dialoguetext: "Don't worry, man, you got a place -- right here." He sounds happy saying this, his limbs a mere shadow below the ceiling.
"My name sets me apart from my fellows. How often do you meet a Raphaël Ambrosius Costeau?"
"Don't think I've met one yet, homes." He studies you silently for a moment.
The lieutenant raises his eyebrows and coughs.
That was him suppressing a chuckle.
"Sorry, you just weren't moving like a human."
"If you're not a crab, then what are you?"
"Did you just climb down from the church tower?"
"Are you human? You weren't moving like a human."
He chuckles. "I am, at least in part, homes... until the Mother's love burns away the crude distinctions of the body."
What does he mean 'in part'?
"If you was to surrender to the Mother -- you know, get a taste of *saeraffic* existence -- you'd never wanna go back."
A body is only crude so long as it's unformed, son. That's where your training comes in.
I don't want to argue with him. He's kind of scary.
I don't know, I think he may be onto something.
"I think having a body is great! I don't want to burn away any of its distinctions!"
"That's because you're soaked through and through with *al gul*, bro. Keeps you heavy and grounded. Then fools you into thinking that's a *good* thing."
What's next? A raw food diet? You're a disappointment.
"Sure did, homes."
"You know, there are some speedfreaks around here who call you 'the crab-man'."

"Wait, did you carve those sculptures?" (Point at the nearest pillar.)

"...now I use those same hands in service of something greater than my own restlessness."
"Just thought you should know."
"It don't bother me none. Crab's no worse than a man, if you think about it."
(Rub your chin.) "You've got some nice... curves going there."
(Squint your eyes.) "These seem a tad... derivative."
"You're promoting the objectification of women with your reactionary depiction of female bodies."
"There must be something illegal about living in a church ceiling. I don't know what yet, but there must be."
"Oh, man, I'd love to see that statute." He pauses to think. "I'm sure I'd be 'trespassing' if the church was in use -- but it's not, hombre."
"Okay, I have other questions."
What is this? Is this what you've been training for? So you could wuss out when push comes to shove?
"I've done my share of illegal shit. Used to be in a gang, the whole deal. But even memories of that time are fading... Most of them are already gone."
"What's 'Mesque'?"
"You sound like you're not from around here."
"Space? Jobs?" He laughs. "Do you see anyone taking swings at me for my place on the rafters?..."
"And it's great! Such diversity is a boon to the economy."
"So you're another immigrant, come to take up space and steal jobs..."
"Haven't you ever met a Mesque before, *cabron*? Surprising number of us around Revachol..."
"You talk funny."
"Well, at least, you're human. That's a relief."
"Glad you're feeling more comfortable." He grins. "First-timers are always nervous."
Yeah! My *body* is my church!
Tell him, son! Show him you're not going to be bent out of shape by his *philosophies*.
He laughs. "Not sure I'm contributing to the economy none, homes."
"You know, I'm not so sure myself anymore." He thinks for a moment. "Don't really matter, though."
"It's all just for the Mother, man. No need to overthink it."
"It's all just for the Mother, man. No need to overthink it."
"I thought you'd be offended. Go and scare them or something."
"I can't leave my post here." He smiles. "Besides, it don't bother me none. Crab's no worse than a man, if you think about it."
"She is a cavity, in the dark, beyond sense. She saved me... but I couldn't describe her to you. No one can, homes, and no one ever will."
"Some ravers want to turn this place into a nightclub."
"The ones in the tent outside, right? I seen 'em. Guessing they're the ones who call me a crab? Probably scared of me..."
"The ones in the tent outside, right? I seen 'em. Think they're scared of me."
"Wait, do they have *reason* to be scared?"
"So, what do you think? About the nightclub, that is."
"Turning a church into a nightclub -- I have to say it's a great idea. You should support it."
"I trust you won't get in the way of some enterprising youth? Their business looks promising."
"Naw, man. They look pretty funny. And I don't harm no one anymore anyway."
"Why not? They wouldn't bother me none. I'm usually way up there, imbibing. Ain't no music on Earth that can reach where I go."
"Absolutely, man. Wouldn't bother me none to have 'em spin music in here. I'm usually way up there, imbibing."
"Wouldn't bother me none to have 'em spin music in here. I'm usually way up there, imbibing."
"Might even be nice to have some company..."
He said that in spite of himself. He's more attached to the human than he'd like to think.
"This is a special place. There's a perforation in the world up there. A way out, into nothingness." He nods toward the ceiling. "This church was built around it, for purposes of veneration."
"I circle it, nurtured by the silence bestowed by the Mother. One of these days, I'll be pure enough to go drink from it directly."
"You sure you didn't just switch one drug for another?"
"Police raid a while back," he responds, his voice suddenly flat.
"You've been here for a long time. Did you see the police raid that took place here?"

dialoguetext: "It's not like that at all, man. It's just faith and joyful service."
"Faith is a kind of drug."
"Let's agree to disagree." (Proceed.)
"I was being insensitive. Sorry. Let's move on." (Proceed.)

"I've heard that before, wey." He shakes his head. "And I know I can't convince you on the spot. But think -- when's the last time you woke up from *silent communion* with a hangover, regretting what you did last night?"
"No worries, man. I know this shit takes time."
"Right. I had other questions..."
Too gleeful, those words -- he is lying. Not to you -- to his very own self.
"What will happen once you drink from this 'perforation'?"
"I will be incinerated, but not destroyed -- finally at one with the state of the world before reality began."
"Is this what you meant by 'saeraffic existence'?"
"I still don't understand what you're doing in the church."
He said something about "saeraffic existence" before. Maybe this is what he was talking about?
"Right on, homes. You're catching on. Yeah, you see, I'm sort of a saeraff to the Mother... I sing her glory."
"I'm a saeraff, homes. I sing the Mother's glory."
"It doesn't really make sense for you to sing if she's the Mother of *Silence*."
"Can you sing for me? Sing for me something."
"I ain't from no *marietti*, if that's what you're thinking. And the song I sing is silent as the Mother."
He laughs. "I don't mean *literal* singing, homes. This is the Mother of Silence we're talking about. It's the singing of a burning heart..."

Accept this contradiction. The man's obviously deranged.

dialoguetext: "She took you for a good spin, huh?" He looks at you gravely. "Don't worry, bro, that love is but a drop compared to the ocean of the Mother's love..."
"I guess you have a point." (Proceed.)
"...the Mother will eat all of you, and never spit you out."
"I know it'll take time. Don't sweat it."
"Did you witness it?"
Could it be that he just doesn't want to discuss a police raid with another police officer?
"Did you see what happened?"
"How did you even find this place -- this church?"
"Hard to say. I think I did some construction work here, back when I still had material worries. Up there, I realized what the true purpose of the church was..."
"Been spending a lot of time here ever since. The past is nothing to me now, wey. It didn't belong to me."
"Keep the flame in your soul alive, though. One day you'll make it up here, if you put in the work."
Some people will find that attitude admirable... but it's not going to help you scale these beams.
Seriously what were you even thinking? You haven't been putting the work in to pull off a stunt like climbing to great heights like a cat.

"What were you even trying to do, man? I believe you can overcome your problems eventually, if you purge yourself of your wilfulness and seek the Mother's guidance. But *this*, right now, would be some suicidal shit."
I feel like I am failing as a man. I am ashamed.
Yeah, sure. There are other things we could do. But, man, it would have been cool.
You might be that numerically, but you've really done a number on yourself too.

There still may be time to recuperate. Just grit your teeth.
When your mind is clear of the neurotoxins you've been injecting it with for years, and your body regains some nimbleness and swiftness, you might achieve such a feat.
That's just whiny bullshit. Get it together.
One day, you may be able to scale this tower. But it won't be today. Neither your sinews nor your spirit could handle this ascent.
"Hey, man. I see it in you -- you are prepared to surrender yourself to the fire of revelation. But you're still a bit shaky spiritually." He looks you over. "You're also just, physically, shaking."
Oh well, didn't really care about climbing up some stupid beams anyway.
And your mind's pretty clear, all things considered. In fact, it's too clear for you to be buying into this climbing vision quest.
(Look at your bottle.)  But it makes me feel more powerful...

But, can't deny it -- your mind's pretty clear, all things considered. In fact, it's too clear for you to be buying into this climbing vision quest.
I don't care about the physical stuff -- I'm in it for the spiritual experience.

Sorry, but you just don't have it in you right now.
When your mind is clear of the neurotoxins you've been injecting it with for years -- and your body regains some nimbleness and swiftness.

"Hey, are you a boiadeiro?"

"What were you before you became a crab-man?"
"To be fair, it's really more like a spider. But everyone calls you the crab-man."
"So you've got nothing else to tell me? How she looks, what she does, who *is* she?"
"I'm afraid not, ese. You just have to wait until she comes back or..." He shrugs.
Or search through her radiocomputer.
"Something like that," he responds, his voice suddenly flat.

Hmh... does it mean he witnessed the police raid?
"Honestly, I don't get it. All these figures look half-finished."
"I see what you've done there. It's as if these figures are trying to become one with the church -- or perhaps with the Mother herself."
"Honestly, I don't get it. All these figures look half-finished."
"I see what you've done there. It's as if these figures are trying to become one with the church -- or perhaps with the Mother herself."
(Rub your chin.) "You've got some nice... curves going there."
(Squint your eyes.) "These seem a tad... derivative."
"You're promoting the objectification of women with your reactionary depiction of female bodies."
*Sssurveys* are a good way to fish for personal information, especially in the name of public sssafety...
"Just tell me what's the password." (Step closer.)
"Yes, it's for a first-degree murder investigation in Martinaise."
"Honestly I just want to break into a radiocomputer, see what's on it."
The lieutenant raises his eyebrow, but doesn't say anything.
"Hey, it's your neighbours who came up with this name, not me."
"Never known myself to be a *crab*. But if that's the name you've got for me, I won't stop you from using it."
"I don't do names either. Names are *out*. I don't care what mine is."
"My name's Harry." (Extend your hand for a greeting.)
"That's just the thing, homes -- none of that *matters*..." He ignores your hand, his limbs a mere shadow below the ceiling.
"My name's Harrier Du Bois, and my place in the world is lieutenant double-yefreitor."
"That's just the thing, homes -- none of that *matters*..." He sounds melancholy saying this, his limbs a mere shadow below the ceiling.
"Wait, so there *is* another person living in the church -- and it's a *viejita*?"

Wait, what if it's Ruby?
"Did it ever seem to you like she was hiding here from something?" The lieutenant seems to be thinking the same. He takes out his little notebook.
"You mean like a fugitive?" He glances at the abandoned radiocomputer on the other side of the nave, pulsing with light. Then he shakes his head.
"I see." The lieutenant seems contented with that answer. "And where is she now?"
"I told you, homes -- I don't know."
"Right, thanks. I'll see if I can find her some other way..."
"You just have to wait until she comes back or..." He shrugs.

"Did it seem like she was hiding in here? Or running from something?"
"You mean like a fugitive?" He glances at the abandoned radiocomputer on the other side of the nave, pulsing with light. Then he shakes his head.
"No, man, quite the opposite -- I don't think she cares much about authority or, anything else for that matter. Maybe only about her machines."

"I can see, and it saddens me. But devotion can save you -- it saved me."
(Let's keep moving on.) "What were you before you became a crab-man?"
(Nod.) "Singing is good. We should all sing a bit more."
"That was... an interesting conversation."
"However, I'm still not sure how it's relevant to our investigation."
"However, I'm still not sure whether we'll find our suspect here."
Uhm.... oops?

Fuck you, crab-man, you don't tell us what to do. Tell him.

There are drugs darker than alcohol circling your system.

Though he used to. A long time ago.
Viejita is... grandma?

dialoguetext: "Sorry, but... who *are* you? What are you doing here?"
All you hear is the accelerated heart rate in your ears, pounding at 100bpm. Beat by beat, your blood readies for conflict.
You're not really feeling it, but you should try to force it, anyway. Maybe she won't be able to tell?
"He's seen *you*."
"And?"
"And? *The crab-man* has seen you!"
"I don't care, I don't care about crab men." She barely looks up, now tinkering with the machine's printer.

"Exactly, what *does* it mean?" There's something frantic about her as she locks her gaze with you, eyes shining like pearls. "Up to now it has been impossible to say what it is, because it's impossible to measure *nothing*."
"What do *you* think it is? What qualities does *nothing* have? How do you measure something that does not exist?" She's suddenly absorbed in the conversation, waiting for your answer.
Easy, you measure it by the world around it.
"What?" She squints her eyes. "I hate it."
"A youth centre would be nice."
"A petting zoo, a place for animals!"
"Maybe some community space to help the elderly?"
"I'm still convinced they want to establish a nightclub for anodic dance music -- they said it's their *dream*."
"But honestly, it's not progressing very well." She grows silent, staring at her circle of basins -- it looks like some ancient ritual.
"It sounds like you're not worried about him at all."
"No, you're right, I'm not..." Her voice trails off, as she bends over to tinker with the machine's printer.
"I don't know, I'm not here for some science, I just want to solve a murder so I can go home."
"You measure it by collecting data on its surroundings, on that which exists."
"Exactly," she nods, "very true! That's what I've been aiming for, that's why I have those basins. I've tried using hydrotransducers to record the silence -- to find out where it *begins*."
"Isn't your Rehm Prefect radiocomputer made exclusively for the government-use?"
"So you do know *something* about computers." She looks up, almost proud of you. "You're right, Prefect *is* used mostly by the government peeps."
"I can't even understand how we're talking about something that doesn't exist, let alone measure it."

"You measure it by its surroundings -- by that which does exist," she replies, "which is what I've been trying to do. I've tried using hydrotransducers to record the silence -- to find out where it *begins*."
"What if you *didn't* have to leave? I talked to Andre, he wants to make it work."
"Those ravers won't be bothering you anymore -- I arrested them because they were planning a drug trade."
"You arrested them..." She looks up, surprised. "Didn't think the cops in this place had it in them," she murmurs.
A small satisfied smile breaks free on her face, infuriatingly triumphant.
"I'm protected by the Wayfarer Act."
"What's the Wayfarer Act?"
(Cross your arms.) "There is no Wayfarer Act."
"The Wayfarer Act states that citizens have the right to gather in public spaces unless they're disrupting the public order."
"Ah, but there *is* and it *protects* me!"
Did she say *over 16 years of experience*? She must have started programming when she was still a teenager.
Look at how pleased she is with herself, playing with her 'important science machines'. Academics!!
"Wait, I have my... I have my..." (Take out your gun.)
"You're right. The Wayfarer Act is the foundation of our legal order. I can't cross it on a whim. You're welcome to stay."
"Have some dignity," the woman sighs, turning back to her radiocomputer.
"You're leaving this church..." (Take out your gun.) "...one way or another."
But you don't take out your gun -- instead you fumble with the holster, desperately trying to free the weapon from its pouch... It looks pathetic.
"God..." The girl immediately steps back and raises her hands. "Easy now, I'll go, it's not an issue! Can I pack my things first?"
(Nod once.) "Just make sure you're gone by the time I get back."
"You better start going if you don't want to be frogmarched to the jail." (Roll up your sleeves.)
"God..." She immediately steps back and raises her hands, sensing the aggression. "Easy now, I'll go. It's not an issue. Can I pack my things first?"
She turns off her computer and leaves.
"Miss, I need you to be gone from this church when I come back." (Put away your gun.)
"Detective..."
"Put the gun down, detective." The lieutenant's voice is low and firm.
"I'm not putting down my gun unless she promises to be gone when I come back."
"I promise, I promise!" she exclaims, words echoing below the ceiling rafters.
"Good." (Put away your gun.)
"Please just go, will you? Please... Pretty please, I don't want to fight. Fighting is scary, and gives me breathing difficulties."
"Of course I can stay. It wasn't even a question."
"I don't want to make anything work," she replies, her expression unchanged.
Put on the headphones.
And then the pressure changes.
All you hear is your own breathing, heavy and hoarse from all the nights spent drinking... It's the breath of an old man.
"A chance to cook some speed, you mean?" she asks sourly, crossing her arms.
"They *promised* they'll do it clean."
"Uh, *did they*?" she asks, clicking her tongue. A moment passes.
"Alright, this is all very good and sad, but I have my research to finish. Trust me, this is far more important than the fate of some local speedfreaks and their dance music."
"What if I helped you *finish* your project? Then you could leave -- and they could come in."
"Well?" Soona asks as soon as you take off the headphones. "Did you hear anything?"
"No, nothing. It's just silence."
"Yeah..." Her voice is bitter with disappointment.
"Why can't you go and get the filament yourself?"
"Where is your old workspace?"
Hold on... If it's called an off-site copy, then why is it still *on*-site?
"If it's called an off-site copy, then why is it still on-site?"
"Oh god, not *this* again..." She takes a deep breath, before letting it all out: "It is not *on-site*, it is *in the basement*, perfectly safe and not connected to the front *at all*."
"And where exactly is the off-site copy?"
"There's this giant ice bear fridge in the building's cellar -- it's there."
"I found a note from the ice bear fridge. It said the off-site copy had been moved to 'a safer place'."

"Zawisza, of course..." She relaxes. "Our project lead Sulisław Zawisza. God, he was always so hell-bent on keeping the copy somewhere 'safe'. And feature creep..." she mutters, "and the Valley of the Heads..."
"Is this the filament you're looking for?" (Show her the production schedule.)
Wait, no! That's dangerous, she shouldn't do it!
"Don't waste your time printing it out, there's nothing but ink there. It's broken."
What an interesting proposition! Truly a task for the intellectuals -- solving the puzzle of water bowls.
Yes, but you like moving things around. Moving things around is calming.
"I moved the water bowls to the right position, just like you asked. What's next?"
"Because it reminds us of death. And we humans tend to think that death is pretty scary."
"It's scary, but we just have to face it."
Despite her fear she was hoping for something extraordinary to take place.
"MAXIMUM!" shouts Egg Head, a great smile still adorning his face, larger than a red dwarf star.
"Why do you need an antenna?" (Point to it.)
"What about those bowls of water over there?"
"What are you doing with your radiocomputer?"
"Why are there so many machines in this place?"
"I brought them here. These are my machines. Please don't touch anything."
"What are you doing in an abandoned church?"
"Do you have any idea where this hole might be located?"
"A hole in the world... What does that mean exactly?"
"Okay. Wow. That was quick. Why do you hate it?"
"Maybe I'd have to be *on drugs* to get it, but to a sober mind it just sounds like uninspired rug whipping. No idea what it has to do with either dancing or music."
"Right, right... but how do you feel about a *club* for anodic dance music?"
"This is about those speedfreaks in the tent, isn't it?" She looks up, shaking her head. "I've got some news for you, it's not a *nightclub* they want to build here..."
"What do they want to build then?"
"Take a guess, why don't you?"
"I heard they're also planning on building a drug lab."
"Bingo." She snaps her fingers. "That's exactly what they're up to."
"Wonderful," the lieutenant whispers, admiring the embellished pillars and the spectacular architecture in the church.
"Good."
"Really?"
"No, of course not." She turns her tired, sardonic eyes to face you. "I feel even worse about drugs than I feel about nightclubs."
"I feel that's illegal."
"I see you've talked to them, good. Drugs are illegal, and I'm not leaving this church -- especially because of some corrupt drug lab idea you've cooked up in that tent."
"Right, isn't that what makes it fun?"
"Your feeling is right, manufacturing drugs is a little illegal."
"No, certainly not. I've got a citizen's investigation to run and I want nothing to do with local vices."
"Yes, I know that."
"They're just encouraging an active *youth culture* here, nothing wrong with that."
"Mind-altering substances are a vital part of anodic club scene, it helps to bring the community together."
Say nothing.
"So that's settled, great." She supports her chin on her hand, visibly pleased: "No nightclubs in the church then."
"Yeah, what I said before... Not possible to appreciate that kind of music without being high as a kite."
"I'm just encouraging an active *youth culture*, nothing wrong with that."
"Wonderful," the lieutenant whispers. "Now this place is also going to be a drug lab. Always something fascinating happening in tents."
"Mind-altering substances are a vital part of anodic club scene. It helps to bring the community together."
Say nothing.
"No, don't mind me, go on with your little project. I'm sure you can spin it as an under-cover op. Many cops do."
"It is, yes. It's against the law. We're cops -- the law is *important* to us."
"Gotcha. It's almost party time!"
"How could you? This is a completely separate issue!"
(Ignore him and address the lead programmer) "I want you to take your belongings and leave within an hour."
"Interesting, a police officer trying to evict a citizen from a public space despite the Wayfarer Act."
"Apologies, I was just thinking out loud. Go on."
"No, please, not the Wayfarer Act again..." (Close your eyes.)
"Yes, thank you. Now, if you'd only let me work..."
"And before you go on, I am *not* disrupting any order here, I'm a circuit bender and no one has anything against circuit benders."
"I'm a circuit bender and no one ever has anything against circuit benders."
"I don't *care* about the Wayfarer Act! Get out of here!" (Stomp your feet.)
I can't do it. I don't *feel* scary.
"No, but you see, it doesn't matter whether you care about it or not. It's the law," she explains to you without even sparing a look, "I'm not going anywhere."
She's still typing behind the radiocomputer, her sweater-clad frame hunched over the machine.
"Hold on, you don't want to make *anything* work?"
"Yes, *anything*. I don't want to make anything work."
It's not the anodic dance music that's made her bitter... it's the failure of Fortress Accident.
"Are you bitter because your radio game project failed?"
"That's right." Something strange shines in her eyes. "If we couldn't get our *welkins* to happen, I don't want anything to happen. Ever again."
There's not a trace of irony in her voice. She means it.
Don't bring it up.
"This is Martinaise, what can you expect? They're the product of their surroundings."
"Very cool, but I don't want any part of those 'surroundings' myself, good or bad."
"On Rue de Saint-Ghislaine in the East Delta Commerce Centre." She wipes some hair off her face and sighs.
"The bookstore lady hates me -- says I'm part of the *curse*, whatever that means."
"Wait -- bookstore lady -- you mean Plaisance?"
"That's her name, I believe."
"Why does she think you're part of the curse?"
"Because she's from Martinaise and people from Martinaise have never ever seen a radiocomputer. She thinks it emits elemental *evil*."
"By your old workspace do you mean the studio of Fortress Accident in the Doomed Commercial Area?"

This is clearly a painful topic for her. She must have had to explain herself numerous times.

"You put it there..." She leans back, massaging her eyelids. "You put a dead body inside the ice bear fridge..."

"Lintel was able to divine the location of the anomaly from this broken copy. I want to repeat their calculation, only this time with better equipment."

This is wrong, machines shouldn't behave like that.
It's the abyss staring back at you.

Cold sweat trickles down your spine... This is spooky as hell.
"Huh?" She looks up, puzzled.
"You okay?"

"I *am* being careful. Treat it as a mere technical anomaly, makes it easier to bear." She runs her hands over the printout, searching for something...
Soona doesn't reply, her hands running over the printout. She's looking for something -- for her morning star -- eyes scouring the millimetres.

"Hold on a moment --  does it mean we're now living in a world that has *holes in it*?!"
"I don't know, are we? That's what I'm trying to figure out here. But how *do* I figure it out?"
"No, my hypothesis was wrong. According to this, I should have *heard* something if I got the coordinates right. Like I said: silence is only what surrounds it."

"But this..." She raises her head, staring at all the machines that litter the church, cables coiling up on the floor like pests. "This is just another failure. Silence sounds like silence. That's all it is."
"You can try on the headphones, see if you can hear anything, but don't get your hopes up."
Form a theory on the two-millimetre hole in the world.
"Bingo."
"I do have one mystery that still needs solving... the radio ghost in the Doomed Commercial Area's electronic doorbell."

dialoguetext: "The creepy woman!" She slaps her forehead. "We were wondering about that when we worked there... but I had completely forgotten about it ever since!"
"It must be entroponetic crosstalk. The one you get in radios and long-distance calls... Now it makes sense, with the pale right on the doorstep."
"Entroponetic crosstalk?"

"It's quite common actually. When the signal gets routed through pale, all kinds of irregularities take place. You may hear snippets of someone else's conversation, or the voice of your former lover, or an echo of an event that took place 100 years ago."
"Pale is a shroud of memories and it doesn't really distinguish to whom those memories belong to. You could hear anything."
"I should let people still working in there know about this. They might be affected."
"That makes sense. Thanks for explaining that to me."
"You mean... Plaisance and the dicemaker? There was almost no one left when we packed up."
"Anytime." She smiles.
"No, just the dicemaker. I don't think Plaisance would survive this knowledge."
"No, just Plaisance. I don't think Neha is playing fair in this game."
"Then go tell them." She smiles, suddenly encouraging.
"Yes, both of them deserve to know."
"Then go tell her." She smiles broadly.
"Then go tell her." She smiles broadly.
"Incredible..." the lieutenant murmurs. "This would also explain why we get it on the police radio all the time."
"Have you seen anyone suspicious -- say, a woman named Ruby?"
"What? No. No one suspicious around here."
"What is an off-site copy and why do you need it?"

"It's a back-up of my former employer's project -- the radio game we were working on. It's stored on a *filament memory* just like the one inside this radiocomputer." She points to the glowing cube inside the machine.
"The backup itself is destroyed now, but I'm hoping to use what's left of it to pinpoint the exact location of the anomaly. You just have to go to my old workspace and get the filament."
"Wait. Are you -- part of the curse?"
"Of course not." She crosses her arms. "Anyway, I don't have my keys anymore and she won't let me in."
"So what I need you to do here is -- go have a talk with her, say that you're a policeman and need to get to the building's basement. Then bring me the off-site copy. Alright?"
"Actually, I've already been inside the Doomed Commercial Area."
"Good -- then you might know the giant ice bear fridge in the building's cellar. The filament is inside the fridge -- just go and get it."
Hey, maybe if you were to find out more about her previous company, Fortress Accident, you'd have something new to say...
She sounds mildly annoyed by this line of questioning, her hands typing hundreds of commands into the machine.
Wait! she doesn't want to share the space with them -- help her finish the research, then she won't have to! Offer to help.
Wait! She doesn't want to share the space with them -- you can help her finish the research, then she won't have to! Offer to help.
"What if it *does* emit elemental evil?" (Narrow your eyes.)
"It doesn't *emit*, it receives..." She stops explaining. "You sound just like her. She started praying when she first saw my Rehm. Turned to higher powers."
She's making it *extra simple* for you.
"In the giant ice bear fridge -- I just told you. It has red glowing eyes, it's impossible to miss. You just need to get the off-site copy from the ice bear."
But... you've been to the fridge and it wasn't there. There was a note saying...
Glue-style? Okay, there *literally* is no other way. The mixing desk is glued to maximum.
Not so stoically -- his hand moves to the gun holster.
Her hand is trembling slightly...
"Five..."
"Four..."
"Three..."
"Mute disengaged." She lifts her hand from the keyboard. Complete silence fills the room.
No wind outside. No waves. No floorboards creaking. Total, continuous silence. This is... unnatural.
It's out there now. In the world. Made manifest.
It will devour everything.
The floorboards. The glass. The streets and the people. Nothing will remain.
This fragile world is about to break.
In the basins -- the water looks like it's *boiling*.
"It was... it was *in* me at first..."
Cracks appear on the stained glass window. Cracks run up the wooden pillars in the dark...
THE MIC IS NOTHING. THIS HAS NOTHING TO DO WITH THE MIC.
"Andre, pull the compressor! The place is gonna come down..."
In the mixing desk now. Building into a positive feedback loop.
"That's it, I'm muting it!" She reaches for the keyboard...
"Egg Head! It's in the desk!"
"Egg Head?! Can you stop it?"
"Egg Head -- whatever you do, don't stop it!"
THIS IS IT. A great roar, the vault of the roof twists above you, glass shatters somewhere near the door... it's coming down.

But then it stops. Totally and utterly -- as if there never was a sound. Only your ears still ring from the shock. Everybody is staring at Egg Head -- holding a dangling cable in his hand. A black three-pin connector.

dialoguetext: "Four years..." the woman whispers. "Twenty two people, millions of reáls... All that time *this* is what we were up against? Just erased it..." Her lip trembles. "Sulisław isn't gonna believe this."
"Yeah, but did you record it though? It was dope, I think we can use it."
"Yes, Andre." She composes herself -- wipes the dust off her sweater and rests her hands on the keyboard. "I recorded it. Damn, I need to send some letters now..."
"Thank you all for doing this. Egg Man, you too. And you, officer." She turns to you. "I don't know *what* we've discovered, but I know what it sounds like now. That's a start."
"What *was* that? I've never heard anything like that."
"You're going to write Sulisław?"
"What happens now. Are you going to..." (Conclude.)
"It was mathematical information -- from the anomaly -- presented as a waveform. That's what it was *technically* -- theoretically..." She shakes her head.
"I have no idea. I've never even heard of anything like this."
"Yes. Our lead designer. And maybe some of the producers too. And some of the writers, if they're sober enough to open a transmission. They need to hear..."
That it wasn't her fault. Or theirs.
"They need to hear about this. Don't worry, I won't send the recording -- although I doubt they have the speakers to produce the frequency anyway..."
"Stay here," she cuts you off, her deft fingers already on the keyboard. "I am going to stay here with these lunatics, send letters, maybe meet Sulisław... Also devise further measurements."
"I want you to know that's totally chill with us."
"I don't care," she blurts, then reconsiders: "But thank you anyway."
That's the best she can manage for Andre. It's quite a lot, in truth. For her, at least.
Her voice seems muffled in the silent church. It's your ears adjusting after the exposure.
Some tiny hard thing lets go in your stomach. You're still alive.
"Yes. And we have to get back to stabilizing Martinaise..." He breathes out, trying to shake off tension. "Instead of demolishing it with loud bass noise of unknown origins."
"Now..." Her hands move on the keyboard. "I have a theory to come up with. *Some* kind of preliminary explanation to all this, or the letter will sound like I've lost my mind..."
"Kim, did *you* hear that?"
"It was *very* hard not to. I think you're right," he turns to the woman. "There *is* something going on here -- and you need to be *very* careful with it."
"I promise, officer. We will *not* play it again."
You have an explanation for all this. Somewhere deep in you -- you *know*. The person you *were* knows.
Silence is silence? You're sure there's more to it...
This can't be it. You should have a listen.
You *have* an explanation for all this. Somewhere deep in you -- you just don't have the pieces yet.
You don't know enough about the world. But that *Joyce* -- if you knew all she knows, could put it together...
"But..." She looks up, and there's fear in her eyes as she considers the possibility. "But pale isn't here. We're thousands of kilometres from the edge."
All you hear is silence in your head.
You don't have to. You already *have*. A long time ago.
"Soona, it is the origin point of the pale."
Wait... *how*?
These thoughts formed in you somewhere, in a long forgotten discussion. Behind a kitchen table, in the evening light.
Drinking coffee and smoking. With a friend.
And a woman, she was there too. Her hair smelled of shampoo and she was smoking.
"What?"
"The swallow -- it's how it starts. It's baby pale."
That comforts her.
"No." (Look up first.) "We are twenty metres from the *very* edge."
"The pale is only an effect. A transition between the world -- and *that*."
She looks up into the darkness under the nave, then back at you.
You have her full, undivided attention.
The lieutenant's too. He takes his glasses off.
"Then... what *is* that?"
"It's *less than less than nothing*. The final rest state for reality. Imagine if all this..." (Spread your hands.) "*Never was.*"
It's nothing. No... it's *less* than nothing. No...
"Then the pale is..."
"Simply... *curdling milk*."
"Simply a gradient."
"But the milk -- it clearly hasn't started curdling yet. We're here and the pale is not."
"But the gradient -- it clearly hasn't started yet. We're here and the pale is not."
"One day, when it's larger, it will be."
"I understand..." She closes her eyes. "A theory of the pale where instead of an *outer ocean* it metastasises -- like a cancer or a mould -- erupting in points *inside* the world."
(Nod.) "*This* is one of those places."
She's silent for a second. Then she opens her mouth. "According to this -- how long..."
"...until it starts *swallowing*? It's already started. Starting with sound."

"And information," she nods. "Causing data losses in the East-Insulindian front. Have you considered why it's formed in a church? And, also, *when* or *how* it might start growing? Or -- if it has other effects? In addition to sound and data..."
"It didn't form in a church, the church formed around it."
"Of course! A pinewood sarcophagus, or a..." She looks for words. "A containment facility of some kind, built by the first settlers."
An intellectual hunger fills her now, casting fear aside.
"I also have a question -- since we're piling them on. How do *you* know this? I'm not doubting you," he explains, "I'm simply curious as to how a detective of the RCM..."
... knows how to think this?
"Yes. Acting on an instinctual level. Or religious practices we've forgotten."
"*Or* it can be a coincidence."
"Yes. But still -- I have considered the same. And the bad news is -- there were *seven* such pinewood churches built in the first decade of Revachol's settlement."
"I have considered the same. The bad news is -- there were *seven* pinewood churches built in the first decade of Revachol's settlement."
"Most of them were burnt down during the Revolution, or re-purposed before, during the Suzerain. I'm not saying *all* of them have one in them, but.."
Some of them might. A black grain, hanging in the air...
"All the failed businesses in the Doomed Commercial Area. All the failure in Martinaise..."
"You think the presence of that *puncture* has somehow... influenced the outcome of events here? Even, say, software development?"
"Yes. Even the Revolution was defeated here. I mean a kind of... entroponetic history."
"All the failed businesses and ideologies -- there's something *wrong* here."
"No. We're reaching. People fail on their own."
"Tiago -- under the roof -- he said he's circling the spot, like a saeraff. He seemed to have lost his mind."

"I told the producers we need to go and move to a normal office building, with amenities. But no -- the artists like the *milieu*. The writers like the *history*..." She shakes her head. "I told them."
No -- It's better they don't know.
"I told them, but no -- normal office buildings are *bourgeois*..."

"True, we never should have upgraded to Vox '50. And the spec kept changing. And those damn *Heads*... but still, the anomaly caused a massive data loss. So -- it had a part to play. It does *something*."
She already made up her mind when she heard it. Some kind of great and uncaring force had to play a part... it wasn't *only* them.
"The crab-man... From what I've heard, his state could be reminiscent of pale over-exposure. Time-perception related illnesses, memory malfunctions, thought insertion."
She's agreeing more and more. Partially because she *wants* to.
(Conclude.) "One day all the world will be like that two-millimetre hole."
And then there is you. And what happened to *your* mind. Are you not a saeraff in worship too?
She falls silent. The wind blows in through the hole in the stained glass window. Cold and moist.
"I think I've had this thought before. That's how I know."
"An amateur-entroponetic police officer... I'd like to say I've heard stranger things, but I'm not sure. This is a hell of a guess, however. Well worded I might add..."
"Yes, it is *very* interesting, but I wouldn't say you *know*. This is a guess. One that's going to have to be *proved* -- by entroponetic scientists."
"I'm going to leave that out -- but the rest... some of this I can use to *start* to explain this to the rest of the team. Maybe I'll sound mad, but..."
"Ma'am, you will *certainly* sound mad."
She shrugs. "One more thing -- maybe a club for anodic music isn't the *worst* thing you can erect around this particular... *point in space*?"
She shrugs. "You know -- maybe a club for anodic music isn't the *worst* thing you can erect around this particular... *point in space*?"
"Perhaps not."
"Yeah, that's still insane, but then again -- so am I."
"The club is the only thing keeping this place -- and the rest of reality -- together."
"Actually, now that I think of it, maybe it's dangerous?"
"I wouldn't go so far as to..."
"YEAAAGHHH! ONCE THE LIGHT IS ON IN THE UNIVERSE -- IT WILL NEVER GO OUT!"
"Maybe, but..."
"Thank you, Egg Head. Let's leave it at that, shall we? We have un-entroponetic detection to perform in this district."
"What is there to add to that? Nothing."
"And here's my Kvalsund multitool. You might need it to hack loose some ice. It opens everything. If you get me the off-site copy, then you can keep the Kvalsund."
The *legendary* Kvalsund multitool! This is prybar version 2.0 -- for *professionals*, like you.
This glorious multitool makes a regular prybar completely OBSOLETE.
There's a solution, but she doesn't want to hand it over to you yet. It's a *thing*, something she holds dear.
It hurts a bit for her to say this -- she's not too happy to be parting with the Kvalsund.
"No, I'm not, it's just me and the..." She looks up at the ceiling without finishing her sentence. "I'm just doing some research. That's all."
"Right, nothing to do with ghosts..."

The machine seems almost alien with its pulsing core, the light casting her face in a strange shadow.
Basement? Sounds like it's *technically* still on-site...

Maybe the speedfreaks can help you with this? Go talk with Andre.

She hast not seen her, sire. 'Tis true.

dialoguetext: She looks up from her monitor. "You're asking me to circuit-bend onto Coalition radio frequencies. You want to know is it possible? Probably. But is it a good idea? I'm not so sure..."
"Do I look like someone who has time for *side projects* at this moment?" She doesn't even look up from her computer.
If you want her help, maybe you should help *her* first...
"The main difficulty will be finding an antenna powerful enough to reach those frequencies. Unfortunately you can't exactly buy mega-longwave antennas off the shelf."
"She's not joking. Even the RCM has to receive special approval from the Coalition to access that kind of equipment."

"There is an old radio relay tower at the very end of the peninsula. It's mostly used to coordinate boat traffic in the harbour, but it's possible that it's equipped to handle mega-low frequencies as well..."
"Assuming the relay isn't too badly damaged, that is. I have work to do here, but I recommend you examine the relay tower and return once you have determined its condition."
"I highly doubt it. That tower is barely able to transmit short-wave signals across the bay. To generate mega-low frequencies, we're going to need a *much* larger antenna..."
"I don't see any alternative. We're just going to have to build the antenna ourselves."
"The radio relay tower at Land's End... could that work?"
She has an idea, though. You can see the tiny signal lights firing inside her brain...
"Where is this relay tower exactly?"
"Alright, I'll check out the tower and report back."
"North of here. Follow the coastline. I do not know how to explain it more simply."
"Very good. I'll be here when you are finished."
"Why don't we just use your AR-1?"
"Wait, we can just *build* an antenna?"
"That sounds hard. Can't we just get one from someplace else?"
"Now we're talking! What do we have to do?"
"We need metal. A lot of it. The taller the structure, the better. Something that is both prominent and easily accessible. If it's near a power source, even better."
"Not the sort of antenna we require. The Coalition has a near-monopoly on mega-low-frequency radio equipment. Fortunately, they do not have a monopoly on physics."
"Yes. From a technical view, it's not even difficult. The difficult part will be finding the *right* location."
"Because it's a completely different class of antenna. It would be like using a high-end racing carriage where a long-distance lorry is required."
"The radio relay tower is in bad shape. I don't think we can use it to reach the Archer."

dialoguetext: "Ah, very good. Let's see what you have."
"Not the most advanced model." She turns a few dials and then sets the transceiver aside. "But at least everything appears to be in order. Yes, this should serve our purposes."
"Ah, you 'found' the transceiver from my old Rehm Civic. Did you think I wouldn't recognise it? No matter. It should work for our purposes..."

"Interesting," she says as examines the transceiver, "an Esterhaz EH-4, heavily customised. This is an advanced model, highly capable. I'll need to replace the frequency dial, but it should certainly work for our purposes."

"Is this... a Kristallsprach?" She looks up at you as she gently opens the case. "The Model 9 is an excellent piece of equipment. I don't know what you had to pay for it, but it should work very nicely."

"I believe that means we're ready to get started. I should warn you, once we begin setting up this antenna, we'll need to see the whole process through. There won't be any second chances, any 'do-overs,' you understand?"
"So if there's anything you'd like to get in order before we depart, I suggest you do it now."
"I got this beauty down at the pawnshop." (Use the highly expensive transceiver.)
"Someone was using this to coordinate a drug smuggling operation." (Use the highly advanced transceiver.)
"I found this in the Doomed Commercial Area." (Use the perfectly adequate transceiver.)
"I found this in an office by the harbour." (Use the perfectly adequate transceiver.)
It's not often that she allows herself to be awed, but the way she holds the Kristallsprach reminds you of someone receiving a precious gift.
She's impressed by your resourcefulness as much as by the equipment itself.
She's not upset. More bemused. This particular transceiver brings back memories, not that she is one to indulge in superstitions.
No further comment necessary.
"Wait, didn't you say we need some kind of power supply?"
"What kind of stuff should I 'get in order'?"
"I'm ready. Let's do this."
"Hang on, I need some time to prepare."
"Very good. If you'll help me with some of this equipment, then..."
"That's fine. Return to me when you are ready to go."
"That's up to you. At a minimum, I would make sure you are physically *and* mentally prepared for an intense and difficult process. Once we begin, there can be no interruptions."
At the very least, you should make sure you're wearing a good pair of gloves.
"Radio-engineers typically carry over-priced solvent sprays to clean the antenna connections, but in a pinch some common ammonia works just fine..."
"Ah, yes. I wasn't sure what to do about that, but then I discovered an abandoned power source down by the edge of the bay."
"Finally, there's the question of *stimulants*. Some people prefer to keep illegal amphetamines on-hand to help with their work. I am not one of them, but they do exist."
It's obvious she's referring to your half-sunken Coupris 40.
An 'abandoned power source'? What could she be referring to?
Whatever it is, it was abandoned for *good* reason. Best to leave some stones unturned...
"You mean the motor carriage that I crashed into the bay?"
"What do you mean an *abandoned* power source?"
"Ah, well as long as it works, I don't need to know the details."
"Ah. Yes, I did notice that it was covered in police livery. Then you already know that the carriage itself is irreparable, but the rear-mounted engine seems to be in fine working order..."
"Someone, I don't know how, appears to have driven a perfectly good Coupris motor carriage into the bay. The carriage itself is a loss, but the rear-mounted engine is still perfectly functional..."
"In that case, let's move on."
"My intention is to run a power cable from the engine up to the antenna. It won't last forever, but it should give us enough time to establish a connection with Coalition Warship Archer."
Pssst, it's the alcohol *in* the ammonia doing the real work, kinda like with you.
"Isn't it a little ironic that you're recommending amphetamines after what happened with the speedfreaks?"
"I try to avoid drugs. Abusing stimulants is *highly* irresponsible."
"So this isn't the first time you've hung around speedfreaks, is it?"
"I'm not interested in irony. I leave that to more *conceptual* types."
"I don't take them because they make me nauseous, but everyone has their reasons. I don't judge."
"It is possible that technical fields attract a certain kind of personality. I haven't given it much thought."
"Back across the waterlock. At least we're getting our *exercise* in today."
"If you'll please carry that amplifier and cables, officer. We have quite a lot to carry..."
"I'm ready now. Let's contact Archer."
Come up with a site for a mega-longwave radio antenna.
That's easy! Antennas are basically just tall things, right?
"We could use the steeple of *this* church." (Point up.)
Alright, brainstorming time. Remember, this is just the ideation phase. There are no *bad* ideas.
Your thinking about this has gotten way too rigid. Time to flip the whole *antenna paradigm* on its head.
Nope, nothing. The idea factory is closed until further notice.
"No, we could not. This church is made from wood. I am not sure you understand how radios work."
Okay, that's a fair point. But don't worry, your next idea will be better.
"I've got it. Why don't we use the mast of a giant *boat*?"
"Here's an idea: Maybe there's an antenna in the harbour we could use?"
"Do you have access to a giant boat?"
"Don't you think the Union would object to that?"
"I could ask the representative from the Wild Pines. She's a friend of mine."
"No."
"Something tells me Ms. Messier would be *less than thrilled* to hear you plan to commandeer her boat so you can talk to a Coalition warship."
"I very much doubt anyone from the Wild Pines would allow us to turn their boat into a giant radio transmitter."
"Yes, it is not a very likely scenario."
"That is why we don't use it, then."
"No way, me and Evrart are tight."
"Hmmm, maybe."
"Problematically so, one might even argue."
"I do not think that the boss of the Union would like us using his equipment to contact the Coalition."
"I don't know about your relationship to the Union, but I do not think they would appreciate us using their equipment to contact the Coalition."
"Hear me out: What if we built the antenna *underground*?"
"Then it would be very difficult to propagate the signal through the air... which would defeat the purpose."
"To be perfectly frank, I'm not sure your ideas are really helping."
"Detective, does the 41st not require its officers to pass Elementary Radio Operations? I thought it was an RCM-wide policy."
Okay, wow, that's some harsh feedback.
Close your eyes. Unfold your mental map of Martinaise. It's morning. You're standing on the plaza before the Whirling-in-Rags.
Turn to face the bay.
Turn to face the apartments.
Turn to face the roundabout.
Your eye follows the tiles west. You see a bench and a few twisted, pitiful trees. Then, just water...
Beyond the unkempt backyard rises a monstrous assemblage of concrete, plaster, and corrugated sheet metal...
The voice again, more urgent now: 'Nay!'
Just a moment. That voice isn't human, and it's not saying 'Nay!' -- It's saying 'N-n-n-neigh!'
You turn around. The morning sun is blinding. You bring your hand to your brow and a great shadow materialises before you. A towering beast, frozen in mid-air...
"The horseback monument."
"Come on, that's..." She was about to dismiss your latest idea out of hand, but something gives her pause.
"The dead king and his horse. It could work..."
"... not the worst idea..."

"We'll need an adequate power supply, and a great quantity of cable. If we connect the cables to some of the stranded lorries, we could theoretically increase the antenna's wavelength *exponentially*..."
"Quiet, I'm doing maths... Yes, assuming we can find just a few pieces of equipment..."
"It's completely ridiculous, but I believe we could transform the entire roundabout into one solid, *fractal antenna*."
It may work, you think, but why do you feel like there may be a terrible cost?
Whatever ambivalence she had about your project before, she's now fully engaged in solving this technical puzzle.
"So you're saying..."
Let her think.
A note of awe in her voice. She's shocked and pleased by her own audacity...
"About time, those other antennas were cramping my style."
"We shall call it: The Herald of Destruction."
"As long as it gets the job done, I'm not interested in the details."
"Are you sure that's legal? I feel like I'm going to need to apologise to someone."
"That's... a very big antenna."
"What you choose to call it isn't my concern. I'm only here to tell you what's feasible or not from a technical viewpoint."
"Very well. I will get straight to the point, then." She nods, seeming to appreciate your cold practicality.
"If you would like to apologise, that is your business. I am only here to tell you what's feasible or not from a technical viewpoint."
"Yes, very likely the largest private antenna in Revachol."
"Your sense of style isn't my concern. I'm only here to tell you what's feasible or not from a technical viewpoint."
"I have plenty of cables and amplifiers on hand. The power supply I will secure on my own. All we require now is the radio transceiver itself."
"In any event, just leave that equipment here. I'll put it away later. If you'd like, you can take one of the extra headsets. I don't need so many spares."
"Well, this was an *interesting collaboration*."
"We make a pretty good team, Soona."
"What do you think? Could I make it as a radio engineer?"
"Perhaps. You're certainly resourceful. That is a good trait in an engineer..."
"You decapitated our antenna. No, I do not think it's a good idea for you..."
"Now you'll excuse me. I have to get back to my own work."
"Perhaps. You're more reliable than the writers I used to work with, though that is not a difficult bar to clear..."
"Really? I do not think we were all that successful. But maybe the RCM has a different definition of success..."
"That is why we don't use it, then."
"Where am I supposed to find a radio transceiver?"
"Alright, I guess I need to find one of these transceivers then." (Conclude.)
"In the meantime, I will gather the rest of the materials. We will meet back here when you have it."
"And before you ask: No, you can't have the radio from my Kineema."
"That sounds like a perfectly adequate radio." She nods.
"There is no need to go out of your way to find a *top-shelf* radio for this purpose. As long as it's functional, that is what counts."
"That will be fine. As long as the radio is *functional*, that is what counts."
"You know what, Kim? I'll find an even *better* radio on my own."
"Certainly, though it requires a fair amount of technical finesse to remove them. Frankly, it's not worth the bother. Just find a regular radio."
"I highly doubt that. When I crank the volume on my DynaWave, it's like you're in the front row at the National Concert Hall."
Wasn't there a *highly functional* radio in that abandoned lorry by the roundabout?
"I didn't know *Speedfreaks FM* had a concert series."
"Alright, Kim, challenge accepted."
"On second thought, this is childish. I'm just going to look for a regular radio."
"I think I saw a radio in that office near the harbour..."
"Possibly. It's worth a look, at the least."
"Do radiocomputers have transceivers in them?"
"Joke all you want, detective. Whatever radio you manage to scrounge up won't lay a *finger* on my set-up."
"A radio transceiver. Cool. I've got this. I've seen *plenty* of those lying around."
"Do you think the pawnshop will have one?"
"Of course you have. They aren't exactly rare."
"I cannot answer that for you, but I don't expect it to be *that* difficult. There's no shortage of radios around here."
"If you have reál to spare, you might even be able to *buy* one. But it doesn't really matter where it comes from, so long as it works."
"Can't we just use your radiocomputer?"
"Absolutely not. My Rehm Prefect is my livelihood. If something were to go wrong, it would be a disaster."
The wind pushes a piece of tare across the cracked tiles. From the north comes the malicious laughter of two children...
From behind you, a low, spectral voice whispers: 'Nay.'
The programmer gives you an impatient look before returning to her radiocomputer.
"I wasn't kidding earlier about contacting Coalition Warship Archer. Can you help me?"

dialoguetext: In white, silver, and apricot faïence, the young mother of humanism stands above you. A crack runs across her body. She is impossibly tall, oval-faced and sad -- a dark and radiant majesty.
Reconstruct the cracked glass.

A jigsaw of broken shards falls into place in front of you: a ghostly reconstruction of the stained glass window. Before it was shattered there was an older woman beneath the younger one -- and a text, a *leitmotiv* below them both.

The shards glimmer in the dark -- you see little pearls of light on the edges of the crack that splits the female figure. Something was written there... remains of broken letters line the emulsion. What it said, you do not know.
Turn away. [Leave.]
How did I know this is the *mother of humanism*?

Despite the damage you've done to yourself, the title appears lodged in your hippocampus. This is Her Innocence Dolores Dei -- the innocence of humanism, internationalism, and the welfare state -- perhaps the most famous human being ever to have lived.
It's a mystery. A mystery sprinkled with self-pity and regret. For some reason, unknown to your mind, looking at her delicate eyes makes you feel like you're ready for drowning...
No amount of *Commodore Red* can wipe her sad smile from your brain-thing. It has survived the deluge and haunts you still. And will haunt you forever, as it haunts all men.
All you know is, this is the young mother of humanity -- and that you should go. Do something else! Escape her sad, worryworn look.
Kneel.
Your knees touch the floor. The floorboards are hard and cold -- there you kneel among the snowdrifts, diffuse light falling on your hands from beyond the glass.

Cradled in her arms are a pair of glowing lungs, clearly visible from underneath her flowing dress. 

You should kneel.
She acknowledges the passing of someone who is still alive...
You.
The mother of humanism stands above you -- a precious and complex wax painting on a single pane of glass. A crack runs across the length of her body, her face oval and sad.
Look up.

The woman looks down at you kneeling. She towers among her followers: architects, laymen, courtiers. There is a sad smile on her lips and a glint in her green-blue eye -- of what? Compassion? Remorse?
No.
Close your eyes first.
The world is silent, but for the creaks and cracks of the massive wooden structure behind you. It covers you from the wind outside.
In the darkness, you sense her eyes on you, inspecting you with their multicoloured glass. As if you're a bug under a microscope.
Cold air seeps in through the crack in the glass, cooling the sweat on your forehead. Makes you shudder...
The ocean feels distant. Its ebb and flow blocked off by the centuries-old pinewood sarcophagus around you.
No, she doesn't care about you. She only cares about her shiny sovereign's orb and her silk robes and getting to the aerodrome on time -- to *leave*!
This is Her Innocence Dolores Dei.
Cold wind seeps in from the crack in the glass. Snowdrifts cover the floorboards at your feet. Above, you feel her multicoloured eyes on you. Inspecting you.
Look up.
No.
As if under a microscope.
No. I am not your bug.
It's compassion.
It's remorse.
It's mourning.
It's not possible to live.
As that soft word passes through your mind, the lieutenant draws an x-shaped cross from shoulder to shoulder.
As that great and desperate thought passes through your mind, the lieutenant draws an x-shaped cross from shoulder to shoulder.
As that bitter thought passes through your head, the lieutenant draws an x-shaped cross from shoulder to shoulder. With three fingers.
That bitter thought passes through your mind as you stand in the apricot-coloured light of the window. The woman keeps smiling her distant smile above you, sundered by the crack in the glass.

That great and desperate thought passes through your mind as you stand in the apricot-coloured light of the window. Above you, the woman keeps smiling her distant smile, sundered by the crack in the glass.
That soft word passes through your mind as you stand in the apricot-coloured light of the window. The woman keeps smiling her distant smile, sundered by the crack in the glass.
As that useless word passes through your mind, the lieutenant draws an x-shaped cross from shoulder to shoulder.
That lonely word passes through your mind as you stand in the apricot-coloured light of the window. The woman keeps smiling her distant smile above you, sundered by the crack in the glass.
As that terrible word passes through your mind, the lieutenant draws an x-shaped cross from shoulder to shoulder.
That terrible word rings through your mind as you stand in the apricot coloured-light of the window. The woman keeps smiling her distant smile above you, sundered by the crack in the glass.
Do the same as you get up.

Your fingertips touch your chest four times. Then you rise from your knees, into the apricot-coloured light of the window. Above you, the woman still smiles her distant smile, sundered by the crack in the glass.
"Who is this, Kim?"
