dialoguetext: "...AS ALWAYS IT'S DJS MESH AND FLACIO AND YOU'RE LISTENING TO S-S-S-SSS-SSSPEE-EED FREAKS FM, BRINGING YOU THE HOTTEST, THE NASTIEST, THE MOST VULGAR..."
Right away the lieutenant reaches into the cabin and turns off the radio. He's not looking at you as he says:
"Someone must have been messing with the radio, or maybe it picked up a random frequency... You wanted the primeline, right?"
"Sorry about it, I wanted to contact the dispatch." (Pick up the radio and turn it back to PRIMELINE.)
"*Speedfreaks FM*, huh?" (Look him in the eye.)
"Oh, is that what it was called?" He's trying hard to act surprised.
"...AND DE FACTO THE FASTEST MUSIC IN ALL OF R-R-REVACHOL R-ROCK CITY. ALL YOU HOOLIGANS, DOWNTOWN DRIFTERS, SIDEWAYS SALLIES AND POWERSLIDING PIERRES...
This radio station is even worse than Cuno -- it feels like someone defecating right into your ear.
This must be the most annoying thing you've ever heard -- it feels like someone defecating right into your ear.
"... GET INTO GEAR, DROP THE MOTHERFUCKING CLUTCH AND LET THE P-P-PPP-PPPPOWER TAKE YOU ON A JOURNEY OF A LIFETIME!"

"... AND NOW FOR SOME MUSIC!" another voice screams into the microphone. Rhythmic rock music fills the cabin, as the back-to-back DJs mix it with sounds from car crashes and illegal speeding competitions.
This is art... *underground* art... a *scene*.
"This is Precinct 57," the operator greets you through the static. "How may I assist you?"
Pick up the radio again.
"Right, you don't want to get into this, no problem."
"Nothing to *get into* really, but sure, let's focus on the important things." He pats the motor carriage.
Go for it -- turn the radio back on while it's still on the Speedfreaks FM!
"...SSSSOUPED UP MOTOR CARRIAGE FOR ONE BAD BAD MOMMA'S BOY, F-F-F-FFFOR THE H-H-HEAVY OF F-F-F-FFFOOT AND FREAKY IN..."
"God-damn-it!" The lieutenant moves quick as a viper as he switches off the radio and sets it on primeline. Then he turns to you:
"Look, it helps me to stay alert on long nights, okay? It's a method. I'm not some kind of *speed-freak* or..." He shakes his head, furiously staring at his feet.
"What about *heavy of foot*?"
"Sure, you don't have to explain yourself. I'll just forget about it."
"Thank you." His eyes glide over the plaza, making sure that no one heard the sudden blast from the radio, before he turns back to the cabin.
"You would be too if you had this motor carriage," he snaps half-seriously.
Take the hand-cranked flashlight.
"I have something here we could sell. Look in the back, in the suspect transport enclosure."
Transport enclosure? Regular people just call it *the cage*.
The cage at the back of the motor carriage looks rather uncomfortable. Four shiny hubcaps are stacked against the seat. Their silver edges sparkle in the dark.
"I confiscated these four a little while back. We can take them to the pawnshop down by the Martinaise Canal."
"Yes, there's one 100 metres south of here, I think it's called Roy's Nest or something. If I'm not mistaken it should be open late."
Those are some fancy words. Most people would just call it *the cage*.
"I have something in the back we could sell so you can pay for your room. Open the suspect transport enclosure."
"You mean the cage, right?"
"Yes." He frowns. "I've never liked that crude name. It doesn't do much to improve the RCM's reputation."
Open the door.
"What *are* those things?"

"They're spinner hubcaps -- frivolous things you put on your wheels. When the wheels come to a stop," he makes a spinning motion with his hands, "the caps keep on spinning. There's no real use for them, it's just for vanity."
"Thanks. I appreciate your help." (Take the spinners.)
The lieutenant nods as you take the spinners.
"You said something about a pawnshop?"
"I need to report a dead body on the Martinaise boardwalk."
"Connect me to Jamrock Public Library."
"Hold on, officer."
"I've got Central Jamrock Public Library on the line and I've already introduced you to their librarian. Connecting the call in 2... 1..."
"Yes, this is Central Jamrock Public Library here." A male librarian answers the call. "How can I help you, officer?"
"I'm afraid they're closed. It says here that the library is open from 10 AM to 6 PM."
"Could you connect me to the 41st Precinct? I have something I need to report."
"I was told I need to connect to my station... the 41st lazareth."
"Have you heard back from the ICP about the serial number?"
"Could you run a serial number from a pair of armoured boots for me?"
"Did you find out more about the owner of the armoured boots?"
In the cabin you see a set of steering levers, a radio on a hook, a pull-out toolbox and the soft glow of the fuel pre-heater gauge.
"Yes, hello? Who is this?" There's a pause. "My records show this channel is used by Lieutenant Kim Kitsuragi."
"Who is this?" There's a pause. "My records show this channel is used by Lieutenant Kim Kitsuragi."
"Yes, I know Kim! He's my partner."
"This is... Harry. I guess. Lieutenant Kitsuragi is my partner on a case."
"Oh. Do you have permission to call from the lieutenant's vehicle?" Her voice doesn't sound very friendly. "Where is he?"
"Lieutenant Harrier Du Bois, reporting in. I'm on a case with Lieutenant Kitsuragi."
"Uh, the name's Mr. Costeau. Raphaël to friends. Kim's my friend."
"I prefer to be called Tequila Sunset. Kim's my partner. We're solving a case."
"From the 41st Precinct. Where is Lieutenant Kitsuragi?"
"Mr. Harry, do you have permission to call from the lieutenant's vehicle? Where is he?"
"Right... Mr. Sunset." Her voice does not sound friendly. "Do you have permission to call from the lieutenant's vehicle? Where is he?"
"Mr. Costeau... if that is your real name, unauthorized use of a police officer's radio is a *major* crime. I will have to alert my colleagues."
"He's resting. It's been rough around here. Listen, I need assistance."
"He's investigating a lead on his own. Listen, I need help."
"Affirmative, Lieutenant Du Bois." There's a pause, tense with anticipation.
"No, wait! We're solving a murder case in Martinaise."
Hang up quickly.
Her voice does not sound friendly. "Where is the lieutenant?"
"I don't know, it's not like we're joined by the hip. Anyway, I need assistance."
"I'll contact him later for a full report." Her voice hasn't become any friendlier. "For now, I'm Officer Alice de Mettrie, how can I help you?"
"Why aren't you using your own radio to contact your precinct?"
"That's one of the things I may need help with." (Cough.)
"Reasons... uh, for one, I don't know where my radio is."
"It's a long story. Bad shit has gone down."
"A-ha. Sounds like trouble." She seems to sigh. "Alright. Next time, have Lieutenant Kitsuragi with you."
"That is a pretty big problem, yes." She seems to sigh. "Alright. Next time, have Lieutenant Kitsuragi with you."
There's a pause. "Alright. Next time, have Lieutenant Kitsuragi with you."
Take the red-tipped prybar.
"Kim, what are we looking at? What is this machine?"
"This is the Coupris Kineema, my motor carriage. You can use the toolbox and the radio if you'd like." He nods at the cabin.
But this is different -- this is a sports model.
"This must be what woke me up when you arrived in Martinaise. The infernal noise."
"Yes, it's my patrol vehicle. You can use the toolbox and the radio if you'd like." He nods at the cabin.
"Do all policemen in the RCM have such *cool* motor carriages?"
"Yes, sorry about that... the Coupris Kineema does have a rather... distinctive engine sound."
He says it with very badly concealed pride.
(Squint your eyes) "Okay, but what *is* a motor carriage?"
"The Coupris MotorCorp does provide most of our patrol vehicles, yes."
"I might be wrong, but this one is a *sports model*, right?"
"You're right." A vainglorious smile spreads over his face as he pats his machine. "I didn't take you for a motorcar enthusiast. Do you also like TipTop, detective?"
"Can we turn it on and drive somewhere?"
Look around the cabin again.
"No, I'm afraid not." He straightens his spine. "We have a murder case on our hands, remember?"

The TipTop Tournée is an interisolary racing series, mostly known for its high speeds, ludicrous sponsorship deals, and high death toll. In Revachol it's held quadrennially on the prestigious Zéro Carrousel racing circuit.
"An interisolary racing series. You should definitely give it a go if you like motor carriages -- it has fantastic competition." He smiles again.
"What's TipTop?"
"I'm pretty sure I like neither motorcars or any 'TipTops'."
"TipTop? Adore it!"
"No, I don't care about motorcars, I just know about random things."
"Oh." He looks visibly disappointed. "I guess it's not for everyone."
"Really?" the lieutenant looks at you. "Well, I'm not indifferent on the matter either." He adjusts his glasses, visibly pleased to have found a fellow fan.
Nothing. Nothing. It's probably nothing, forget I brought it up. Please proceed with the carefree lollygagging.
Motor carriage, motor carriage... Something bad with a motor carriage.... A dark lump rises in your throat.
What is this sinking feeling I have with the words *motor carriage*?
The radio DJ stops. For a moment it seems like he has ran out of things to say...
Turn the radio back to PRIMELINE.
Turn it off, this isn't music!
He's still avoiding your gaze -- and his ears glow red.
"But seriously, let's quit joking around, alright? We have a case to investigate." He turns back to the cabin.
The entirety of Martinaise is watching you!
A flock of seagulls takes off nearby, startled by the roaring radio.
"I feel deprived of human contact."
"We should try again during business hours."
"Anything else, detective?"
"Do you like to party, Alice?"
"Now, how can I help you in your *investigation*?"
The soft purr of electrical kittens -- radio waves cast far and wide over the metropolis. A woman's voice greets you through the static:
"Hi, Alice, I'm a policeman too. Nice to meet you."
"Operating a radio is easy." (Speak into the microphone:) "Come in Delta-Ten, this is Firewalker, copy!"
"Hello... hello... hello...." (Mimic echo.) "Is there anybody out there?"
As you tap on the gauge, the indicator pin jerks as if startled. It's in the large orange sector, indicating the engine is warm. Next to the gauge is a red switch labelled HEAT.
As you tap on the gauge, the indicator pin jerks as if startled. It's in the small blue sector, indicating the engine is cold. Next to the gauge is a red switch labelled HEAT.
"There's no use pressing the HEAT button," he says and jingles his keys. "It won't start without the ignition key."
He's downplaying his excitement -- the lieutenant is more than happy to show off his precious carriage.
The dashboard lights up with orange glow. The rounds per minute gauge jumps and the engine of the Coupris Kineema comes to life with a whiny growl.
Like a leopard, waking from its sleep. Yawning and roaring at the same time.
That sound. You feel the wind in your hair as if you're already driving -- but where?
Yes -- where?
Press the button labelled HEADLIGHTS.
Down a narrow street lined with shabby wooden houses, the 8/81 motor-tract coiling like a serpent high above. Children play under the viaduct. Eyes turn to watch you as you pass...
What's ahead?
The Valley of Dogs -- and before it, a familiar dome, like a ladybug without the colours. The building has a designated parking place for *your* carriage.
This is Precinct 41 -- as close as you have to home now. It's far away...
The button stays in the dash for a few seconds, then jumps out and... nothing happens.
The Coupris Kineema cannot be started without an ignition key.
Press HEAT.
The prybar feels nice and cold in your hand. Heavier than you'd think.
Cold and heavy -- like truth. You feel like you're reunited with *truth* once more.
The handles are long and sleek. *Snap-snap* go the cutters in your hand.
You can do good work with these: cut chains, locks, and ropes -- especially belts...
Useful for opening all sorts of doors and lids...
It's robust, weatherproof and well made. Police issue -- blue.
Let's you see things in the dark you would otherwise miss...
"Take what you need, officer. It's going to be a long case. I'm not *protective* of my tools. Like some men are..."
He's clearly *a little* protective of his tools, but what can you do? Work is work.
How do I turn on the headlights?
Translation: We're not going anywhere right now.
Tap on the fuel pre-heater gauge.
Uhm... When Lieutenant Kitsuragi is here? It's his MC.
You need his key to turn on the engine if you want the foldable lights to pop up.
Press ENGINE START.
"There you go. I'll turn them off from the remote once you're done -- we just need to stand in front of the machine now."
Look in the suspect transport enclosure.
"What do you mean you 'confiscated' them?"
"A couple weeks ago I stopped a young man for going slower than the speed of traffic. Turns out he was some Coalition official's son -- and high."
(Look at Kim.) "Isn't that *corruption*?"
"I don't know, is it?" The lieutenant looks back, stone-faced. "I was going to take them into evidence, but they weren't necessary for conviction. He never asked for them back."
(Look at the spinners.) "I get it, I would have confiscated them too -- they're mesmerizing."
"That they are." The lieutenant looks at the spinners and sighs. "I was going to take them into evidence, but they weren't necessary for conviction. He never asked for them back."
A vanity he wouldn't mind.
"Sorry, I can't take them. It wouldn't be right." (Don't take the spinners.)
"All right, let's *not* take them now, then come back once we realize we have to -- have this conversation *again* and then take them."
Operating the radio is easy. Just be confident -- you've probably done it a thousand times.
Inside you see a set of steering levers, a radio-microphone, a pull-out toolbox, and the soft glow of the fuel pre-heater gauge.
"So you took his spinners?"
"Mhm," he nods. "I took them *and* arrested him for driving under the influence."
Sounds likely.
In the cabin you see a set of steering levers, a radio on a hook, a pull-out toolbox and the soft glow of the fuel pre-heater gauge.
Damn it -- the lieutenant had the number and he's not here.
"This is Precinct 57. Can I connect you to someone?" The voice on the shortwave repeats.
"Please connect me to Sylvie again."
"Yes, hello." You recognize her voice.
"Sylvie Malaìika on the line for you, officer."
"Just a second, officer..."
"Officer," she finally returns. "I have Sylvie Malaìika on the line for you."
"Give it a minute, she might be busy at the moment... takes a bit to get to the phone."
Just wait. Relax.
What is *wrong* with you? Why did you ask to be connected to her? Who *does* that?! Act professional now.
"Alice this is Firewalker. Re-connect me to the 41st."
"Alice, please connect me to the 41st again."

dialoguetext: Alternative translation: Don't even *think* you can drive my MC.
"A motorized vehicle, officer. I'm sure you are familiar with the concept. We've had these for nearly a century."
Honestly, that sounds like an *amazing* physics demonstration.
"Um.... did you want to put these spinners on your machine?" (Point at Kineema.)
"No, no. That would be silly. I just..." He hesitates. "I don't know why I kept them. It doesn't matter. I couldn't put them on this MC anyway. A cop with spinners -- that would be outrageous."
"Yes. Too wacky."
"Yes. Outrageously cool."
"I'm sorry you have to sell them because of me."
He flashes a smile, barely visible in the dark.
"It's only right that we sell them."
"Exactly."
Say nothing.
"As I said, they're useless anyway. I should have remembered I have these earlier..."
"Don't make your unpaid hostel bill a *moral boon*, officer. It won't stick."
Shot down. I've nothing to add.
But thank you.
The spinners shine so bright they reflect on the lieutenant's glasses. He doesn't say anything either.
Pick up the radio again.
Just nod.
He turns the pre-heater on, waits, takes out his keys and says: "All right. Ready. I turn, you press START -- it's next to the pre-heater."
*You* told him to do that stupid thing...
"Isn't that dangerous?"
"Okay." (Turn off the radio.)
"No more dangerous than stepping between three armed mercenaries and eight Union men, I hope." He glances over his shoulder.
"I don't like it either, but that's the way it is. The streets seem safe enough to me. If anything, taking out the mercs made things calmer. For now..." He flicks off the radio. Silence.
They're shutting you up. Silencing you. Don't fucking drop your guard.
Everything sounds okay. No drumbeat of total war yet. If anything, everything sounds *too* okay...
Silence.
Something is wrong. Only static hisses through the speaker.
"Precinct 57, we've been attacked. I repeat -- Lieutenant Kim Kitsuragi and..."
"Hello?"
No reply. Only the mindless drone of static, crawling through the air.
"It's been this way for a while now." The lieutenant shrugs. "My guess is, the Union is listening in on our conversations -- and jamming outward communications to protect themselves from Krenel."
"It only happens when someone mentions the attack -- the rest is unaffected. Our best bet is to carry on like nothing happened -- that is, if we don't want us cut off the grid completely."
Turn off the radio.
If only Lieutenant Kitsuragi were here to make sense of it...
"You can try calling again -- just don't mention the tribunal. And remember, they're listening in."
He sounds worried, yet ready to assist. This is how people get when the police call.
Wait, what? 'Wild one'? That doesn't sound right...
C'mon, wake up! The way she said she's not Sylvie -- practically begging you to make a move. Just go for it.
Hold on! As a feminist I find these implications offensive.
Oh, did you hear that? Pure lust. She's a wild one! Throw her a curve-ball, see if she's down to party.
Oh, did you hear that? How she said 'officer'?! She's a wild one, wants it bad, bratan. Get that party going!
Offensive-smoffensive, just ask her, alright!
As your parasympathetic nervous system I call bullshit. Now ask her!
Yeah, bratan, otherwise you're always gonna be wondering what could've been. Just ask her!
"Sir, how can I help you with your *investigation*?" The voice on the other end is becoming impatient.
"Sir, you're already connected to the 57th Precinct." Her voice is sharp and noticeably less friendly.
What an unbelievable prude... Oh well, at least now you know.
Odd... she didn't sound menopausal. Must be frigid or something. Oh well.
"Who doesn't," she states matter of factly. "Now, how can I help you in your *investigation*?"
Change of plans -- *her* number.
A dark feeling. This is going wrong. Let go of the clutch.
So strange. The machine is not on the bottom of the sea at all. It's right in front of you, well kept. Why did it say that?
What?

dialoguetext: "Come again, officer?"
"Speedfreaks FM. A radio station. It's for the case."
"I said 'Speedfreaks FM'. Kim's a big fan."
"Really?" he says, low and tired.
The lieutenant sighs under his breath.
"Okay, officer. One moment."
"Right... One moment, officer."
"Excited, Kim?"
"No."
"Sorry, officer. Your radio personalities are unavailable, probably until tomorrow. Is there anything else I can assist you with?"
"I have *DJ Mesh* on the line. I'll connect you now."
"Yo!" The word shoots out of the man's mouth like a bullet.
The starting gun fires. And we're off!
"Yo yo!"
"Yo yo yo! You got DJ Mesh here, my man. I got a few minutes before I gotta go back on air. What do you need?"
"Hello, is this DJ Mesh?"
"It is. I got a few minutes before I gotta go back on air. What can I do for you, cop-man?"
"The Lamb is calm before its slaughter. It does not know what will befall it."
"Uh... What?" He laughs, confused. "That's the wildest shit I heard today. You are a cop, right?"
"I'm so sorry to bother you. I just have a question."
"Ain't a bother, brother. Anyway, I only got a few minutes before I gotta go back on air. What do you need?"
"Yes. And I have a question."
"You aren't the only one. Anyway, I only got a few minutes before I gotta go back on air. What can DJ Mesh tell the RCM?"
"I'm just calling to confirm -- did you debut a new track from DJ Flacio a few days ago?"
"'An Asshole Is A Mouth For Shit (And I'm Puking).'"
That's the name of the song. Vulgarity is la belle du jour.
"Great title, man! Number one stuff."
"I'm guessing that's the song."
"... What?"
"An Asshole Is A Mouth For Shit (And I'm Puking)?"
"Okay... But what is the song called?"
"Are you insulting an officer of the Law, punk?"
"What? No, I'm not telling you off, man. That's the name of the song! 'An Asshole Is A Mouth For Shit (And I'm Puking).'"
"Yeah, that is the song. 'An Asshole Is A Mouth For Shit (And I'm Puking).'"
"An Asshole Is A Mouth For Shit (And I'm Puking)!"
"'An Asshole Is A Mouth For Shit (And I'm Puking),'" he says more slowly.
"It ain't just a song! It's the shit-hot new single from DJ Flacio that's shredding up the sonic waves."
"Thank you very much! Yeah, it's the shit-hot new single from DJ Flacio. Really shredding up the sonic waves."
"Do people like it?"
"They're lovin' it, man! The requests keep coming in for more."
"I really think it's the future of music, I do. Fuckin', like, stinkcore, or something. Shit's so nasty, those stinkwaves come up like soundwaves, you know what I mean?"
"Is that legal to play?"
"It's illegal not to play, man. When you got that kind of music in you, the universe demands you let it out, know what I mean?"
"Plus, Flacio and I got it in our contracts that we could play our own tracks. So really, it would be illegal not to."
"Okay. Let's move on. We talked to some kids who said they heard it in their heads. Do you know how that could be possible?"
He sighs. "Is that what this is about? Listen, it's not our problem if kids decide to tune into R-R-R-Revachol's hottest station."
"It's not that they played it on a radio. They heard it in their heads. Do you know how that's possible?"
"I don't understand. Are you asking if we can, like, play our station into people's brains?"
This is preposterous. Neither sound nor scent work anything as he's describing. What does he even *mean*?
"Sure, man. I'm young, cool, and with it."
"I don't have any idea what you mean."
"Very cool, man, I'm dead serious when I say, Flacio is going to make it big in this world."
"Doesn't matter. Listen, I'm dead serious when I say, Flacio is going to make it big in this world."
"Sure! Forced radio. Can't tune out. You'd make a killing on ads!"
"Yeah. Like a new way to equalize people, getting them all on the same station. A great tool for Communism."
"Exactly like that. Because I think you're an enemy of traditional values forcing your filth on the innocent."
"Yeah, like that. Maybe it was part of your civic duty, you were just testing it out for the government."
"Speedfreaks FM is elective listening, man. We don't want to force the people to adopt our thinking. That's fascist bullshit."
"No, I was just asking -- and dreaming up a bold new money making scheme."
"Right, well -- no, we don't force radio into peoples heads. Don't know how you'd even do that, man."
"Was there anything else you need to know?"
"No, that wasn't my fascist line, that was my ultraliberal one. I can do the fascist one if you want."
"You're a fucking wild man. Sure, let's hear it."
"Okay, the fascist thing was me calling you an enemy of the state for force-pumping filth into children, thus corrupting traditional values."
The radio host doesn't try to contain his laughter. "Oh, man, I love it! You're great. No, we didn't do anything like that. Wouldn't know how to -- we just played it on air like normal people."
"Right on, brother. We gotta make sure everybody tunes into this sonic revolution!"
"But we didn't, like, force it into people's brains. Got no idea how to do that, short of them just tuning in on their favourite radio receiving device."
"Okay. I'd recommend looking into it, though. For the revolution."
"I understand. Thank you for clearing that up."
"Revolution-brain-broadcast. Got it. Yeah, we'll look into it."
"My pleasure, comrade cop. Is there anything else you needed?"
"Was there anything else you wanted to ask?"
"We ain't testing anything out for the Man, unless it's how many bricks you need to break all of his windows."
"That wasn't a threat, by the way. Just a figure of speech, I'm a spoken word guy. Now, is there anything else you needed?"
"Shit keeps getting weirder with you, man. Fucking unbelievable."
"No, we didn't force radio into people's heads. The fuck is it with you fascists and conspiracy theories?"
Tell him the truth, bröther. Even if he isn't *hard* enough to hear it.
"It's not a conspiracy theory, it's logic. The lesser races, still fresh and DRIPPING from the proto-slime, can't beat us outright -- so they resort to impossibly devious schemes."
The lieutenant stares at you, his jaw clenched. A vein strains on his temple.
"You know, it'd be one thing if you were just crazy. Like, I could forgive you then. I know lots of crazy people."
"But you're just fucking hateful. And I got no time for that shit. Anything else you need, or can I hang up?"
"I'm just thinking of the children."
Say nothing.
"Right. Is there anything else you need, or can I hang up the fucking phone now?"
"Just one more thing -- give a shoutout Lieutenant Kim Kitsuragi. He *coincidentally* has you saved to his radio."
"No, that was it. Thank you for your time."
"Huh?" The sound bubbles out of him, even to his own surprise.
"Okay, cop-man! Can do, will do!"
"DJ Mesh out."
"Not going to happen, you fascist prick."
"Not going to happen, you fascist prick. Tell your friend to not listen to us any more."
The lieutenant's breath catches in his chest.
No parting words; only the dull cry of the dial tone.
"Nah, man, thank you. This has been an absolute pleasure."
"Later, cop-man."
You crossed a line. This will not be forgotten.
"The party has terminated the call. Is there anything else I can do for you, officer?"
You should check the radio again!
You should check the radio!
Look at that! His eyes dilate. That's joy, my man. You wouldn't be able to tell, but his glasses *just* magnify it.
Press the button labelled "Saved" and turn on Speedfreaks FM.
It requires no adjustment. The radio is already set to Speedfreaks FM.
"...SPOKE TO THE W-W-WILDEST COP IN REVACHOL."
"FASCIST PIGS, I SWEAR. YOU SHOULD ALL..." The assault gives way to burning quiet.
"...SPOKE TO THE W-W-WILDEST COP IN REVACHOL. HE ASKED US TO GIVE HIS BUDDY COP, LONG TIME LISTENER KIM KITSURAGI, A BIG SHOUTOUT. KIM, WE LOVE YOU."
"FASCIST PIGS, I SWEAR. YOU AND KIM KITSURAGI SHOULD ALL..." The assault gives way to burning quiet.
Another equally furious voice seizes on the silence. "HERE'S SOME MUSIC."
The lieutenant snaps off the radio, turning it back to PRIMELINE. He stares at you silently.
An audio-assault descends full force on you. Sonic daggers fly forth from the Kineema's speakers. The soundwaves would slice you if they could.
Turn the radio back to PRIMELINE.
"KEEP IT FREAKY," another voice cuts in, "LIKE DJ MESH, DJ FLACIO, AND YOUR W-W-W-WILD FRIEND. THIS ONE'S FOR YOU!"
"We aren't discussing this." After a few bars, the lieutenant turns the radio back to PRIMELINE.
If, when a motor-carriage's engine was ignited, it could drive by its own accord off to a high mountain and there write a song -- perhaps it'd be something like what you're hearing now.
What a reserve of willpower. It's taking all he's got to not smile.
Elsewhere in Revachol, the lieutenant has also just turned on the radio. In his privacy, he doesn't even try to stop himself from smiling.
The lieutenant snaps off the radio, turning it back to PRIMELINE. He stares at you silently.
Another equally furious voice seizes on the silence. "HERE'S SOME MUSIC."
"DIDN'T EVEN GET HIS NAME. BUT WHOEVER THAT MYSTERY COP WAS, WE SALUTE HIM."
An audio-assault descends full force on you. Sonic daggers fly forth from the Kineema's speakers. The soundwaves would slice you if they could.
"I HOPE HE'S R-R-R-ROCKING WITH US A LONG TIME," another voice cuts in. "THE WORLD NEEDS MORE FREAKS. THIS ONE'S FOR YOU, MYSTERY COP!"
That quickfire patter -- is this the voice the twins heard?
"That's DJ Mesh! That was Speedfreaks FM!"
"Isn't that the station we have to call? Speedfreaks FM? Why's it saved as 'favourite'?"
The lieutenant is resolutely silent. Staring at the console.
A look of betrayal. The secret has been revealed!
"Aw, man! You should have told me you liked them! I could have asked for a shoutout."
"It's okay to like what you like, Kim."
"You lying to me right now, Kim?"
"I don't listen to them," the lieutenant says sharply.
"I don't like it." He shrugs very slightly. "I don't know how that channel got marked."
"Excuse me?"
He's too stiff. Like a grunt during a military inspection, hoping their commanding officer overlooks them.
Why the fuck can't he just admit it? Don't let this go. Hound him until he admits it.
Just leave it alone. He clearly doesn't want to share this with you.
"I said, are you fucking lying to me?"
"Nothing. Never mind."
The lieutenant raises an eyebrow. The ocean wind blows, bringing in the smell of salt.
"Mhm." The lieutenant frowns at you.
That eyebrow! He's using his Authority against you... you... can't resist...
This has gone far enough. You're going to show dignity toward your fellow officer and *apologize*.
"I... gah..." (Grab your head.) "I'm... sorry, Kim."
He remains silent.
"C'mon, man! You can tell me!"
"Wait! Can you send me any Speedfreaks merch?"
"I can understand why you'd ask, our shit's hot. Think we gave the last of it away at our last live show, but -- what's your address anyway?"
"Uh, I'm gonna need better than 'streetless shack' if you can get that for me."
Merchandise. Ask for Speedfreaks FM merchandise.
"Send it to the Whirling-in-Rags, in Martinaise."
"I'm staying in a shack by the coast, in a small fishing village near Martinaise."
"I don't really know my address..."
"Thank you!"
"Wait! Don't you need to know my name?"
"I don't want to know, man. I like leaving it to the imagination. Now, anything else?"
"Hey, don't thank me yet! Again, I don't think we got anything left, but, well... Anything else?"
"That's, uh... Well, have you got *any* address I can send shit to, man?"
"That I can do. Whirling-in-Rags, Martinaise. Got it."
Even if a package arrives, how will it get to you if it hasn't got your name on it?
"Now, was there anything else you wanted to ask?"
"Sergeant Torson here is wondering if you are still in possession of your genitalia. Over."
"Yes, I lost my wiener too, just lay off, okay?"
"I left it at his momma's after I fucked her ass all night. Tell him that."
"I don't need to listen to this. Firewalker out!" (Turn off the radio.)

dialoguetext: "That did not go well. I guess the important thing is that you followed protocol and reported your lost items."
"Did we need anything else here?" He looks around in the cabin.
The silence is almost deafening after you flick off the switch, severing the connection.
"Thank god for that! That would have been a nightmare. I don't even want to imagine the poor prick who has to relay that kind of news to the captain."
"This might sound odd, but there's *personal details* I'd like to discuss."
"I guess I can hold off the report for a few days." Oldboy lights another cigarette.
"Uh, can you repeat that?"
"This shit does *not* leave this room! Not a word of this to the captain or anyone else. We'll give him a couple of days to pull his shit together!"
The fuck do you need a gun for? Look at the pythons on your arms. You *are* a gun. The biggest one in the world.
She sighs. "Right... please hold."
"Just a moment, officer..."
"I'm not going to..."
"Ask him!"

"Mack, man the door," he gestures Torson to block the doorway, then turns to Minot. "You know what he told me? 'I don't want to get better -- I want to get worse.' Those were his words." He sighs heavily and turns to address the room...
"I just know we can't give up on him when he's at his weakest. He wouldn't..." The crowd in the room has started fidgeting uncomfortably. Someone's trying to slip out unnoticed.
"Just a second, officer..." She puts you on hold, the static crackling softly like a bonfire. After a while you hear an old man greet you from the radio. His rattly voice is oddly familiar:
"That's a negative. Not going to say that. Over."
"What's he saying? Share with the class!"
"Yeah? How do you fucking plan to do that, huh?! Get him off the drink?! Go jogging with him in the morning and get him on carrot juice?! He's a lost man!"
"He... He said he sodomized your mother."
"We must help him." Minot looks down at her neatly polished black shoes. There is a quiet firmness to her voice when she speaks.
"The prick ate momma's vanilla waffles at the captain's birthday party! Some nerve he's got..."
"Sure her vanilla waffles were the only thing he ate?"
"Shut up, Chester, this isn't funny. This is my mom we're talking about!"
Say nothing.
"Tell him to apologize right now!"
"10-4, come in, officer! Over."
"Sergeant Torson requests that you apologize for the claims you made about his mother. Over."
"10-4, come in..." He hesitates. "...*Fire walker*. Over."
"Yeah, Mullen was fucked alright. Sounded fucking drunk to me."
"Okay, tell him I'm sorry -- It was just banter, I thought that's what cops do."
"He says he's sorry and he didn't mean nothing by it."
"He what...? He lost his badge?!"
"Okay, tell him..."
"Enough!" The commotion dies down. All eyes turn to Satellite-Officer Vicquemare. "None of this is funny! It's fucking sad, that's what it is. He's a cop. He's one of us, goddamn this..."
"Tell him to find his *goddamn* badge and gun, that's the *only* thing that matters here!"
"10-2, 10-5. This is 41st, come in! Over."
"I'm his *goddamn* partner!"
"Yeah, Mack's right, that was some gnarly shit there..."
You *really* need to get your shit together, this is nearing a complete meltdown.
"Fire. Walker."
"Fire-*water*? He's lost it... Fuck it, tell him to find his goddamn badge and gun, that's the only thing that matters!"
"Hey, if you don't like the fallout, maybe *don't* fuck with the Firewalker!"

"Yes, please do try. It's imperative that we learn whose armour this was."
"Armour like this isn't mass-produced -- it would have probably been fitted. Perhaps there's a record of who signed for this particular suit of armour."
"Is there any way to find out who got this particular suit of armour?"
"Yes, but the ICP tends to be reluctant to share private sector records. I could try to talk them into it, though."
"Hard to say. Their client list is rather diverse. And... incomplete. The only constant seems to be that the mercenaries are always deployed in third- and fourth-world countries."
"Sure. Call back tomorrow. Hopefully I will have more information for you then."
This is a fun challenge for her, an opportunity to contribute beyond doing her job by rote. She'll gladly put in the extra effort for team RCM!
"Yes, thank you, officer. I really appreciate your efforts in this case."
"You are my beautiful conquering heroine."
"Glad to help. Call back tomorrow. Hopefully I'll have more for you then."
"I'm going to ignore that, officer. Call back tomorrow. Hopefully I will have more information for you then."

dialoguetext: "I'm glad the inquiry was helpful to your investigation, officer. Did you have any other questions?"
"A name -- this is very good. Ellis Kortenaer..." he says to himself.
Joyce said the dead man went by Lely. He must have gotten that from *Lelystad* -- the name of the county.
According to Klaasje, Lely said his real name wasn't really *his* -- perhaps that's because he was fostered?
"Okay."
"Was there anything else?"
I don't know about you, but I really, really enjoyed it. Worked out really well in the end.
I knew this would lead to something good!
We're still glad you did it, my liege. This was good training. For when you need to lie to save your life maybe?
You hear her fingers on a keyboard. "No, they were called *Sediment*. And *Somatosensor*, it seems. All that during the last nine years."
"The world will end soon."
"Okay." She's not worried. "Does that mean you're ready?"
"Neonatal Care Unit?"
"He was found as a newborn, in a leaf compactor, near an abandoned farm. He spent four months in the neonatal unit -- survived, apparently -- and was assigned to a foster family at two."

"Then the armour followed him to Semenine -- or at least I assume it did. And that's it. There are no records of his employment in Krenel. Or any of its other incarnations. Or him even entering Revachol.
The lieutenant leans in to listen, notebook in hand.
"So all we have to connect him to Krenel is the armour."
"Even that is a small miracle -- these *organizations* usually double check their inventory." He leans closer and shouts: "Thank you, Alice. Great work!"
"No problem, lieutenant." She sounds pleased.
"Even that took quite a bit of convincing to retrieve the information from the database, officer."
A compliment from Lieutenant Kitsuragi! Not bad.
"Wait, he was found in a... leaf compactor?"
"It's a garden tool used to press leaves into these... cubes. It's a detail the hospital had -- the only detail in these files. So I thought it would be good for you to know."
"It is! Thank you, Alice!"
"Any information on his foster parents?"
"None, officer. Sorry."
The lieutenant nods -- then jots it down in his notes: "Lelystad -- Lely. I like that."
"If you say so, officer -- of course."
"So his name wasn't *his* because he was fostered?"
"Hah! Yes -- what Klaasje said. Very good. That makes sense to me." He takes a quick note.
"I... don't know what that means. But -- sure."
"Well, we have his name and service record now." (Move on.)
"I'm glad the inquiry was helpful to your investigation, officer. Did you have any other questions?"
This means something to him. To know that name. Like naming a case. It's important.
"Sorry, sir. I still haven't heard back from the database people. Try calling again later. Is there anything else I can do for you?"
"Still no word I'm afraid, sir. I know it must be frustrating. Was there anything else you wanted to ask?"
"It was part of a special order for Corps de Pharmacie, a security firm contracted to protect the interests of Oranjese pharmaceutical companies. In the Semenine conflict."
Sometimes police work is about human dignity -- about giving back names to anonymous victims.
"One moment..." You can hear her shuffling through some papers.
"Can you please describe the body -- age, sex, cause of death?"
"An unidentified middle-aged man. Looks like he slipped, fell through a hole in the boardwalk and hit his head against the metal bench."
"An unidentified middle-aged man. Height 170-175 cm, dark hair, medium build. Looks like he slipped, fell through a hole in the boardwalk and hit his head against the metal bench."
"Any signs of violence?"
"No, seems like it was an accident."
"Someone might have... pushed him?"
"No field autopsy necessary..." she repeats.
"Did you perform a field autopsy?"
"No, it's still just a theory."
"What about his belongings? Did you examine his clothes?"
"He was wearing boots, trousers and an old leather jacket with a bright blue lining. I found a library card from his pockets."
"Any information on the library card?"
"It's from Central Jamrock Public Library. It belongs to someone named Billie Méjean."
"I haven't examined it yet."
You can hear her sigh audibly on the other side.
"Do you and Lieutenant Kitsuragi want to take the case or should I assign it to someone else?"
So unprofessional of you... Pity!
"Good, you have a lead."
"We're taking the case."
"Please assign it to someone else."
"I have assigned the case to Lieutenant Kim Kitsuragi. Please follow up on this library lead to identify the man. We'll send someone to take the body to the morgue."
"Great, I'll give it to your colleagues. You don't have to worry about the case anymore, we'll send our officers to take away the body."
"That's all for now. Thank you for reporting in. Is there anything else I can do for you?"
"That's all for now. Thank you for reporting in. Is there anything else I can do for you?"
"Assign it to someone else, Alice -- we've got enough on our plate."
"It looked like an accident to me, Alice," the lieutenant rushes in to say. "But that's for the guys in processing to confirm."

"The man was about 173 cm tall, stout, with dark hair and a moustache. We suspect he might have been inebriated when he slipped -- there were bottles all around him, and traces of vomit on his shirt."
"We suspect he might have been inebriated when he fell -- there were bottles all around him, and traces of vomit on his shirt."
"There might be a *sequence killer* on the loose."
"A sequence killer." You can hear her stop typing. "Are you suggesting that this might be connected to the case you're working on?"
"No, we're not," the lieutenant rushes in to say. "There is no evidence to suggest that this man was connected to the lynching -- or that we're dealing with a sequence killer here."
"It looked like a simple accident to me, Alice. No field autopsy necessary."
"Yes."
"No."
"Actually, scratch that -- there is no sequence killer, I just made it up."
"You just made it up?" Silence. "I see."
"What about his belongings? Did you examine his clothes?" She goes on as if nothing happened.
"No? It's some *other* sequence killer?" Silence. "I see."
"I see." Silence. "This is something you should discuss with the Lieutenant Kitsuragi, as you're sharing the case."
You can hear her quickly typing in the background.
"I'm looking for any information that you can provide on Billie Méjean, a reader."
"Billie, Billie *Méjean*, you said? Give me a moment, I'll have to check our database." He puts down the receiver.
"Yes, hello, are you still there?" You can hear him fiddle with the printout. "I found Billie Méjean's home address, is that alright? No phone number unfortunately."
"Yes, home address is fine."
"Here we go, sir: Rue de Saint-Ghislaine 33B, apartment no 20. It's in Martinaise, I believe... Capeside Apartments, it says. That's all."
"I'm not really that good with addresses."
"Maybe you can write it down? It's Rue de Saint-Ghislaine 33B, apartment no 20. It's in Martinaise, I believe... Capeside Apartments, it says. That's all."
"Do you have any other information on Billie Méjean?"
"Thank you. That's all from me, I have no other questions." (End call with the library.)
"It says here that they returned their last book just a few days ago, but I wasn't at work that day."
"Happy we could help. Good bye, officer." The librarian hangs up and the call gets redirected back to the station.
"Anything else you need from me?" Alice asks.
"Do you know someone who was?"

"Marie?" He covers the phone with his hand and yells out into the room behind him: "Marie! Do you remember a reader named Billie Méjean? They returned a Thibault book the other day..." You hear someone answer from afar.
Loos, Radio City? That's the same book the working class woman was reading at the bookstand...
Something unpleasant twitches in your stomach.

"Yes, it was my colleague Marie," the librarian is speaking into the phone again. "She said that it was Billie's *husband* who returned the book. He also asked for this new sci-fi release "Loos, Radio City '87", but we don't have it yet."
"So Billie Méjean is a woman, not a man? How did your colleague know that it was her husband?"
"Can Marie describe to me what the husband looked like?"
"Marie knows Billie, she's been working here longer than me. Sometimes her husband returns some books for her."
"She said it was an older man... And that she's pretty sure he had had a drink or two the last time she saw him."
"Thank you. That's all from me, I have no other questions." (End call with the library.)
"Happy we could help. Good bye, officer." The librarian hangs up and the call gets redirected back to the station with a soft click...
"Anything else you need from me?"
"What was he wearing?"
"Uh, one second..." The librarian turns away from the phone again and relays the question.
"Sorry, Marie wasn't really paying any attention to that."
"Do you know the husband's name?"
"Sorry, no -- Marie only knows him by sight."
They're too poor to have a phone line.
"Maurice, what?!" a woman yells. Then: "Yes-yes, okay, if it was the police..." She starts explaining something.
Good. You have a name now.
And then goes for a little drink later, on the lookout...
"Marie..." A moment passes.

On Meroe drive in Central Jamrock -- in a darkened hall lit by orange desk lamps -- far away from the noise outside -- a middle-aged man taps commands into an old radiocomputer. A printout falls on the desk. Behind him, a lonely reader scours some dusty bookshelves, looking for a paperback...
That's where the smoker on the balcony lives, isn't it?
By the pier, north of here. Those big apartment buildings there.
"It will take just a moment, officer..."
Her voices fades out into the familiar radio static.
You hear a man clearing his throat briskly, then an answer: "Gottlieb. What'd ya want?"
"Gottlieb. What'd you get yourself into this time?" The question is followed by the sound of someone taking a long drag.
"How did you know it was me?"
"I've been shot..."
"I've been bad and I want someone to abuse me."
"Didn't. But now I do. How's the drinking going?"
"I decided to stop. Completely. Forever."
"I'm trying really, really hard not to."
"It's going great! I feel like it's really helping me with this case!"
"Great to hear it. Stop by some time when you're done with your case -- I'll draw some blood, run it through -- let you know how much 'forever' your liver's going to give you."
"Great. Have a medal. I have an autopsy to attend to. An autopsy of one Chester McLaine, who died of *fish poisoning*."
"Fucking... I'm not dead, it just hurts, okay?"
"Ah, it's you. Walking, talking, though?"
"Yes, but..."
"Great! How's the drinking going?"
"Oh, it's you. I know a woman skilled at that sort of thing over in Jamrock... but I wouldn't want to inflict you upon her. Best of luck, detective."
"I guess that's it for now." [Hang up.]
"Mhphm." The phone clicks. Suddenly you hear the already familiar voice...
"You know who I am?"

dialoguetext: "I think I've developed extreme photosensitivity..."
"I think I've had a heart attack..."
"Gottlieb. What is it now?" There's not the slightest hint of wanting to know the answer in that familiar raspy voice.
He's carelessly chewing on a piece of hard candy.
"I don't want to talk about this anymore."
"Great. I have an autopsy to attend to. An autopsy of one Chester McLaine, who died of *fish poisoning*."
"I was told to call the lazareth. People are worried about me..."
"I'm in a bad way, doc. A real *bad* way."
"Just a routine check-up."
"Oh," the man is unpleasantly surprised. "It's you."
Was that a snarl or a suppressed groan? No love for you here.
"Yes, there's no end to the misfortunes fate has seen fit to rain upon me."
"Good fortune, you mean good fortune, right? You're basking in the floodlight of my glory."
"Yes, we live in difficult times. But at least it's over. Almost over, that is..."
"I'm sorry I've been such a bother to you..."
"I don't know anything about fate. I just wanted to talk about a medical issue."
"Sure, sure -- but can you tell me about myself? As in, who I am?"
"*Who* you are? You lost your human visage a while back. Now let's get on with it -- I've got more important things to do."
"Then let's get on with it. Clock is ticking."
"Oh, spare me the sad drunken blubbering and get on with it. What's your complaint?"
"For you it probably is. I'm counting on my lungs outliving your liver by a wide margin." He pauses. "Not that that's anything to fête."
Was he speaking about his longer life or your shorter one when he said it was no cause for celebration?
"Basking in your glory, yeah. Practically drowning in it. Please, tell me what your complaint is before I am completely submerged."
A bit of both. But don't flatter yourself -- he's not sorry for you.
Don't flatter yourself -- he's not going to miss you.
"Great! Any other complaints?"
"I couldn't reach up and grab a tie from a spinning fan without unbearable pain shooting through my arm."
"I've lost my memory. All of it."
"Doc, someone broke my heart."
"Look, pal -- getting *pumped and dumped* is not a disease. People live through it all the time. You should be happy for her."
"Hard to tell exactly what it was over the phone. Could be a combination of peripheral neuralgia and high blood pressure. Could be that you were having a heart attack..."
"...or, actually!" He seems to be positively surprised by the idea. "It could be *both*, given your profile."
"Wait... both? But that sounds bad."
"Yup."
"So what do I do?"
"Cut down on the drinking, pal. In fact, cut *off* the drinking. The drugs too. Anything else?"
Oh, but speed, sweet speed... It goes so well with alcohol, too...
What's he going on about? You know that speed is great for you. But, shh, don't tell him -- he won't understand.
"I still *feel* pretty good though. I can probably take a lot of damage."
"Yes, positive thinking is a well-known cure-all. My suggestion is to exercise a lot."
Which reminds me -- when are we finally going to get that speed?
"That's because you're hungover -- even the radio waves coming from your direction smell like liquor." He pauses. "Do you feel like your eyes are twitching too?"
"Yes."
(Lie.) "No."
"That's the tiny vessels pulsating from high blood pressure, stupid officer. You might be sustaining permanent damage to your vision as we speak. Not much I can do about it. I'm not an *eye* doctor."
"But... what kind of doctor are you then?"
"The busy kind. It's not life-threatening, just annoying. For you. I've got more important things to do here."
"Good. It would be an awful nuisance if your experiments with your blood pressure were to cause permanent damage to your vision. A nuisance to you, that is."
"And you survived it! Congratulations. Are you mobile?"
"Even better! Anything else? I wouldn't worry about that. Officers your age have coronary trouble all the time. Also -- death is a natural part of life."
"With all the damage you've been dealing yourself with drugs and alcohol, I'm not surprised."
"What else? I'm not a *brain* doctor. Look on the bright side -- you've got a whole new life now. Use it wisely."
"Isn't there *anything* you can do for me?"
"What, you want me to do blood work for you again, tell you just how bad things really are *across the board*? You want another rundown of everything collapsing inside your body?"
"Yes. I want the truth!"
"No, that doesn't sound like something I can handle right now..."
"I see your point. Might as well just get back to work."
"Do that. I need to go. Some idiot has glued his eyelids shut with Cyanoacrylate. It *looks* like Mack Torson, but it's hard to say because his eyes are swollen..."

"And then that motherfucker Gottlieb -- reeking of schnapps -- ordered me into his butcher's room..." Officer Fischer is in a storytelling mood -- he continues: "And I ask him, 'You sure, doc?' and he's cool as can be, 'Yeah, if you're in pain, we've gotta get that baby out...'"

"...and so he removed my appendix *on the spot*, while the party was still on in the other room. And I was delirious with pain and all the schnapps I'd had, but I remember thinking -- man, that Gottlieb can stitch..."

"Only a month later, when I got a chance to properly thank him, did I find out that *he* had no recollection of the event -- that's Gottlieb for ya. In league with some devil, he is, I'm sure of it. Cheers!" The clinking of beer glasses is drowned in group conversation...
"Yes, it's Firewalker here."
"Firewalker? Yes, yes you are. Just don't breathe in the general direction of your fire-feet. Actually, wait..."
"...do exactly that. Put yourself out of your misery. Take a deep diaphragmatic breath in and..." You hear an exaggerated inhale and a long exhale on the other end of the line.
The firewalker cannot die.
Self-immolation has been all the rage in Lo Manthang for a while now, especially among university students. It is particularly popular in Co Hoi, where such acts get the most press.
But why?

Young religious people protesting the Seraise government, which they consider to be oppressive. It's also got something to do with the encroaching Occidental influences on the local way of life. You have to *not* like a lot of things to set yourself on fire.
A glorious sight: your body, tired from the vastness of the visions that haunt it,  burning up in a flame fed by your own living breath.
"This has been my plan all along. I want to protest the Coalition government."
"The smell of my own flesh cooking... I wonder what it would be like..."
"I feel like you're making fun of me."
"'Cop Sets Fire to Himself.' That would be quite an interesting conceptual piece, don't you think?"
"Sounds more like a newspaper headline that will surprise absolutely no one. Now, do you have any *current, pressing* medical problems?"
"From what I can tell, you're just playing into their hands -- disabling yourself from doing any actually useful work. Now, do you have any *current, pressing* medical problems?"
"Please wonder on your own time. Now, do you have any *current, pressing* medical problems?"
"I'm the most serious person at this station, detective. Now, do you have any *current, pressing* medical problems?"
It would be an artistic statement of some kind or another.
Young people are stupid.
I wish I was young and on fire.
They should be forced to serve in the military.
That's awful. I don't want to think about it anymore. [Ignore thought.]
Yes, especially young people in young countries. Anyway, answer the man.
You can still be. There's time. Anyway, answer the man.
Uhm... they already are. Anyway, answer the man.
"So you see it too? That my body is to become the last torch in the darkness?"
"I see third-degree burns and a referral to a plastic surgeon whom you won't be able to afford. But that's in the future. Do you have any *current, pressing* medical problems?"
"No wonder I'm in so much pain. I feel like I've been... damaged."
Ignorance is bliss, as they say. Go ahead, answer the man!
"Yes. Probably in more ways than one."
"You want the real, honest-to-god truth? Stop drinking, eat magnesium and vitamin D. Our station is not a retirement home. We don't have the funds to deal with *rock stars* past their prime."
"Anything else I can help you with, officer?"
"You're not surprised? Okay. Anything else?"
This is *not* about self-immolation in the Samarskilt AR.
Of course, yes. You were having health trouble.
He sounds very careless about it all. Positively breezy.
You're detecting very little in the way of empathy from Dr. Gottlieb.
Abstinence *could* have immediate positive effects on your health.
It certainly does not help with aiming...
Accept it. The body is an object and objects break down. Do what good you can with yours, before the rest goes too.
Sort of. But by god does it *burn* in your chest...
There is no surprise in his voice. Only careless superiority.
It's hard to say if he doesn't believe you -- or doesn't care.
"And no, I *don't* want to hear a *political commentary* on the topic. In fact -- I've got work to do. Some idiot has glued his eyelids shut with Cyanoacrylate. It looks like Mack Torson."
"It's not fucking cryo-actilate... it's super glue, doc."
Cyanoacrylate *is* super glue.
The money is probably going to some old, oily...
"Doc, someone broke my heart."
"Wait... pumped and dumped?"
"Do you know who this person was, have I told you..."
"That's what the guys say, officer. That some chick pumped you -- and then dumped you. Threw you away like an empty juice carton."
"You must have me confused for a close personal friend... I am not. I am a medical professional -- with a constant *idiot* emergency on my hands."
Don't take it personally. There just wasn't any *juice* left in your carton, pal.
You hear someone whine in the background. "My eye, doc... my eye..."
One needs tending to right now, he thinks, looking around the room. God, these apes...
So it's political! You're being *neglected* because of political reasons...
As you hold your ledger's clip under the headlamp, a shimmering iridescent pattern appears. One you've definitely seen before...

Look at the shimmering street grid.
Look at the perforations.
"Okay, let's go." [Put the ledger away.]
There are many of them. And they are divided into three separate rows.
Tally up the different rows.
The first row has 18 dots.

The next is the longest. It runs all the way around the border and then some.
There are so many it's hard to count. More than 150, at least. Maybe even 200.
What about the last row?
The last row has three perforations.
Three, that's it?
That's it.

"The first row represents your years of service. *Eighteen* years? Okay -- not bad at all. What did you do before you volunteered?"
"Got drunk like a megastar?"
"I walked the land telling whores and liars of the End to come. There are 9,855 days remaining."
"Do you really think I have any idea?"
"Yes, that *does* seem quite likely. Your youth coincided with some heady days for Revachol. But let's move on, shall we?"
"Fair point... Let's move on, shall we?"
"Cool. I'm glad you joined us. Not a lot of money in doomcrying... Let's move on, shall we?"
"I was a hobo and I lived under a boat."
"You know, the RCM is a volunteer's organization. We would have no qualms with vagrants joining our ranks were they qualified... but let's move on, shall we?"
"No shame in working a regular job, detective. Sometimes after a long day of doing *this*, I even envy it... Let's move on, shall we?"
"Probably a some boring office job. Same as everyone else."
"I feel like I just went around apologizing all the time."
"Maybe you were a diplomat? Or in PR? Doesn't matter, I suppose... Let's move on, shall we?"
"This next row -- the one that wraps all the way around -- is your number of closed cases. *Closed* is good. It means finished. You've got, let's see..."
"Wow, more than 200!"
"Two-hundred sixteen, to be exact."
"Is that a lot?"
"I would have thought there'd be more."
"It's *quite* a lot, even for someone who's been on the force for nearly two decades. Usually clearing more than 10 cases a year puts you in the 90th percentile of *all* RCM officers..."

The lieutenant nods with evident respect. "It's quite a lot, even for someone who's been on the force for nearly two decades. Usually clearing more than 10 cases a year puts you in the 90th percentile of *all* RCM officers..."
"So you're saying I used to be a *supercop*?"
"I used to be good. That's some solace I guess. What's the last number?"
"I don't think I can ever *re-become* this person... What's the last number?"
Doesn't that tingle in your index finger give it away?
"Right. Those are your confirmed kills. You've got precisely *three* perforations there."
"So I'm a killer..."
"I was expecting a higher number, honestly."
"That's not... too many."
"Is now a good time to pour one out for the fallen?"
"Definitely not."
"Call it what you want. You were a valuable member of your precinct. Now, let's look at the last row..."
"Have you ever killed anyone, Kim?"
"How do you handle the strain?"
"Thanks for this." (Conclude.)
The lieutenant nods.
"Everyone has their own method of coping, some more effective, or self-destructive, than others..." He gives you a meaningful look.
"Yes," he says, declining to elaborate.
(Let's look at something else.)
Right. The meaning of the perforations remains opaque to you.
As you look at them you feel your index finger reflexively contract three times.
Seems like something I've done before.
A memory, an echo in the recesses of your amygdala.
Must be a muscle spasm.
And something you'll do again, before this is all over.
You know the answer already. The tingle in your index finger gave it away.
"Those are my confirmed kills. Three of them."
"That's right," the lieutenant says, gauging your reaction. "How did you know?"
"Because I felt a twitch in my index finger."
"Because I feel like a killer."
"Just a lucky guess."
"Ah, right. Sometimes the brain's able to preserve certain responses even when conscious memory has been... let's say... *misplaced*..."
The rectangular watermark is overlaid with the logo of the RCM, and yet the major arteries of Revachol are all recognizable. They shimmer in the Kineema's headlights.
Wait... look around you.
"Where are we on this?" (Point to the halogen map.)
You catch a faint glimmer from a broken beer bottle. In the distance -- sounds. Two men engaged in a drunken argument, followed by the closing of some distant window.
In the middle of a broken plaza, illuminated in a cone of light, two men, one slim, the other sturdy. They are on the city stage, but only one of them knows his lines...
"Ah, Martinaise at night," he smells the air and says.
"Let me see." He takes the ledger for a moment and inspects it.
"Right here," he says, his finger near the top of the map, on a segment of coast jutting out into the great ocean.
Count them individually.
You count 216 perforations. Considering that nice, large number, a wave of pride washes over you, though you can't say why, precisely.
"For an RCM officer -- especially Precinct 41, which is in the Jamrock Quarter -- it's rather... tame. I mean that in a good way."
"What's it feel like to kill a man, Mr. McCoy?" a young woman asks the man across the desk from her...

"Honestly, babe," says John McCoy, crossing his ankles over said desk, "I don't feel anything anymore. It's just like brushing my teeth -- I do it once or twice a week and don't really think about it." There's no trace of guilt in his voice.

"There are certain officers who treat their kills like some kind of ghoulish game. If they do happen to *solve* a case it's usually by accident." It's obvious the lieutenant doesn't think very highly of these officers...
"But it seems as though you are, or at least *were*, one of the good ones. So we have that to be thankful for."
"Maybe I should pour one out for the boys? The fallen?"
The lieutenant sighs.
"If you want to pour out the booze you've been carrying around *on duty*, I'm certainly not going to stop you..."
"Actually, I'm just gonna hold onto this."
(Pour one out on the ground -- ceremonially.)
A dark pool of cheap wine appears at your feet. It shimmers in the lights of the Kineema.
Honourably done. You have given up some of your own blood -- for theirs.
"As you will..."
"The Gloaming comes for all, but it came first for you."
"I'm sorry for killing you."
"Here's to you, honoured dead."
"I will make it okay with the power of rock and roll."
"I'm not really sure what you're supposed to say at these things."
"Very noble of you. Are we done here?"
"Personally, I find it helps to keep up a few hobbies."
"Like what?"
"Oh, this and that. Let's not get into it now."
"Maybe I should find a hobby?"
"Hobbies are lame."
"Suit yourself..."
"Why not gardening? You've already got the yellow gloves..."
"Why not historical reenactment? You've already got that antique carabineer gear..."
"Why not take up a sport? You've already got that FALN gear..."
"Why not historical reenactment? You've already got that turn of the century revolutionary hat..."
"Anything's better than annihilating yourself with drugs and alcohol..."

dialoguetext: A dark pool of moonshine-spiked borscht appears at your feet. The chunks of beet shimmer in the lights of the Kineema.
A dark pool of pale-aged vodka appears at your feet. It shimmers in the lights of the Kineema.
A dark pool of cheap pilsner appears at your feet. It shimmers in the lights of the Kineema.
It seems as though you don't have anything to pour out. Too bad for the boys.
"Seems nice."
"Seems like a shithole."
"No -- it does *not*," the lieutenant says without optimism.
"It has its problems..."
A rat brazenly darts past you and disappears amongst the stopped lorries. In the distance -- a child somewhere shrieks, a woman reprimands her in a voice no quieter than the child's cry...
"Ah, Martinaise," he smells the air and says.
In the middle of a broken plaza, in a cone of light barely visible in the daytime, two men, one slim, the other sturdy. They are on the city stage, but only one of them knows his lines...
"I know you've killed some people in the line of duty..."
"Right. I'll go turn off the lights..." He presses a remote control on the key.
You can now see your statistics on your JOURNAL page -- to the right of the task description.
"I'm sure I've seen worse."
"Oh yes. Coal City, Le Royaume, the Burnt Out Quarter..."
All of them worse than here.
*Alpha male officers who are proud of their numbers* often do -- it's meant.
Son, here is where we score your life performance. You better hope it's good.
That's right. A killer of humans.
*Confirmed kills*? That sounds pretty evil. A *drink* would soften that feeling.
It's not a problem for him to state it, however.
It's meant in earnest. Please don't mistake it for a jab.
"Neither am I. Are we done here?"
"Wait, *eighteen years* I've done this?"
"That's what it says. I might've guessed even longer based on your age... what did you do all those blissful years of your youth?"
Not bad.
Not bad for what? You don't even know what it means yet.
He's sincerely glad you're not a scary predator. Not to say relieved you're competent.
"Let's start from the top."
"You humiliated me. I don't care what your political beliefs are, but you painted me with the same brush. Publicly."
"I have been defamed over *live radio*. That has never happened to me before. And it *never* will again."
"If you ever dare do anything like that again -- even close to it -- I will have you sanctioned. That was abhorrent."
This hurts. It should. Apologize and try to make it right.
"I fucked up. I'm sorry. Can I make it up to you?"
"I just said what was in my heart. I can't apologize for passion."
Say nothing.
"No, officer. Short of undoing it, there's nothing. Let's just finish this case."
"You don't surprise me anymore, officer." The lieutenant's gaze cuts through you. "Let's finish with this case. I want to be done with it, now."
"Let's finish this case." The lieutenant shakes his head. "I want to be done with it, now."
"There's no doubt the twins heard Speedfreaks FM," he says, still tempering his anger. "I still don't know how, without a radio -- but they did."
The road to healing is going to be a long one. Stay the course. You will make it, some day.
"There's no doubt the twins heard Speedfreaks FM. I still don't know how, without a radio -- but they did."
"Hold up, Kim. Aren't you going to say anything about meeting your radio heroes?"
"Spooky shit. But what does it... mean?" (Squint in thought.)
"We're not any closer to knowing *how* they heard it, though, are we?"
"Nope."
The final word on this matter has been spoken.
"I don't know what it means." The lieutenant's gaze travels toward the coast, toward the fishing village so far away.
"No... We're not." The lieutenant's gaze travels toward the coast, toward the fishing village so far away.
"I mean, a weird voice in *my* head said to talk to the kids. Maybe it's related?"
"Guess we're stuck then."
"I don't think the voices in your head are related to this, no."
The lieutenant turns his attention away from the coast, back to you.
"Not necessarily. We've learned something. No idea what. Something, at least."
"Did we ask where the kids were when they heard the voice?" The wind picks up, blowing a stray strand of the lieutenant's hair out of place. He smooths it back.
"But it didn't sound like one of my thoughts. Sounded like a lady."
"Probably not. Sorry, Kim."
The lieutenant gives you a long look.
Sincere worry, officer to officer. He feels you need help and regrets that he doesn't know how to offer it.
"I don't know what to say to that, or what you want me to say. I'm sorry."
"I didn't. Sorry."
"Are you criticizing me, Kim?"
"Nope."
"No need to apologize. I was just going to say it'd be a good idea to ask them."
He sighs. "No. I was just thinking that it'd be a good idea to ask them."
"We could ask where the kids were when it happened."
"And, detective..." He turns to you. He smiles. "Thanks for this. It's been interesting."
You see a set of tyre tracks in the brown slush that covers the plaza mosaic.
Not now. [Leave.]
The hole in this fence doesn't look *that* huge.
Reconstruct the movement.
No, these tracks are not interesting at all. Let the street sweeper just sweep them away.
The tracks are as they have ever been. A bit more worn, perhaps. Fortunately, the street sweeper still hasn't noticed their presence.
...and then accelerated straight into the fence.
I think I got it. [Leave.]
What kind of vehicle drove through here?
Hard to say.
The tyre tracks were left here by an unknown event that took place some days ago. It's a message, written in the language of burnt rubber.
Some of that rubber stuck to the tiles right in front of the Whirling-in-Rags. This is point A. The driver started there...
The driver proceeded to back out of the yard, barely stopping before hitting the adjacent building...
...before heading south. Must have been in a hurry.
This is significant somehow.
Maybe. Probably.
The hole is not that impressive.
"A car drove through the fence."
"You are correct. This is a rather motor carriage-friendly city."
An ominous warning of bad things ahead.
This is the point of departure of the motor carriage that crashed into the Samaran Butter sign, right?
Why yes it is! Good connection.
This is where I started off with my motor carriage.
What happened next?
Hard to say. Your vision is blurred and you are having difficulty concentrating thanks to your relentless hangover.
Okay. What happened next?
Yes. And ended up half-sunken in the sea. You must have been drunk when you left off.
Damn bartender.
He was exaggerating. People blame *cops* for everything that goes wrong in the world. This has nothing to do with you.
"This is where I started off with my motor carriage... before sinking it in the sea."
"Yes, it is. Well," he gestures toward the gaping hole in the fence, "you did provide us with a very convenient access point to the crime scene."
"This is the point of departure of the vehicle that crashed into the Samaran Butter sign."
"Well," he gestures toward the gaping hole in the fence, "you did provide us with a very convenient access point to the crime scene."
"No wonder the cafeteria manager seemed frustrated when he was giving us directions to the yard."
The lieutenant follows the tracks with his gaze. "That's plausible. A similar... reckless abandon seems to be in evidence."
Somehow that makes you feel... scared. You don't know why.
As a matter of fact, you don't even know why you stopped here. You would never drive recklessly like this. And you don't have a car.
"Is this connected to the case?"
"I'm not sure... there are plenty of traffic accidents waiting to happen in Martinaise. With the jam right here on the roundabout. I would keep them separate."
Why am I looking at this?
Cop habit. You look at everything.
This isn't case-related, you think.
You could *follow* the tracks south. There seems to be a canal there. See where they went. (If you find the time.)
She is appraising you scientifically, the way she would an exceptional zoological specimen. It's not *like that*.
"I've gotta get going now." [Leave.]
"You seem to be in a chair."
"Are you okay? I am very sorry I crashed into you earlier. I don't know what got into me."
"How'd you like to roll with me?"
"Sweetie needs money. Do sweeties get money?"
