dialoguetext: "I don't know if you've noticed, but I don't know where I am, or what I'm doing. Or *anything*."
"Oh sweetie." Her expression becomes very serious. "I heard your conversation with the manager about your... financial troubles. When do you get your next paycheck?"
You've got guns of steel and a chiselled jaw (somewhere under the bloated alcohol layer). Maybe she'd like to sponsor you?
"Yes, dear, I am a paraplegic."
"What did you do, then?"
A paraplegic is someone with limited or no ability to use the lower half of their body. Paraplegia is caused by spinal cord injuries -- like falling from a great height, or a grenade explosion!
"What is a paraplegic?"
"I'm sorry, it was rude of me to mention the wheelchair. Let's move on." (Proceed.)
"That's quite alright. I'm used to people asking questions. I know they're thinking about it anyway."
There is no bitterness in her voice. She accepted the curiosity her condition inspires a long time ago.
"No, dear, I'm not quite *that* old, although I was injured in the line of duty."
"It means I can't use my legs. I was in an accident some years back, injured *in the line of duty* as they say."
"Were you a... tightrope walker?"
"Were you a... mountaineer?"
"Nothing so glamorous, dear, though when I was young, I dreamt of planting the Revacholian flag on some figurative peak."
Her eyes light up. "Whatever do you mean?"
"Roll us some cigarettes. I'm jonesing for a smoke."
"Oh, I'm perfectly alright! I'm more worried about you. What was that?"
"The 'Whirling-in-Rags' cafeteria? It was on my keys."
"We're in Revachol."
"A war zone. At the edge of the world."
"I don't really know... some seedy hotel?"
"That's right, and where is the Whirling-in-Rags cafeteria itself located?"
"We're in the city of *Revachol*, dear." She flashes you a worried look.
"That's right! In a hostel called the Whirling-in-Rags, to be precise."
"It does still look like that in some parts of the city, doesn't it..."
"We are in a hostel called the Whirling-in-Rags, dear. And the Whirling itself is in the city of Revachol."
"A seaside hostel called the Whirling-in-Rags, to be precise. And the Whirling itself is in Revachol."
"Speaking of history -- you know what *year* it is, yes?"
That tape you picked up said '43. You seem to be a hip modern man who listens to hip modern records, so it must be '43.
"It's totally '43."
"It's the spring of '51."
"All I know is: we are approaching the *end times*."
"I can tell that this is taxing for you, so I'll just ask *one* more question. What regime are we living under? What mode of government?"
"I'd *like* to think it's the dictatorship of the proletariat, but something tells me it's not."
"Could I become a paraplegic?"
"Nothing so extravagant, dear, though what young girl doesn't dream of soaring over a crowd?"
"I was a training and development manager at a rapidly expanding mail-order shoe company."
"You'd think it would be a safe job. But I had to be everywhere -- and, well, once I happened to be under some faulty scaffolding."
"I was lucky. This was almost twenty years ago, and I was compensated exceptionally well. One can only dream of such pay-offs nowadays." She runs her hands over the chrome wheels of her chair.
"I hope not, although the work you are doing for all of us *is* quite dangerous." Her eyes glimmer with admiration as she looks up at you.
Towering over her in your insignia, you make her feel safe.
(Nod grimly.) "Someone *has* to do it."
"But not you. You're volunteering. So thank you, sweetie."
"Maybe it wouldn't be so bad, hanging out in a chair, playing pinball..."
"Actually, this machine is broken." She taps on the greasy glass of the pinball machine.
"I'm not sure I should be in this line of work."
"You're a man at the peak of your physical and intellectual powers. You will find another calling yet, I'm certain of it!"
"Thanks for clearing that up for me. Let's move on." (Proceed.)
"Sequence killers, oh my..." She sounds impressed. "But I think you already have a partner, sweetie."
"I want you to be my wheel-chaired partner in fighting crime, helping people, catching *sequence killers*."
"A partner who needs you to get back to helping the people of Martinaise."
Her face flushes with excitement, but she instantly recomposes herself. "I wouldn't be of much use to you, sweetie."
"Thank you, but..." She looks out the window wistfully. "Martinaise isn't the most wheelchair-accessible place, you see. I'd slow you down."
"Why? Three heads are better than two."
"You're probably right."
"I really would like to help out, but I don't want to slow you down. If it weren't for all the stairs and potholes in Martinaise, I'd join you for sure!" She looks out the window wistfully.
"I know, I know. But there are also *side mysteries*. Sequence killers and forays into the para-natural."
"You're no fun, Lieutenant Killjoy."
"Now, gentlemen, no need to squabble." She turns to you. "I wouldn't be of much use to you anyway, sweetie."
"Oh, no-no-no, I haven't smoked in years..."
"Does that mean you don't have tobacco? Or rolling paper? Or any cigarettes at all?"
"Why don't you smoke? It's great!"
"Good for you. Smoking is a stupid habit. Maybe I should quit too."
She shakes her head slowly.
Wait! Maybe she knows where you can get cigarettes. Delicious toasty cigarettes stuffed to the tip with *love*. You should find out.
She looks embarrassed. "Cigarettes are a luxury, sweetie. Besides, I have to mind my health."
What are you talking about? Smoking is one of the last remaining pleasures in this world. Trust me, there's not much out there for you.
"Can you tell me where to get cigarettes?"
"I thought you were cool, with your wheels and all."
"It's probably for the best. I don't really need a cigarette right this minute."
You would do well to follow her example. Smoking is the reason you feel like a rag. It's painful for you to even ask these questions.
"An old woman in a wheelchair just doesn't look good holding a cigarette. Though I'm sure it lends *you* a roguish charm, sweetie."
"I'm glad to hear you say it! Smoking can do some real damage to your respiratory system. But I think you already knew that."
"You should really ask someone younger and more mobile, sweetie."
"Yes, officer, you look rather dazed... like a stunned fox. But surely things can't be *that* bad?" Her eyes follow your movements with some concern.
"I was hoping you could be my *sponsor*."
"What is a pay check? I haven't seen any pay checks..."
"It isn't easy for me to ask this of anyone, but I am at the end of my rope. Any money you have could help me."
"You must be joking." He pauses, reflecting. "Although our pay does sometimes feel like a joke."
"Officer." He leans in so that only you can hear, but his tone is forceful. "Get a hold of yourself, please."
"Sweetie, I only have a few cents on me. But... I could give you this to pawn, just to tide you over." She unfastens a gold commemorative pin from her left jacket pocket and drops it into your palm.
If she could, this woman would feed and clothe you and every other sad, lost person on this earth.
"Right. Let's change the subject."
"It's a bad year in my late forties, or fifties? I don't even know how *old* I am."
"Oh no, dear! It's the early spring of '51."
"Perhaps, dear, perhaps. But for now it's just the spring of '51."
"There, there. The year is '51, and spring has only just started. I'm sure there are better days ahead."

Outside, the melting snow seeps into the cracks in the walls and the cobblestone streets. All the way down into the sewers... Above ground, the first May bells blossom. You can feel it. A great cold. Then the shiver passes.
"We're dead. Haunting each other. We're ghosts."
"Now, now." She tilts her head as she looks up at you with maternal solicitude.
"The edge of civilization."
"On something called *the urban coast*."
"In... Revachol?"
"In hell. We're all in hell."
"We are alive -- in a hostel called the Whirling-in-Rags. And the Whirling itself is in the city of Revachol."
"Honestly, I don't know diddly-squat about Revachol. What kind of place is this?"
"All I know is that Revachol used to be really cool in the Thirties."
"Yes, we're in Martinaise, on the coast of Revachol."
"Yes, indeed. We are in the fine city of Revachol."
"I know it's the '50s, but I'm not sure about the year."
The New was in the Thirties, and two decades have elapsed since The New, so it must be the Fifties now.
"Good, dear, you got the decade right! It's the spring of '51."
"I can assure you, with absolute certainty: there are no sequence killings taking place in Martinaise."
He scans your face as though searching for clues. "I did not know murder investigations are supposed to be *fun*."
"The New! Disco dancing! It seems like a lifetime ago..." Her eyes are filled with light reflected off those gilded years, when the city seemed full of possibility.
"How would I even begin to tell you?" Her grey eyes widen. "Revachol is the most beautiful city in the world. We're fortunate to be here, you and I."

"I haven't seen very many other cities personally, but everyone says so. Revachol is a rare jewel. This city used to rule the world... Though it has seen better days." There's a pause as she studies your expression. You must look quite lost.

"Much has changed, but it is still the most beautiful city in the world, a rare jewel set in the sand between the pines. Everyone says so, even foreigners." There's a pause as she studies your expression. You must look quite lost.
"I believe Revachol is being managed by something called... the Coalition?"
"Precisely, sweetie! Revachol is what's called a Zone of Control, led by an alliance of foreign powers. We have almost no government of our own, sadly..."
"Oh sweetie..." she smiles a sad smile. "It's really not. There used to be people who thought that way -- other people, who wanted those things -- but... they all went extinct."
"I feel like *I* was in a war..."
"Oh my! What happened?"
"I think I lost."
"I think I won."
"That's how I feel about the accident..." She looks down and then up at you again. "I was a training and development manager at a rapidly expanding mail-order shoe company."
"Were you a... rugby player?"
"You're probably right, Kim."
"Kim -- of course! I forgot I had *you*!"
"Yes, and it seems to me that you'd do well to stick close to him. He has the look of an upstanding officer of the law, someone you can lean on -- and, sweetie, you *are* looking unsteady."
"Yeah, what *was* that?"
"That cafeteria manager is a bad man, a man without honour or compassion."
"I drank so hard I forgot *literally* everything."
She leans back in her chair, alarmed by your answer.
She is perturbed by your not knowing what year it is -- but not by your mention of the apocalypse. It *must* be the end times.
She looks flustered, her hands smoothing out the creases in her blanket even as she attempts to reassure you.
Though she praises you, it is clear that she was taken aback by your response.
Her relief is palpable. She was getting pretty worried about you there, but now she relaxes her shoulders...
The lieutenant tries to pretend he's not hearing it and is out of the conversation.
The lieutenant studies you, rubbing his chin.
I'm beginning to suspect that you might indeed be completely adrift in this reality, thinks the lieutenant. How can it be *that* bad? Never mind -- we're in this now.
"We are governed by intelligent machines that perform calculations to determine the *freest* market. Everyone hustles and grinds like a bad ass visionary."

"Oh... no, nothing like that, dear. Revachol is a Zone of Control, led by an alliance of foreign powers called the Coalition. We have almost no government of our own. And certainly not one who's horseback."
"Our leaders are fierce warriors who traverse the plains on steeds. Civilization cowers before us."
"I hope you're right. I hope it's not too bad..."
"Yeah, I'm blowing this whole thing out of proportion. Forget I said anything."
She nods, but still looks worried.
"You know where we *are*, right?"
"On second thought, things *are* bad. I don't even know enough to know what I *don't* know about this world."
"Oh, no, far from it. Although..." Her eyes glimmer mischievously. "I did come out to watch the boys play when I was in school. All those tan calves..."
She blushes, surprised by her own boldness.
"It seems to me that you lucked out with your partner. He has the look of an upstanding officer of the law, someone you can lean on -- and, sweetie, you *are* looking unsteady."
"Quitting smoking is one of the best things you can do for your health, officer."
You would do well to follow her example. Smoking is the reason you feel like a rag. It's painful for you to even ask these questions.
"But I'm not going to quit *today*."
"But I have to smoke. It's part of my cool guy persona."
"You are my witness: I pledge to never pick up another cigarette as long as I live!" (Try to stop smoking.)
She sighs. "I know it's not easy, sweetie. But keep thinking about it."
She sighs. "I'm sure it lends you a roguish charm, sweetie."
She smiles, obviously pleased. "I support your decision, officer."
She won't judge you, no matter what you say.
Wait, who's *sweetie*?
Her eyes move up and down your person as though taking your measurements. Her attention is *scientific*.
"You shouldn't keep your colleague waiting." She nods toward the man in the orange bomber jacket.
"Hello, sweetie."
"Hello again, sweetie." Her grey eyes shine above the rims of her glasses.
"Radios are being used to control people's minds and distort our perception of reality, concealing our true masters: foreigners and *women*."
"From where I was standing, it looked like you were about to pull out two guns, but drew two... akhem... birdies instead. Well, I'm glad you're weren't injured."
"He's just on edge because of the lynching. Don't judge him too harshly. Anyway, I'm glad you weren't injured."
"It was like my body had a will of its own. I was running, my torso turned, my hands made this lewd gesture... I'm sorry you had to witness it."
"Don't beat yourself up over it too much, dear. People do strange things when the old fight-or-flight kicks in. I'm just glad you weren't injured."
"It's not easy to assert your right to a decent living wage when you don't have a strong union behind you... Maybe you should talk to Evrart, the Union leader?"
"No problem." She nods, smiling up at you from behind her glasses.
Tug on her heartstrings.
Your deportment remains dignified -- as you shed a single, manly tear.
Try to force a tear out of your duct. Really *rip* into the whole emotional aggression thing.
"Oh god, I'm going to die on the street aren't I?"
"Sweetie, I'm sorry, but I think you need more help than I can give you." She looks distressed and even a little frightened.
"Hmm, a grenade? Did you fight in a war?"
"And even if he weren't there, I don't think you'd have much use for *me*." She looks down.
"But you're the most mobile person of them all!"
She chuckles. "I'm glad you think so, but I still don't know where you can get cigarettes."
"That's right, dear! How splendid! Here, take this pen. Knowledge should always be rewarded."
"What do you mean?"
"He was tormenting me with outrageous demands for *money*."
"Hello, sweetie." The elderly woman turns to you with a smile.
"Hello again, sweetie. I see you've met up with your colleague." She looks at the lieutenant.

The pin is round and slightly tarnished. Three sailboats in bas-relief with the sun hovering over the water behind them. A chipped green banner at the bottom reads "Saint-Batiste Summer '31 -- Dinghy Races."
"Where can I pawn the pin?"
"I promise I'll buy it back for you once I have more money." (Conclude.)
"What is 'to pawn'?"

"It's easy. You bring a valuable item to a 'pawnbroker' who then gives you money for it. You can get it back later for a slightly larger sum if it hasn't been sold, but you never end up doing that anyway..."
"This will help me out, Lena. Thanks." (Conclude.)
"Oh, it's not an ancient family heirloom or anything, but... I suppose it *would* be nice to get it back."

"Cross the plaza and follow the road along the coast. Down by the water, there will be a shack nestled against an old stone façade. That's the pawnshop. An old friend of my husband's goes there often. He says the owner is quite helpful."

The Saint-Batiste Dinghy Races were conceived as a biennial civic pride celebration (and cash cow), but only took place twice, in '31 and '33. The '31 races are the subject of fond reminiscence: Those who were there will tell you of sun-drenched bleachers, pink bubbly, and bronze-legged studs in white shorts.
"You're quite welcome, dear." She smiles up at you.
"Of course, dear! I just wish I could have done more."
"I decided not to pawn it. You should have it back."

dialoguetext: "I just wanted to thank you again."
"Aw, thank you, dear. I confess -- I am glad to see it again. Very honourable of you, officer."

"So, about your husband... Does he often go missing?"
"Hello again, ma'am. So why did you need to make that call?"
"Is everything alright, ma'am?"
"You see, Morell, my husband, and Gary were supposed to get back Monday night, but they're still missing and I haven't heard from them..."
"Truly -- a lot of legwork. My partner *adores* these kinds of things..." The lieutenant is still catching his breath.
"You see, Morell, my husband, and Gary were supposed to get back Monday night, but they're still missing and I haven't heard from them..."
No mystery here -- this is Klaasje's handiwork. She cut the line.
It must have been the Whirling landline that Klaasje "nicked."
Why would he be *vague* about phone problems? This is something to look into later -- ask Garte maybe.
"What does your husband look like?"
"Oh! Well, he's a bit shorter than you but with a larger frame. And he has longish white hair -- usually a bit uncombed, you might say *wild* even..."
It's always a challenge to describe the person you know best in the world.
"One other thing -- he'll likely have all kinds of *field gear* on him, even if he's not out in the reeds. You know, just in case."
"You never told me you've *seen* the phasmid!"
It must have been the Whirling landline that Klaasje "nicked."
Why would he be vague? This is something to look into later. Ask Garte maybe.
No mystery here -- this is Klaasje's handiwork.
"Word around the canal is some weird new cryptid destroyed it."
"Probably just some technical problem."
"Oh, now you're just having fun at an old woman's expense! In any case, thank you for looking into this. It takes a weight off my shoulders."
"Well, whatever the cause, I'm thankful. You've spared me another sleepless night."
"Listen, sweetie. I hate to ask, but if your investigation happens to take you to the other side of the coast, please do keep an eye out for my husband..."
The water lock! That was broken. Could this be it?
"Oh, thank you sweetie, truly. I'll be right here if you come across any sign of Morell."
"The water lock to the other side of the coast is broken. They're probably just stuck over there." (Proceed.)
"Tell me more about this *rare insect* your husband is looking for."
"Oh, sweetie, it's *fascinating*..." She catches herself. "But I shouldn't bore you with entomological minutiae."
"No, I want to hear about the insect."
"You're right. I don't have time for insect facts right now. Let's talk about something else."
The lieutenant gives you a sideways glance.
"Of course, dear."
She was about to launch into an impassioned description, but stoppered herself. Why's that?
"Well," she hesitates. "It's a *phasmid* technically, but..."
Ah, yes, *phasmatodea* -- a diverse group of insects whose bodies resemble twigs, leaves, that sort of thing. "Ghost insects," colloquially.
"... where other phasmids imitate sticks or leaves, this one's a living *reed*. It disguises itself among the reeds here on the Insulindian coast."
"Hence its name: The *Insulindian phasmid* -- perhaps you'll end up co-discovering it with us, officer?" She looks you in the eye and nods thoughtfully.
"I knew it. "The lieutenant sighs. "We're gonna be chasing made-up insects with *cryptozoologists*."
There's a touch of *awe* in the way she enunciates the creature's name.
"It's not made-up, officer, I can *assure* you."
There's a hint of defensiveness to her retort, but also confidence. She seems to sit up a little straighter in her chair.
"It's simply *elusive*, so much so that most *establishment* zoologists doubt it exists at all."
"So... is it dangerous?"
"Is it valuable?"
"Does it have cool powers?"
"Okay. What's so *special* about this stick-bug then?" (Move on.)
"Yes! It can blend in almost *perfectly* among the reeds." Her face lights up at the thought of it. "It's how it's stayed hidden all these years. Centuries even."
"Oh, I doubt it. No one gets into cryptozoology for the *money*, sweetie."
She chuckles to herself. "Not at all. Why else would it hide itself so carefully?"
"Oh dear, I'm afraid I'm not explaining this very well. It *is* very special..." The woman's face flushes with embarrassment.
"Morell can explain it all much better. I wish you could hear him describe it. Then you'd understand, I'm sure."
She's skipping over some important parts... perhaps you'll find out more later.
"And if you see him, let him know Lena is waiting for him here at the Whirling. He gets so tangled up in his work that he may not know the water lock's been repaired. And it's *cold* out there..."
"Hmmm. Well, his expression is slightly grumpy, but his eyes are always bright and curious, like a small boy's. And his palms are quite coarse from all the field work, but he's quite gentle..."
You can't go around Revachol feeling grown men's hands. If you want to find her husband, you'll need more *concrete* information.
"Let's try again. If I were trying to meet him on the street, what would I look for?"
The lieutenant pulls out his notebook and begins jotting down the woman's description.
"That's good enough. Let me ask you something else."
The woman's face flushes with embarrassment. "I'm sorry, sweetie. I'm afraid I'm not very good at this sort of thing."
"Of course, most phasmid sightings turn out to be *false alarms*, but their description matched the Insulindian phasmid *perfectly*, and they didn't even know what they were looking at!"
"I suppose I have something of a *personal* connection to the Insulindian phasmid... All scientists have their little hobby-horses."
She laughs. "I doubt it. It's not like teenagers need much encouragement in *that* regard."

"Well, some teenagers making out in the reeds saw one. They didn't know what it was, of course, but there was a brief article in a local newspaper. About their encounter with a *ghost insect* that looks like the reeds. Gary sent us the clipping."
"What makes you think the phasmid is around here?"
"So a newspaper clipping is all the evidence you have?"
"You seem really excited about this cryptid."
Interesting. Maybe the phasmid *made* the teenagers make out?
Enthusiasm has wiped the worry from her face. Her eyes sparkle behind her glasses.
"Maybe the phasmid *made* them make out?"
"Yes." She smiles a cautious smile. "Field work is a young person's game, as they say..."
The lieutenant stares at his shoe, caked in mud. He doesn't say anything.
You've come so far. You can't leave those locusts there, waiting on the ghost reed with no one to witness when it appears...
"Oh... you don't want to hear about some old woman's ramblings..."
"'Ramblings'? Nonsense! Your description of the phasmid is the most precise I've ever heard!"
"But darling, I didn't even get the *size* of it right."
"You were a *child*, my dear. Really, it's extraordinary what you were able to describe. Now go on, tell our friend about it. He's proven his interest in the field."
Reflexively, the lieutenant readies his familiar notebook.
"Well, it was summer," she starts. "I was building a racing track out of sand on the beach near a tall stand of reeds. Quite a tall one, many times my height, I remember. When all of a sudden..."
"You must be mistaken. I'm a connoisseur of delusional ramblings."
"Let's change the subject for now."
"That's kind of you, but I've got to demur. It's hard to tell a story you don't really believe in anymore..."
"I ran back home to my grandmother and asked her if *reeds* could *walk* and told her they were looking at me." She chuckles. "Of course, she just laughed at me, but I knew what I'd seen..."

"For years it was a story I told at parties, when I wanted to impress *boys*, that sort of thing." She brushes her hair back. "Of course, most people just took it as a strange, amusing anecdote. So did I, honestly. But then I met Morell..."

"That's true, yes. I'm almost certain neither my mother nor my grandmother knew of it. It was only when I started telling my story as a teenager that boys would tell me: Lena..." She lowers her voice, imitating a boy.
The glance is tender, yes, but tempered by something else, a thought she can't express even to him... Interesting.
"Are you saying you *made it up*?"
"The story is real to you and him. That's what matters."
"So you haven't seen it? I should arrest you for lying."
"No! At least... I don't think I did. But Morell was so eager to believe my story was *evidence* of the phasmid's existence..."
"No, sweetie," she shakes her head, "there's more to it than that. Morell was so eager to believe my story was *evidence* of the phasmid's existence..."
"Oh, sweetie, I wish it were that simple. But it's not. Morell was so eager to believe my story was *evidence* of the phasmid's existence..."
"That I'm some Queen of the Cryptozoologists... That... And for years his belief made *me* believe too."

"But now we're both getting old, and he's still working himself sick out in those reeds, looking for it..." She shakes her head, still unable to meet your eyes. "But what if I was just *wrong*? I think I was..."
The lieutenant opens his notebook but doesn't write anything.
First, tell her that her marriage hasn't been a lie.
An acorn is not the same as the tree. That requires time, diligence, and care...
But it *has*, hasn't it? A seed can only bear what's inside it. The seed of love is black and oily.
"Wrong or not, your relationship with Morell isn't just about the phasmid."
"But it *is*. We've spent years searching for the phasmid, hunting it together. Without it, what are we? Just another pathetic old couple..."
"Morell hated lecturing. You convinced him to do something real in this world."
"Normally when I think about stuff like *women* and *marriage*, I feel *bad*. When I think about you and Morell I feel okay. That counts for something, no?"
"If I hadn't led him down this path he could have a steady job lecturing at a university."

dialoguetext: It has a taste *you're* quite familiar with.
"Lying has gotten you this far, why stop now?"
"You know, the Perikarnassians theorized that *love* was the key to immortality..."
"Oh, sweetie. I don't think the Perikarnassians were thinking of people in *my* situation." She looks down at her legs...
"But if the dream comes to naught, what good is it? No, the thing is..." She looks down at her legs...
"Oh, of course it counts for something. But we've had our hard times too..." She looks down at her legs...
"I broke it. Drove my motor carriage into a billboard above the lock, blocking the gates."
"Oh, sweetie... Well, I'm glad you survived that. And I'm grateful for the information -- it will spare me another sleepless night."
"Just a moment, officer..." She smiles up at you nervously. "If you run into my husband again... do tell him I'm worried, and to hurry back."
"Sure thing, ma'am." (Accept the task)
"I'm sorry, I don't want to get involved in your affairs." (Refuse the task)
"Oh, thank you so much sweetie. Good luck with your investigation now."
"Of course, sweetie. Good luck with your investigation."
"My apologies, ma'am. I did not mean to undermine your hobby."
"It's not a hobby, dear. It's a *sub-field* of zoology, one specializing in animal species that are so exceedingly rare that many assume them to be *extinct* or even *fictitious*..."
"It's just police-work."
"Yes, but a junior officer could..." He takes off his glasses and thinks. Then puts them back on without wiping.
"Fine, our victim's already been dead more than a week. One more diversion won't change anything."
Oh yeah. Here comes the *interesting*.
There's a touch of *awe* in the way she enunciated the creature's name.
That's not special at all. Of course it blends in, most insects do. You don't even have to be a stick insect for that...
"I'm basically also a cryptozoologist now."
The little silvery knob holding the tie together feels warm in your hand. It's in the shape of an avian skull. With *eight* eyes.
You could ask her about this, when you get the time -- it's probably a cryptid. But the phasmid, of course, is more important...

"Well, in that case sweetie, let me give you a small token of my gratitude." She hands you a ribbon-tie held together by a silver bird skull. "It's a tie, Mesque in origin. The pin is an antique... quite special to the cryptozoological community."
Measuring things is important. How did she get the size?
That is a way, *way* bigger compliment than it sounds like.
"Wait. Where was this and how old were you?"
"Ah, I'm getting ahead of myself. I was five and a half. In Betancourt, in the suburbs. My grandmother had a summer home there."
"What happened?"

"The strangest moment of my life: I looked up and one of the reeds *moved*. Not like a plant, but like a living thing -- it stood up and looked at me. Its body unfolded like some antique toy... I've never seen anything like it."
She'd just started forming memories. Real memories, not the billowy haze of infanthood.
Betancourt got bombed in the war. It used to be quite near. Circa 20 kilometres from here.
She had no fear. Just surprise.

"I looked up and one of the reeds moved. Not like a plant, but like a living thing. It stood up and looked at me. Its body unfolded, like some antique toy..." She shakes her head. "I'd never seen anything like it. The reeds turned into a creature."

"I didn't know this can happen, so I reached my arm and touched the thing. It felt just like a stalk of reed, but it moved. Swaying, towering above me..." She looks at you. "After a while -- 20 seconds? a minute, maybe? -- it left. Went into the reeds."
"Did you follow it?"
"I tried, but I was only a child. There was mud and high water, I couldn't see it anymore. I was just standing there, knee deep in mud, looking around me..."
Where did you go? Don't go...
"Then what?"
"We were on a date, can you imagine? She tells me a story and it's the most detailed report of the Insulindian phasmid I've ever heard. The sounds -- she told me it hissed..."
"It did, yes -- like reeds in a gust of wind."
"...the way it moved, the colour, how some of its limbs were white like marble..." He breathes excitedly. "It matched *perfectly* with what I know from other accounts! It was amazing."

"If it weren't for Lena, I might've given up hope years ago. It's no exaggeration to say that she restored my faith in my profession." He looks at her with admiration, forgetting a wide smile on his face.
"Its limbs are white?"
"Maybe you imagined it, Lena?"
"Kim, what do you think of this?"
"Thank you for sharing this with me." (Conclude.)
"Not all of them." He answers for her. "There is some white colouration reported, along with beige, where the camouflage ends."
"How could she? Who imagines this? She didn't *know* about the phasmid. This is the main thing here, what makes it a confirmed sighting -- she had no previous knowledge of the insect."
"You were on a date?"
"Our first, yes." The old woman looks at her husband tenderly...

"'You tryna' tell us you saw the Insulindian phasmid out there in those reeds? Get outta here!'" She smiles. "They'd just give me a cider and ruffle my hair and tell me to stop dreaming -- but I saw it."
"I thought it was a wonderful story, ma'am." He closes his notes and gives her a simple smile.
But I don't believe it. A child, left unattended, on a warm day. Children make up stories and then end up believing them.
"You're welcome, sweetie. I do appreciate the chance to relive it, whenever I get one. It was just..." she sighs. "Such an impossibly sunshiny day. So warm."
And she could get up and walk -- right into the reeds on her own. Into the mud. Anywhere.
"How big was it?"
"It's hard to say how big things are when you're quite *small* yourself. To me, it seemed to be taller than I was then... but that's probably not the case."
What if it *is* the case?
"He gives up and *I'm* running around?"
"I'm sorry, dear. It was me -- I made him go home. He gets *so* stubborn about these things -- luckily his cough kept him from arguing with me."
"I'm sorry, dear -- you've had to drudge through them so many times. Such is field work -- a young person's game as they say."
Be real -- Gary is not going to help with this.
"Once more onto the breach, then!" (Take it on with undue optimism.)
Fuck that cough. It's not happening. The insides of your lungs are lined with *tobacco*, a powerful antibacterial agent. You are unstoppable.

"Officer... I hate to ask, but perhaps you could check those traps one more time? Only if you're in the area... In truth, I know Gary won't be up to it, and I'm concerned about my husband's health..."
"Alright, when you put it that way -- I'll help." (Accept task.)
"Sorry, I have too many other things on my plate. Wish you the best of luck." (Reject task.)
"Oh, thank you so much. And don't catch a cold out there!" She smiles up at you brightly.
"I understand. Best of luck with your work as well." She smiles up at you, doing her best not to look disappointed.
She frowns, looking you over. "Surely things can't be *that* bad?"
"We're in the Whirling-in-Rags cafeteria."
"We're in Revachol."
"A war zone. At the edge of the world."
"I don't really know... some seedy hotel?"
"That's right, and where is the Whirling itself located?"
"We're in the city of *Revachol*, dear." She flashes you a worried look.
"That's right! In a hostel called the Whirling-in-Rags, to be precise."
"But -- maybe a *fresh set of eyes* is what the world needs? And -- while I'm no doctor -- such bouts of amnesia are often temporary. So I wouldn't worry *too* much."
"It does still look like that in some parts of the city, doesn't it..."
I'm just a poor woman, she thinks. What do I know of these things. And how can I help you?
"We are in a hostel called the Whirling-in-Rags, dear. And the Whirling itself is in the city of Revachol."
"A seaside hostel called the Whirling-in-Rags, to be precise. And the Whirling itself is in Revachol."
"Speaking of history -- you know what *year* it is, yes?"
"If there's no government, how come there are cops?"
That tape you picked up said '43. You seem to be a hip modern man who listens to hip modern records, so it must be '43.
"It's totally '43."
"It's the spring of '51."
"All I know is: we are approaching the *end times*."
"I can tell that this is taxing for you, so I'll just ask *one* more question. What regime are we living under? What mode of government?"
"I'd *like* to think it's the dictatorship of the proletariat, but something tells me it's not."
"You're joking. Try again, one more time. What year is it?"
She means this sincerely. Worrying won't do you any good.
"It's a bad year in my late forties, or fifties? I don't even know how *old* I am."
"Oh no, dear! It's the early spring of '51."
"Perhaps, dear, perhaps. But for now it's just the spring of '51."
"There, there. The year is '51, and spring has only just started. I'm sure there are better days ahead."
Outside, spring rain seeps into the cracks in the walls and the cobblestone streets, and into grated storm drains. All the way down into the sewers... Above ground, the first May bells blossom.
"We're dead. Haunting each other. We're ghosts."
"Now, now." She tilts her head as she looks up at you with maternal solicitude.
"Sure. It's the year 973."
"The edge of civilization."
"Yes -- and Revachol...?" She examines you.
"On something called *the urban coast*."
"Mhm, okay."
"In... Revachol?"
"Cop. We are living under the cop-regime."
"In hell. We're all in hell."
"I don't even know what to say. I'm so disappointed."
"We are alive -- in a hostel called the Whirling-in-Rags. And the Whirling itself is in the city of Revachol."
"Some kind of democracy maybe?"
"Honestly, I don't really know anything about Revachol."
"All I know is that Revachol used to be really cool in the Thirties."
"Yes, we're in Martinaise, on the coast of Revachol."
"Someone more educated in these things than me? Someone rich, maybe? Wealthy people are educated. Though I don't know where you would find a wealthy person in Martinaise..."
"Yes, indeed. We are in the fine city of Revachol."
"I know it's the '50s, but I'm not sure about the year."
The New was in the Thirties, and two decades have elapsed since The New, so it must be the Fifties now.
"Good, dear, you got the decade right! It's the spring of '51."
"The New! Disco dancing! It seems like a lifetime ago..." Her eyes are filled with light reflected off those gilded years, when the city seemed full of possibility.
"Of course." She turns to you. "Then I don't know. Someone rich maybe? Wealthy people are educated. Though I don't know where you would find a wealthy person in Martinaise..."
Her grey eyes widen. "Oh my. How would I even begin to tell you? Revachol is the most beautiful city in the world. We're fortunate to be here, you and I."
"Actually..." She raises her finger. "We are *not*. You could say that about almost any other nation, but not Revachol. Try *one* more time, officer -- what mode of government?"

"I haven't seen very many other cities personally, but everyone says so. Revachol is a rare jewel. This city used to rule the world... Though it has seen better days." There's a pause as she studies your expression. You must look quite lost.
"Yes, great, see -- we're getting somewhere. What else do you know about our city of splendour? Tattered as she may be..."

"Much has changed, but it is still the most beautiful city in the world, a rare jewel set in the sand between the pines. Everyone says so, even foreigners." There's a pause as she studies your expression. You must look quite lost.
"I believe Revachol is being managed by something called... the Coalition?"
She's trying to avoid the foreigners part. This is because she's a woman. She may be *lying* to you...
"Precisely, sweetie! Revachol is what's called a Zone of Control, led by an alliance of foreign powers. We have almost no government of our own, sadly..."
"Oh sweetie..." she smiles a sad smile. "It's really not. There used to be people who thought that way -- other people, who wanted those things -- but... they all went extinct."
"No." He looks away. "I'm not an encyclopedia. I won't be a guide either. I'm a police officer."
"Things aren't *bad*. They're catastrophic."
"Someone more educated in *sweeping* matters? Maybe you should ask..." She turns to the lieutenant.
"Revachol is the disgraced capital of the world. Something like that?"
"It has something to do with everything. I really don't know how to explain it better..."
"What does that have to do with there not being any cops?"

"A defeat, I'm afraid. The people of this archipelago tried to build something new, something *different*. The rest of the world didn't like it, so they came and ended it. This was forty two years ago."

"Nope. Sadly not. Revachol is what's called a Zone of Control. Under an alliance of foreign powers called the Coalition. We have no government of our own and what democracy we have is..." She thinks. "Market driven."
Oh no. We've arrived at some sort of *weak* world, where everyone's a nansy pansy...
She leans back in her chair, alarmed by your answer.
She is perturbed by your not knowing what year it is -- but not by your mention of the apocalypse. It *must* be the end times.
She looks flustered, her hands smoothing out the creases in her blanket even as she attempts to reassure you.
Though she praises you, it is clear that she was taken aback by your response.
"See -- I have no idea."
I don't know... still looks like there's a lot of hustling going on. Maybe she's wrong. Also...
Damn it, I was really hoping it would be a Cop World. Okay, well, let's see...
"I hope you're right. I hope it's not too bad..."
Her relief is palpable. She was getting pretty worried about you there, but now she relaxes her shoulders...
"Yes, but, more specifically -- on the coast of the city of Revachol, in the district of Martinaise."
But they still have cops...
"On Insulinde?"
"You were doing quite well up until the end there. It *does* look like you're having trouble remembering things. History and places. Remembering *Reality*, in a word. It's very odd..."
The lieutenant tries to pretend he's not hearing it and is out of the conversation.
"Oh... no, nothing like that, dear. Revachol is a Zone of Control, led by an alliance of foreign powers called the Coalition. We have almost no government of our own -- certainly no machines."
She's scared now. She's realized you really are brain damaged.
Meaning: buying is voting.
The lieutenant studies you, rubbing his chin.
"That's right! We're on the coast of the city of Revachol, in the district of Martinaise."
I'm beginning to suspect that you might indeed be completely adrift in this reality, thinks the lieutenant. How can it be *that* bad? Never mind -- we're in this now.
A sigh. The lieutenant buries his nose in his notebook.
"We're in Martinaise."

dialoguetext: "We are governed by intelligent machines that perform calculations to determine the *freest* market. Everyone hustles and grinds like a bad ass visionary."
"You didn't do very well, dear. It does look like you're having trouble remembering things. History and places. Remembering *Reality*, in a word. It's very odd..."

"Oh... no, nothing like that, dear. Revachol is a Zone of Control, led by an alliance of foreign powers called the Coalition. We have almost no government of our own. And certainly not one who's horseback."
"Our leaders are fierce warriors who traverse the plains on steeds."
"What is the *Revolution* you mentioned?"
"It is quite disappointing, yes. A lot of people would like some form of representation. There's *talk*, but... for now, the RCM is all we've got."
"Yeah, I'm blowing this whole thing out of proportion. Forget I said anything."
She nods, but still looks worried.
"Revachol is a Zone of Control, led by an alliance of foreign powers called the Coalition. We have almost no government of our own. And *certainly* no dictatorship of the proletariat."
"You know where we *are*, right?"
"Who could tell me more?" (Conclude.)
"That's right, dear! How splendid!"
"Radios are being used to control people's minds and distort our perception of reality, concealing our true masters: foreigners and *women*."

"Oh dear, this *is* troubling. You really ought to know that -- being one yourself. There aren't *really* any cops in Revachol, not in the traditional sense. The status of law enforcement has been a complicated matter since the Revolution..."
"So -- how did I do?"
"But we should stop for today, sweetie. You look like you need a break. Besides, I'm not the best person to explain the *big* things to anyone..."
You sense that she won't judge you, no matter what you say.
"That's right, dear! How splendid! Here, take this pen. Knowledge should always be rewarded."
"Oh... no, nothing like that, dear. Revachol is a Zone of Control, led by an alliance of foreign powers called the Coalition. We have almost no government of our own. And certainly no matriarchy..."

"Oh dear..." She shakes her head, suddenly very worried. "And you were doing so well. There aren't *really* any cops in Revachol, not in the traditional sense. The status of law enforcement has been a complicated matter since the Revolution..."
"You don't notice this about me, but actually -- I have lost all memory of the world and myself and I have no idea what I'm doing."
"On second thought, things *are* bad. I don't even know enough to know what I *don't* know about this world."

dialoguetext: "But thank you, sweetie. You did make me forget about my worries for a while." She smiles up at you, but concern is creeping back into her expression.
"I hope I've been useful."
"Don't worry. You've asked me to look into it and I will."
"Thank you, sweetie. I'm awfully sorry to impose on you like this -- maybe there's something *I* can help *you* with in the meanwhile?"
Her voice is shaky. What is going on here?
Very strange... why is she not letting you do this? It's like she's given up.
Very strange... you get the sense she wouldn't have let you do this even if you did volunteer. Why?
"Lena, what's wrong? You seem different."
"Different -- how?" The half-moons of her glasses reflect you as she looks up at you.
Answering a question with a question, for example -- defensive isn't her usual style.
"You're... on the back foot."
"You've given up on the phasmid."
"You're not telling me the whole story."
"Never mind."

"Although the 'low' part is a little ironic -- the Col Do Ma Ma Daqua makes, or, rather, *is* such a high-pitched sound that other animals, including humans, can't *hear* it. It could be everywhere, all of the time -- and we wouldn't know."
"Well, dear -- they cancel each other out. And these tests were performed so recklessly that when they happened upon the right frequency... well, they wiped out most of the population."
"Fine I'll bite." The lieutenant looks at her sceptically. "How can an animal be a sound?"
"I don't know."
"But how can an animal be a sound?"

"Plenty. It's the evidence that led to its discovery. In the Twenties, a group of Areopagite ornithologists -- that is, scientists who study birds -- were trying out a new recording technology for capturing sounds outside the range of human hearing."
"Many scientists have asked the same question -- some have claimed that it isn't *itself* a sound, but a tiny *corpuscle* that emits sound waves. But there's no evidence to support this theory."
"Extinction?"
"Could it be *here*?" (Look around.) "Right now?"
"Interesting. What about..." (Conclude.)
I wouldn't be so sure. What if the damage is *also* invisible?
"Exactly... And these tests were performed so recklessly that when they happened upon the right frequency... well, they wiped out most of the population."
"It's not. Don't worry. If it were predatory we would have found it by the damage it inflicts."
"They cancel each other out."

"The scientists soon discovered they could track and even *predict* what appeared to be feeding, mating, and migration patterns based on sound waves in a *strictly delimited* range of ultrasonic frequencies -- even higher than those of the highest-pitched bat calls."
"They realized that they had discovered a new species -- and called it the Col Do Ma Ma Daqua. After the Perikarnassian name for the voice of god, which is said to be *very* silent."
"No, dear. They cancel each other out. And these tests were performed so recklessly that when they happened upon the right frequency... well, they wiped out most of the population."

"That is a sad story." She frowns. "A group of university students assisting with the field work, in their enthusiasm for the project and, no doubt, because they were preoccupied with impressing their professors, nearly drove it to *extinction*."
You have *no clue* because you're not a DWEEB.
This lady really should be a teacher. She's really good at the explaining things thing.
Psst. They cancel each other out.

She nods gravely. "They tried to communicate with it, and had no other means but sound. So they started sending out sound waves at frequencies they thought might match the Ma Ma Daqua's. And what happens when a sound wave meets another sound wave of the same frequency, dear?"
Maybe it's predatory?
"Sequester. Thyme. Josquin --" She nods. "Those are but some of the Ma Ma Daqua they followed individually."
"They amplify each other."
He nods approvingly.
The lieutenant pauses thoughtfully.
"Ah, fuck it. Let's have more cryptids."
"Right, okay, we can move on for now." (It'd be dishonourable to renege on the promise.)
"But, Kim... Don't *you* want to hear about another cryptid too?"
Something in him breaks.
The lieutenant leans in. "Hey, you promised you'd only ask about one cryptid."
"Well, the answer is: yes, there is an invisible cryptid."
"This has been educational, sadly we need to discuss something else." (Conclude.)
"Of course, dear."
"Yes, that's another translation." Her eyes light up behind her glasses. "They're both quite lovely, aren't they?"
"They grew quite obsessed with these little birds -- even though they couldn't see them, they could distinguish among individual birds and," she smiles, "even began to *name* some of them."
"Wow."
"Go on."
"Is this bird a cryptid?" (Point to the tie she gave you.)
"No." Her eyes narrow mysteriously. "It's *the* cryptid."
"Wow. *The* cryptid?"
"Okay. What *is* this bird?"

"The eight-eyed teratorn, the largest flying avian ever discovered -- with a wingspan of 11.5 metres. It was thought to have gone extinct 3,500 years ago, some even doubted the *fossils* were real. A mutation, they said. Until..."
"Oh yes." The small silvery skull shines between your fingers, its beak sharp.
"Until?"
"Until it was *sighted* by renowned Gottwaldian explorer and naturalist Uwe Plattenkalk in '21."
"What happened?"
"Alone in the blasted desert heat the doctor wandered eastward, where man hasn't stepped foot in over a thousand years -- since the fall of Perikarnassis."
"Mutation..." the man scoffs. "All of evolution is a mutation."
This *renown* seems a bit dubious -- your own catalogue comes up completely empty, but -- of course -- you are not all knowing.
"Okay -- and Uamrao is..."
"The world's largest canyon system, sweetie. It's a barren waste east of the Erg desert -- an ancient riverbed, completely dried up."
"He was lost, without any navigation equipment and desperately low on water. After a day or two he noticed a bird high in the noon sky. A great black bird, it seemed gargantuan."

"Every now and then, the bird would dive down to feed on an animal carcass somewhere on the horizon. But by the time Uwe got there, the teratorn had taken off already -- and the carcass was picked clean. This happened many times."
Eat the bird, Uwe. It's the only way to survive.
"I understand. He started hunting it."
"He was following it?"
"It followed him?"

"Yes. A bird that big has a lot of blood in it and he was dying of thirst. For many days Dr. Plattenkalk followed the teratorn. Until they reached a great canyon wall, where the bird finally landed to rest."
"I need to hear about this sighting."
"Okay. Not now, let's back up a notch."
"Of course, sweetie. Do you want to hear about another cryptid? The teratorn is, by many accounts, the greatest though..."
"It happened on a botanical expedition into the vast and unexplored Uamrao canyon in southeast Iilmaraa. Dr. Plattenkalk got separated from his group during a sandstorm..."

"Yes. Or, rather, *hunting*. A bird that big has a lot of blood in it and he was dying of thirst. For many days, Dr. Plattenkalk followed the teratorn, until they reached a great canyon wall, where the bird finally landed to rest."

"The professor climbed up there, with a rock in his hand. He found the bird sleeping with its head tucked under its wing. A great black pile of feathers on the perch. So he approached, slowly squeezing the rock in his fist..."
Watch out!

"Then the teratorn suddenly looked at him. He could see it had *eight eyes* -- four on either side of its skull, like a spider -- and the man couldn't move. He was paralysed, frozen into place with the rock in his hand. Whatever he did, he could not get closer to the bird."
"The bird was controlling his mind. It *kept* him from approaching. He could step back, but every time he stepped forward -- paralysis. Uwe spent three days trying, until the bird flew away."

"More like *he* followed it. A bird that big has many litres of blood in it and he was dying of thirst. For many days, Dr. Plattenkalk followed the teratorn, until they reached a great canyon wall, where the bird finally landed to rest."
"Yes way, sweetie," she smiles, used to derision. "Cryptozoologists have been tracing it ever since, but Uamrao is vast, mysterious, and holds many secrets."
"Hold on, how did he survive to tell the story?"
"An eight-eyed mind-controlling bird. Fuck yes."
"An eight-eyed mind-controlling bird? C'mon..."
"An eight-eyed mind-controlling bird? No way."
"The eight-eyed teratorn was indifferent to him, as long as he didn't get closer than two steps. It even let him feed on some carcasses up there -- and the two unfertilized eggs it left behind."
"Absolutely, sweetie," she smiles, glad you agree. "Cryptozoologists have been tracing it ever since, but Uamrao is vast, mysterious, and holds many secrets."
"Yes way, sweetie," she smiles, used to derision. "Cryptozoologists have been tracing it ever since, but Uamrao is vast, mysterious, and holds many secrets."
"This one -- I liked," the lieutenant puts down his notes. "Not only does it have eight eyes, *and* is a living fossil, *and* the largest bird ever to live. It also does mind control."
"Modern radar telemetry shows great promise -- we *will* confirm this one. By the end of the decade, latest."
He's sincere. He likes the audacity of it.
"So that was the last anyone saw of it?"
"Okay. So it's never been seen again."

"Sadly, yes. But there are numerous reports of eight-eyed bird skulls from Iilmaraa. And then there's the striking resemblance to the Perikarnassian Imperial Eagle -- an ancient heraldic symbol -- that is hard to pass off as coincidence. The imperial eagle, too, had eight eyes."
"Very, *very* hard."
"This one's very famous, everyone knows it. People will be looking at that tie on you and thinking: that man is into cryptids." She winks. "So -- what else do you want to know?"
"There are limits, you see, to how large a metabolism an ecosystem can beget. Some say a gravity anomaly below the Koko Nur desert might allow the creature to grow to these *gargantuan* sizes."
Great. This is great shit. You need more.
Gravity anomaly? Diggin' it. Diggin' this para-scientific stuff right here.
Not *really*. It's just stylization. The way they drew eyes -- it's not a zoological drawing.
"The Gnome of Geroma? That doesn't sound too bad."
"Oh -- it is. None of its victims survived. Grieving relatives never even found their bodies because the Gnome's venom *dissolved* organic tissue."
The lieutenant throws you one of his *looks*. "*One* cryptid -- like you said. One. This can't turn into some kind of cryptid extravaganza. We have things to do."
Whooh... tough choice there.
She *transforms* when speaking about these strange animals -- into a confident woman.
"Mhm. They grew quite obsessed with these little birds -- even though they couldn't see them, they could distinguish among individual birds and," she smiles, "even began to *name* some of them."
Great regret washes over her. A wending cloth.
"Why?"
"Where could he be..."

dialoguetext: A scattering of bullet holes is spread across the cracked wall, reaching from one corner to the other.
Why this many bullet holes?
Walk away. [Leave.]
A row of ghostly shades stand facing the wall. There are many of them, a dozen at least, their heads lowered and eyes blindfolded. It's quiet. No sound, no movement.
Unable to piece together the *big picture* just now. There's a hole in the hypothesis.
Who were they?
Comrades. The forsaken, the wretched, who tried to rise against the horrors of the world.
Foreign dissidents, unwashed criminals, and hoi polloi. Such is your belief, officer.
Leeches, fleas, and thieves. All the freeloader scum living off the hard work of others. Such is your belief.
Collateral damage on the path toward normalcy and progress. Such is your belief, officer.
Ordinary people -- familiar, each and every one of them.
"Hmm, correct." The lieutenant examines the wall closely. "The density of the bullet holes is unusual, even in a general *average bullet hole frequency in Martinaise* sense. Grim affairs."
The density and spread of these bullet holes is surprising -- this takes *a lot* of bullets. Fully-automatic rifle fire.
"Oh my god, look at all these bullet holes! I haven't seen any other bullet holes in the walls before, somehow."
Even more bullet holes. Something has definitely happened here.

Ten metres away -- other shades are lined up in an orderly manner, automatic rifles primed. A gust of wind blows by -- the coats of the firing squad flap slowly in the breeze. A single person stands on the side.
A long time has passed since the moment of this fusillading. Rain and brine have since washed all the blood away. Not a trace remains.
Who was who in this execution? I need to understand.

At first the lieutenant doesn't say a word... he just stares at the wall. "I don't know," he says finally. "I don't know who died here, lined up beside that horrible wall. It could have been any of the parties involved in the Revolution."
"What about people from the Coalition? The so-called moralists?"
"Yeah... it's very unlikely the Coalition forces were the ones who died here. They were always the *last* ones against the wall."
Seven men in combat uniforms and dark coats, holding automatic rifles aimed at the people. Soldiers from some side... but from which one?

The abundance of bullet holes leads to two options: either an inordinate amount of executions were performed here, or they did not use a *conscience round* -- where only one soldier has the loaded rifle. Looks like this was a mass execution with everyone fully armed.
I'm just a representation of your mental faculties... piecing together any available information. You should probably ask the lieutenant.
"To be honest, if a Coalition member was anyone in this situation -- it was the commandant. The superior giving the orders."
Look at the line of soldiers.
Look at the people against the wall.

A host of men, probably in everyday clothes -- ragged from the conflict and covered in dust. They were not sitting (a common practice for executions in some nations), as demonstrated by the height level of the bullet holes.
The commandant -- the one who gives the order. Machine gun fire crackling through the air, the lights of the muzzle flashes dancing on his face...
Good bye. [Leave.]
A cold sea wind blows away the figures.
"Kim, who was who in this execution?"
A row of ghostly shades facing a crumbling wall, with another seven shades standing ten metres from them. A single person stands on the sideline.
"Another likely scenario." The lieutenant nods.
"Meaning, this is *a lot* of bullet holes." He brushes the wall with his hand. "Looks like fully-automatic rifle fire. Something you don't see these days..."
"Why not?"
Say nothing, just nod.
"The manufacturing and sale of automatic rifles was curtailed after the Revolution. The destructive power of such tools proved to be... too much. We do need to retain some humanity in this world."
The lieutenant also nods. It is quite a scene -- the two of you standing next to the broken wall of an abandoned building... nodding. Nodding along.
Two officers of the law against the world. Nodding in unison. It is your source of power. The bond of camaraderie between you... is palpable...
Nod even more.
Shake your head.
The lieutenant is nodding so hard it looks like his head is about to snap off his neck.
He nods in agreement -- it really is a very serious scene, worth shaking your head over.
The lieutenant gives a terse nod. "Nothing for us to do here. Let's move along."
"Alright," the lieutenant coughs abruptly. "I'm glad we stopped when we did... my neck was starting to hurt. If there's nothing more, we should get going."
Follow your brother into death itself.
Phew! All that nodding was rough on the old neck. Close to feeling that twinge...
Don't stop nodding.
Stop nodding.
The lieutenant matches your nodding pace. He's a true professional at this.
The nodding's reaching critical mass! You can't take this much longer, captain!
Keep nodding, goddamn it! Stay the course!
A small bead of sweat runs down the side of the lieutenant's face as he maintains his nodding...
Abort! Abort! No... shit, it's too late!
Your neck couldn't withstand all this effort... it's too much!
Almost snapped your neck... but I fucking got this. No pain... no pain...
It's too much! You can feel your vertebrae starting to crack, your muscles groaning...
Just one more nod.
As the lieutenant takes out a handkerchief and softly taps the sweat off his temple... a faint crack echoes through the coast...
Whew, got off lucky there... that could have resulted in a world of hurt.
Whew, got off really lucky... that could have resulted in a world of hurt.
"Busted the neck, did you?" He cranes his neck left and right, stretching. "Glad I stopped when I did... my neck was really starting to hurt. Don't worry, it'll mend... now, we should get going."
"OH SHIT FUCK HELL!"
He would follow you into death itself... and you would do the same for him.
"Alright," the lieutenant coughs abruptly. "It's a good moment to stop. My neck was starting to hurt. If there's nothing more, we should get going."
They stand, facing the wall... It's impossible to discern any details about their personality or background.
"What if it was the Feld personnel when their assets were being seized by the revolutionaries?"

"Perhaps the ones executed here were the loyalist-conservatives -- killed by the communists at the start of the civil war. Or it could have been the communists, put to death during the last stretch of the conflict by the Coalition forces."
The morning sun rises beyond the horizon, radiating the first light of the day. The order was carried out at dawn.
The sun blazes high up in the sky... baking the planks, the sand, your skin. The order was carried out in the afternoon.
The sun falls slowly toward the horizon... the last light of the day. The order was carried out in the evening.
It's dark, very dark... faint lights flicker at the edge of your vision. It's rare for the order to be carried out at night...
Droplets of rain fall on the wooden planks, the surrounding sand dunes. The clouds block out any rays of light...
Snowflakes fall on the wooden planks and the surrounding sand dunes, covering the land with the white of innocence...
Look at the person standing on the side.
Men of duty. Dark duty.
Who were they?
Overpriced mercenaries putting down some rabid dogs. Someone's gotta do it, right?
In all truth, violence offers no answer... It's only the last available resort when all mediation fails. And here, all did fail.
Martyrs of the Nation, the ardent knights. The few who had the guts to do this.
Murderers. Twisted by orders. Young boys forced into killing.
You, your friends, your family. Everyone you had ever known. This was *you*.
Soldiers... people in a bad spot they probably did not choose, ordered to commit acts they wanted no part of.
"It could even have been the employees of the Feld R&D Center down the coast, as their building was taken over by the revolutionaries."

Behind this building -- the other one. Once filled with engineers and designers of Feld Electric, now collapsed and dead, but for some rats... You feel drawn, for some reason, to the faded mural again.
"You mentioned Coalition forces. Could it have been them against the wall?"
I'm dumb.
Fine. Okay.
The scattering of bullet holes looks like one giant smiling mouth. Smiling its deadly smile.
The scattering of bullet holes looks like one giant smiling mouth. Smiling its deadly smile. Laughing at you and the world and the living.
What *is* this...
Maybe you should change it. They were praying... screaming...
Remember what Trant Heidelstam said about Feld.
Or maybe...
The man sees you approaching and turns away...
"Officer..."
"Mr. Villedrouin..." The lieutenant nods.
"Mr. Villedrouin..."
"I've been looking all over for you."
"Look what the tide dragged in."
"I must admit. I did not take you for a sightseer. What do you want now?"
"Is that so? Have you come to *enforce* an arrest warrant?"
"Is that an RCM *term of art* for the *wrongfully accused*?"
"Listen, about what happened earlier..."
How do you expect to assign la responsabilité if you won't apologise for your own mistakes?
"Sorry, bad joke. I wanted to talk about what happened earlier."
"Let's get right to it. I have something to say."
"Yes?" He turns to face you.
"And what is that, officer?" He turns to face you.
"I'm listening." He turns to face you.
"It seems we had a little 'misunderstanding.'"
"I would like to sincerely apologise for my behaviour. It was completely inappropriate, and I accept full responsibility."
"I'm still pretty sure you were in the wrong, but I'm willing to forgive you."
"Unbelievable. I have never seen the nerve before..."
"Especially from a common officer of the Revachol Citizens Militia."
"Does this behaviour represent the RCM's *official stance* toward its Coalition partners?" He turns to the lieutenant.
"That is certainly a *euphemistic* way to describe what I recall..."
The man considers your words a moment, then nods slowly...
"I accept your apology, officer, out of my *profound* respect for the RCM, and the importance of our continuing partnership."
"Now, what brings you down to the coast?"
"And now, this conversation is over. Good day, *officer*."
"Perhaps he does, perhaps he does not. In any case, this conversation is over. Good day, officers."
With that, he turns his back to you once more.
You aren't going to get out of this with evasion.
Do you hear that contempt in his voice? He's always considered himself *above* you.
Do you hear that contempt in his voice? He's always considered himself *above* you.
"I must apologise on my partner's behalf, again. Please believe me when I say that he does not speak for the RCM in *any* capacity."
The lieutenant stares at the man's back, then steps away. He makes sure no one else can hear him as he turns to face you...
"I don't understand why you have it in for this man. He's never been anything but gracious and helpful to our cause. Why do you feel the need to insult him?"
"I'm sorry, Kim. I just can't help it."
"It feels like he holds us in contempt, like he thinks he's better than we are."
"I just don't like his face, okay?"
"Good god, couldn't you *try* at least?"
"Of course he does, he's from the Moralintern. But that doesn't mean *we* don't have standards to maintain..."
"Good god, couldn't you *pretend* at least?"
"I'm not even sure why I'm bothering. This is *your* side task, after all..."
"Now, let's go. You've done enough damage here."
"Ah, super, here you are again, officer. How can I help?"
As you approach, the man turns and greets you with a polite wave.
"Ah, super, it's the officer! I was not expecting to run into you again, but things have a funny way of turning out, no?"
"What brings you down to the scenic Martinaise coast?"
He appears completely at ease, like a common holidaymaker.
"I need your help forming a committee. I'm trying to assign *la responsabilité*."
"Thank you for your time." [Leave.]
"Actually, I was wondering what *you're* doing out here."
"My friend, if it's *la responsabilité* you're after, I have good news for you: There's no need to form such a committee, because it already exists!"
God, of course it does. These Moralintern types...

"The Comité de Responsabilité de Revachol. It acts as a sort-of clearinghouse for Coalition activities. To put it simply, they are the ultimate arbiters of la responsabilité in this part of the world."
Yes, this is just the sort of reasonable authority you're looking for!
"I would offer to connect you with the committee myself, but alas, I am not actually *in* Martinaise."
What? Where is he, then?
You *knew* there was something strange about this one! He's an astral projection, a bureaucratic phantasm!
He's speaking figuratively. He means he's not in Martinaise in his *official* capacity.
"What are you talking about? I'm looking at you right now!"
(Attempt to stick your hand through his astral form.)
"I got it. You're only here on *personal* business."
"So... where *are* you, then?"
"Of course, we are speaking informally, but *officially* I am still in La Delta, preparing for an upcoming conference on fuel oil derivatives..."
"Précisément. *Officially* I am still in La Delta, preparing for an upcoming conference on fuel oil derivatives..."
"Why, *officially* I am still in La Delta, preparing for an upcoming conference on fuel oil derivatives. I'm only in Martinaise in an unofficial capacity..."
"Mais que faites-vous, officer?" Your hand bumps up against the man's solid if somewhat fleshy chest.
"That's why it would be extremely irregular, or potentially even *inappropriate* for me to intercede with the Committee concerning a district I'm not officially in."
"Yes, I was wondering the same thing. What are you doing?"
"You said you weren't really here. I had to make sure you weren't an astral projection."
"Nothing, just lost my balance a moment."
"No, no, don't be silly. We're simply speaking in an informal capacity. *Officially* I am still in La Delta, preparing for an upcoming conference on fuel oil derivatives..."
"Perhaps your blood sugar is a bit low? As I was saying, *officially* speaking I am still in La Delta, preparing for an upcoming conference on fuel oil derivatives..."
"But this is an urgent matter. I *need* to get in touch with the Committee."
"How am I supposed to contact the Committee then?"
"Are you saying I should just give up?"
"Yes, you've made your *persistence* quite clear. Under normal circumstances I would have to insist you go through the regular channels."
The man frowns. "Well, under ordinary circumstances, the Committee contacts *you*."
"I don't mean to discourage you, of course, just to say that it won't be *easy* to reach the Committee."
No, no. You can't let them give you the runaround.
In other words, the Committee only knows what it *wants* to know.
Not exactly a model of accessible and accountable governance...
"But if you have information of a vital interest, they might be willing to entertain an exception. In which case, I would advise you to contact them via Coalition Warship Archer."
"Wait, what's Coalition Warship Archer?"
"Why do I need to go through Archer to speak to the Committee?"
"So how does one go about contacting a Coalition warship?" (Proceed.)
"Officer? You mean to say you haven't noticed the giant Coalition aerostatic peacefully patrolling the skies over Revachol?"
You follow the man's gaze out toward the west. There, hanging some distance above the horison, you can just make out a strange silhouette...
You follow the man's gaze out toward the west. There, amidst the low-hanging stars, you can just make out signs of motion...
It looks, to your eye, like some kind of long, metallic fish, suspended beneath a number of ceiling fans...
You look around, but you don't see anything unusual. Then again, your eyes aren't the sharpest...
It's a set of position lights moving in unison, like a restless constellation...
You can't see anything. But then, it's dark, and your eyes aren't the sharpest...
Not just any fish, it moves like some ancient bottom-feeder gliding over the ocean floor in search of prey...
Don't let the paintjob fool you, it's a goddamn killing machine, and there's nothing you can do to stop it!
It's about four-and-a-half kilometres from your position, you estimate.
No, it's more like a creature from the abyssopelagic zone, a great dark bioluminescent fish...
Don't let the shiny lights fool you, it's a goddamn killing machine, and there's nothing you can do to stop it!
"Oh, right. The *Archer*. I thought you said... something else."
"I don't think I've ever noticed it before."
"Ah, well, I'm glad to hear that at least. It would really be *quite unusual* for you to have never noticed it before..."

"Interesting. In a sense, that's the very idea. The Coalition doesn't want the people of Revachol to feel that they are under a *military* occupation. That is why the Archer is always careful to maintain a constant, discreet distance."
"It's amazing. An inspiring symbol."
"It looks like a fish."
"It looks like a killing machine."
"Huh. Can't believe I never noticed it before."
"Isn't it? A triumph of both technical ingenuity and international cooperation. I, for one, feel much safer knowing it's up there, watching all of us."
"Fascinating. I always thought it was more like a dragonfly. But isn't it interesting how humanity always finds inspiration in nature?"
"Well, of course it *is* a heavily armed and armoured warship with a full complement. But I assure you its purpose in Revachol is to *keep* the peace, not disturb it."

"That is part of the idea, of course. The Coalition doesn't want the people of Revachol to feel that they are under a *military* occupation. That is why the Archer is always careful to maintain a constant, discreet distance."
"You see, in addition to being an airborne artillery platform, Coalition Warship Archer is also the linchpin of the Coalition's surveillance and communications infrastructure in Revachol."
"And listening! It has the most objective vantage point in the entire city. Not to mention a vast array of radio, photographic, and meteorological monitoring instruments."
"I find it a great comfort to know there are benevolent powers watching over all, in strict accordance with the Wayfarer Act and the Bristelmüne Conventions."
"Hold on, it's *watching* us, too?"

"Hmmm, this is quite the problem, very tricky. Of course, the Archer has orders to fire on any unidentified aerostatics that might approach it, so it might be safer to get in touch *from the ground*..."

"But in that case, you would require a radio transmitter capable of broadcasting on Coalition frequencies. And that kind of technology naturally isn't typically available for non-Coalition use. Yes, it *is* a bit of a conundrum."
"I suppose there might be some way to *circuit-bend* your way onto those frequencies, but you'd have to be one of those *techno-tinkerers* to do it."
"Do you know any of these tinkerers?"
"Is that... legal?"
"So what am I supposed to do?"
"Unfortunately not, no, I don't have the pleasure. I am merely a representative of the Coalition Government, not very well-versed in technology. But you..."
"Unauthorised circuit-bending is a very serious matter with grave security implications, but as of the moment there is no specific law *forbidding* it, in Revachol at least..."
"That, my friend, is your responsabilité. I cannot take it from you, nor can you delegate it to someone else..."
"Always my pleasure to be of assistance to the RCM. Godspeed, and if we don't meet again, bonne chance!"
"Already leaving?" He shakes his head merrily. "À tout à l'heure, officer!"

"Mm, well that's très simple. I was visiting the fishing village just north of here. They have applied for a series of micro-loans to revitalise the old market, and well, I wished to see the situation *first-hand*..."
"And then, well, I had some extra time on my hands, so I decided to stroll down here. It's quite peaceful, isn't it?"
(Look around.) "Yeah, it's lovely."
"It's not quite my scene."

Man up, this is about having structured fun! All you have to do is read an intricate rulebook, study an assortment of maps, unfold the illustrated gameboard, and start rolling dice.
It's not dangerous, it's fun, structured fun! All you have to do is read an intricate rulebook, study an assortment of maps, unfold the illustrated gameboard, and start rolling dice.

In no time you could be romping through grasslands with low-level characters, hunted by iyskel riders... or battling unspeakable monsters in endless dungeons fraught with danger and despair, conjuring up forceful maegics to aid your quest.
Don't forget heated arguments escalating to physical confrontation with your friends.
And beer. Lots of beer.
And most importantly, never forget to rage-quit if the dice don't go your way!
It's not. It's for pansies. Man from Hjelmdall is way more awesome.

Yes, the Wirrâl setting is known for its complicated system of political alignments. But if you're not into that you can just hack your way through dungeons in search of loot. That's what most people do.
None of that witless Man from Hjelmdall fascist dross hidden behind faux-realistic allegory. Wirrâl is no cliché-ridden apologia for colonial violence. Wirrâl is pure *imagination*.
Open the box.
A quick guide to the maegical races of Wirrâl. Create your own hero choosing from any of these completely unique and fantastical backgrounds.
The options are, in order of importance: the welkin, the dweorgr, the humans, the faerie folk, and the pygmies.
You pry open the box. Inside you find a folded-up map, a small booklet, a 24-sided die, and a little plastic figurine.
The welkin -- tall, lithe and graceful, with long flowing hair and pointy ears. They're known for being powerful maegic users, but can also hold their own in a brawn-driven fight.
Read about the welkin.
Put the booklet away.
Read about the dweorgr.

A grand race of industrious mountain people. They're short, stout and muscular, and enjoy digging for gold and other precious minerals. They're also well-versed in the art of combat, where they prefer to use axes and hammers.
The dweorgr also come in a few different sub-races: hill dweorgr, shield dweorgr, and dark dweorgr.
Look at the die.
Take the die.
