dialoguetext: "Kim, we ready to do this?"
She means her kids.
"For the case I need to get *in tune* with the coast."
"And its people?" She bursts out laughing. "Glad to be of assistance then."
So fast as to make it seem like the weather turns at her command.
Say nothing. It's stupid. A stupid idea.
Say nothing? Well, now there's silence. She's looking at the sea. You hear yourself breathing.
You should say something. Anything. Maybe the Tequila Sunset thing?
"Oh."
"Oh indeed."
Uncomfortable shuffle of nylon.
Too morbid. Why am I not getting good ideas?
"So now that you know -- you keeping the name?"
Not terribly impressed, not surprised either.
"Because it's not human. Humans betray you."
"There's an explanation to this. And it's political. You see..." (Begin a long, impassioned political tirade.)
"Do they? Some of them do but..." She shrugs. "Sounds to me like you should choose your allies better, that's all."
"Aye, aye -- it's political." She stops you. "No need to step on a soapbox about it. What if we *disagree*?"
See? She doesn't *want* to disagree. Good sign. Keep it at that.
She's right. They're made mostly of plastic. A cheap novelty gift you can buy from a flower shop or a kiosk.
"So... who do you think killed the hanged man?"
"Good one. I'm gonna go with *the rope*."
She thinks it was a riddle. She must not even know of that business. Better that way.
As she walks off the wind picks up, and the light from the sun seems to fade -- the crumbling silhouette of Feld Electrical R&D towers in the distance, beckoning.
Say something about the sun.
Here we go. Two different approaches to cap this off with style.
"The only fault with the sun is -- it shines on us as well as our *enemies*."
(Stare into the sun.) "Yeah, a massive thermonuclear reaction, five billion years old -- the sun is a god."
"Aye," she nods. "And a benevolent one. When did you last have one of those on your side?"
"That it does. But then... we are also enemies to our enemies, eh? And so she shines on us. The cops and the commies, the killers and the saints. You know..."
"In my early twenties, maybe?"
"When I had my love with me."
"Never."
"I still do. I'm righteous."
"Well -- now you have that giant thing to watch over you. So... to hell with youth." She smiles. "You know..."
"The wind's gonna pick up soon and I have to go, but..." She takes her sword out of the scabbard. The blade reflects the sunlight, a dark orange.
"Well -- now you have that giant thing to watch over you. So... to hell with love." She smiles. "You know..."
"Well -- now you have that giant thing to watch over you. So... to hell with cruel gods." She smiles. "You know..."
"Well -- maybe it's that god that makes all those atoms burn up there in that big thing..." She smiles. "You know..."
"Have this. The sun's good but it doesn't *stick* things -- I've no use for it anymore."
Say what? Something *interesting*? IMPOSSIBLE.
"Thank you for coming on this walk with me." (Conclude.)
"Think we can do this again sometime?"
"Farewell." She nods to you and turns to go.
"Doubt it." She smiles sadly. "But thank you for the company."
"That sun thing was very pretty, I'm sorry I don't have anything to add..."
Please, this is important!
"Sometimes I feel like I don't have a good brain."
She turns her head and the plastic fish-hooks rattle in her ears. Nothing share-worthy takes place in your head.
Relax. This was still good.
"Aye. Brains, generally, aren't very good, are they? I prefer backs, arms, shoulders -- lungs, too." She smiles. "You know..."
"Thank you. Out there on the other planet -- the sea -- you start seeing things in a strange light. I'm glad I got to share it." She smiles. "You know..."
The lieutenant looks at the sword with distrust in his eyes.
"Are you sure you don't need the sword?" (Look at it.)
"No. Men around here are too drunk to pose a threat to me."
Do not bring it into a gun fight, he thinks. Please understand it's merely ceremonial.
This is as far as it goes with her. You'd need to put a year between you and your last drink for anything more.
As she walks off the wind picks up, and the light from the sun seems to fade -- the crumbling silhouette of Feld Electrical R&D towers in the distance, beckoning.
"I hope this has been refreshing for you, detective," the lieutenant says, watching her leave. "Let's return to our search with a fresh pair of eyes."
True, you ought not love ruins and hell -- and the fading scent of apricots.
You would be incinerated. Or worse.
Maybe some general remarks before you say something big? Work your way up to the *cool*.
"There's an interesting lilt in your voice."
"Thank you. I'm half Ubi. My mother was from Ubi Sunt?. Not a lot of sun there, I hear, though I've never been..."
Is there something here that would indicate a sniper used this place as a nest for taking the shot? Just some urban detritus, a bottle and a dilapidated old comms tower.
Maybe the campfire was used by the perpetrator?
Maybe the assailant climbed the comms tower, took the shot there?
What about the cigarette butts?
Look over the water -- to the Whirling-in-Rags.
The wind picks up. Fine sea foam lashes your face. It feels like needles. You can take it -- just raise your collar, detective.
In the distance you can hear the breakers roar.
A smoking assailant who favours Tioumoutiri to Astra or Drouin? Cigarette butts are part of the campfire set -- they're also everywhere.
The salty water has corroded the ladder to nothing but two thin orange rails. In addition, there is no stable nest up there. It would have been useless.
To warm his hands before he pulled the trigger? There are no markings on the ground for a tripod, he would have had to lie on a mattress. This is simply not a good spot for a 1.2 kilometre shot.
Tioumoutiri was a Revacholian colony on Iilmaraa. The suzerainty's population was mostly Iilmaraan Areopagites -- up to 97%. The region was known for its tobacco export. Hence the name.
I want to know *a lot* more about this.
Enough. The cigarettes are unimportant.

Oh, you do! The butts you saw had a silhouette of a boy wearing a kofia hat -- a tobacco picker. This boy is the Tioumoutiri brand logo. Contemporary Revacholians prefer Drouin (a local blend from the southern islands) or Astra, a legendary cigarette from Graad. Tioumoutiri is favoured by older men who like its old fashioned paper filter tips, insane amount of tar and the sweet smells of colonialism and halva.
Nothing is unimportant, detective.
"Those?" He points to them. "A smoking assailant who favours Tioumoutiri to Astra or Drouin? Cigarette butts are everywhere. This is a common brand for old men."
"I don't see it, officer. I don't see a person take a shot here and hit something there..." He looks east, over the coast. "In the Whirling-in-Rags."
"It's not possible to climb that ladder and even if it were -- why? There's no platform up there to aim from." The lieutenant looks up, raising his collar.
He looks like he's cold out here at the tip of the coast. The jacket is warm, but not for this weather.
"Kim, you look cold -- maybe a thicker coat?"
"Kim, you look cold -- maybe a little pilot cap?
"No."
No what?
"No what -- you're not cold?"
"No what -- an orange pilot cap would not help?"
"Yes, that one. No to the orange pilot cap." He turns to face the sea.
"No, an orange pilot cap would not help." He turns to face the sea.
"I'm okay. You on the other hand -- look like you're about to turn into a popsicle."
"It's my style. Superstar cops don't wear parkas. They rock out."
"What if I *want* to be a popsicle?"
"You're right. I should look into this situation before I die of hypothermia."
"That seems smart, yes."
"Absolute idiocy," he nods in acknowledgement of the idiocy on display.
"Don't be silly, no one wants to be a popsicle."
Technically speaking that would be a...
"Copsicle. You meant to say copsicle."
"No. I did not. We *Seolites* don't do paranomastic humour."
"To warm his hands before pulling the trigger? Perhaps. But anyone could have made this. The coast is specked with fires this time of year." He looks around.
"Truthfully -- this seems like a very poor choice to take a 1.2 kilometre rifle shot from. Visibility is awful, there's water vapour everywhere -- I think we can rule out... B double prime, was it?"
[Finish thought.]
Are you sure? You haven't ruled out the shot coming from here yet...
I said finish the god damn thought.[Leave.]
Oh right...
So?
There, 1.2 kilometres over the wave-crossed bay, through heavy, dark grey curtains of rain you see the smallest rectangle, barely visible.
A glowing light on the third floor of the Whirling-in-Rags. With binoculars you would see a young woman's shape move behind the glass, her limbs long and slender.
Smoking. Drinking. Being happy and elated. Without you -- because you're here, freezing in the wind, aren't you? Doing your *detective work*.
There, 1.2 kilometres over the cold water of the bay, through a thick snowstorm melting flake by flake in the waves you see the smallest rectangle, barely visible.
The light is off on the third floor of the Whirling-in-Rags. The young woman is gone, in Precinct 57. Safe, closed off. Her form no longer moves behind the glass there...
It's late. There is no light on the third floor of the Whirling-in-Rags. No shape moves behind it. Klaasje must be out on the town.
It's glowing in the dark night. The lights are on. Klaasje must be in there... looks like she's kept her promise not to go out at night anymore.
There, 1.2 kilometres over the cold water of the bay, blue from the distance and the air, you see the smallest rectangle, barely visible.
Such a good girl, you think.
The light is off on the third floor of the Whirling-in-Rags. The young woman is gone who knows where. Safe, closed off. Her form no longer moves behind the glass there...
Still, you felt it was important enough to make a mental note. That means *something*. You didn't pay attention to any of the other cigarette butts on the coast.
How do you respond to a pithy *no* like that? He's just into pilot caps, it seems.
It does look *extremely* rickety. And wouldn't help much either.
An old door, worn by elements, guards the depot. The wind has blown a sand dune in front of it. The door hasn't been opened in a long while. You see a handle.
Walk away. [Leave.]
Yes. Better that way. You can't even fathom the rabbit hole you might find yourself in otherwise.
You rattle the handle a bit, then push on the door with all your weight -- it does not budge. Not only is it locked, it's also *jammed* shut.
Huh... I wonder what's inside. How can I get in there?
"Whatever, door." [Leave.]
You can't. This door cannot be opened...
The lieutenant shrugs. "We don't get in there."
"What do you mean? We get into... like... everywhere."
"Come on, we even got in the Light Bending Guy's container, but you're saying we can't get in here?"
"Frankly, you're just going to have to accept the fact that you can't get in through every single door."
No-no, we've gotten into every door thus far. That's what we do -- we open doors. We're cops, that's our perk. Even Evrart knew that's a part of our M.O.
"But that's who I am. Who *we* are."
"Yeah, I understand you, I like opening doors as much as the next guy, but this one is simply beyond repair and we don't have the resources needed to open it."
EVER.
No-no, we've absolutely gotten into everywhere thus far. That's what we do -- we open doors and go through them. We're cops, that's our perk.
"I'm not gonna accept this. The door could be part of the investigation."
"Relax. No one's hiding in there. If we can't open it, others can't either -- and thus they can't get in." He looks at the door with a rueful smile.
What is this thing anyway?
"It's military -- a service depot of some sort."
The concrete structure looks *military* in origin. Over half a century old at least, but sturdily built.
"From here to the Whirling? I can't see how..." He looks southeast and blows on his fingers: "The church is in the way."
"Used to service what?"
"Probably something that is no longer there." The lieutenant looks at the hunching, concrete toad in front of him.
It may have been used to service an aerostatic battleship in the atmosphere? Or a fortification, like a seafort in the bay.
"Could this structure have been used to take the shot?"
Open the door.
There is no success. You didn't succeed here. It's impossible. The door does not open. It is not only locked, it is *jammed* shut.
For servicing an aerostatic battleship in the atmosphere? Or a fortification, like a seafort in the bay?
"Okay. I can live with this." (Accept it.)
"What else is there to do? *Not* accepting isn't gonna bring the fire brigade in..." He looks at the door with a rueful smile.
At least you can *think* about opening it. About doors in general -- they are, after all, fundamental to your life. Perhaps something useful will come from this?
Relax, he thinks. There's no one in there. If we can't open it, neither can anyone else.
At least you can *think* about opening it. About doors in general -- they are, after all, fundamental to your life. Perhaps something useful will come from this?
He catches your glance and nods. "This is the uniform of the Royal Carabineers in service of Frissel the First, Guillaume *Le Lion*, and the valiant King Filippe the Fifth before him."
"Don't you mean Frissel the Fun?"
"*You* do not speak his name, craven! Although he was a clown..." he adds. He turns back to you. "But he was *our* clown. Ours to ridicule -- and to mourn."

It is the *Croix de Bravoure* -- Cross of Valour. The Cross was the highest battlefield decoration in the Suzerain's armed forces, awarded for exceptional bravery in the line of duty in service of King Frissel the First.
*The Setting Sun* was a decoration used to distinguish seasoned combat veterans in service of King Frissel the First during the Revolution.
Look at the cross.
Look at the sun.
A crowned head in front of two crossed rifles. The medal hangs from a blue striped triangle.
A small blue star inside an orange sun. It has the word *Vaillance* written below.
"The medals." (Point to his chest.) "Did you get them for..."
"That's no dink, that's a fighter!"
"For bravery," he interjects.
"So I grabbed the *dink*," he says, with a stern look, "and started crawling. Kept going until the 59th Cavalry picked us up."
It's a conflicted topic for the old veteran. There must have been a number of controversial episodes in his service days.
"For bravery?"
"Not for raping women or...?"
"Not for killing babies or...?"
"That's what I was going to say, bravery."
"When I came to, it was all over," he continues, ignoring his companion. "It was just me and jawless Drysant, gurgling in the blood-soaked mud right next to me."
"The dink had taken numerous flesh wounds and lost a lot of blood, but despite missing his jaw he seemed hesitant to die. Tougher than he looked, that one."
"Then his horse, driven mad by the noise and smell of gunpowder, stepped on my leg and shattered my knee." He pats his right thigh.
"Do not speak of what you know nothing about, poltroon!" He slams the heel of his boot in the ground. "*Duty* is something you will never understand."
"So, did you?"
"No, I really wasn't, I'm just asking."
"I'm sure. But I know this uniform's reputation: You were also wondering if I got these for raping women or killing babies."
"I grabbed my sidearm and shot the beast in the head. Then everything went black."
"*Capitaine Arnoux -- le fléau des chevaux*!"
"For doing my duty in the heat of battle, for looking my mortality in the eye, when men like Gaston here hid in the bushes and shat themselves..."
"So what *did* you get the medals for?"
"He saved some *maudit* princeling who foolishly strolled into the front line in his gown of velvet and gold."
"The rebels were smart. They let us come real close before opening fire. Suffice to say, it was carnage."
"Saved a princeling?"

"Alas, the young Drysant was all piss and no vinegar, wearing a tunic of purple velvet and cockatoo feathers to battle." He spits. "Even his rifle was *gold-plated*. Shone from five klicks away. Can you imagine the asininity?"
"It was on the first months of the Revolution here in Revachol. Unrest was spreading like wildfire. Marauders had taken most of the Couron and were getting *really* ambitious."
"Oh no, you have to get shot." He nods eagerly. "Repeatedly. And you need to get your hands bloody too. Really *really* bloody."
"Through some miracle we both survived. And the jawless freak convinced Frissel to give me a medal for not leaving him to die in his own blood, piss, and shit."
"Okay... then what did you do?"
"What a dandy!"
"King Frissel thought he could end it all in one decisive strike." The old carabineer runs his fingers over the larger medal. "Sent his cousin, Drysant, to put an end to the unrest."

"He was the commanding officer and I was on duty. Just doing my job. Shouldn't hand out medals for that..." He shakes his head. "Thirteen months later I received 'The Sun'. For distinguished service. It's not worth mentioning."
You sense he's downplaying it -- he did a lot more than his duty. More than anyone's duty. It's in his spine, in his billowing breast. An untarnished self worth.
"Maybe, maybe, but also bear in mind, officer..." He points to the sun-shaped medal on René's chest. "They don't hand these out for anyone with a service record."
"I got shot in the left shoulder and went down. Just a flesh wound, but just as I turned over, the prince fell into the mud next to me. He was missing his lower jaw."
"And that even whilst crawling with a mangled half-dead prince on his back, he still managed to murder three rebels on his way."
"What *Monseigneur Modestie* is not telling you is that he crawled over seven kilometres before the cavalrymen found him and Drysant. Two days later that was."

"To keep the long and bloody story short, Drysant marched us against the partisans in Couron. And when I say 'marched', I mean made us walk into captured enemy territory single-file, like toy soldiers, while he rode in front on his giant red stallion."
"Sounds like you're being modest, René."
"I'll leave you to it..." [Leave.]
"I don't know the reputation of... *anything*. Don't even recognize the war."
"Son, we should never forget our past. Lots of mistakes were made back then, but they were also lessons." His voice takes on a tutor-like quality.

"No -- we were the last ones to keep all the baby killers and rapists in check, and let me tell you, son..." His eyes find yours. "If there hadn't been Royal Carabineers, Revachol might not be standing at all."
"Thanks for the story, René!" (Conclude.)
"Bah!" His gaze wanders over the bay. "There were many such stories in those days. Many such men too. True Revacholians, men with *backbone*."
Shush! Ignore them! They don't know what they're doing. They're *old*! You are letting down yourself and the team. Get in the damn game already!
"See? Your munching and complaining have ruined my concentration." The man throws a metal ball toward a smaller, wooden ball in the sand, missing it by a metre.
Trying to throw something as close to a predetermined point as possible... measuring... this must be the age-old game of pétanque.
"Have you no shame," the man says to his partner, "whining about your back every time you bring out the measuring tape?"
"A moment of your time, fellows." (Don't get involved in the game.)
"I hope you pass out from it, you goddamn jellyfish. Men like you are the reason this nation is sinking." Standing tall and proud, he looks at his partner with disgust.
Better observe them first.
You're such a wuss!
"René, you're a man with a fork in a world of soup. Please... let's just try to enjoy the game, alright?" The other one is eating a big sandwich.
That's the spirit! Don't even waste your breath asking about the game. They wouldn't know anyway. They're *way* past their prime.
No, you got this! There's the ball -- you're the game!
Alright, I got this -- ball time!
Shouldn't I ask what game it is first?
These manly men are playing *balls*. This is a *ball* game. Grab a ball and play it. Don't ask questions. Shoot first, ask questions never.
"René, you're a man with a fork in a world of soup. Please... let's just try to enjoy the game, alright?" This one's still chewing on his sandwich.
"Sure, officer. I am René, René Arnoux, and my *specially abled* partner here is Gaston Martin. How can we help you?" The man in the uniform stands before you tall and proud.
"Right." The old man stands tall and proud, looking at you inquisitively.
"You seem to be playing in a crater."
"Do you know anything about the man hanged in the back yard of Whirling-in-Rags?"
Look. Look! In his hand, going into his mouth! The sandwich, it's hauntingly beautiful!
"I'm trying to, but you keep breaking my concentration. You're old, I can see that. We're both old. Now stop grabbing your ass like it's a girl."
Could the objective of the game be to throw the metal ball so it lands by the wooden ball?
"Watch out, Gaston..." He points at you. "It's Inspector Oaf. Come to throw more of our stuff into the sea, officer?"
"I like playing in the dark. Sharpens your nocturnal instincts... Feels like being on recon again."
"The purity of snow always reminds me of the purity of a man's soul...." He looks at the falling snow. "If he's got principles."
"Your munching has ruined my concentration!"
"Offic... argh..." He rubs his chest and spits. "Goddamnit... pull yourself together, René." He turns to you. "What do you want?"
"Forgetting those times means the mistakes were for nothing. That all those people died for nothing."
"Quite impressive. It's men like René who made Revachol great once."
"I'm not impressed. All those heroics and where is he now? No, you gotta play to win. Look after *you* first."
"René, I found your guard booth."
"Yes, the Débardeurs' Union pays me to stand vigil during the nights." He looks down. "Not out of any *political* allegiance, mind you."
"I'm an old man, don't sleep more than a few hours every night anyway and... money is tight," he adds with a slight sigh.
He feels like he has to justify himself for some reason.
"Got it, thanks." (Conclude.)
"Yes, yes. Like I said," he brings it up again, "I would be up *anyway*, so might as well keep an eye out. It keeps my senses sharp."
His features stiffen and he gets a cold look. "She... is nobody. This is none of your concern and I refuse to discuss my private affairs with the RCM."
"The lady is Jeanne-Marie Beaulieu." Gaston speaks with a soft voice. "And she sure as hell wasn't a nobody."
"I understand Jeanne-Marie meant a lot to you?"
"I was 22 when I returned from King Guillaume's Ikeira Operation in the south and found my sweetheart in the arms of this wretch..."
"There's nothing for you to *understand* here," he snaps. "It is not *her* death you are investigating."
"Were the circumstances of her death in any sense...*unusual*?"
"Absolutely not." His voice is coarse. "She died of pneumonia in her bed at the age of 79. This is highly... usual."
"Alright, let's back up to a less sensitive subject, okay?"
His face is motionless like a marble mask. He doesn't comment.
"What happened with you, Gaston, and Jeanne-Marie?"

'The Ikeira Operation' was a seven-year campaign during which Suzerain Guillaume's army forcefully united the people in the southeastern part of Le Petit Continent, collectively known as the Ikeira tribes, under the Revacholian banner.
He gives Gaston a hateful look. "I won her back, but while I was dealing with some... issues..."
"You were like a dark cloud sucking the joy out of every living thing around you, and you..." He quickly glances at you. "You... *hurt* her."
"Where was the photo of you two taken?"
"I... uh... I..." He looks down at his boots, lips moving, but the words are inaudible.
"Those days and memories are gone." He nods and looks René with something resembling compassion.
The old soldier says nothing, but when his glance quickly runs over Gaston's face, there's an odd look in his eyes.
"Revachol Fair of '91 in the Faubourg district." His eyes turn to the sea. "A parade was held to honour Guillaume *Le Lion's* name-day. And the carabineers marched in the place of honour."
"You looked happy in the picture. Smiling."
"Okay, thanks."
He nods.
"This was the happiest day of my life." This is said in such a matter-of-fact tone, it leaves no room for doubt.
"We're still waiting for a replacement for the *boule* you sent sinking."
"Vigilance, officer!" He salutes you. "What can this old carabineer do for you?"
"Can you please stop whining for one second and let me take the shot."
"René, you are the angriest man in the world."
"Ah, *mon dieu*! The pain in my back is unbearable. I can't even say if it's in my back or hip anymore. Feels like it's in *both*!" He tries to measure the throw.
This man seems to be experiencing a mild to medium level of congestive heart problems, either due to narrowing of the arteries or high blood pressure.
"I found you guys a new *boule*." (Hold out the ball.)
"Now-now, no need to get angry again, René. I'm sure the officer tried his best. It's not like there's a *boule*-kiosk here in Martinaise."
The old veteran stares at the shot put ball in silence, then speaks in a reserved voice: "What is this? Are you mocking us? This isn't for pétanque."
"Fine." He takes the *boule*. "You tried to right a wrong. It's still a gram better than actual *nothing*."
Grab the ball and show them how it's done!
"Exactly. And I *really* did try."
"There's not gonna be an alternative. I suggest taking it."
"I'm very sorry. It's the best I could find."
"*Trying* is worth as much as is accomplished. In this case -- almost nothing."
"I said I wouldn't do it, but I found you a new *boule*."

dialoguetext: "See, René, I told you he was one of the good guys." He chuckles. "You should have more faith in people."
He mumbles something to himself. It seems to be a variety of curses.
"That's what it was all about?" He takes the sandwich. "Gaston is a snivelling rat -- I've known this my whole life -- but an RCM officer bullying an old man? Robbing him of his meal?!"
"You deserve it more than anyone." (Hold the sandwich out to René.)
"NO," the old soldier exclaims sharply. "I don't understand, what you're trying to accomplish with this... sandwich *bonanza*, but I already don't like it." He crosses his arms.
"Listen, guys, in these dire times we are all brothers. Let us dine together as one." (Hold out the sandwich.)
Cautious nature prevents him from voicing more objections, but he will always remember the cop who bullied him -- of that you can be sure.
The old man looks devastated as he observes you and René strengthen your  manly bond over his culinary wonder.

"*Silence!*" he snaps at Gaston, then turns to you: "Since you put it that way, I *symbolically* accept your cordial gesture." He eats the sandwich-half in two well-measured bites and nods. "For Revachol."
"What? No!" He gasps, looking like he's about to cry. "Old angry René doesn't even have taste buds -- it would be a complete..."
"Let us -- true Revacholians -- symbolically share this meal. For Revachol!" (Give half the sandwich to René and eat your half.)
"No-no, officer! René doesn't know what he's saying." The jolly one jumps in.
"No reason, never mind." (Keep the sandwich.)
"Everything *you* do reflects on the idea and the people you are representing. When we," he says, pointing to Gaston, "think of the RCM, we think of *you*. Please make it a pleasant thought."
"Yes," he says impatiently. "I was standing right here. I saw it. Why are you telling me this?"
"I managed to get my hands on Gaston's sandwich."
Judging by his attitude -- probably the second one.
Wait, what team?
I'm on it, coach!
Does it matter what team? Pick a team, any team, the blue team -- you're letting them down! GET IN THE GAME AND THROW THE GODDAMN BALL!
EYES ON THE BALL, DINKY WINKY!
What is it about this old soldier that makes him stand so proud?
"I saw a horseback monument near the roundabout."
All you observe is a veteran refusing to let go of the past and his old uniform. This is not uncommon.
As René turns from you to his partner and back, the medals on his chest rattle and glare. He keeps his spine straight and his ribcage lifted, displaying them proudly.
"Not this again..." you hear the lieutenant mumble under his breath.
Two. The larger one is shaped like a cross, while the smaller medal resembles the sun.
How many medals are there?
"Ah, yes, King Filippe III on his steed -- a reminder of what Revachol once was..."
"How should a true king rule?"
"What was that about cocaine?"
"Oh absolutely..." He smiles as if reliving a pleasant memory. "At the mercy of a cocaine-snorting tyrant who emptied the treasury so he could sleep on a bed of gold?"
"...a superpower, feared and respected. A testament to what this country *can* be under the leadership of a True King, someone who knows how to rule."
"*Decisively*. Without fear of offending the sensibilities of the frail and weak-minded among his subjects! This is something the insurgents never understood..."
"You can't even take responsibility for yourself -- how could you fathom the responsibility weighing on the shoulders of a ruler?" he asks, obviously annoyed.
"Oh yes, René, yes..." The jolly man nods meekly. "Men were bigger, girls were prettier, and everyone was a *fascha* -- Lord, please bring those days back, if you can!"
"I... saw a picture in there. You were in it. Who's the girl?"
"Let's talk about something else."
Cocaine? Cocainum? Sounds like our kind of king. And -- just imagine! -- what kind of cocaine a king would have had...
"Oh, old Filippe was a *big* fan of the purple nose candy the nobility loved so much. A cocaine-connoisseur of sorts." He chuckles. "His egocentricity is borderline legendary."
"Seems to me a leader should take care of his *people* before himself."
"Powerful leaders -- not afraid to do what *must* be done -- that's what this country needs."
"I'm not sure how I feel about that."
No, he really believes what he's saying -- he has completely accepted the narrative of transcendence through cocaine use.
"You haven't lived as long as I have, son. With age, a man learns certain things about real power -- or else ends up a spineless socialist rat, like Gaston here."
"Revachol would be a different place if more people realized that." He gently rubs his chest. "We could still be the..."
"A nation is only as strong *as* its leader. That's why it was such madness to try to..."
No one and nothing can change this man's mind -- he is as rigid as they come, still in that antique uniform -- it's a symbol for him.
"And the worst part of that, officer," he says, face terrified, "is having to spend your days playing pétanque with an angry snake."
"Don't get started on that again. What happened, happened." There is some weariness in his voice now -- he's heard this rant many times before.
The carabineer doesn't reply, but his entire being communicates unbreakable resolve.
But imagine -- purest cocaine... Now that would make you feel like a king. Not that you can afford it. But a man can dream, right? In another time and place...

"Filippe III was even brought into this world with the help of cocaine -- the court medic administered a dose to his mother when she was in labour. And it is well known that with the help of cocaine -- only the purest, of course -- he was able to connect with higher realms..."
But imagine -- purest cocaine... Now that would make you feel like a king. Not that you can afford it... But what about speed? Speed is cheap. And good.
'Higher realms'? Of course -- it all makes sense...
"I too have travelled to higher realms..."
"What was that about higher realms? Sounds interesting."
"Seems like irresponsible behaviour for a monarch. Drug users shouldn't even operate heavy machinery, much less rule countries."
"It's really not." He turns to René. "Please do spare us the cocaine fairy tales."
"Yes, indeed. We are not here to investigate the drug trade of centuries past."
"Such responsibility requires a boost every now and then. I sometimes need one too..."
"Please, officer! Don't encourage him!" He quickly turns to René. "Do spare us the cocaine fairy tales. The RCM isn't interested in them."
"Thanks for clearing that up. I have some other questions now."
"I'm listening." He doesn't sound too pleased to have his praises to the miracle of cocaine-fuelled kingship cut short.
"From what I've seen of the officers of the RCM..." he begins, looking you over, then stops himself. "But I don't want to get into a debate about drug policies."
"Do *May bells* mean anything to you, René?" (Show him the flower.)
"That's how it is, huh?" The man slowly nods, exhales sharply, and takes the ball. "Fine. I guess you did attempt to right your hooliganism... Consider it forgiven."
"The best, huh?" he says inspecting the ball. "This isn't even a *boule*, but... Fine. I guess you did attempt to right your hooliganism... Consider it forgiven."
Dark cloud? That sounds unpleasantly familiar...
He glances at it and frowns. "I prefer the old name -- Insulindian Lily. Girls brought them to young cadets when they entered service. Wearing them on your cap was supposed to bring good luck."
"Hold on, is this a *royalist* military tradition?"
"Did they bring you good luck?"
"It used to be," he says with a sigh. "But the communards were fond of them, too. Called them *revolutionary* flowers, bells of the Revolution..."
"You know what..." He falls silent and the emerging smile withdraws. "No. They brought me misery, false hope, and disappointment. The *revolutionaries* sullied them."

"But it wasn't the revolutionaries that *sullied* the idea for you, was it?" He looks at the old soldier almost gently. "She gave them to me too and your jealous little heart just couldn't accept it."
You stirred up some bad memories there.
She? Must be the woman from that picture -- Jeanne-Marie -- again.
Why are you so mean to me?
Consuming food is mechanical process for him. He doesn't enjoy it, just goes through the motions and moves on.
"Excellent job bullying that old man, officer," the lieutenant says with a frown. He looks impatient and not happy. "He'll be sure to put in a good word for the RCM in the future."
"I do not approve of this *abuse* of power nor your *redistribution* efforts." His features stiffen. "That's not the Revachol *I* fought for. Here..." He hands the sandwich to Gaston.
The man looks at his partner with suspicion, then his eyes light up, he pockets the sandwich and chuckles. "*Merci beaucoup, Capitaine Arnoux*!"
"Hopefully it will finally take your fat ass to the other side of a cardiac arrest, Gaston." His words are slow and deliberate. "This doesn't mean anything. Doesn't *change* anything."
You can feel the jolly man pull back. This hurt. More than he was ready for.
"He's right, you know?" The lieutenant nods towards René. "We're supposed to protect people -- not take advantage of them. Now wrap this up."
He doesn't think it was an excellent job at all -- he's disappointed.
"All of *this*..." -- he points to you -- "is very unprofessional. Makes me think the Citizens Militia is nothing but a badly organised band of bullies and jesters. Again: I *don't* like this."
"We're not, the officer was just..." The lieutenant falls silent, looking for words to justify your sandwich antics.
Should have just eaten the damn thing.
Like a machine.
He seems agitated. Trying to control himself.
He's afraid, what might happen if his *opinionated* partner is allowed to speak his mind freely.
It's clear these words mean a lot to him.
"You're right, I should have thought about it."
"That's just *your* opinion."
"No. It isn't. He's absolutely right." He shakes his head. "I don't like it and I feel confident saying absolutely *no one* in your precinct would approve of this either."
"That's right." The former soldier nods, his fists curling in a ball. "And I'm *sharing* it with you so you can better yourself..."
"Now, gentlemen..." The lieutenant addresses the men in a casual manner. "If my partner doesn't have any other questions, we'll take off."
"Yes, well..." The lieutenant looks uncomfortable. "Let's just wrap this up and try to think about these things in the future."
"Fine. You live, learn, and move on." The former soldier nods in agreement. "The matter is closed. Now what can this old carabineer do for you, officer?"
Not a soul.
"Officer," the other one jumps in. "Let's not get sidetracked here with this nasty business. I know you wanted something from old René or me. Let's talk about that instead."
"You are representing an organisation, an insignia, an idea." The old man continues in a softer tone. "You need to understand that."
"C'mon, I was only joking around."
"I didn't find it funny."
"Me neither." The lieutenant looks weary of this whole situation. "I don't think anyone did."
"It was quite funny, officer." He lets out a keen laughter. "I thought it was very funny."
"Unbelievable... How can you even walk up straight with that liquid backbone of yours, Gaston?" He shakes his head. "Officer, what do you want?"
"I'm just gonna go -- we'll all forget about it at some point." [Leave.]
I'm satisfied with this explanation.
"I myself use *speed* to transcend..."
"I drink alcohol and go to heaven..."
"Pyrholidon helps me connect to higher realms..."
But imagine -- purest cocaine... Now that would make you feel like a king. Not that you can afford it... But you could do a bit more speed. That would be okay. Would help you stay sharp.
"Sounds like there's a story there, but I'd like to talk about something else right now."
"Sounds controversial. Let's talk about something else."
"I didn't think you had the stomach for it." He nods grimly. "And I can usually tell."
"Didn't think you had the stomach for it." He nods grimly. "Kids don't these days. I'm used to that."
Whoaa... sounds like you're about to open the gates of conversation -- this man will literally talk your ear off, if you let him wander off to Memory Lane.
"Honour is everything to me," he says with grim finality.
"Listen, René, I might wanna hear that story later, but right now I have more important things to discuss."
"Fine," he snaps at you, obviously annoyed for the interruption. "What is it then?"
"Purple velvet tunic," the lieutenant says thoughtfully. "That isn't exactly *camo*."
"So what happened?"
It's painful to even think about.
Hang on to the story -- veterans get sentimental after such *retellings* -- this might yield something useful.
He really despises that Drysant fellow.
"Shattered knee... interesting. Actually, can we pick it up later and do questions now?"
"Ugh..." The old man looks at you, obviously annoyed by the interruption. "Sure. Yes. Yes, you can ask your questions."
The bane of horses.
"I'd give up. Can't imagine living without my jaw." (Touch your jaw.)
"This would never happen to Johnny Law-jaw." (Point to your jaw.) "My jaw is tight."
"I've been through worse."
"He didn't." A shadow of respect crosses his face. "I hoisted the prick on my back and started crawling. Kept going until the 59th Cavalry picked us up."
"Right, right..." -- he doesn't get sidetracked -- "so I grabbed the prick and started crawling. Kept going until the 59th Cavalry picked us up."
"I doubt it," he remarks dryly. "Anyway, I grabbed the prick and started crawling. Kept going until the 59th Cavalry picked us up."
Duty, medals, honour, chain of command -- I like this guy. He's not a pansy. I don't like pansies.
"I'm *not* getting into this with you again." He mumbles through clenched teeth and turns to you. "Officer, was there anything else?"
"Why do you despise Drysant so much?"
Is that... pride in his voice? It's deep down, but -- maybe even unbeknownst to the man himself -- it's there.
"Hold on, you're just a *little bit* proud of René's heroics, aren't you?"
"Sorry, officer, but you're reading me all wrong." He chuckles. "I'm a man of peace and these kinds of bloody 'heroics' are only impressive to men like René himself. Certainly not to me."
He's lying.
"How did *you* find the story to be, officer?"
"This doesn't seem like a good moment to express an opinion." (Lean closer.) "I don't wanna risk it."
"*Bon dieu*," he mumbles, slowly shaking his head. "You and Gaston must be related. His blood runs yellow too."
"René, I wanted to ask, what *did* you actually get these medals for?"

dialoguetext: "René, the medal story -- Drysant's horse stepped on your knee, then what happened?"
"Already forgotten, officer."
The old carabineer stands quietly like a statue, his features motionless.
René told you his war story, now impress him with *your* heroics.
You should try to come up with a heroic story of your own -- impress this old soldier.

"That's why the Filippian kings used cocaine -- for clarity of vision, to aid in their work... Regnum Cocainum -- Revachol's finest years." He seems to grow taller, brimming with pride about the past.
"Of course," the lieutenant marks dryly. "Clarity of vision. *Awareness*."
"They used cocaine for *clarity of vision*?"
You can. It's very *asinine*.
"Because he was a *god damn* dandy!" he exclaims furiously. "Had no business leading men or even being on the battlefield. All he was, was *related*. That's it."

"Royal blood alone doesn't make army commanders. He was a stupid kid, only interested in horses, hair styles, and *manloving*." He spits. "And *seven hundred and eighty two* Royal Carabineers are dead because of his incompetence."
Whooa, *manloving*? Is that even a word?
It is not.
"You must have seen *something* on the night of the murder. Your booth looks right into the yard."
"Yes. It does." He nods. "Unfortunately I wasn't working that night. Been on a two-week leave since last Monday."
"No one. The booth has been unmanned since last Monday." He looks suddenly very old and tired. "There's no other guard. It's just me."
"Hold on, why are you on a leave?"
"So who was working your shift that night?"

"Evrart *created* this job for René, because he knows the Royal Carabineer's pension of honour and PTSD isn't something a man can live off. 'A decorated kingsman collecting tare reflects bad on the whole neighbourhood.' -- his words."
"It's a private matter," he says with dignity. "Nothing to do with your investigation."
"Look, officer," his partner jumps in. "The container yard doesn't actually need a guardsman. Never had one before René. Mr. Claire had that booth built specially for him. It's mostly *decorative*."
"You see, officer, René is the kind of man who'd rather die than admit he needs medical assistance or -- god forbid -- seek it. A real man's man. He's just gonna *ride it out*."
"The container yard has been unguarded for a week?"
"I'm fine, goddamnit! Mind your own business!" The outburst makes him clutch his chest. "It's nothing, just got to cut back on coffee."
"The *possibility* of someone being in there is enough to discourage any ill-minded individuals..." he tries to argue.
It's his heart.
"No one has been guarding the container yard since last Monday?"
"Yes." He nods, before hesitantly continuing. "It's... it's not actually an issue. I mean..."
"Evrart gets it. Big guys looking after the small and everyone working together -- I love it!"
"Such dependency only weakens a man further. Do or die -- there is no middle ground."
"René is but one man. We need a program -- get all the elderly back in the job market, keep folks motivated."
"René should *rent* out his services, invest the profit, get few more guys, expand and repeat. Wagework is a dead end."
"There's absolutely *nothing* wrong with tare-collecting. It's my side-thing too." (Proudly hold out the tare bag.)
There's a grimace of pain on the old soldier's face. Looks like he wants to argue, but can't find words. Finally his lips move: "Can we conclude the topic of my guard booth now?"
"It's not charity. Not to me..." There's a grimace of pain on the old soldier's face. Looks like he wants to add something, but can't find the words. Finally his eyes light up and he says:
"Look, officer..." He pauses like he doesn't actually know how to reply. "Can we conclude the topic of my guard booth now?"
"Yes, yes, yes," the carabineer utters angrily. "Can we conclude the topic of my guard booth now?"
"Oh, I didn't mean to imply there's something *wrong* with that," the jolly man says quickly. "I do it too. Everyone does it. It's an excellent side-thing."
Still, all you see is an old soldier refusing to replace his uniform with a civilian attire.
"Anything else I can assist you with, officer?" he asks impatiently. "We still have a game to finish."
"Is there anything you can tell me about this rifle?" (Hold out the antique firearm.)

dialoguetext: "It's a *Belle-Magrave*," he says, taking the rifle. "4.46 calibre, breech-loading, Revachol-made. Good weapon, accurate and reliable."
His moves are quick and precise as he first checks the weapon, then aims it at the sea. This man knows firearms *intimately*.
"This one's inoperable. The bolt-spring is missing and the mechanism is jammed shut. Still a beauty," he adds, handing the rifle back. "Where did you find her?"
"In the basement there." (Point at the book shop.)
"Sorry, I can't divulge that information."
"What do you mean *find*? This is my rifle, I always have it with me."
"I'm not surprised." He looks at the building. "There are probably lots of forgotten war-time weapons lying around here. Back in the day, everyone had *something* stashed away."
He nods. "I understand. Unfortunately, I don't know what else to tell you. These BM's are an antique. No one uses them anymore. The ammunition is impossible to find."
"As for the rifle -- I don't know what else to tell you." He shrugs. "These BM446s are an antique. No one uses them anymore. The ammunition is impossible to find."
"Up there I give it all I got. I *earn* my keep." He looks towards the guard booth and sighs. "But you're right officer, there is no middle ground. It's do or die."
Something about him has changed. He's calmer somehow.
He wants to argue, disagree -- but feels he's got no right, being at the mercy of Mr. Claire.
"Mostly decorative?"
"So it doesn't matter, if you're there or not?"
He is not going to become an entrepreneur.
"Thank you for your time!" [Leave.]
Could it be... guilt?
"Did you ever use artillery fire against the *communards*?"
"Pretty damn clever indeed."
"Bastards..." (Slowly shake your head.)
"Must have been a bloodpath."
"May bells don't blossom yet, do they?" the lieutenant quickly asks.
"Maybe on some remote parts of the city they do." The old carabineer shrugs. "But I think you have to wait for at least a month."
He's just making excuses for the king's habits, isn't he?
There's something you missed... You will get to it, don't worry.
"Enough," he cuts in sharply. "I can go over these matters *in detail* with you, Gaston, but not while we have company. So officers...?"
"René... I need to go back in time. Can you help me?"
*Something* isn't right about this game.
The jolly-looking man in the checkered jacket moves lazily. Like a giant tomcat stretched out in the sun...
Despite his limp, the man in the uniform moves with efficient grace. His motions are measured and precise.
Take a closer look.
That's none of my concern. [Discard thought.]
...then suddenly he leans forward and uses the 0-end of the measuring tape to nudge his opponent's balls further from the small brown sphere in the pit. As he does this, he complains about his back.
Apparently oblivious to his partner's treachery, the uniformed man grabs a ball and takes aim again.
"So the wind is... yes, perfect."
"Is my aim really *that* off?"
"Strange, I could have sworn..."
"Stop complaining and hurry up!"
"Don't get mayonnaise on the measuring tape."
"I feel 20 years younger every time it rains."
"I'm fine, just a little heart burn..."
"*Mon dieu*, how much can a man whine, Gaston?"
"Goddamn ticker..."
"It's a different game in the snow."
"Wouldn't even pick it up, if my heart wasn't in it."
"Build a solid routine and stick to it. That's all there is."
"*Mon dieu*, the pain is exceptionally bad today..."
*chews loudly*
"Not bad, René, you might stand a chance this time."
"Argh.. my back! I swear it's getting worse..."
"I'll just measure... *ouch*. I can barely move..."
"Yes, yes, the good old days. The all or nothing days."
"Would you like to play alone tomorrow?"
"How long have we known each other? Almost eighty years?"
"You are the angriest man I know, René."
"You mentioned Jeanne-Marie Beaulieu. Who is that?"
"Tell me, what do you know about the dead man?"
"Bye for now." [Leave.]
"I'm obliged by the law to tell you there's been a breach of *ethics*." (Wink and point to the balls.)
"What are the rules of this game?"

dialoguetext: "This... this isn't right, officer." He shakes his head. "René wanted to be buried in his uniform, but..."
"Officer..." The jolliness is gone from Gaston's face. "Care to play a game with a lonely old man?"
"Actually never mind... Wouldn't be the same..."
"Oh, sweet Jeannie..." He gets a dreamy look in his eyes. "She was the finest woman in all of Revachol. Maybe the entire world."
"Do not *defile* her memory, Gaston." There's an almost imperceptibly small tremble in his voice. "Let her rest in peace."
His tone lacks its usual intensity, like he doesn't feel he has the right to speak on the matter.
"So you both know her?"
"What happened to her?"
"Sounds like this is between you two. I have other matters to address."
"Sure, officer." He nods. "It's better for  René's flickering ticker too. Not that he'd ever admit anything there needs tinkering."
"We knew her, alright..." His friendly face lights up. "Lived on the same street our entire lives, just two houses apart. The three of us have been best friends since we were four."
"She was René's first girl, back when the prick was sixteen." He looks at the carabineer almost gently. "They were courting till he decided he'd rather die for some great *idéal* than just be hap---"
"AND THEN YOU STOLE HER FROM ME!" He jerks forward, but then grabs his chest and stops.
"Easy fellows, no need for this to get ugly."
"Oh, officer..." Gaston is unfazed by the outburst. "It already got ugly nearly eighty years ago when the three of us were just learning to walk and talk."
Do not intervene.
"Sorry, but I *really* wanted to just ask some questions."
"It's okay, officer." He smooths his white whiskers. "You might have just saved René from a heart attack."
"Well... technically *you* stole her from *me*, because we'd been pretty close ever since you two had that falling out over the ink you spilled over her pretty yellow dress..."
"You stole her from me," René repeats, trying to steady his breathing and still clutching his chest.
"We were just boys, then. This was different. *You*..." The tall veteran looks at you and nods.
"No point starting this all over again, for the thousandth and the first time. Especially when we have company." He turns to you: "Officer?"
"She died of pneumonia two winters ago. It was a quiet passage. Peaceful." He smiles faintly.
"René and I were both by her bedside when she..." He pauses, searching for the right word.
"Died," he sharply fills the silence and adds: "No use sugar-coating it. Won't bring her back, will it now?"
"Departed," his partner finishes his sentence, then chuckles: "Until the very end she couldn't decide between us. The most indecisive woman I've ever met."
A quick grimace of pain passes over René's features, but he immediately regains control. His face now a dispassionate mask again.
"Did you love him?"
"We've hated each other our entire lives. So much in fact that..." He falls silent and looks at you, eyes filling up with tears.
"You always confused her, couldn't let us be happy..." He says with heavy resentment. "Seduced her with your fancy words and *pastries*."
"Why do you think she was indecisive?"
"She could never make up her mind about anything. What to have for breakfast, favourite colour or which one of us to marry." The look in his eyes is happy and distant.
"She was always leaving one of us for the other, but never long enough to actually get married."
"Heck," he says with a chuckle. "*Technically* we're both still engaged to her."
"That's a bit odd."
"Women, right?"
He suddenly remembers *you* are still there, falls silent, and turns away.
"Of course, officer," he says with a smile. "Memories are all we have left."
"Thanks for sharing." (Conclude.)
"*Mon dieu*, officer!" He looks at your wounds. "It is worse than I thought! Believe me, I know all about that kind of pain, I've had hip trouble for the past... week."
"The prick is gone," he replies, trying to smile. "I... I can barely believe it, but he's really gone."
He is trying to retain his jolly façade, but the underlying sadness casts a deep shadow over his wrinkled face.
"Gone? Gone where?"
Gaston sighs and mumbles, more to himself than you: "Hell, most likely. He was an absolute cunt..."
"Was he really that bad?"
"How did he die exactly?"
"Do you know what happened to his medals?"
"I offer my sincere condolences." (Conclude.)
"Old people die, you better get ready too." (Conclude.)

"His angry little heart finally gave out." He sighs. "The dockworkers found him in the guard booth this morning. Wasn't even supposed to be working for another week, but he just had to prove how tough he is..."
"Guess he was about to head home, 'cause when the dockworkers found him he was wearing civilian clothes and not the cockatoo uniform I saw him in all the time."
"Sometimes I thought he was wearing it just to piss me off." Gaston smiles a sad smile. "Now the joke's on him, 'cause he's gonna be buried without it."
"Well, you took one of them." He shakes his head. "Still can't believe he gave it to you, but that's how rigid he was. Once the offer carelessly left his lips it was irrefutable..."

He looks at you for a moment and then speaks quietly. "I took them for myself. Took them to remember that old cunt. Nobody knew him better than I did, and I want to remember that old cunt by something."
"The other one I took for myself." He looks at you defiantly. "No one knew him better than I did, and I want to remember that old cunt by something."
Strange how  *old cunt* sounds almost gentle when he says it now.
"I repeat -- an *absolute* cunt." He turns to look at the crater. "Even his old army buddies didn't want him around. He was like an old viper."
"The only people who could stand to be around him were Jeannie and me..." He pauses. "She saw something in him when we were just kids, and..."
His voice trembles. "...a-and she never lost sight of it. And I thought if the most beautiful being in the world can love him, then there must be something worth holding on to..."
"Yes. I... I loved that angry prick. He didn't deserve it, but I did." He wipes his eyes with a sleeve. "You know what his last words to me were?"
"Some right-wing royalist slogan?"
"Something mean?"

"'In Guillaume's time you'd have been shot without a trial'. That's what he said to me." The old man gathers himself and wipes his eyes again. "He lived a cunt and he died a cunt. Let's leave it at that."
"Yes." The lieutenant nods. "We are both very sorry for your loss."
"Maybe it's time to slow down, enjoy life a bit?" He smiles apologetically. "Anything I can do to assist you?"
"I guess it doesn't really matter anymore. You do what you have to, like the rest of us... So how can I help?"
"Oh... sorry, officer... What do you want?"
Host almighty, he's a total bummer now!
"Yes..." A strange expression runs across his wrinkled face, then vanishes without trace.
"*Mon dieu*, you set it on fire!" He looks at the plaza. "What kind of a policeman are you?"
"I uh... don't know. It was an accident. I'm sorry."
"Policeman of the state yet to come."
"The herald of the apocalypse."
He finds comfort in the thought.
"We all got to go some time, officer. Everyone I love is already there. Probably waiting for me." He smiles faintly. "I'm not afraid to die. It's been a good run and I really miss my friends..."
"Hey, Gaston, I found you a new *boule*." (Hold out the ball.)

"Keep it, it's not even a real *boule*." He waves you away. "Besides, it doesn't really matter now. I've never seen anyone else play pétanque in Martinaise."
"But you probably had some official business too?" he asks and puts the hat back on.

dialoguetext: "It really wasn't bad."
Make it... *lively*!
He stares at you, aghast. "What a waste..."
"It was (*burp*) great! Nutritious as fuck! I could go all night on one of these pocket rockets!"
"Truly a masterpiece of modern gastronomy. Or should I say... *GASTONomy*." (Give the man an approving wink.)
"I don't mean to keep Gaston's tongue from your rectum, officer, but do you actually have any *police* business with us?"
"Very nourishing. Thank you!"
"I guess you don't really need taste buds for police work." He looks disappointed. "Is there anything else, officer?"
"Ugh... thank you, officer." He looks at you with disgust. "Please tell me there wasn't anything else?"
"Coming from an officer of the law, this appraisal means an awful lot to me." He bows slightly. "Thank you."
"It was a sandwich, I don't know what to tell you. I was hungry and now I'm not."
"I suggest naming it 'Gaston's Shit Sandwich', that's what I think."
"Yes, yes... and the taste?" He leans even closer. "How was the taste?"
"Taste? I just ate it, forgot to check the taste."
"*Very* nourishing indeed." (Rub your belly.)
"Oh..." He doesn't look up. "Good. Good for you, officer. I'm just wondering if René ever... never mind. Can I help you with something?"
"I uh..." He rubs his chin, not knowing what to say. "That's nice. Uh... better somehow. Can I help in any way?"
"Oh, okay..." He seems to edge away from you. "It's perfectly alright. No harm done and it's really none of my business anyway."
"Oh, okay..." He seems to edge away from you. "Well *I* certainly have full confidence in your competence. And the future," he adds quickly.
"Apocalypse?" He backs away, visibly worried. "I uh... I don't know, what this means, officer. I'm sorry. But thank you! I'm here to cooperate any way I can."
"Looks delicious." (Point to the sandwich.) "Can I have a bite of that?"

dialoguetext: "When the dissidents come to *rape* our country, he hides, but try to get a bite of his dear sandwich and he gets claws? You're a special kind of a vermin, Gaston."
"Sorry, officer, I'm sorry, I didn't mean it in a bad way," he continues cautiously. "But the sandwich is mine, I'm not gonna share it."
"Believe me, officer, I wish I could help you, but I need this sandwich to keep my blood sugar stable." He's squirming, avoiding your gaze. "In my age you need to pay attention to these things."
"FUCK OFF, it's mine!" He jerks away, immediately startled by his own reaction.
"You're not hearing me, man. I *need* the sandwich!"
"*Please*, friend, let's just share it."
"I'm sorry, officer, but I really don't share food," he says and quickly adds: "Nothing personal, it's just a principle."
"The only one you have."
The sandwich looks like a culinary wonder, well made and abundant in components. The author sure knew their craft.
Suddenly you realize how hungry you are. The last time you ate must have been... god knows when.
"Don't be a dick, Gaston, there's plenty for everyone."
"Please, man, can I just have a bite?"
"Okay... I'm not that hungry anyway."
In addition to the obvious slice of ham -- a fat one -- you notice a brim of a tomato peeking from below. And... is that mayonnaise?
You can barely hear him. The sweet smell of pickles in harmony with garlic butter and marinated onions emanating from the sandwich is driving your mind in a singular direction -- it must be yours.
"Oh, that's good, that's very good." He's visibly relieved. "You must have other business then?"
"Firewalker. I walk in the flames."
"A beacon of light in the dull shores of mediocrity. You're welcome, Martinaise."
"Oh, uh... Well thank you, officer. It certainly lightened the mood." He laughs nervously. "Very cosy, like a little street fair almost."
"The fuel oil was an environmental hazard. I had to get rid of it somehow."
"Oh..." He glances at the burnt writing. "Of course. I didn't think of it. Good job officer!"
Did he feel like he *has* to prove he can still pull his weight? Doesn't need hand-outs?
Wait... did he push himself to prove he can pull his weight and doesn't need hand-outs?
"That he's sorry?"
"Do you think our conversation about his job pushed him to go out there?"
"The irony isn't lost on me, but I wanted to ask about something else."
"I'm glad to assist you if I can, officer," he replies, voice tired and breaking.
"No," he replies quickly. "René was the most stubborn man in Revachol. Nothing you or I could say would ever *push* him to do anything. The man was completely immovable."
He has doubts, but right now he just wants to move on and not think about it.
'Do or die -- there is no middle ground' -- that's what you told René. Perhaps he wasn't *completely* immovable after all?
"It was over so quickly I didn't get a chance to form an opinion."
And *then* it hits you -- the brilliant bastard has drenched the entire sandwich in honey mustard. That's incredibly decadent. And delicious.
"No, you are not. Enforcing proper conduct in an amateur pétanque game is not something the RCM involves itself in." He smiles. "It doesn't matter."
(Whisper.) "Kim, cheating in sports is *unacceptable*. I got this."
"You're right, that's none of our business."
"What is... actually never mind." He smiles a clever smile "I'm sure there's *something* I can help you with, officer."
Doesn't matter?! Integrity in sports *doesn't matter*?! Hold me back, sonny-Jim... GODDAMNIT, it's *all* that matters!!!
Aeons ago. Probably when you were still a child.
A glimmer of respect flashes in René's eyes.
... and it's gone.
"Here, something to remember your friend by..." (Give him the photograph of René and the girl.)
"Let me see..." Gaston takes the photo, hands trembling. "This was 60 years ago! We all went to that parade. Young René looks so happy and Jeannie..." Eyes blurry with tears, he has to stop.
"I'm sorry, officer, I just..." He dries his eyes. "Thank you, *thank you* for this little memorabilia. It really means the world to me."
"That was nice," the lieutenant smiles. "A small thing for us, but invaluable to him. He probably didn't even know René had the photo."
"It is what it is, part of life really," he mumbles, only half-listening to you. "But to know someone for 79 years, then one day they're just *gone*..."
"I just don't know anymore... about anything really." He slowly shakes his head, then remembers your presence. "But you... you must need something?"
Despite their differences these men played such a significant part in each other's lives that now that one of them is gone, the other feels... just lost.
"We are both very sorry for your loss," the lieutenant bows his head. "Death of a friend is a terrible thing."
"It is what it is... part of life," he mumbles, only half-listening to you. "But to know someone for 79 years, then one day they're just *gone*..."
"I'm not afraid of death either."
"I don't want to die."
"I'm not afraid of dying -- I'm only afraid of not really living."
"I'm pretty much on my wait out myself too... can't wait to die!"
He will never play pétanque again.
That means the uniform could still be in the guard booth -- something to keep in mind if you *really* plan to give yourself to Revachol.
"Tell me."
"Something forgettable, like 'See you tomorrow' probably?"
Teacup? Oh, because of the ceramic armour. Clever.
"Let's talk some more about Jeanne-Marie."
"Sweet sweet Jeannie..." He nods, smiling. "Ask away officer, I knew her all my life."
"I want to go over few more things about René, if that's okay?"
"Sure, officer." He smiles. "They are the good guys around here. What do you need?"
"Yes?" he looks up. "What about, René?"
"Nothing wrong with weighing your options first."
"Guess he was about to head home. The dockworkers found him in his civilian clothes and not the cockatoo uniform you... ugh... confiscated."
"What? Was he killed during the mercenary tribunal?"
"Oh, he would have liked that." The old man slowly shakes his head. "Violent lives ending violently... That's how he wanted to go. Sadly it was not the case."
"Too bad René's gone, I was hoping to ask him about May bells..." (Hold out the flower.)

dialoguetext: The old man stares at the flower, then sighs and says: "René wasn't really what you'd call a botanist, officer. And believe me, he didn't like Insulindian Lilies."
"Wait, Insulindian Lillies?"
"Why didn't he like them?"
"Mhmh," he replies with a slight nod. "That's their old name, dating back to the time of kings and crests and all that other stuff he loved so much."
"There were many reasons, but mostly it was the communards. They called them 'The Bells of Revolution'." A sad smile passes his face.
"I guess in the end the Insulindian Lillies were just another piece of the Old Insulinde, the royalists had to surrender to the Mazovian insurgents. It doesn't really matter anymore."
But you feel the dried flower in your hand somehow still *does* matter. Although not to this sad old man.
Of course he didn't, flowers are for pansies. Stop wasting time with them.
"It is such a pleasure to see you again, officer. How may I aid the Citizens Militia on this fine day?"
"Officer!" He exclaims. "The mere sight of police in Martinaise makes me feel safer already. How can I help you?"
"Hello, officer." He turns to you. "How might I be of assistance on this fine day?"
"Yes, that's what you need, Gaston. More padding on that fat ass of yours. I hope your heart gives out."
"René, tsk-tsk. It's the little pleasures. Life doesn't need to be a.... *mnjam mnjam*... a struggle."
"I have really outdone myself..." He takes a bite out of his sandwich. "This is divine."
"Hey, Gaston. No comment on the duds?"
"It... isn't right." The old man doesn't even bother looking away. "René wanted to be buried in his uniform. But I guess it doesn't matter now..."
The lieutenant gives you a long, slow shake of his head.
"May René rest in peace." (Conclude.)
"Yes..." A strange expression runs across his wrinkled face, when he repeats: "in peace."
"Shame, I didn't get to ask him how to turn back time."

dialoguetext: "Real shame..." The old man nods, eyes still on the ground. He's not really paying attention to your words.
You're not gonna get anything out of this guy. If the old carabineer knew something, it will be buried with him.
No worries, just a small setback. *Movere tempore*, kingsman. For the tenacious no road is impassable. Just got to stay moving.
"Icebreaker, I plough through every ice sheet on my path."
"I uh..." He rubs his chin, not knowing what to say. "That's nice. Uh... If I'm in your way, I'll move! Or can I help in any way?"
"Gender equality is a very noble, very *modern* idea, but in real life, primal roles prevail. But I do not wish to discuss this matter further."
"No reason to even feel bad about that, it's just the way of the animal kingdom."
"And... most of the locals?"
"In Martinaise, the Union is the law, so can you really blame them?"
"But you don't have a problem with cops?"
"*Cop* is a pejorative term. I don't have a problem with policemen. On the contrary, I admire the effort to bring order to our streets."
"Unfortunately, I don't." He shrugs. "Unlike most of the locals, I have no qualms about assisting law enforcement, but this affair has passed me by completely."
"What about policewomen?"
"I am merely stating that Nature, in her infinite wisdom, has made men more fit to perform certain... more challenging tasks than women."
"I'm confident they are indispensable in regard to all the paperwork and other administrative duties."
"Not to mention keeping the station tidy and the men fed and happy."
"There are no duties RCM women couldn't carry out."
"You better not be implying that women are unfit for fieldwork..."
"There's no point in getting angry at nature, officer. This is just the way we are *made*."
"No man can afford to turn his eyes to the horizon if his rear isn't secured. If the womenfolk take care of that, then men can tackle the bigger issues."
"I try to avoid voicing opinions on controversial matters. Let's just drop it."
"Great minds think alike, René. You and I really seem to have it all figured out."
"Yes, I guess that's true."
"Really, officer?" He smirks. "Match an average woman against an average man in a dark alley and see who comes out on top."
"I guess, it might not be as black and white, but disagreeing makes me uncomfortable."
"Remaining headstrong, making tough decisions on the spot, or even tackling physical obstacles are a few examples of such *challenges*."
"I don't want to get into this argument with a police officer," he replies calmly. "Let's just say that in the last eighty-two years I have repeatedly seen my beliefs confirmed in full."
"But you must agree that Nature, in her infinite wisdom, has made men more fit to perform certain... more *challenging* tasks, don't you, officer?"
"Well, I'm glad at least some people bearing your insignia have kept a level head in these turbulent times."
"You're a bit of an asshole, aren't you, old man?"
"No, I don't think there's *any* evolutionary inequality at play here."
"You know, I'm getting second thoughts about this."
"It's as good a time as any to turn our attention to a different topic, officer," he says, adjusting his cap.
"Tell me something you are really good at and I'll find a woman who's better."
"The RCM doesn't discriminate," the lieutenant marks dryly. "Women are held to the same standards as men. And -- as reflected in the quarterly statistics -- are equally effective in their jobs."
"Unlike men, they also have to deal with the very same mentality you two are displaying right now." He frowns. "If it weren't for *this* they would outperform us."
"I know the kind," he says with a frown. "Gaston here is the same. A weathervane. Never stood up for anything in his life either."
"Oh, René..." He smiles wide and friendly. "If you only knew life beyond confrontations, conflict and extremities..."
That woman, who couldn't choose between him and Gaston -- Jeanne-Marie -- *she* must be the reason René is so bitter. He holds her indecisiveness against all women.
"So, again: you don't know anything?"
He doesn't know about the crime. Your time is better spent discussing *politics*.
"If I knew, I would not be *afraid* to tell you. I simply don't. I am an old man, not a coward. The daily business of the riff-raff no longer concerns me."
'Tis true sire. He knows nothing.
This is a man with a lot of past, but little present. And almost no future.
"Thank you, René, I am honoured." (Reach out your hand.)
"I don't deserve this." (Don't take the medal.)
"Kim, should I take it?"
Flashes of bloody and terrible scenes of war. Men dying, horses shrieking, blood sinking into sand and snow and asphalt and fertile black earth...
The man shakes his head, mumbling something under his nose, then turns back to you: "Can we get back to our game now?"
"Of course not." He doesn't even look up from his notebook.
"I uh... I had a dog -- 'Fifi'. Took her fishing late one autumn but the boat rocked and she fell in, so I jumped after..."
"And I thought getting my knee shattered and surviving on rat carcasses in the trench was bad... here, have one of my medals! You've earned it, *officer*."
"Right when you are willing to do just about anything to make it stop, you open your eyelids..."
"For your information, alcoholism is a terrible, debilitating ailment."
The veteran of numerous armed conflicts extends his right arm with the *Setting Sun* in his clenched fist and an expression of utter disbelief in his eyes.
The veteran extends his right arm with the sun-shaped medal. It glimmers in his wrinkled and scarred palm.
"Yet you do not *comprehend* the suffering of enlightenment I have endured."
"I don't think there was anything else he wanted. Was there? You got the medal, now let's solve the crime."
"Everyone can see that, yes."
"SILENCE! You know not of which you speak! I have danced with Al Gul for one thousand nights!"
"This deity of yours has quite the following in Martinaise..." He straightens his back. "None as zealous as you it seems, though."
Go long, go deep, go unconventional!
Unfortunately there doesn't seem to be anything worth mentioning among your achievements. You should resort to good old lying.
"My story doesn't have gunfire, blood or spilled guts, but let me give you a *different* take on heroism."
"Yes. Alcohol."
"Look, I don't think anyone's ever been so drunk. It must be a record."
"Imagine just flickering into existence from nothingness."
"Imagine pain that makes giving birth seem like a mosquito bite. But *inside your head*." (Point to your head.)
"You mean alcohol?"
"I'm talking about so much more than that."
"Well..." (Drag out the pause.) "In essence, yes."
"How dare you belittle my voyage through the void?!"
"Was the vessel you boarded the 'HMS Commodore Red'?"
"How so, then?" He leans in with his hands on his hips.
"Sure, officer." Already he looks sceptical. "Let's hear your *take*."
"No, I have found *The Source*. The Source of The Flow. I have found... Al Gul."

All of this, accompanied by a musical composition telling of the heroism of old, when men were bigger in both body and heart. You feel strange kinship to this old soldier. You and him are the same now.

dialoguetext: "You already threw their ball into the water, took a sandwich from one of them, and a medal from the other. What more could we possibly want? Perhaps we're done bullying these citizens?"
The old carabineer stares at you for a moment, then tension leaves him and he asks: "Was there something else you wanted to take from us?"
The man stares at you, silently frowning.
"I'm not following you."
"It must have been -- there was a magnum-sized bottle in my room..."
The carabineer crosses his arms and spits in the crater.
"You already threw their ball into the water and took his medal, perhaps we're done bullying these citizens?"
The carabineer stares at you with a frown. Doesn't look like he's buying it.
"The boat capsized and sank. Fifi was already tired. She was almost 11. I took her on my back and started swimming..."
The name echoes through the deep dark halls of history... it calls to you and your kin!
"I'm sorry, I think I just fell off the wagon that's all. I lack character..."
"It was a transcendent event. I saw behind *The Veil*."
He'll get it. Don't worry, just continue -- he's *gonna* be impressed.
"Imagine knowing nothing but the sweet oblivion only to wake into unbelievable pain..."
