dialoguetext: Too late. It's impossible to keep it in. Your body curls and pushes it out. Burst by burst...
You feel a great force wringing you from the stomach. Your body curls and pushes it out. Burst by burst...
The smell of Commodore Red rises from the pool. Among it, distilled spirit and bits of shish-kebab.
The corpse looks at no particular direction with its bulging eyes. Its mouth is silent.
"I'm sorry."
"Fucking corpse."
"Keep it." The lieutenant hands you a blue checkered handkerchief.
"Thanks." (Wipe your mouth.)
"I don't need your pity."
"It's not *pity*. You should wipe your mouth after vomiting." He pockets the handkerchief.
"It's okay, happens to everyone." The lieutenant hands you his white handkerchief: "Keep it."
"You think ammonia would help?"
"If you can handle the headache," he nods. "Some officers use it to deal with cadaverine odour."
"I don't need that shit."
"Sure you do. You just threw up *a lot*."
"That young woman, the gardener, mentioned she used salts for the smell." He nods toward the plaza.
"There's Frittte nearby, east of the hostel. They usually have a small apothecary. If they don't..." He points to the greenhouse.
"There's a greenhouse here -- and a gardener with a wheelbarrow on the corner of the Whirling-in-Rags. If she works here she might have something for the smell."
"God... this sucks."
"What now?"
"Fucking corpse."
If the lieutenant were here he would have an idea what to do. But he isn't. He's somewhere filling paperwork. Looks like you'll just have to work it out on your own.
The second time -- not so much. When the vomiting is done your cheeks are wet with tears.
"The ammonia didn't help at all..."
Spit and wipe your mouth with the handkerchief.
Spit and say nothing.
The weight is reassuring. Like a crenel on solid fortification. Pat pat pat...
"Nor does the wind right now..." You feel the lieutenant pat your back, rhythmically.
"I've seen strong men turn themselves inside out for hours. You're facing tough odds here. Alcohol withdrawal makes it considerably harder."
"Are you okay, officer?" You feel the lieutenant pat you on the back. Heavy, rhythmic pats.
The weight is reassuring. Like a crenel on solid fortification. Pat pat pat...
"You're facing tough odds here. It's aggravated further by alcohol withdrawal."

"I've seen *captains* puke their guts out. It never gets easier, you never get used to the smell. Every Monday is cadaver day -- throw up, investigate, throw up, initial autopsy, throw up, bag it..." He pats your back again.
"I failed *AGAIN*!"
"Why can't I keep it in if I've been a cop my whole life?
"This is *bullshit*. I don't wanna do this anymore. I don't wanna be a cop."
"Can't we do something else? I think I want to solve something else now."
"You seem to be fine."
"Okay."
"Then drive to the station, maybe throw up on the way there if you didn't bag the thing tight enough."
"I think I've lost my sense of smell." There's a pause.
A white lie.
"Not being hungover helps too."
"Monday -- make sure you bring a handkerchief."
"Get a hold of yourself." You feel the lieutenant pat your back, rhythmically.
"I think I don't wanna be a cop anymore..."
"Do it without me. I just can't keep it down."
"Okay. You've said it. You needed to say it, and now that you have..." He withdraws his hand from your back and looks you in the eye:
"You need to get your shit together."
"That's probably a good idea. Clear our heads. But before we can do that..." He withdraws his hand from your back and looks you in the eye:
"No. This is a two-man assignment, because it needs two officers to complete. I need your help." He withdraws his hand and looks you in the eye:
You are being weak. This is weakness -- and it cannot go on much longer, or you will LOSE.
"Give me a moment. I got this. Let's try *again*."
Say nothing -- just nod.
"Okay."
"An appropriate attitude." He withdraws his hand and looks you in the eye:
"But I don't wanna get my shit together!"
"But my shit already *is* together!"
"No, it's not officer."
"Then the world will turn away from you, and leave you behind."
(Shake your head.) "No."
"No?" The lieutenant's expression is stern and impenetrable. He points at you: "You *will* get your shit together."
You're sure this has not affected his impression of you in a good way.
"We should go talk to the locals, find something else to do while the wind changes. It's pretty bad right now."
"Give it half an hour, get yourself together, then come back and have another go."
WHAT IS HAPPENING TO YOU?!?! Are you going to CRY now, son?
You heard the coach! This is weakness. It cannot go on much longer, or you will LOSE.
For a moment, the hanged man appears to smile. His lips are red like a clown's.

It's especially painful this time. You've thrown up so much there's nary anything left down there. Hot tears of pain streak down your face -- you're crying too. Crying and convulsing at the same time.
Just cry.
The lieutenant is clearly at a loss.
Little black bubbles pop on the corpse's lips, decay liquid like tar. It's like he's gurgling.
"What do I do now?"
"Officer, you just need to be stronger. Learn to keep it in long enough for us to work. There's nothing else *to* do."
Your muscles tense up. The vision in your dead angle darkens. You feel the sudden urge to push your hand into his soft gut.
The spell has no effect. You stand eye to eye with it, the odour washing through you.
This delicate machine, ready for picking... Instinctively you crack your fingers.

The material appears to be ceramic. Its clean white stands in stark contrast to the decaying flesh above the knee. The man wore thick polymer socks, probably for padding. A fine array of interlocking plates covers them.
Knock on the boot.
Pull the boot off.
A small bell-like sound fills the air. Like tapping on the side of a porcelain cup.
Delicate and fragile, they feel alien to the world around you. Out of place somehow.
"The material looks out of place here."
"It is. It's expensive." The lieutenant draws a line in the condensation on the ceramic -- with his index finger.
"We've requested similar material for our tactical units for years now. The Constabulary's deemed it too costly. In that time, we've lost six men to semi-automatics."
"How much are we talking about?"
"For a full set -- about four years of wages."
For the Northwest Region of Revachol, an officer's average yearly income is 5,500 reál (unadjusted for rank).
"Wait -- my yearly pay is 5,500 reál?"
"Ka-ching, baby!" (Nod to the boots.)
"Not too much, yes."
"By *ka-ching* do you mean..." He tilts his head. "'Let's not log them as evidence, let's steal them'?"
The only difference is a barely audible *click* underneath. Sounds like the end of a long dice roll.
"These aren't just boots, are they -- they're armour."
"No. That's not what I meant."
"If this *Constabulatory* is dragging their feet why not start ourselves, before more good men die?"
What was that about the Constabulatory before? You need to push some buttons if you want to recruit the lieutenant in a conspiracy.
"It's enough."
"Pathetic. I need to hustle more and hate less."
"Sounds puny. No wonder I can't pay my hostel bill."
"I have no idea what that means."
The lieutenant nods, wiping his finger on his sleeve.
"It's a sorry situation, I agree."
Swing the prybar at the boot.
"Sounds fragile."
Punch it harder.
Suddenly your biceps coil up. Your elbow is sharp and cocked for a punch.
The prybar in your hand is itching for some action.
The metal connects with the same *ding*. The sound does not appear to get louder...
The lieutenant cups his ear: "Did you hear that? A click?"
"What do you mean?"
"Yes, like dice rolling."
"This material is a kinetic re-distributor. It spreads kinetic energy horizontally. From plate to plate. When the plates connect there's a click." He points to the toe. "See these lines?"

"This is a kinetic re-distributor. It spreads the incoming energy horizontally, from plate to plate. When the plates connect, there's a click. That's the sound you heard." He points to the toe. "See these lines?"
These are clearly not boots, they're *armour*. Possibly part of a larger set.
"Ceramic plate. Zirconium dioxide most likely. This is where the make would be..."
"Indeed..." With his notebook under his arm the lieutenant crouches to inspect the soles: "Technically speaking these are *sabatons*, not boots."
Oh! The lieutenant uses a Mnemotechnique A6 -- that's not just any notebook, it's a classic!
Thanks, super useful to know.
Forget about the notebook -- tell me about the armour!
It's clearly some manner of super-armour. Or future armour? Super-future armour? I'm useless.
It's all you, baby.
"What kind of armour is this exactly?"
"Where?"
"Under the heel. Fairweather..." He turns the boot slightly. "Fairweather model T-500 / VE. I'm guessing that's 'vitreous enamel'. This is advanced stuff."
The sabatons dangle off the man's decaying form, ageless and synthetic.
"The locals probably scavenged it -- it would be odd if he had more on after *seven* days."
He nods: "Piece by piece. He's been out here for seven days -- it would be odd if they didn't."
"No. He must have worn something precious underneath his clothes. They've removed all his clothes to get to it -- they did not just strip him for the putrid rags."
"What if they told him to strip before they hung him? To demean him?"
"*They* usually hang them completely naked for that. La Puta Madre, the Mazda, the Besmerties, and the like. This one still has his underpants."
"Then where are these clothes -- have you seen any around?"
"Someone could have cleaned the yard. But that's a question for... the red-haired thing."
"I hear you, f****t cop. Talking shit 'bout the Cuno. Come here and say it to Cuno's face!"
"Cuno this boot-shit is super boring and the guys are total *vittupää's*."
"What are you tryin'a ignore me now, fuck face?"
"Fuck you, Cuno!"
"You wanna fuck me, huh? You wanna FUCK the Cuno?"
"What happened to the rest of it?"
"Maybe he was just wearing these boots and there is no rest of the armour?"
"Of course." He nods.
The lieutenant nods often. It's part of his un-plastic expression range, communicating both professionalism and sarcasm. This time, the latter.
"So they don't get shot in the foot? I think our *extremities* are fine without a dead man's boots."
"Yeah."
Oops. Well, no one said it would work. Back to detecting now.
"That's a lot, I take it?"
"As a wage, it's regrettably small. But for a piece of hardware -- yes, that's a lot."
(Point to it.) "Looks like there's a serial number on the right sabaton."
"Good. Can you read it to me?" He tips the drying ball point of his pen on his tongue.
"We have a make and a number -- that's something. We can use the radio in my Kineema to run it later. Either station can chase it for us."
True. It didn't have the cadence and logic of a real manufactured item.
"Officer, the decomposing corpse has temporarily suspended my sense of humour. Let's continue in a less playful manner." He pauses to think. "Anyway..."
"We have a make and a number -- that's something. We can use the radio in my Kineema when we're done. Either station can chase it for us."
"That doesn't sound like a serial number. Where's the structure and logic of a line of manufactured products..." He pauses to think. "No matter. We should run it anyway."
"Understood."
Your fist connects to the boot with the same *ding*. The sound does not appear to get louder.
"It's anything but. This material is a kinetic re-distributor. It spreads kinetic energy horizontally, from plate to plate. Dissipating it entirely." He points to the boots. "See?"
Faint, organic lines cover the plates where they separate into smaller ones. These plates then divide into smaller plates, until there are hundreds of them altogether...
"How could this man afford such expensive hardware?"
"That's for us to find out." He checks his notes. "Mr... Garte implied he was security personnel for the harbour company. This confirms my own assumptions."
"That's for us to find out. My initial report on the area suggests he was a security guard for the harbour company -- but that's just hearsay."
"These look pretty advanced for a security guard."
"Okay. Makes sense."
"No." He shakes his head. "Your first instinct was correct. This equipment is way beyond what a security guard can afford."
"I agree. This equipment is *way* beyond what a guard can afford."
"What kind of boots are these?"
Back off.
"They're armour, not boots." With his notebook under his arm the lieutenant crouches to inspect the soles: "Technically speaking these are *sabatons*."
"Okay then -- what kind of *armour* is this?"
The cadaver slowly twists on the cargo belt, his torso covered in tattoos and extremities blotched pink and blue.
(Back off and look at the corpse.)
The stench fills your nostrils. As you push downward, an ominous creaking sound comes from above.
"Stop!" The lieutenant's voice is sharp. He looks at you, with the boot under your arm.
"What?"
"Lieutenant, you seem distressed -- why?"
"Oh! This is a bad idea, isn't it?"
"You're going to pull his head off."
"Do what?"
"I'm gonna pull his head off, right?"
"Pig's gonna pull his head off."
"Brutal."
"Yes, that's what I said. You'll compromise the coroner's case if you do. So please *don't*."
"You're about to pull his head off."
"Even the mongrels can see you're about to pull his head off."
"Do it, homo!"
Indeed. From this angle it does look like the neck isn't going to take much more. Being dead for a week has all but liquefied his muscles.
"I'm not a homo."
"Stop obsessing about your sexuality officer, you're about to seriously compromise the coroner's case."
"*Pull his head off*. There's no point performing an autopsy if you do, we'll have compromised the coroner's case."
"What are you trying to achieve anyway, why are you hanging on to that boot?"
Let go of the boot.
"What's wrong with you, asshole? Why's he letting go, Cuno?"
"I don't know, baby," Cuno shrugs. "I don't know why he's such a f*g."
"Officer, if I may ask -- what were you trying to achieve by pulling on the deceased foot?"
"These boots would go super well with my bell-bottom pants."
"This is advanced enemy technology. We should conduct research into their weaknesses."
"Are we not detectives? There may be *clues* inside the boot."
"They look fancy. I thought I could pawn them, earn some *lucre*."
"It's that Constabulatory thing I said before. With the dead guys. I wanna *protect* them."
"I'm sorry. I didn't even want to take them off, I just thought I should try."
"This is not the *enemy*, this is the deceased. The victim. In a murder investigation."
Is he now? A sense of danger emanates from the remains of the person in front of you.
...like whorls of floorboards. The design looks organic, influenced by highly resistant wood materials, like Lignum Vitae and ebony perhaps.
For a quarter of a second he appears to be looking at you. The stench of death makes your eyes well up.
"I feel as though we may cross paths with him yet. One way or another."
"You're right, that makes sense."
"Better safe than sorry."

"There's no way you're getting them off. All the organic matter in his body has been flowing down into the boots. For *seven* days. They're *fused* to his feet now -- why do you think they're the only thing left on him?"
"You do understand the boots are steeped in cadaverine odour, don't you?"
"So are my pants."
"Can't I just wash them?"
"You're right. I didn't think this through. It was an impulse thing."

"There's no way you're getting them off. All the organic matter in his body has been flowing down into the boots. They're *fused* to his feet now -- why do you think the locals haven't scavenged them yet?"
"You'd have to boil them in acid. Besides..." The lieutenant taps on the boot.
"You have a point there, detective. You have a point. But..." The lieutenant taps on the boot.
"That doesn't mean anything, detective. Besides..." The lieutenant taps on the boot.
"It *does* make sense, doesn't it? Besides..." The lieutenant taps on the boot.
"One way or *another?* I can't even think of the *one* way... *magic*? *Semenese corpse salt*? Besides..." The lieutenant taps on the boot.
You're *sure* there's a way to peel them off -- but first the body needs to be down. And second, it would probably be better if the lieutenant wasn't around...
"How many clues do you need? You already found the number. Besides..." He taps on the boot.
"Maybe we should concentrate on what's outside the boot and leave what's inside to the boys at Processing? Just this once? Besides..." He taps on the boot.
It's hard to get a read on the lieutenant. What would he do if you stole them? Would he report you, or not? Surprisingly, you feel like he probably wouldn't.
"For a full set of armour I wouldn't blame you. But these boots are hardly worth a disciplinary hearing. There are better ways to pay a hostel bill. Besides..." He taps the boot.
"Honestly -- a whole set of ceramics: the breastplate, the pauldrons... I wouldn't blame you. But these two? Not worth bringing Internal Affairs into your life over. Besides..." He taps the boot.
"Okay. Fine. You want to protect the *feet* of six dead men. That's commendable. But..." The lieutenant taps on the boot.
"I don't think we should *do* anything just for the hell of it. Besides..." The lieutenant taps on the boot.
This feels... dangerous. Are you sure?
There might still be a way to peel them off, but first the body needs to be down. And second -- it would probably be better if the lieutenant wasn't around...
Sounds like a plan. (Accept.)
Steal a dead man's boots? But that would be *DISHONOURABLE*! (Refuse -- for honour.)
The anticipation makes you crack your fingers. Feels nice. Nice and *cracky*.
All right then, you can pay the hostel bill in *honour* points. How many honour points have you collected?
There are honour points?
"What's going to happen to the boots then?"
"Okay, got it."
Of course there aren't, don't be naive.
You still feel as though there might be some honour points. And if there are, you've surely earned one.
"Processing will take care of them. With the situation in the morgue, it will yield nothing. But we must pick our fights." He looks toward the boots. "Should we continue?"
Grab the boot under your arm.
Better not even try.

The man before you is naked, but for a pair of underpants and white boots. His skin is marbled with decaying veins and blotched by lividity. On his chest: a fading web of tattoos. The cargo belt used to hang him from the tree looks reinforced.
"Initial report?"
"Just something I scraped together from my station. An area report on Martinaise. I'm sure you did the same..."
He's not actually sure of that. He's just being tactful.
As you narrow your eyes, the monster before you blurs into a violent mess of green and pink.
Only the lower extremities are pink with a dash of blue: his fatted hands, thighs and his neck, just above the noose. The rest of the corpse appears dark green in the cold spring air.
Observe.
Stop, relax your eyes.
"His face and hands are pink. Thighs too."
"I'm squinting, Kim. Why am I doing it?"
"How should I know why you're squinting, officer?"
(Squint harder) "His face and hands are pink. Thighs too. The rest is greenish."
(Stop squinting) "I don't know either. Maybe I should just stop."
"Oh," he snorts. "You're trying to assess *lividity*."
The monster comes back into focus: an explosion of colour, coursing with dark marbled veins. His stomach appears pregnant with something -- black liquid streams down his thigh and onto his boot.
"I see it." He adjusts his glasses. "His neck too, the lividity goes right up his chin. We have good, well-pronounced discolouration here..."
(Cover your nose.) "Something is coming out of him."
"Should we worry? His stomach looks like it's gonna explode."
A pool of blood and faeces has eaten into the frozen mud below the man's feet. Purge liquid is dripping into it, drop by drop.
"The victim appears to have contained no more than half a kilogram of digestion at the time of death."
"We got lucky."
"Maybe he went to the toilet some time before death?"
"God damn right I'm a f****t!" (Turn around and yell.)
"Did we? I don't *feel* lucky."
"Maybe." He doesn't *really* want to dwell on it too long.
"F****ts talkin' 'bout shit."
"The fuck he sayin'?"
Malicious laughter erupts in the yard. Sounds like seagulls.
The lieutenant's face is made of stone.
"Pig said he's a f****t."
"I think he was upright immediately after death. Blood has gathered in his hands and feet. And his neck." He points to his fattened chin.
"Could it still be he was moved after death?"
"Maybe he was strangled by someone?"
You would still like the hypostasis marks in the neck to be a *bit* more pronounced.
"For some reason my brain would like the pink to be more pronounced, especially in the neck."
"Maybe it looks faint to you?" He leans closer, covering his nose: "It *could* be more pronounced, actually. Dûment noté."
"Yes, there's always a chance we're wrong. We should check for ligament marks on his neck to see if they're in tune with the belt. We'll have to get him *down* first..."
"There's always a chance. We should check for ligament marks on his neck to see if they're in tune with the belt. We'll have to get him *down* first..."
(Back off and catch your breath.)
But there is no breath to catch -- only the cadaver filling the air and your nostrils. He slowly rotates before you, decomposing.
"I don't know what to think. What do you think?"
"There's a..." his eye twitches for a moment, "a strong build-up of gases, yes. Rigor mortis becoming livor mortis. He'll be fully limp by tomorrow. I don't think he'll explode... I *hope* not."
"I've kept an eye on the forecast. It's been below freezing since last Sunday. Today is the first chance to thaw. Things would be... *worse* if it had thawed earlier."
"As I said it's been below freezing since last Sunday. Today is the first chance to thaw. Things would be... *worse* if it had thawed earlier."
The hangman's knot is pulled tight by the weight of the corpse below. Yellow, hard-edged polyester cuts into his neck. Above, a sliding buckle ties the belt to the branch.
"We should have a look at that belt before we even *consider* taking him down. It looks worrisome." (He points to the belt around his neck.)
This is a steel-reinforced cargo lashing belt, big brother of the regular cargo belt. It's used for tying cargo under six-rotor airships.
"What kind of rope is this?"
"Don't ask me how I know -- but this is a lashing belt used for airlifting cargo."
"Industrial strength. The kind used for tying cargo to lorries."
Relax your eyes.
"For a week he seems *well* preserved actually."
For seven days the cadaver is quite well preserved. Surprisingly so -- there's no deflation, no apparent fly larvae in the abdomen.
"He's beaten up -- see the bruises?"
"I do. Most of them are postmortem. Maybe even all of them. The delinquents have made our jobs harder with their little sport."
Keep it to yourself.
Good. Death does not care for your smart alecking. It reeks and disintegrates in a feast for cadaverine bacteria.
"Stop talking in riddles, coin slot."
"He means you fucked him up good, Cuno," the girl yells. "Fucked him up brutal-like."
Oh my, there's something on the belt... a familiar word that speaks to the *thirst* within you.
What was that? A word?
VERMILLION, in yellow letters along the length of the twisting cargo belt. Only a deep longing for Vermillion *Golden Spirits* lets you decipher the fading logo of the local brewery.
"I should get a drink."
"No. You should *not* get a drink. You should perform an initial inspection of the victim's corpse -- we're on the rope part."
"Airlifting? I thought it was used on lorries -- for strapping cargo to them."
"Apparently this is the reinforced kind. For air transport. My brain tells me so."
He nods. "The local harbour uses six-rotors to shuffle containers around. I get the sense they used whatever was on hand, without paying much attention to not incriminating themselves."
"Then again what do I know? I don't even know what an airship is!"
"No, you're right. The harbour uses six-rotors to shuffle containers around. They used whatever was on hand here. Without paying attention to not incriminating themselves."
"We're assuming dockworkers from the harbour did it?"
"I'm still approaching this as a lynching, yes. Motivated by the ongoing strike." He politely raises an eyebrow: "You?"
"Like in a harbour?"
"In a... I can't come up with anything other than a harbour."
"Yes. It looks like they used whatever was on hand, paying no attention to not incriminating themselves."
Like in a circus! When the circus leaves town and they tie a black spotted giraffe to the wall of a carry-pen!
"Like in a circus, for transporting black spotted giraffes?"

"Uhm..." He considers it: "No. More like in a *harbour*. Like the one just east of here. I get the sense they used whatever was on hand, without paying much attention to not incriminating themselves."
"The brief suggested as much. Politically motivated by the ongoing strike... did you not get a briefing?"
"Uhm, yeah."
"No. They might have forgotten to brief me."
"Then you should ask me the first moment we get."
"My past has undergone total annihilation. Nothing remains -- my mother, the love of my life. Certainly not a *briefing*."
"Okay." He blinks. "You should ask me for one the first moment we get."
"Makes sense. Believably mundane."
"I feel like it was something else."
"Don't ask me, I'm just lumbering from one moment to the next."
No. You *feel* like it was something else -- but what?
"Yes." He covers his nose. "It often is. This belt worries me."
"Seventy percent of the cases I get are just filling in the blanks on the initial report." He covers his nose. "This belt worries me."
"We all are." He covers his nose. "This belt worries me."
(Back off and look at the corpse.)
"They sure wanted him to stay there. The polyester seems strong."
"I was afraid it would be..." He rises to inspect the noose. "Thin steel wiring, parallel strands. This makes getting him down more problematic than I had assumed..."
"It's not merely polyester -- it's steel reinforced." He rises to inspect the noose. "See these lines? This is where the wires run. I see rabbets for more than twenty strands."
Ignore it.
It's hard, but somehow you manage not to see it. The corpse looks at you sideways, from an unnatural angle.

An intricate web of blue lines stretches across the torso. From the right shoulder to the solar plexus, each time they intersect a small white star is formed in their crossing. Hundreds of fading asterisks riddle his skin, their concentration is highest around his heart.
His corpse is marked by stars.
What will mine be marked by?
Alcohol and heartbreak.
It will be marked by bullet holes.
Your fist clenches suddenly.
It will be riddled with disco.
"Is this a map of the night sky?"
"Is this a micro-electronic system?"

"At least *something* good came out of all this." The lieutenant glances at the badge in your hands.
The man in the photo looks at you solemnly.
Study the badge.
[Leave.]
You see: a photo, a name, a rank, a document number, the date of issue, and -- in the lower right corner -- your precinct.
How old?
Eight, maybe ten years. The guy in the picture is rather good looking. He's got a nice haircut and is distinctly lacking in massive sideburns.
And he's winking? Why?
Why do you think? His face is already contorted by the Expression. Although it looks less grotesque on him than it does on you now.
It looks better on him because he isn't in as much *pain* while producing it as you are now. Although there's already a hint of that pain, certainly.
Don't be fooled. The bad times have already begun.
Wake up the past and tell it to stay awake -- the bad times are here to stay.
No, he's not. He's going keep calling you "officer" when he's angry with you -- and "detective" when he's not.
It's meant to keep you safe.
...from bullets, hunger, shrapnel, kidnappings, and worse.
He's not going to call you Harrier. He'll keep calling you 'officer' when he's angry with you and 'detective' when he's not.
"What is a 'lieutenant double-yefreitor?'"
"The lieutenant is a rank above sergeant and below captain. It's the highest rank in the RCM that still does field work. I am a lieutenant."
"And double-yefreitor?"

"The title of yefreitor is added to your rank when you decline a promotion to a higher rank -- in your case, captain," the lieutenant explains. "You have declined twice. Thus you're double-yefreitor."
"Declined?"

"There are many reasons one would do this. The rank above you in your precinct's *décomptage* might be taken. Or sometimes promoted officers do not *want* to replace their superiors -- out of respect."
"And sometimes," he continues, "they just prefer the type of police work available to their current rank -- in your case, lieutenant."
Heavy-duty case-solving machine.

The countdown is modelled after the dual-leadership system employed by the Left during the Revolution. Which in turn was developed by last century experimental psychologists in the University of Koenigstein.
"The lowest rank is junior officer -- usually teenagers. Then there are the patrol officers. Then sergeants, lieutenants, and then a captain. That's basically it, except for a few kinks."
"What kinks?"
"Kinks like satellite-officers and the additional yefreitor rank I already explained."
"Wait -- satellite-officers?"
"Thanks for explaining all this." (Don't mention it.)
"My pleasure."
"You are given the title of 'satellite-officer' if your partner is quickly promoted through the ranks and you rise with him. You don't seem to be a satellite..."
"So you've been putting up with all my bullshit because I'm your superior?"
"So you've been putting up with me because we're of the same rank?"
"I'm not putting up with anything," the lieutenant says with a little smile. "You put your life on the line and we came out on top. That matters."
"No. I've been putting up with you because, despite an unconventional approach, you're doing good police work."
"More than driving your motor carriage into the sea. The upside of that is, of course, you finding your badge."
"It matters more than driving your motor carriage into the sea." He smiles encouragingly. "And now we've even found your badge."
Don't be fooled. The bad times have already begun.
The numbers are not there for 'good measure'. They have an administrative purpose. One that's unfortunately been erased from your memory.
The lack of alcohol swelling is a bonus. Though there's a *pinch* of that in your cheeks already.
A name like armour.
The badge in your hands shines as you rotate it, catching light. You see lines of information:
He trusts you -- for now. Try not to spoil it.
Still -- he doesn't trust you completely.
Such a small yet precious thing. Expensive paper caught between thick plastic like a fly in amber. It reads:
The long and short of it is: you're his superior.
"A new badge usually comes with a new rank. You seem to have been... doing well then."
But the badge is new. You used an old photo for a new badge.
Good choice. A newer photo would look... different.
"Four months ago? Seems like a new document was recently made. One is handed to you as part of a promotion, or... if you lose the old one.
A new document is given to you as part of a promotion. Or when you lose the old one.
The pain in your chest tells you you were working yourself to death to earn that rank.
The case created a lot of *edge* you have to *take off*. The death march really gets us going.
You're pretty sure you weren't doing *well* -- but better? Probably yes.
I remember that time... the tie around your neck feels tight suddenly. That was a good time. We had a good work/drink balance going. What happened, man? Pump it up.
"What?
"It's a *tough* station to work in. You have all of Jamrock to cover -- that district should have *three* precincts, but money is what it is."
It's no wonder you are like you are, he thinks. But then again...
"But then again..." A faint smile. "It's a legendary district. And a hell of a station too. It must be an honour and a curse to work with people like Pryce, McCoy, Berdyayeva..."
And you? Is it an honour to work with you? Don't ask him, ask yourself.
He knew all those people although they're not from his station. They must be big.
...Roberts, Feuerbach, De Mettrie... suddenly names from your décomptage flash in your forebrain.
A crumpled billboard reading "SAMARAN BUTTER" soaks in the canal. Two ugly lines mar the bright countenance of the blond boy depicted.
What is Samaran Butter?
Whatever it is, the boy on the billboard seems very happy about it.
Goat milk butter. The Samaran terrain makes it easier to raise goats than cows, and the local goat farmers produce high-quality meat and dairy staples that add variety to other nations' diets.
It's an acquired taste.
Attempt to reconstruct what happened here.
Just some tasteless advertising at the bottom of a canal. No use rubbernecking now.
Judging by the size of the impact and the parallel lines of burnt rubber, the cause was probably a motor vehicle.
Look at the crater.
Look at the roof of the shack.
Look at the broken posts.
Look at the sign.
Look at the opposite bank.
What was the model of this phantom vehicle?

dialoguetext: Nothing more to see here. [Leave.]
There are two good candidates: the Coupris 40 and the Linnea G22.
Why the Coupris 40?
Why the Linnea G22?
It's about the right size, and the tyre marks look like they came from the skinny tyres frequently found on that motor carriage.
Very sturdy but light motor carriage. More likely than most to survive that jump.
Blink. [Leave.]
What now?
The SAMARAN BUTTER billboard still looks freshly painted, suggesting it took the plunge recently.
How recently?
Within the past 72 hours.
The black marks on the roof indicate that the vehicle *vaulted* from the crater to the roof of the shack.
Side slip marks indicate that the vehicle was travelling up the crater at 35 km/h.
The vehicle soared through the air, hitting the billboard and upsetting the posts. Then it continued its flight, taking the billboard with it.
The sign broke the vehicle's fall into the canal.
Look at the sloping metal roof panel.
The panel served as a take-off ramp.
Still speeding, the vehicle made a loop and vanished into the fog along the coast.
The Coupris 40 is a very popular model with bank clerks, topping-pie delivery drivers, secondary school teachers, cops, strippers dressed as cops, undressed strippers...
The Linnea G22 is not a particularly popular model due to its peculiar proportions, which the manufacturer's design team probably thought about for too long.
These look like the same tyre tracks I saw earlier -- in front of the Whirling-in-Rags.
Now? You'd have to follow the tracks to be sure.
The crumpled SAMARAN BUTTER billboard still soaks in the canal, marked by tyre tracks.
The lieutenant looks on, waiting for you to wrap up your analysis.
These match the tyre tracks you saw earlier -- *your* tyre tracks.
"Yup -- *I* did this."
"Yup -- *I* did this."
Clearly. The motor carriage in question was a Coupris 40 -- mere minutes before it took a final voyage into the ocean.
"Clearly, yes. Dwelling on it longer only makes it worse."
The sign billboard has fallen on the water lock, keeping it open -- and thus out of order.
He's well composed, but underneath it you sense *psychedelic* processes, bubbling. Some kind of drug maybe?
"Do you know anything about the traffic menace on the loose?"
His courtesy is not insincere, but he prefers being alone with his projector, just watching the movement of light across the walls of the shop.
"I have other business to take care of now." [Leave.]
Is Roy high -- and if yes, then what is he on?
Nope, still no clue. You obviously haven't been doing enough drugs lately.
Feeling warm and enthralled by the movement of light, while the mind continues to race forward? Lucky bastard -- he's probably on Pyrholidon. It's tough to come by on the street.
Okay, he definitely *is* high. Whatever it is you've probably done it -- and many other things besides. But you can't cut through the jumble of sensations to get to the answer.
"Is it just me, or is it really warm in here?" (Look around.)
(Get straight to the point.) "So, where does a man get Pyrholidon these days?"
There's a note of indignation in his voice. Interesting.
"No judgement -- just curious. I probably did loads of Pyrholidon before I lost my memory."
"I've *had* to take it, you know, since the People's Pile clean-up," he responds carefully. "I was with the Emergency Relief Brigade."
"It must have been tough -- radioactive clean-up."
"How did you end up running a pawnshop?"
"There's something I'd like to sell."
"Let me have a look."
He takes a step back, studying you. "How would I know?"
He tilts his head. "I try to keep the shop at a comfortable temperature."
"Traffic... I'm sorry, officer, but I don't drive."
"It's pretty obvious that you're under the influence, sir."
"Chill out, man -- I'm a chill out cop who just wants some of what you're having." (Wink.)
He frowns. "Pyrholidon is just something I... you know, since the People's Pile disaster." He coughs, as if to mark his words.
"I was with the Emergency Relief Brigade. Had to take it for radiation sickness."
"I lived by the river since I was a small boy. The Esperance... didn't have the heart to let it all go to shit without trying to *do* something, to help out."
He hesitates. "There's a reason why everyone's tried to forget any of it ever happened, and why no one has tried to repair or replace the Pile."
"Whose fault was it that the generator failed?"
"No one's, everyone's..." He sighs and shakes his head.
"The clean-up happened fifteen years ago. I was young then. Later my second aunt died, left me this shack and the assorted junk in it."

"So I came to Martinaise. People told me don't go there, it's a *shit-hole*. I said: people, we just had a *nuclear pile meltdown*. I'm gonna get as far from Faubourg as I can. Still in the same city, but..." He shrugs.
"Thank you for telling me." (Conclude.)
"But didn't you hear it when the traffic menace drove over your roof?"
"Now that I think about it, I do remember hearing a thunderous noise the other night -- some kind of powerful electric vortex hitting the shop and then moving on..."
He shrugs. "I like theory more than story. Outward movement, not vortices."
"Someone else came here earlier today asking the same question -- I promptly sold her the gun you pawned a couple days back."
"Wait, I *sold* you my gun?"
"Was the buyer a policeman too?"
"Any idea where I can find this buyer?"
"At least now I know how I lost my sidearm. Let's talk about something else." (Conclude.)
"You were adamant about getting rid of it, officer." He hesitates. "Said you were *undeserving* of a service weapon of the Revachol Citizens Militia."
"And I don't like keeping guns around the shop for long. Off-the-charts photon emissions. The unhealthy kind."

"She didn't seem like a policeman, although she kept referring to herself as a *Pig*. Which was odd. I found her interest in the gun a bit... obsessive. But I was just happy to get rid of it. And of her."
"Truth be told, she was terrifying."
"Right, so let me get this right," the lieutenant turns to you, "you sold your sidearm, issued by the Citizens Militia, and now a civilian is running around the streets of Martinaise with it."
"There is only one explanation. She must be one of my rabid fans."
"Maybe she's a vigilante. Wants to prove she can do our jobs better than we can."
"I don't like it either. What if she intends to commit a crime and blame it on the Citizens Militia?"
"She must be one of my adoring fans. Just wanted to feel closer to me, you know."
"Maybe she's a vigilante. Wants to prove she can patrol the streets more effectively than the Citizens Militia."
"What if she intends to commit a crime and blame it on the Citizens Militia? On *me*?"
"You gotta help me find her, man."
"In that case, she'll be happy to get a visit from us. *If* we can find her..." He looks around, worried.
"It's possible in these parts of town. We ought to find her and discourage her from taking justice into her own hands." He looks around, worried.
"You're right that she could cast aspersions on the force. We have to find her." He looks around, worried.
"Sure, man."
"Oh... I certainly hope not."
He tenses. "I hadn't considered that... This is why I don't like to deal with guns."
"I wish I could help with that, officer, but I don't know where she was from or where she was going."
He considered it, but his priority was to get rid of the gun as quickly as possible -- albeit for a price.
He's trying to ingratiate himself with you by anticipating your questions. He knows he shouldn't have sold the gun.
He's doubtful, but doesn't see the point in contradicting a notion that is so dear to you.
He steps further back behind the bullet-resistant glass, visibly perturbed. He doesn't want to be involved in any *incidents*.
"My apologies, officer, but I have no idea where she was coming from or where she went."
"So much disappointment -- and early deaths, cancer mostly. And we knew all that was coming even as we were *cleaning up* as best we could."
"The People's Pile? What's that?"
"Tell me more about this Emergency Relief Brigade you were part of."
He points at the white triangle on his orange safety jacket. "We were an all-volunteer force, self-organized. Tried to help fire brigades contain the spill."
"That sure narrows down our list of suspects."
"Does that mean you don't have any idea who the driver was?"
He shakes his head slowly.
"A vortex? Sounds fascinating."
"Yeah, it was pretty wild. I didn't really know what to make of it, but I know it meant *something*."
"Wait, why don't you drive?"
"I just don't like it very much. Movement on the road never really gelled well with the movement of my thoughts."
"Yet another sign that the end is nigh... It must be destiny that brought me here. Tell me more about this vortex?"
"The end... I don't know about that. Seemed more like a sign of a large-scale transformation. Shook the entire shack."
"I don't have anything to sell at the moment."
"Anything else you're thinking of selling?"
"I'd like to sell my clothes."
"I have a fascinating photo of a corpse here." (Show him the photo.)
"I'm not purchasing any more clothing at the moment..." He looks you up and down quickly.
Suddenly, his gaze fixes on your tie. He steps back from the glass. "And *especially* that tie. It swallows photons around it. I have no need for *necrotic* objects."
"You might be able to aid my investigation."
"I doubt it, but I can try to answer any questions you may have."
"Know anything about the recent hanging?"
"Think you could help me get a corpse out of a tree?"
"Oh... no, I don't like those kinds of objects. No sale." He barely even looks at it.
"By the way... do you, um, happen to have any *guns*? Like the ones carried by cops?"
He's not telling you the whole story. It seems he's trying to spare you.
"I feel like there's something you're not telling me."
He probably has a good reason for that. (Drop the matter.)
He looks away. "You weren't quite yourself, officer."
You sucked on a gun? Good. Good. Very normal.
"What was I like?"
"Happens to the best of us, I guess."
"I'm so sorry you had to see me in that state. We don't have to talk about it any further."
"No apologies necessary, officer."
"It certainly does, especially in Revachol."
"You were very distraught. You said the gun was a threat to your life, and... that you can't *trust* yourself with it tonight. And you need the money."
"When I said that I don't normally buy firearms, you put the gun barrel in your mouth and sort of... sucked on it. Then I agreed to take it."
"Wait... how much did I sell the gun for?"
Say nothing.
The light swirls in his face and glasses. He doesn't know what to say either.
"Fifteen reál."
The lieutenant looks from you to Roy and then back to you. It's clear that he hopes this tableau might still turn out to be a bad dream -- it's not, though.
What is a particle decay generator?
Why is it called the *People's* Pile?
Why did it fail? (Conclude.)
A primitive nuclear reactor, also called a *pile*.
Construction began during the Commune of Revachol. The *people* continued work on it after the Commune fell -- they wanted a cheap source of energy for Revachol West.

An emergency valve defect resulted in steam pressure blowing the turbine, taking the fuel containment vessel up in the explosion. Both the faulty design and lack of finances contributed to the catastrophe.
With Kim here too?! That just sounded really, really bad.
"Do you know what the tattoos mean?"
He frowns. "Aphotic paths? Counter-radiance networks? Antimagnetism? It's darkness. That's all I know. Sell me something *lighter*."
"Another time, perhaps."
"I didn't mean to offend you." (Drop the subject -- you don't want drugs.)
His loosens up. "I'm not offended, officer."
"Care to share your Pyrholidon with me?"
It's almost like he's worried for you.
"I ride the *pyrho* every day."
"Every day?" He tilts his head, studying you, then nods. "You look the part."
"Here you go, man." He presents a large cap-shaped object on the palm of his hand. Very odd-looking...
Yes, darling, that's the Coalition Government ordained Pyrholidon -- straight into your gut!
Not so sure about this.
Wait, why wouldn't I be sure?
Because it's an anti-radiation drug and you're a cop, not a post-apocalyptic scavenger?
"Thanks, man." (Take the pyrholidon.)
"Actually, I changed my mind. I don't need any Pyrholidon." (Refuse to take the pyrholidon for now.)
He looks down. "Of course."
"I respect your decision, officer. What else can I help you with?"
"I can understand how you would mistake Jacob Irw for a powerful electric vortex."
"Jacob Irw? The great TipTop champion? Yes, yes..."
His forehead creases. "Do you think it may have been... Jacob Irw who drove over your roof?"
"It's a logical explanation. I felt within that thunderous crash a soul plunged into chaos."
"I felt within that thunderous crash a soul plunged into chaos."
"The vortex is going to become much bigger -- it is an integral part of how it all ends."
"An *end* implies a stable state, whereas we can see from experience that everything is in fact always transforming. Thus, there can be no end."
"But that is merely our meagre sense experience. There are dark forces at work now that we cannot even envision, much less see."
"The dark always has its counterbalance in light. Neither will prevail. The cycle will continue." He folds his arms with finality and turns away from you, concentrating once more on his light show.
"The corpse behind the hostel, I assume..." He looks into the swirling lights, then to you: "I don't have a truck with a mounted platform or anything of that sort myself..."
"Ask around the harbour. There might be some workers there who'd be willing to help."
"I do my best to keep my distance from all manner of butchery. Bad for business, bad for everyone."
'This mess' -- he means *your* mess.
Needless to say: things didn't work out.
"You... uhh..."
"Have you tried it before?"
"Actually, that's all I've got."
The pawnbroker's gaze is already fixed on the dancing colours.
Roy takes the hubcaps from the lieutenant and inspects them. The spinners appear iridescent in the dancing light of his pawnshop.
He marvels at the cobalt shimmer, and nods: "Yes, these are very, very good. Did you defraud some foreign prince for them? Jump a Mesque banger? No matter... I'll give you 200 reál."
"Thank you." He takes the cash, then turns to you.
"Here's the 30 reál you need for your bill. Do *not* waste it." The rest goes in his pocket.
"Here's the 60 reál you need for your bill. Do *not* waste it." The rest goes in his pocket.
"Here's the 70 reál you need for your bill. Do *not* waste it." The rest goes in his pocket.
"Here's the 100 reál you need for your bill. Do *not* waste it." The rest goes in his pocket.
"Here's the 130 reál you need for your bill. Do *not* waste it." The rest goes in his pocket.
"No one was defrauded or *jumped*, I assure you," the lieutenant explains as the pawnbroker opens the register and counts the cash.
"Of course. I meant no offense. 200 reál for you, officer. Delightful doing business with you. Do come again."
"Hello again. How can I help you?"
"Hey, do you know how to fix this?" (Show him the bundle of magnetic tape.)
He looks at the bronze-coloured bundle in your hand. "You mean re-spool it? Yeah, I do, but..."
He slowly finishes his thought: "...but I'm not some Mr. Fixit, I'm a pawnbroker. If you want to pawn the tape, sure. Although it looks pretty... worthless."
"Hmh, maybe you can help me some other way, then."
Just explain why you need this so much. He's bound to understand.
"Wait, but you tinker with film tapes all the time. Isn't that the same?"
"No, it's different... those film tapes actually *mean* something to me, but this is just a worthless bundle of old tape."
"Is it any good? The music, I mean."
"I helped them up the bass beat. It's getting pretty *hard core*, but there's something missing. A melody line to complement the beat. I'm feeling this tape might be it."
"Okay, I'll help you out. It's going to take a moment though, so just sit back and relax..."
"Sure..." he mumbles as his eyes once again start following the light show around the pawnshop.
"Yeah, I bet they would... all those lights in a massive church hall..." He stares at the intricate interplay of light and shadow all around him, suddenly moved by the idea.
You take some time to look around the store... The play of visuals all around the pawnshop is mesmerizing. Suddenly, Roy turns back to you with a reel of tape in his hand and coughs.
You know, these visuals would look *super cool* in the church.
"Well, thanks for the help." (Proceed; take the repaired tape.)
"Yeah. My pleasure. I do what I can for true passion projects... Just try not to use this tape for negative photon emissions. Take responsibility, okay."
"A sanctuary filled with hand-picked positive photons... There would be no room for sadness in such a place. It's a brilliant vision..."
"I rather like it *here* too, so yeah -- I'm not giving you my projector. This tape is all I can do for you and your friends' nightclub project." He nods at the fixed tape on the counter top.

"Yeah, man, no." He shakes his head. "I rather like this place happy too. You know -- where I work. This tape is all I can do for you and your friends' nightclub project." He nods at the fixed tape on the counter top.
Poor apes on a stupid ball, with never enough money to do anything remarkable.

He looks off to the side, then down at his hands. "Can't say I'm a huge admirer of Wild Pines, and I certainly wouldn't trust any silver-tongued spokesperson of theirs. Fortunately, I have no reason to get involved."
"Ever had any dealings with the Union Boss?"
"Know anything about the Wild Pines representative that's in town?"
"He's been by the shop a couple of times." He gives a lazy half-shrug.
There was something awfully deliberate about that laziness.
"Did he discuss union business with you?"
"Did he buy anything?"
"Why do I feel like you don't want to talk about him? Are you hiding something?"
"Wait... what do you have against Wild Pines?"
"Have you *met* the Wild Pines rep?"
"He tried. Wanted to come to some *mutually beneficial arrangement* around my dealings with the dockworkers... I politely declined to *hear him out*."
"He purchased a remarkably garish paperweight the first time he was here... Nothing the second."
"They weren't the most... pleasant interactions. Small-town Big Wigs always want everyone to play a part in the play they're staging."
"But I bowed out at some point. I prefer to watch from afar while the Big Wigs come and go."
"I have other questions about this."
He nods reluctantly.
"So you don't know what kind of arrangement he was talking about?" The lieutenant studies the pawnbroker suspiciously.
"As I said, I refused to talk to him. That's why he came back a second time. That's *also* why he hasn't come back a third."
For a moment, his jaw tenses up, and his gaze is sharp and clear. Then he relaxes again.
"What kind of *arrangement*?"
"No, just -- people like that make everyone else see the world somewhat askew... at an angle that is convenient for them. Now -- you have more questions, or are we..."
"What should I have *for* it?"
The People's Pile was a Type U particle decay generator that failed immediately after entering service, releasing radioactive waste into River Esperance.
Those triangle patches on his vest... you have a feeling they *mean* something. Like they're similar to the halogen rectangle on your jacket.
(Point at his clothes.) "Say, what's with the triangles on your vest?"
He hesitates. "I was... I was with the Emergency Relief Brigade. You know, after the People's Pile disaster." He coughs, as if to mark his words.
"Had to take Pyrholidon for radiation sickness. That's what you were hinting at just now, wasn't it?"
He's taking it for mental and emotional, not physical pain these days.
"I'd like to buy back the commemorative pin I sold."

dialoguetext: Buy the pin.
His eyes move from you to the lights dancing on the walls.
"Greetings on this fine night. What brings you here?"
"The pawnshop is always open."
"You do know that it's not really a 'fine night'? The weather is terrible."
"How come you're still open?"
"It's cool that you're still open. Big city vibes."
"Top of the morning to you. How may I be of service?"
"Isn't being forced to get up for work at dawn a little inhumane?"
"Early bird gets the worm, huh?"
"I'm so glad you're already awake. It's so lonely in this city at this hour!"
"Is it?" He turns his head to the right and then to the left, as if looking for non-existent windows. "Spring is capricious, yes."
"Perhaps." He shrugs. "I just like being awake for the transition between night and morning -- bearing witness to the first hints of light on the horizon."
"It's not often that I see officers from the RCM in my pawnshop." The man at the counter turns to you slowly.
"Oh, no, not at all." He flashes a smile. "I guess I haven't had many customers lately, RCM or otherwise."
"Who are your customers usually?"
"Sorry, I feel like I'm interrupting you."
"Now that the RCM is here -- tell me, have you had any trouble lately?"
"I haven't had any problems myself... though some of my customers have complained about inconsistent law enforcement."
"All kinds of people come through here... Locals, travellers. People looking for a deal. People looking for a keepsake. People who are terminally bored."
"I see you were wounded in the recent... altercation." He nods gravely at your leg. "A speedy recovery to you, officer."
"Now, what can I do for you?"
"As you can see... I have a wide selection of goods for everyone to choose from."
(Shake your head.) "It's shameful, how insufficient the police presence is in these parts!"
"This business plan is all over the place. You should specialize, zoom in, recapitalize."
"I see you were wounded in the recent... altercation," he says with a grave nod. "A speedy recovery to you, officer."
"Hello hello! Let me know if I can help you with anything."
"It keeps me entertained." His attention is drawn once more to the play of light and shadow on the walls behind you.
(Look around.) "Typical vacuous consumerist objects."
"Honestly, I think some of your selections are..." (Press your finger to your lips) "...more tasteful than others."
(Nod.) "Quite the collection indeed."
"Between you and me," he looks you up and down, "this is why I don't get involved in local politics."
"You're calling this *politics*?"
"So it goes." The pawnbroker nods gravely, then shrugs. "Now, what can I do for you?" he asks.
"What can I do for you?" he asks.
"Who are your customers usually?"
"It keeps me entertained," he responds, unimpressed with your critique.

"Yes. All the good conflict corridors: Supramundi, Yeesut, the Semenese islands. Countries that don't have a good record reporting *atrocious* military conduct on their soil."
"Okay. Anything else you can tell me?"
"Sadly -- no. Before this happened I had little interest in them. Now that I do -- I don't have the resources." She thinks.
It's the *expression* she objects to?
"What? *Going native*?"
"Yes."
"It sounds like you object to the words 'going native' more than him raping and killing people here."
She's picked a strange hill to die on. Strike!
She's silent.
"What is the purpose of this, detective?"
"This is where you draw the line -- *going native*? Not at hiring a paramilitary death squad?"
"Paramilitary death squad is a bit rich." She remains calm: "But yes -- were it up to me I would have at least *vetted* them more thoroughly."
"Never mind. Forget it."
Should have cornered her. Maybe it would have yielded something...
"I have no idea what you're talking about."
"Probably."
"I'm gonna say no."
"In my line of work it pays to do your research. I was prepared to deal with the RCM. I did *not* think I would be dealing with a group like *Krenel*."
"Ah yes, your condition. The International Collaboration Police maintains a database for these sorts of things. Perhaps you should consult it. It was just a suggestion."
"Perhaps the arrangement no longer stands... excuse me, it's not my place to pry. If it does you should take advantage of it. Just a suggestion."
"Or he *didn't*." She tilts her head. "This is information passed on to me from some teenagers loitering around the canal. I cannot testify by it. "
"Who did the passing on then?"
"What did these teenagers by the canal say?"
"That the man was killed because he assaulted a local woman. I've asked around a bit -- this seems to be the accepted story around Martinaise."
"It's the first time I've heard of this. Where did this assault take place? And when?"
"Last Sunday night, at the Whirling-in-Rags -- the hostel by the gates. Supposedly the colonel was drunk, maybe on narcotics too."
"If you mean did I see him alive -- yes. But I did not *know* him."
You don't know how you know -- it's not written on her face, nor in her voice -- but she had sympathy for this man.
"You liked him."
"His name was..."
"*Liked* is a bit strong," she tosses her head. "He... he was the most charismatic among them. He handled all the talking. His departure left a major gap in the group's *communication skills*."
"Lely. His service name, a nom de guerre most likely. He wouldn't divulge his full name. Only one of them did -- a bad sign if there ever was one."
"Tell me about the others first."
"This Lely -- anything else? Nationality? How old would you say he was?"
"One is a man, *Korty* they call him. A nickname as well. The other a woman, Phillis de Paule. Korty is... *the gunner,* I believe. De Paule is a radio operator."
The lieutenant cuts in: "What would you say was his eye colour -- the deceased's?"
She closes her eyes, trying to picture the man's face... then shakes her head...
"I can't remember." There's a pang of regret to her voice.
"That's alright, ma'am. Anything else -- nationality? What would you say was his age?"
"He was forty. Or fifty. It's hard to say which, he had a combat injury on his lower jaw. It made it difficult to estimate his age, or gauge his facial expressions."
"Indeed. This matches the dental reconstruction we saw on the body," he says to you, then turns back to Joyce. "What else? Nationality? Accent?"
"What else? Nationality? Accent?"
The lieutenant was testing her -- asking a small detail first to see if she knew him better than she let on. She passed.
"He was Occidental I think. Light brown hair, a mix accent. Oranjese, or Messinian maybe? His injury gave him an accent all his own..."
"In a way it was humanizing. He had to learn to speak *through* it -- through the injury." She nods. "That's all I know, I guess. I only met him once."
"What else? Nationality? Accent?"
"And that seems to corroborate the ethnicity we gave." The lieutenant is pedantically happy about it.
The lieutenant jots something down in his notebook, muttering to himself: "Had him down as Mondial... should change it to Occidental."
Like a crossword puzzle solver. Or a master at the guessing game Peng.
"They've gone to ground, as it were. I don't recommend seeking them out." She puts her foot on the guardwire, for balance. "For one -- they're almost certainly armed to the teeth."
"They don't have the same respect for the Revachol Citizens Militia as I do. To put it bluntly they think you're vigilantes, *ghetto savages*. It will not be a fruitful meeting."
Vigilantes? You're a professional officer of the only *legitimate* authority in Revachol.
"I still need to know where they are."
"Okay, I'll steer clear for the moment."
"I'll confront them directly."
You should show those meatheads exactly how *savage* you really are.
"They just need someone to put the *Fear of Revachol* into their hearts."
"Vigilantes? The RCM gets its authority from the Coalition. Where does theirs come from?"
"You're likely to run into them eventually. When that happens, I'll be in a better position to mediate if I don't appear *involved*."
"That's wise," she nods. "Our goal is to *avert* catastrophe. Besides," she sighs, "You're likely to encounter them sooner or later."
"That is a *bad* idea, one I won't be a party to." She shakes her head emphatically.
"Somehow I doubt that lecturing them on the legitimate use of force will persuade them to stand down."
She reaches for the photo; takes it, then holds it in her hand...
She wears fingerless gloves, her fingernails are cut short and fractured. Like those of a working woman.
"It was taken with a Trigat, not long ago. This is the man's upper body. There were no more markings on his hands or legs."
Stay quiet. Observe the woman's expression.
"What do you think?"
Her mouth is relaxed, the accordion lines near her mouth vanish. The pearls of her eyes move slowly on the photo's surface.
She has no excess of emotions for this cadaver. Has she seen dead bodies before? It's likely.
"Sorry," she breaks her concentration. "I was trying to see if I can read the web of interdependencies between these points -- the stars." She points to one on the photo paper.

"I can't. But that's how you read this story. The points themselves don't have letters, numbers, anything. Their size, location on the body and distance from each other tells you what they represent."

"Close," she nods. "Port cities. This is an Oranjese Map of the Waterways -- a sailor's tattoo worn by wayfarers of the Dolorian century, over 300 years ago. The sailors would mark their bodies to map their travels."
"What travels did the dead man make?
"Quite a few. Vredefort -- the Oranjese capital -- traditionally stands on the right shoulder." She points to it on the photo. "He started somewhere near here, I think."

"Revachol," she says. "Those are the two constants: Vredefort on the shoulder and Revachol in the heart. They started the tradition of these maps right after the discovery of Insulinde, at the dawn of the Interisolary Age."
"You said you can't read it."
"Until the executions start? Truthfully -- I don't know. It depends on their progress identifying the members of the lynch mob. And their impatience."
"They don't report their progress to you?"
"Not on this matter. I'm afraid they consider this a personal initiative." There is a brief silence. Seagulls squawk over the bay...
"What? You mean you don't know what's going on?"
"Places? Like stars in the sky?"
"Places? Like vias on a microcircuit?"
"Places? Like blooms in a pattern?"
Say nothing.

"Port cities. On the oceans. This is an Oranjese Map of the Waterways -- a sailor's tattoo worn by wayfarers of the Dolorian century -- as early as 300 years ago. The sailors would mark their bodies to map their travels."

Somewhere in an office lit by a single green desk lamp captain Ptolemaios Pryce -- 58, bald and bespectacled -- is writing in a ledger on his desk. Rows and rows of days and weeks, laconic remarks in a single column: *patrol*, *case*, *vacation*, *injured*...
Vredefort? Vredefort has a military academy. The Semenese islands saw a recent conflict. In Revachol he was executed.
"I can't. This man was no sailor -- and these are no ports. I can understand geographic fragments, but not their meaning."
"What is the use of this map?"
"Who could tell me more?"
