dialoguetext: "Look guys, I've gotta be honest. I may not have 'read' many 'books', but that doesn't mean I don't have *stories*."
"Absolutely. It's the only proper foundation to develop a real understanding of events." He nods in vigorous agreement.
"There might be something to that. I recently finished 'The Greatest Innocence'."
"That reminds me, Kim and I just played this interesting game, 'Suzerainty'."
"But once you've got a political lens, you can read anything critically. Even those Hjelmdallermann books."
"Listen, books are fine and all, but to be straight with you, they're no substitute for a real story."
"Hmm, don't think I'm familiar with it. Give us a quick summary, if you don't mind."
Now's your chance to end this interview on a high-note. You quickly gloss Lopez de Fuego's essential argument, peppering it with your own commentary and asides...
This is a good start. They're starting to loosen up. You feel relaxed and in control. You quickly gloss Lopez de Fuego's essential argument, peppering it with your own commentary and asides...
Like a river emptying into the sea, the discussion winds its way toward the character of the innocence herself.
"... but then, any *critical* account of Dolores Dei's reign has to seriously reckon with her atrocities in Magritania and La Vuelta during the Mesque secession, don't you think?"
"Lopez de Fuego seemed to think she was pretty great regardless."
"Honestly, I did get the impression there was something inhuman about her."
"Exactly. Lopez de Fuego totally glosses over all her mass murder."
"I'm a little rusty on my innocentic history, so it was helpful for me."
"Total nonsense. The greatest thing Dolores Dei ever did was get blasted by her own therrier."
"The whole innocentic system practically requires that. Without true gods we're made to set them up for ourselves." He nods vigorously.
"Ha! It's good you were able to see through even that gauzy nostalgic pulp."
"I'll say that beginnings are very delicate things. That makes it all the more important that you start with *the right books*."
"If he wants a real critical history, he's got to read 'On the Material Conditions of the Mirovan Boilermakers'."
"It's so good. Brutally revelatory."
"Oh, right. We've been meaning to try that out."
Now's your chance to end this interview on a high-note. Soon you're engaged in a thoughtful back-and-forth about the relationship between theme and mechanics...
This is a good start. They're starting to loosen up. You feel relaxed and in control. Soon you're engaged in a thoughtful back-and-forth about the relationship between theme and mechanics...
Best of all, your arguments are liberally seasoned with references to particular historical events and personages.
"... but then my issue with these historical cube-pushers is that they offer the *illusion* of subjectivity even as they reinscribe the logic of colonialism itself..."
"... though I'd love to hear your take on it."
"For me, games are mostly about spending time with a partner."
"I thought it was pretty fun. No need to intellectualise it too much."
"But by allowing players to *recreate* historical events, like the introduction of cocaine to Safre, doesn't it force them to question what 'subjectivity' means in a ludo-thematic context?"
"Hmm. What is it they say about ties? That they're like kissing your sister... or in this case, I suppose, your partner."
"He's only saying that because he got the better of me, somehow..."
"He's only saying that because he *likes* getting thrashed like a schoolboy."
"Yes, and it only took about four hours of our lives that we'll never get back."
"Listen, this is a forward-thinking group. It's entirely your business, of course."
"With his 'partner', he says."

"Anyway, we also enjoy a good board game every once in a while. The other week Ulixes and I tried this new one where everyone is competing to manage their own Zone of Ecological Catastrophe. You should see the components."
"Of course. The one thing capitalism does better than every other ideology is novel and clever distractions. It's all one never-ending dopamine dripper."
Capitalism *rules*, is what he seems to be saying.

dialoguetext: Wait-wait-wait, you were trying *not* to do that!
Ensconced in your ceramic armour, you barely notice the moment of contact. But you do hear the distinct *ting* of your knuckles catching the young man's cheekbone.
Even through the yellow latex shell containing your hand you can feel the force of the impact against the young man's cheekbone.
En route to its target your FALN glove traces a strangely pleasing black-and-white blur through the air, like some kind of ultra-sonic weasel.

At the moment of contact you're reminded of a fight you once witnessed between two homeless men in an alleyway. Could it be that you've set out to recreate that moment now, right down to the smelly fingerless gloves?
You feel a bright pain as your bare knuckle collides with the young man's oddly prominent cheekbone. At the moment of contact his eyes are wide as old silver coins.
Of course, it's not *actually* ultra-sonic, that's just an illusion produced by good branding. Still, the force you've unleashed really is tremendous.
Oh god, tell us you haven't done it *again*. Are you twice the killer now?
Oh, no. Tell us you didn't *really* kill him.
"Good god, detective! What's wrong with you?"
"Steban, can you hear me?"

dialoguetext: "Errrrck." The young man cradles his jaw and looks up, his expression blank.
You're both lucky you didn't shatter his cheekbone. He may want to count his teeth before he goes to bed tonight.
"Oh, god. I'm sorry about that."
"Let that be a lesson to you."
Say nothing.
"*Sorry*? You nearly took my fucking jaw off!"
"What lesson is that, huh? That the RCM are assholes? That they'll take your fucking jaw off?"
"What? You're just gonna stand there after you nearly broke my fucking jaw?"
You think you can hear a slight popping sound as he moves his mouth.
It certainly won't improve your precinct's image within the community.
That's right. You don't *owe* him any explanation.
The lieutenant nods.
"Thank god we avoided *that* fiasco, at least..."
The young man can hardly conceal his disappointment. He was apparently looking forward to being punched by you.
And yet you can't help but sense a slight disappointment on his part. It seems a part of him hoped you would hit the pretentious young communist...
"Well, if you're not going to play along, I don't think we have anything further to discuss. Good evening to you, gendarme."
"I'm ready... let's talk about infra-materialism."
"Yes, let's get right to it."
You'll be leading this conversation, so wherever you take it, they'll be glad to follow.
"I have some questions about the origins of this theory."
"I really want to hear more about these hyper-revolutionary figures."
"It's the theoretical parts I'm interested in. The third-level stuff."
"Oh, it's a great story. You should check out Nilsen's journals if you ever have the chance."
"Ah, yes. That's certainly one of the *least* developed parts of the theory, but also one of the most intriguing."
"Oh, yes. Or the *fun parts*, as we like to call them."
His companion nods in agreement.
His companion leans forward, ready to jump in...
His companion nods his head with expectation.

These two are full of interesting stories and rumours about Nilsen, Mazov, and their revolutionary exploits. Half an hour passes and the conversation gradually wends its way to some unexpected places...
They're impressed that you dove right in to the most advanced parts of the theory. Half an hour evaporates and the conversation is still wending its way toward new and unexpected places...

A cool breeze coming off the bay wraps itself around the Capeside Apartments. In a nearly forgotten part of that glorified construction site, surrounded by rusted pieces of scaffolding and walls of faded tarpaulin, a detective of the RCM debates the intricacies of an abstruse theory with a pair of university students...
"... but if it's true that this individual possesses *so much capital* that light literally *bends* around him, then that must mean..."
"That *capital* produces its *own* form of plasm!"
"That *light itself* is a bourgeois illusion!"
"In 'Innocence of Capital', Puncher and Wattmann argue that communists must possess as little capital as possible, in order to keep their thinking *undiluted* by its influence..."
"*Or* it suggests that capital, in sufficient quantities, must exhibit its own plasm-like qualities..."
Watch out. You call yourself a communist and yet you've been accumulating a *suspiciously* large share of capital in just the last few days. It's almost certainly distorting your thinking.
You've accrued a modest account balance over the last few days, but probably not enough to warp your thinking *too* much.
Nothing to fear. Judging from your account balance, you should be thinking *extremely* clearly.
"Again, he was just a regular high-net-worth individual. There was nothing *extra-physical* about him..."
Now the breeze has subsided. All is still except for the last bits of steam rising from the coffee pot.
"... but my question is where does the RCM *recruit* all these hyper-revolutionaries to join this 'Remote Viewers Division'?"
"It's less that you're 'recruited' into the RVD and more like you're *called*."
"And my *point* is that maybe these *hyper-revolutionary* individuals are more common than infra-materialism generally assumes..."
"Fascinating..."
"Yes, only the detective here would draw a connection between a made-up division of para-psychics and the addled ramblings of a defunct communist mage..."
A fortunate turn that the lieutenant isn't here. Imagine what he would have to say about this.
The young man ignores the lieutenant. "But I suppose it makes sense that some common strain of infra-materialist thought would persist in the RCM, even to this day, given its origins."
The young man nods thoughtfully. "But I suppose it makes sense that some common strain of infra-materialist thought would persist in the RCM, even to this day, given its origins."
"... all I'm saying is if you want to get *really extra-physical*, pyrholidon is the way to go..."
"... anyway, I think I've made my point."
"... or maybe I'm wrong. It could really go either way."
"Undoubtedly."
"... but I'm still trying to figure out how the *pale* fits into all this..."
"... so wait, you're saying that President Knezhinisky has *never opened a book*?"
"The two phenomena are actually deeply intertwined." He nods. "Many infra-materialists believe that pale is actually a manifestation of nostalgia and historical inertia..."
"Those same theorists have hypothesised that revolution may in fact create a *counter-force* that prevents the pale from expanding."
"No-no-no. We're saying he doesn't *need* to open them, because he absorbs all the relevant content just by staring intently at the cover. It's a widely understood second-level effect..."
"We've tried it ourselves, but thus far we haven't been able to absorb more than the preface and table of contents."
The evening is winding down...
"Well, on that note, I think we can call it an evening."
"Yes. One of our better discussions lately, on the whole."
"Hang on, is that *it*?"
"What do you mean, 'is that it'? You've done the reading, we talked about it, what more do you expect from a reading group?"
"What if I have more questions, you know, about communism?"
"Well, you could always *ask*, I guess." The two young men look at each other a moment.
"But it's getting late, so maybe pick the *most important* question?"
"He probably won't get a better chance, honestly."
"Kim, what should I ask?"
"I need a minute to think about it."
Ask the most important question about communism.
"I changed my mind. I don't have any questions."
"Yeah, I'm good. No questions for me." (Cancel task.)
"Detective, how should *I* know what questions *you* have about communism?"
"Come on. We have things to do in the morning."
"He says he doesn't have any questions, Steban."
"Are you absolutely sure? A communist can't be afraid to ask questions, just because they don't know what the answer might be."
In other words, you'll forfeit their respect if you back out now.
"See, Steban? I told you there's no such thing as a gendarme communist."
"It seems you're right, Uli. I should've listened to you." He sighs, then turns to you.
"Now, if you'll excuse us, we have some *group business* to attend to."
The question you mean to ask is both very complicated and incredibly simple...

Alright, here we go. We're devoting all your available brain cells to coming up with a question about communism. Scratch that, to coming up with *the* question about communism, the alpha and omega of communism questions, and that question is:
Take a deep breath. Best to go one piece at a time.
"If communism is all based on *theories* that are impossible to prove..."
"If no one can agree what real communism even *means*..."
"If communism keeps failing every time we try it..."
The young man waits patiently for you to finish.
"... and the rest of the world keeps killing us for our beliefs..."
"... and whenever we *do* try it just devolves into a corrupt farce..."
"... and we keep fracturing over theoretical disagreements..."
"Yes?"
Say it.
"... what's the point?"
The young man considers your words for a minute.
You're witnessing his ironic armour melt before you. This is his *true self* you're seeing now.
He's thinking about someone...
Wait, who is he thinking about?
Forget it.

"The theorists Puncher and Wattmann -- not infra-materialists, but theorists nonetheless -- say that communism is a secular version of Perikarnassian theology, that it replaces faith in the divine with faith in humanity's future..."
Hard to say. Someone dear to him.
Track his gaze. He's looking out past the broken wall, toward the opposite side of the Bay...
Let the thought go.
What's there?
Toward the skyscrapers of La Delta.
They rise like electric obelisks in the night.
Many tall buildings, belonging to a district whose name escapes you.
"Who's in those skyscrapers over there?"
"You're thinking about someone, aren't you?"
"Broken."
"Unfinished."
Say nothing.
The young man looks at you a moment, then at his companion.
He's not accustomed to exposing his doubt like this.
"What could it hurt? Alright, let's give it another go..."

There, in the middle of the floor, the winding spire quivers with an improbable energy...
"Don't apologise. As I was saying, if it were *easy*, it wouldn't require so much plasm to work."
There's no way it should stay up like that. How is the weight being distributed?
But it is! It is!
For a long moment, no one says a word. You're all three transfixed.
"... what do we do now?"
"Shhh. This is the most amazing thing I've ever seen..."
"... and there it goes..."

dialoguetext: "That was weird."
Say nothing.
"My mums." The young man looks surprised. "She works in one of those skyscrapers, but it's not like you think... she's a cleaning lady..."
"Yes, in fact... my mums." The young man smiles sheepishly. "She works in La Delta... in one of those skyscrapers, but it's not like you think... she's a cleaning lady."
"But how did you... oh, never mind. I guess I'm easier to read than I thought..."
"Why do you call her 'mums'"?
"She's given up a lot for you."
"You want her to live in a better world."
"Because I always have. Though I try not to do it too often now... it's kind of embarrassing, isn't it?"
"We all have to make sacrifices for the future. Maybe that's what I was trying to get at earlier..."
"I want us *all* to live in a better world. But yes... she's a part of it... I guess we're all a part of it..."
You made him self-conscious now. He's practically paralysed.
"Yes, that's a good way to think of it, broken, but not irreparable."
"Yes, that's a good way to think of it... a work-in-progress."
"It's a nice thought."
"I don't know if I believe it, though."
"A thought can be a very powerful thing. That's the whole idea of infra-materialism..."
"You've got to believe in *something*. Otherwise, what are you doing?"
His words aren't really directed at you. He's wrestling with himself now...
"Steban, it's getting pretty late."
"You're right... We should clean this up and get going." He gestures to the matchboxes.
The young man appears lost inside his own thoughts...
A cold wind whips at the canvas. From far below, the sounds of waves smashing themselves against the rocks. You are exposed.
Pull your jacket tighter.
Rub your arms with your hands.
(Whisper.) "Are women bourgeois?"
Oh god, that's bad. Surely I can think of something better.
The young man gives you a slightly confused look, as though he's sure you asked something else and he simply misheard.
No, he heard you crystal clear.
Somehow it sounded even *worse* out loud.
You only said what everyone else was thinking. Look around -- do you see any women here?
"He wants to know if women are bourgeois, Steban..."
"Yes, I heard him. Give me a moment." He takes a deep breath, then turns to you...
"What makes you ask *that* question, above any other?"
"Because they can't handle *me*."
"Because I can't handle *them*."
"Because they won't let me forget the life we used to have together."
"I don't know! It's just what my brain told me to say."
"Maybe your problem is that you think it's their job to *handle* you..."
"Maybe your problem is that you think they're *yours* to handle..."
"Ah, gendarme. Your problem isn't ideological, it's personal..."
"That's because your brain is floating in ideology, gendarme. It's practically drowning in it..."
Is "Ideology" some kind of high-proof liquor? Because that's the only thing your brain is floating in.

"You asked that question because you're still under the influence of ideology. That's natural. You're like a fish that's only now discovering that her whole life has been dictated by the movements of sea currents."
"That's what ideology is. It's like there are these invisible forces everywhere, pushing and tugging you this way and that, and you don't even know they're *there*."
"What does this have to do with communism?"
"What does this have to do with women?"
"Is it even *possible* to imagine a world without ideology?"
"Everything, man. That is part of the communist project, to destroy the ideological structures that reduce men and women to these hollow shells of identity."
"Of course it's possible. Just extremely difficult. You practically have to be a world-historical individual to do it."
"Do you know the story of Dobreva and Abadanaiz?"
"You mean the Revolutionary Lovers?"
"I thought that was just some gibberish you made up for the passphrase."
"I don't know what you're talking about. Who were they?"
"No. They were the Revolutionary Lovers, the Dual Commissars of Revolution in Insulinde."
"The so-called 'Revolutionary Lovers'. They were the Dual Commissars of Revolution in Insulinde."
"Not just lovers, they were the Dual Commissars of Revolution in Insulinde."
It's too bad they wound up equally dead on some nameless island in Ozonne...
What became of them, though? There seems to be a blank paragraph in the history books...

"It's from them we get the notion of dual-leadership, the *décomptage*, Revachol's truly great contribution to revolutionary thought. I believe it even persists in some form in the RCM, even to this day."
"It's too bad they died like all the rest of the communards."
"What happened to them, Dobreva and Abadanaiz?"
"Is that true, Kim, about the décomptage?"
"So... you're saying women are only bourgeois because of ideology?"
"I need to take some time to think about all this..." (Conclude.)
"They died on their own terms, like real revolutionaries. There's a lot to say for that."
He sighs. "There's more to it than that. People still make their own choices. It's a matter of being aware what's influencing them."
The young man nods but says nothing. He appears to be distracted by something...
"I had no idea its origins went all the way back to the Revolution itself. But it makes sense, in a way..."
He's wrestling with some question of his own.
He's lost in his own thoughts. You wonder what silt you've stirred in the bottom of his soul.
Maybe in another life, but not this one. Face it, this is *the* question that's been simmering inside you all along.
No-no-no! This was supposed to take your mind *off* the other thing!
Hang on, I thought I was really getting into the theory back there!
Maybe I should keep this one to myself.
Sure, you spent some time getting lost in your theoretical labyrinths, but *this* has been the beast at the centre this whole time...
It's too late. You've already opened your mouth to speak...
"That's enough for tonight. Will you still be here if I have more questions?" [Leave.]

dialoguetext: "Sure, we're here most every night." He shrugs. "Maybe we'll catch you again."
"Sleep well, gendarme."
"Wait a minute, if you don't mind..."
"We wanted to get your opinion on something: a few little changes we we've been thinking about."
"What kind of changes?"
"Nothing *too major*, I think. We were talking, potentially, about relaxing some parts of our admissions process..."
"Hmm. It probably *would* help if you didn't make people go through a whole interview just to join."
"Maybe you should ditch the passphrases and meet in a coffeehouse."
"Have you considered changing up the reading list?"
"No, you should keep it the way things are."
"That's interesting. I thought people *loved* group interviews."
"Hmm. I thought the *cloak-and-dagger routine* made us seem more appealing."
"I suppose we have read through most of the infra-materialist canon by this point."
"Exactly what I've been saying. On fundamental matters there can be no compromise!"
"I thought so, too, but perhaps we overdid it, just a little..."
He sighs. "You're right. It probably wouldn't *kill* us to read more conventional historical materialism."
"I'm not saying we abandon our beliefs. I just think it would be better if our group had more than *two* regular attendees."
"As long as we maintain the appropriate critical distance."
"Good point. Two's not really a 'group,' is it?"
"Nah, two's the best number. Three's when they start cramping your style."
"Plus, all these empty chairs are a little sad, aren't they?"
"Precisely my point. It's about quality, not quantity."
"There was another thing: We were also debating putting up some posters around town."
"Though *some of us* maintain that advertising is an unacceptably bourgeois tactic."
That's what makes it so beautiful. The irony is unbeatable.
Ahem. As a noted art cop you definitely have an opinion on this.
"As someone who's dabbled in murals himself, I support this plan."
"As something of an art critic myself, I support this poster plan."
"Think of it this way: you're appropriating bourgeois methods for revolutionary ends."
"Sounds like something Cindy could help with..."
"Posters are great. Who doesn't like posters?"
"Yeah, posters *are* pretty bourgeois."
"Glad to hear it. I was thinking we might be able to get Cindy to design the posters..."
"Ah, it makes sense. There's already a sub-theme of radical street art running through our reading group..."
"Oh, I *like* that. We're dismantling the structures of capital with their own tools..."
"That's *exactly* what I was thinking..."
"Exactly! I was thinking we could print them in the old communard style, with huge slogans..."
"See? Even the gendarme agrees."
"I suppose that would open us up to charges of hypocrisy... not to mention it might make us *look pretty desperate* for new members..."
"When nothing could be further from the truth."
"Right. We'll have to table this question until we've considered the potential downstream effects."
... and just like that, their ironic defences are back up.
"Plus, I've got the *perfect* place in mind..."
"Put some more coffee on, Uli. We've got a long night ahead of us. We should probably get Cindy in here too..."
"In any case, we've kept you long enough. Goodnight to you."
"Oh! And, gendarme. One last thing..."
"I've been thinking about what you asked before, about women, you know..."
"About that question you asked earlier. It reminded me of a certain poem that you might appreciate..."
"Not that it's any of my business, but it sounds like this question is *really* tearing you up inside."
"So, good luck with that, I guess."
"'In dark times, should the stars also go out?'"
"Anyway, goodnight to you."
Ah, so he *has* read something besides his books of abstruse theory!
"A gang of cheap psychologists and intellectual midgets." His companion sneers. "Typical Gottwalders, in other words."
"... and next thing you know there are *budget cuts*, so now we've got to cut the bean rations in half *again*..."
"Comrade Ulixes is right. The amount of plasm required to strike down an ideological enemy outright is enormous. We're talking second-level effects, at a minimum."
"Or even *third*."
"Nothing, I just thought there would be more..."
"More what?"
"I don't know. More... something?"
"It seems like there's something on your mind. Maybe a question you mean to ask?"  The young man turns to his companion, then back to you.
Hit him as hard as you can.
"Wait, who are these *infra-materialists*?"
"I know who Kras Mazov is, but who is this 'Ignus Nilsen' guy?"
"You're not familiar with them? It's... pretty advanced stuff. You may not be ready for it yet, gendarme." The two young men exchange skeptical side-glances.
"Okay, but then who's this 'Ignus Nilsen' guy?"
"Only Kras Mazov's most trusted lieutenant, the Evangelist of the Revolution, and the founding father of the People's Republic of Samara."
It's hard to overstate how unimpressed he is that you've never heard of this world-historical individual.
No, wait! Can this really be the end? You feel like you've just gotten to the real stuff.
"It's embarrassing, but at that point my political consciousness was still pretty rudimentary."
"Perhaps some vestigial sexual objectification from your pre-revolutionary consciousness." He nods.
No, it was an artifact of your pre-ideological consciousness.
"It happens to the best of us."
... even the lieutenant seems engrossed, despite your revealing details of an RCM investigation...
... even the lieutenant seems engrossed, despite your revealing details of an RCM investigation...
"The matchboxes... you were trying to make the tower from Nilsen's journals."

dialoguetext: "So you really *did* read all the way to the end." A sheepish grin. "Yeah, Uli and I were trying to see whether there was enough plasm between the two of us to hold up a few matchboxes..."
Saying it out loud makes him realise how foolish it sounds.
"Right. Basically an infra-materialist parlour game. Let's forget about it."
"It was just a little *informal* experiment. No reason to take it too seriously."
Say nothing.
There's something going on in there, but his innermost sanctum is still beyond your reach...
"Wait, you're saying communism is some kind of religion?"
"But what if you don't believe there *is* a future?"
"But what if humanity keeps letting us down?"
Has it gotten cold in here? Your arms seem to be covered in gooseflesh.

"Only in this very specific sense. Communism doesn't dangle any promises of eternal bliss or reward. The only promise it offers is that the future can be better than the past, if we're willing to work and fight and die for it."
"Then you don't believe in the historic role of the proletariat, which also means you reject the basis of historical materialism."
"Nobody said fulfilling the proletariat's historic role would be easy." A tight smile. "It demands great faith with no promise of tangible reward. But that doesn't mean we can simply give up."
"It means you're not a communist, in other words."
"Even when they ignore us?"
"Even when they shoot at us?"
"Even then."
"Especially then."
"And of course, we'll be shooting right back."
"Mazov says it's the arrogance of capital that will be its ultimate undoing. It does not believe it can fail, which is why it must fail."
"Yes. Whereas we understand that we'll almost certainly fail, which is what allows us the chance to succeed..."
Why do you see the two of them with their backs against a bullet-pocked wall, all of a sudden?
So young. So *unbearably* young...
"I have to say, I've never *entirely* understood what they mean, but I think maybe the answer is in there, somewhere."
"What are you then?"
"Okay, but what if you *know* there isn't going to be a future?"
"Something else..." The young man shakes his head.
"I'm not sure I get what you're driving at. Of course there will be a future, even if the form it takes might appear unrecognisable. That's the spiral of progress."
"Julia Dobreva came from Graad. Jean Abadanaiz was born in Revachol. She was brilliant, charismatic, a revolutionary comet. He was her partner and stabiliser, the planet who kept her in orbit."

"I guess you could say we believe it *because it's impossible*." He looks at the scattered matchboxes on the ground. "It's our way of saying we refuse to accept that the world has to remain... like this..."
Somehow you only now realise that the temperature has been dropping steadily for the last half hour.
Their faces, blurred yet frozen as though in ambrotype. You were never *that young*, were you?
"We should try again, all of us."
The charge in the air has changed. You allow the moment to pass.
"I'll sit this one out. I don't think you want my *skeptical materialism* interfering..."

The front of this quarterly journal features a large, satirical portrait of the late King Frissel. From the sides of his head, a pair of white antlers spread to the corners of the cover.
Why antlers?
Why Frissel?
Flip through the pages, see what catches your eye.
Because white antlers are one of the symbols of communism. They represent a society in accord with the natural world and at the same time above it.
Because Frissel was incompetent, foolish, and cruel. In short, the embodiment of everything the communards wished to overthrow. It's *satire*, you see.
To your disappointment, there aren't any full-colour pictures to direct your attention, just column after column of closely set text, interrupted occasionally by little doodles in black and white...
No advertisements, you notice. So who's funding this *radical commentary*?
After riffling the pages with your thumb several times, you return to the table of contents...
The magazine is divided into several sections: 'International Developments', 'Kunst und Kultur', and 'Local Concerns'. Just inside the cover there's also an editor's note.
You flip back to the front of the magazine. The table of contents unfolds before you.
A shameful way to treat a former king, even one as underwhelming as Frissel.
I want to catch up on 'International Developments'.
Read the editor's note.
What is 'Kunst und Kultur'?

[Put the magazine away.]

"Comrade, as you know, this journal takes its name from Mazov's immortal expression 'Du cristal à la fumée.' This was his way of describing the way the rigid, crystalline structures of capitalist ideology turn to smoke under communism..."
(Whisper.) "Kim! I think this is a *communist* magazine."

"But like the structures of capitalist ideology, we too are at risk of going 'à la fumée.' Unlike many publications which are content to spoonfeed their readers reassuring drivel, *La Fumée* is committed to telling the radical truth, even when that truth may drive away potential subscribers."

"So please, if you value our radical Mazovian perspective on contemporary politics, culture, and international affairs, please consider subscribing today. 

Yours in struggle, The Editors."
Play it cool. Pretend everything's in order.
"What do you expect? It was laying around the office of the Débardeurs' Union. They're probably *bankrolling* the thing."
Only four issues in and it sounds like they've already alienated their readership.
This section includes a long, tedious critique of the latest round of free-trade negotiations between the EPIS nations and the Free State of Semenine.
You also skip over an article about heavy fuel oil smuggling along the Mesque-Messina border, something about bear wrestling in Samara, book riots in Yugo-Graad...
Face it, you really aren't interested in foreign affairs. You're not even sure where most of these countries are...
Apparently the material conditions of other countries hold no interest for you. Your brand of communism is strictly local. So be it...
It seems to be part of a new public fitness initiative in the People's Republic of Samara (SRV), devised and promoted by none other than President Knezhinisky himself.
According to this extremely credulous account, 'Uncle Sport' (as he's affectionately known to his people) has recently decreed bear wrestling the national sport of the SRV.
Whoa-whoa-whoa. *Bear wrestling*? Flip back to that!
Seems a little too foreign for my tastes.
Alright, let's see what this 'bear wrestling' is all about...
When it says 'bear wrestling', does that mean two bears are wrestling *each other*, or...
Hang on, tell me more about this 'Uncle Sport'.
Based on the description in this article, he appears to be an extremely competent and democratically elected president.
Of course not. The article makes plain that this is man-on-bear (or in some cases, woman-on-bear) competition. Two competitors, one ring, five rounds (or until 'incapacitation')...
According to the SRV's Ministry of Information, the programme has been a tremendous success. Public support stands at 87%, and youth obesity and alcoholism rates are down 12% and 7% respectively.
This is the SRV we're talking about. If you think those are the real numbers there's probably a guy who wants to sell you a bridge in La Cherte.
I guess it's hard to fight a bear if you're drunk.
I guess it's hard to fight a bear if you're out of shape.
Hmmm. Not sure I trust these numbers.
What are you, a statistician? Did the Moralintern send you on a 'fact-finding' mission? This is the SRV party line, comrade.
Precisely. For too long drink has been a scourge to the working class, and President Knezhinisky is deeply committed to supplying the people with more wholesome entertainments.
That's very much the idea. President Knezhinisky has long maintained that a strong body is the best defence against capitalist aggression.
Good thing you're a goddamn ox, son. An ox that fights bears.
In shape, out of shape. You've always preferred to rely on your wits.
The Waste Land of Reality is an unforgiving place, but if you ever encounter a bear wandering its roads, you're pretty sure you could take it.
See? There are plenty of ways to find meaning in life. You don't *need* booze to feel alive.
This is all ass-backwards. Drinking makes it *easier* to fight a bear! Plus, then you'll have a bottle to smash on its head. Easy peasy!
"Kim! Do you think there's any chance our case will take us to the SRV?"

Read the profile of 'C.S.'

"You know, *most* people would just write a letter to the editor..."

If it weren't for the Wild Pines all those moochers would be out of a job.

Wouldn't it be better for everyone if labour and capital could reach some *reasonable* accommodation?
Why should I care? This doesn't have anything to do with me.

According to these editorials, private enterprise is simply a means of organising labour that would already happen regardless...
Sounds like their bodies just haven't been *crushed* enough yet.

The writer G. Martin remarks dryly that 'capitalists *love* wealth redistribution, so long as it's only redistributed *upward*'...

According to these editorials, there can be no accommodation with the forces of international capital or their 'mucilaginous allies' in the Coalition...

Perhaps they've overestimated the market demand for this kind of *commentary*.

"This Brief Look(TM) introduces readers to one of this century's most fascinating and misunderstood theories in a concise, jargon-free manner."

Finish the book.

Known to his numerous admirers as the 'Evangelist of the Revolution' and to his even-more-numerous enemies as the 'Apocalyptic Shrike', Ignus Nilsen remains one of the most controversial and fascinating figures to emerge in the years of the Antecentennial Revolution, second only to Kras Mazov himself.

"Then I was right to spare you from it, no?" He cracks a little smile. "Anyway, the pale is no more terrifying than, say, water. Or death. Or that we're stuck behind our eyes, for all eternity..." He looks around, pensive suddenly.
"You don't look like other people around here."
"That's because I'm half-Seolite. Or quarter. My father's father was from Seol -- so was my grandmother, but from my mother's side..." He shakes his head. "It's not an interesting topic."

"You're only making it *sound* uninteresting. I still want to know more about Seol."
"Okay, I guess it's not interesting then."

"I can see you're disappointed." A brief smile. "You're right to be -- I don't speak a word of Seolite. I've never met either one of my grandparents. I've never been to Seol. I'm a regular, garden variety Revacholiere."

"You're barking up the wrong tree. I don't speak a word of Seolite, I've never met either one of my grandparents. And I've never *been* to Seol." He seems almost proud of these things. "I'm a regular Revacholiere."
He's glad to have shot down your question.
Seol is a protectionist, isolationist panisiolary state west of the Insulindian isola. Actually, it's *quite* interesting; some would even say mysterious...
A point of pride to him.
"I was sent to teach you a lesson in *style*."
"Can we go over the preliminary info again?"
"You mean like a brief? Do you want me to brief you again?"
It's all part of the Masterplan, you see.
Tell him. Tell him why it's you.
"I for one hope I don't have to use my service weapon at all -- like a *normal* police officer."
"Of course." Sounds like you just answered his question.
"Yes, it's a wholly pointless matter. Forget I ever mentioned it."
He's actually glad it's addressed now.

"So no, I don't think they sent you as a joke. And even if they did, they are in for a surprise."
He's right. There are no airtight theories, just paranoia. You've given it some thought, now let it go.
"Safe? No. But you're old. You've made it this far. *Something* has brought you through. We've only just started working together, so I don't know what it is yet. But it's there."

"I checked the records. This jurisdiction dispute -- who polices Martinaise -- reaches back to the Thirties. It's as old as my station. And all this time we can't decide who gets Martinaise? I think, yes, both stations would prefer a win."
"Do you really see me as a safe bet?"
"Ha, so you *are* their finest."
"Safe? No. But you're old. You've made it this far. Something has brought you through. I haven't worked with you yet, so I don't know what it is. But it's there."
"It would be immensely ugly of them, not to mention unprofessional.... But I also think it's somewhat unlikely."
"Why's that?"
"I am the finest of nothing."
"I don't think I can say one way or another. I do think it's somewhat unlikely, though."
"They -- Klaasje, as we've come to suspect -- didn't identify themselves in any way. The tone was muffled using a device of some sort. The desk could identify neither the caller's age nor sex."
"Was there anything else you wanted to ask about the competition? If not, we should move."
That's where his conversations with himself take place.
We all have our different mediums. His is written.
You're super lucid -- yet psychedelic. You don't need office supplies to connect to your nervous system, you're *special*.
(I'm not gonna call him a bino.) "Glasses are cool."

The eyebrow is exercising *psionic* control over you.
It's like you're *locked down*.
Cut this boring stuff off immediately. You know what this case is about!
So desperately mundane. You need to funk this case up.
He's basically *challenging* you to sex it up with some lurid twist. Don't get right into it, sit on it a bit -- then hit him with it!
It can still be an otherwordly sex-mystery *in your head*. With a dark twist, even.
Maybe this is why your chest feels so hollow -- you did an awful thing, and you can't even bring yourself to acknowledge it...

"Nothing. Actually, as I'm saying this, I realize I would not be telling the truth."

He's not the least bit curious about what you planned to say.
"Yes."
Nod.

He turns his attention elsewhere.
"Just one thing though..."
Get back to it. [Leave]

"Are *you* part of the homo-sexual underground?"
"Nothing, let's go." [Leave.]
Uhm... uh...
"Yeah, but..."

"... but am I? I'll spare you another *20 hour mind-project* -- yes, I am. Now let's get back to work."
That's the truth.
"... but *am* I? I'll spare you another twenty hours thinking about it -- yes, I am. Now let's get back to work."
Oh no, you're a cop, you can't go to jail...
"Aren't we going to talk about the boots I'm wearing?"
"Yes, uhm..." The lieutenant stares at your shaven face, his eyes narrowed. "Uhhhh..." he mumbles. "I don't know what to say." He coughs. "Perhaps..."
Damage.
Yeah -- damage. He means damage.
"It's just stupidity." The lieutenant shakes his head.
Yes, but containers *contain*. Things. Shiny things. They're interesting.
"Hold on, and the RCM is?"
"That's us. The Revachol Citizens Militia. We're the police in this city."

The RCM, or the Revachol Citizens Militia, is the police force you and him are part of. A self-organized peace corps of the occupied city of Revachol, the RCM operates within a legal twilight, yet its authority is rarely questioned. It's *super useful* to know this.
"It doesn't *have* to be murder. It can just be sex."

One you should be *ashamed* of. It's no wonder the soft one doesn't want it back. It was right to abandon you...
"Kim! We need to talk about... *responsibility*."
"Ah, I'm glad to hear it, detective. I was wondering when we'd get to this very subject."

"Good. We're on the same page then."

"If you ask me, it's high time for you to put the bottle away. Sober up, get back to basics. That would be my advice."
"If you ask me, it's past time for you to cut back on the smoking. You seem like a man with a death wish. It's quite disturbing."
"If you ask me, it's past time for you to lay off the *street drugs* you've been abusing. They really aren't helping us solve the case."
"If you ask me, it's high time for you to set aside these frivolous *side tasks* and focus 100% of your energies on the case before us."
"And I hope we don't even need to discuss the *street drugs* you've been abusing..."
"Oh, I'm not giving up drinking. It's what got me where I am today!"

"I can't give up street drugs now. I *just* got addicted to them!"
"No, no. I meant like *la responsabilité*. You know, the kind that gets assigned."
The lieutenant's quizzical expression gradually deepens into a frown.
"Why are you pronouncing it like you're a Coalition bureaucrat?"
"You know what? Forget it. What *specifically* are you trying to assign responsibility *for*?"
"So what *are* we talking about, then?"
"I'm talking about *la responsabilité*. You know, the kind that gets assigned."
(Point to the ground.) "For the murder."
(Point to yourself.) "For my disaster of a life."

"But isn't that *our* job?"
"But isn't that *your* job?"

"Next I suppose you're going to tell me you need to form a *committee* to assign this *responsabilité*?"
"No, it's way more nuanced than that. There's like this whole historical or socio-economic dimension to it."
"Yes, exactly."
"How did you know?"
"Fascinating. And here I believed your recent turn toward moralism was just an act."
"Simple, because Moralintern types *love* to form committees."
"In any event, I am just a humble law official. I may work under the Moralintern's umbrella, but I'm certainly not qualified to serve on any 'committee'."
"You know who might be, though? That Mr. Villedrouin, the uh... gentleman you needlessly antagonised in the apartments..."
"If you're serious about this, you might keep your eyes out for any Coalition officials we might happen to run across."
"You know who might be, though? That Mr. Villedrouin, the uh... gentleman you met in the young man's apartment..."
"You know who might be, though? That Mr. Heidelstam, the gentleman near the Feld building with the... distinctive way of speaking."
"If I were trying to get in touch with the Coalition, I would start by seeking him out. But first you might need to speak with his *young companion*."
"If you're trying to get in touch with the Coalition, I would start by finding some way to apologise to him. But first you might need to speak with his *young companion*."
"Now, was there anything else?"
"Hold still a second..." (Try to smell Kim.)

The lieutenant's posture becomes rigid and uncomfortable as you lean forward and sniff the area just above his shoulder blade...

The lieutenant is fastidious as a cat in matters of his personal upkeep. And yet, in the folds of his jacket you can just perceive the stale and acrid traces of oil rags, transmission fluid, and brake pads.

He smells... like a man? A perfectly normal man?

"If you have more questions, don't hesitate to ask."
"Thank you for this." [Leave.]
"How do you think today went?"

dialoguetext: "Then you shot him in the chest, which... wasn't ideal. But we did manage to get him down from the tree. So, as they say, all's well that ends well."
"Our inspection was also very *thorough* -- and we've already started following up on leads."
"I would say our initial inspection was *very* thorough -- and we have solid leads to follow up on."
"Our inspection *could* have been more thorough -- as it always can -- but we have some leads we can follow up on."
"Moreover, you found that the hanged man wasn't just hanged -- he was also shot. That was some *excellent* detective work."
"*And* you managed to locate and pull out the bullet. So we can get ballistics, make of the gun -- all this is invaluable."
"Yeah, I'm a professional."
"No big deal."
"It was the least I could do, given all my past mistakes."
"So what are our powers exactly? The RCM?"
"I hope our investigation will help improve the situation here. At least do *some* good."
"We won't change anything here."
"What the people need is stronger leadership that would put everyone in line."
"Me too," he says quietly. "But I wouldn't count on any drastic changes in our lifetimes."
"Probably not," he says quietly. "Anyway, positive change happens slowly. We never really get to see the impact of our actions."
"That seems unwise to me, but it's too late for an all-out political debate." He purses his lips.
"Now, as for interviews -- my list of people to talk to here in Martinaise, I mean..." He takes a deep drag and looks at the city.
"We conducted an interview with Evrart Claire."
"We couldn't conduct an interview with Evrart Claire because you refused to take a seat."
"We met Evrart Claire, but you left the conversation abruptly before we could really interview him."
"We met Evrart Claire, but didn't conduct a full interview. So that's one for the to-do list..."
"The body is still hanging from that tree, which is... unfortunate. And there's still *much* to do at the crime scene."
"I still feel like we're missing something. And there's still work to do at the crime scene too..."
"I still feel like we missed something, but at least the corpse has been refrigerated. There's still work to be done at the crime scene, though."
"I still feel like we missed something, but maybe the boys in Processing will surprise us. We still have work to do at the crime scene."
"We didn't get to meet Evrart Claire, but we did get into the harbour. It'll be easier to reach him tomorrow."
"We weren't able to find the Union leader, Evrart Claire, much less interview him. So that's on the to-do list for tomorrow."
"We interviewed Joyce Messier, the Wild Pines rep, and learned a lot -- none of it very *good news* for us or Martinaise, but..." He gives you a quick nod of acknowledgement and approval.
"We tried to interview the Wild Pines rep, but she asked us to do something for her first. Fine. So be it."
"We talked to Joyce Messier, but didn't get any information from her." He frowns. "I have a feeling Joyce knows how dangerous the situation really is. We *have* to get her to talk to us."
"We didn't talk to the Wild Pines rep. We really must do that tomorrow."
"Above all, though... today was exhausting. What's with all the *running*? You run a lot. Is that a standard Precinct 41 practice?"
"Yeah, that's just how we roll in Precinct 41."
"I'm training for a long-distance run. I want to raise money for charity."
"I don't like to waste time, you know. My mind moves fast -- the rest has to try to keep up."
"I don't know why I do the things I do, Lieutenant Kitsuragi."
"It's impressive, especially for a man your age -- and in *those* heels..." He nods thoughtfully, tapping his finger on his cigarette.
"Where shall we begin? We should talk about the investigation first and foremost, but I also remember you wanting to discuss the RCM?" He lights a cigarette.

"They're quite limited, actually -- the power officers of the Revachol Citizens Militia exercise most *frequently* is imposing fines of up to 1000 reál for offences, in accordance with an interdepartmental schedule."
"A thousand? Why not more?"
"Wouldn't that be an easy power to... abuse?"
"Okay. What else?" (Continue.)
"Yes, although indirectly, as citizens can always request records from their local station."
"Officers of the RCM have been known to take bribes of less than the prescribed fine amount." He frowns. "It undermines trust in the RCM."
"The RCM's primary role is to ensure safety. We're not really supposed to play any part in the economic structure of Revachol."
"We can arrest people, of course, but, rather than bringing someone in directly, it's preferable to serve a *Station Call* slip. It prevents confusion and overcrowding."
"Wait, how can you be sure the arrestee will show up?"
"I see. And if someone resists?"
"You can't. Those who don't show up become fugitives though, and have fewer legal rights when they are eventually caught. It's about power projection. Thus far they seem to mostly show up."
When power calls you, you come. But power itself is a fragile trick of perception.
"We are permitted to use whatever force we deem necessary. Even lethal."
"Wait, so if I kill someone while on duty..."
"Have you ever killed anyone, Kim?"
"Have *I* killed anyone?"
"You have to supply compelling evidence for why it was necessary to use lethal force. In these cases -- your partner is usually your witness."
"Yes." He pauses. "The last time was four years ago."
"That's an improbability -- perhaps even impossibility..."
"*Not* a good position to be in, by the way. Internal Affairs handles these cases thoroughly -- by cross-examining you for inconsistencies. It is hard to *cover* for anyone. Which is for the best."
He says it matter-of-factly and moves on.
Of course you've killed people. It's somewhere down there, melting in all the drink...
"I must have. I feel it in me."
"I probably have."
"I don't know if I really want to know."
"No. I don't think I have."
"Precinct 41 is known for... a higher-than-average rate of police violence."
"Perhaps. But Precinct 41 is known for... a higher-than-average rate of kills." He raises his eyebrows.
He's not judging you. He's respectfully acknowledging the difficulty of working in your precinct.
"And who makes all these rules?" (Continue.)
"And the Moralintern more broadly, but yes." His gaze is absently fixed on a window below that just went dark.
"The Coalition Government and the Moralintern more broadly."

"The RCM was formed by the Coalition Government to restore order in the International Zone after the Revolution. So we did. Now we attempt to *maintain* that order, no more, no less." His gaze is absently fixed on a window below that just went dark.
"Or... perhaps it is better to say we were *allowed to form*. It's a point of contention whether the citizens of Revachol or the Coalition Government founded the RCM."
"You really got him talking, and now we know a lot about local politics, including Claire's ambitions and drug trade, and also have some viable suspects."
"You really got him talking, and now we know a lot about local politics, including Claire's drug trade, and also have some viable suspects."
"You really got him talking, and now we know a lot about the union, and also have some viable suspects."
"You got him to talk to you about both the Union and the murder, so we're definitely making progress there."
"You got him to talk to you about the Union, but he wouldn't talk to you about the murder without having you do a favour for him first."
"You got him to talk to you about the Union and even his drug trade, but he wouldn't talk to you about the murder without having you do a favour for him first."
"You got him to talk to you about the Union and even his drug trade, but he wouldn't talk to you about the murder."
"You got him to talk to you about the Union, but not the murder."
"Though he wasn't forthcoming about the Union, you got him talking about the murder. Good one, that."
"Though he wasn't forthcoming about the Union, you got him talking about the murder, and now we have some viable suspects."

"Though he wasn't forthcoming about the Union, you got him talking about the murder, and now we have some viable suspects. Moreover, we learned something about Claire's personal ambitions in all of this."
"He wasn't particularly forthcoming with useful information, however."
"Yeah, it's getting very cold now. Let's go." He puts out the stub of his cigarette and looks to the door.

Go for it -- the lieutenant has his eyes set on the fat guy. Push Angus. We're almost there.
"You hanged a corpse to cover up the real cause of death -- the bullet in his head."
Fat Angus. The powerful guy. Mr. All Muscle. The time has come -- put him in the pressure cooker.
"You hanged a corpse to cover up the real cause of death -- what was it?"
Suddenly there is an awful ringing in your ears -- your body temperature spikes. You're burning all over -- with fear.
"You just killed yourself. Like I said you would -- suicide..." He shakes his silvery head; his calm voice is almost kind now.
"Goddamn right! Don't *come around* if you're not *from around*!"
"You hanged the corpse to cover up the real cause of death -- the bullet in his head."
"Fine. I'll tell him. After a long walk along the *coast*." She walks off without looking back.
"Wait. Let's go back. I want to say something else..."
"You hear that, Angus! They're gonna kill me too!"
"They club you -- from behind -- string you up and go back to drinking."
"We're not sure. Probably a bullet. The wound was difficult to see."
"They drag you out back, light your corpse on fire and piss on you. They don't care."
"You hanged the corpse to cover up the real cause of death -- what was it?"
"Wait. Stop. Let's go back. I want to say something else..."
"Goddamn right, this is Uniontown! You work for the company -- we *will* kill you!"
"Me too."
"Fuck, Dennis, we don't kill you if you work for the company! Half the harbour works for the company..."
"We didn't kill him! We didn't even *hang him*, he was dead when..." He takes a breath, wheezing.
"Work for the wrong company," he jots down, "and they execute you."
"They kill you," he jots down, "because they think it's *funny*."
"I'm sorry I made you guys fight."
You only manage to perform one more movement. An instinctive jerk to your left. Then -- no sound. No one screams. It's impossible to say where it comes from...
"Lizzie." He turns to the fixer. "Your help is no longer needed here. Go tell Evrart."
"It wasn't for your fucking entertainment, Dennis. She..." He gets a hold of himself.
"What do you mean, old man? What suicide?"
"DENNIS!" Titus roars. "Stand down or I'll beat your head in. Theo --" He points to the old man. "Take your hand off the belt -- this isn't '31. I've got this under control."
"So you *didn't* kill him. He was already dead."
"Yeah, let them know!" The little guy slams his fist on the table. "We'll kill you dead."
What? What does that mean?
"No." You see him shake his silvery head. His calm voice is almost kind now. "*I'm* not gonna do it. I'm too old for a shot like that now..."
You caught the leader off guard. Now strike.
"Angie, where's your goddamn inhaler? You sound like you're dying."
Look at Kim first.
The man's fists under the table are balled -- you can tell from his neck and shoulders. He means it.
(Turn to Angus.) "Or what? You're gonna kill me like you killed him? FOR NO FUCKING REASON?"
"It wasn't that. It wasn't..." the fat man says with a wheeze. "We didn't hit him, okay?"
"I left it home. I can't get it, I'm too fucked..." He grabs his chest. "I'm sorry."
"We didn't light him on fire!" You hear the fat man wheeze. He's trying to get up. "No one pissed on him either!"
That's it, that's the weak one -- you flushed him out. Now go in for the...
"Officer, you *will* be next if you don't shut up." The old man reaches for his belt, but his voice is strangely calm.
(Turn to Theo.) "What happens if I keep talking? You gonna *kill* me too -- in this bar?! FOR NOTHING?!"
"Why are you so fucking FAT, Angus?!" Lizzie snaps at him. "Now it's all pointless, because of *you*. You wasted my time. I told you, Titus --" she turns to him. "I told you to just give her up."
Steel yourself, push on. Just ignore Theo.
Firearm! A Glace 08, or a .38 calibre pistol -- either is small enough for you to have missed.
He's on to you. He knows what you're trying to do...
Another nod.
He nods.
He doesn't think she did. Or at least he *hopes* she didn't.
"What happened Sunday night?"
"Klaasje came down." He points to the stairs. "She seemed really out of it. Drugged up -- even more than usual. Bug eyed and gurning, you know? Not in a *fun* way."
"Cause the girls asked us to. They were in some shit."
Girls plural? There's another girl? Two of them? Take note of this. They'll probably say more about her later.
"Why?"
"If Klaasje didn't kill him -- why the cover up?"
"So, *who* killed the merc then? Any leads?"
So there *was* a wound -- you should try looking for it one more time, before you send the body away.
At least you'll know what to look for now -- when you get around to doing the autopsy.

The coroner and his assistant are wrapped in blue: hands covered in blue gloves, mouths covered by blue masks, bodies by blue aprons. The coroner wipes his brow, scalpel still in his hand. "Get the light. Shine it in his mouth," he tells his assistant. The coroner squats, to better see as the light illumines the darkness inside. "Well, shit. Can't blame them for missing that. Get the saw, Alan. This just got fun."
"It looked like she'd redosed after something went down. I've seen that look before, she was scared. I knew someone had died."
"How did you know?"
"What happened then?"
"I've done this job for ten years. I've seen it before. It's the politician in the motel room with the dead hooker scenario -- only in reverse."
"Did *she* kill him?"
"Did *she* kill him?"
"Cop, I have no idea -- the girl says she didn't..."
"Good analogy, boss." The rat-faced man snickers.
"You don't get to talk yet, Shanky." He points at him. "You're still on the bench -- and you keep taking it easy too, Angus." He turns back to you.
That's okay with the fat man, still wheezing there. He couldn't speak if he wanted to.
"We went upstairs. Sure as day the merc was dead. And there was a bullet hole through the window. Fucking..." He scratches his chin. "Dirty sheets and bottles everywhere."
"Tibbs patched the window. And the corpse -- we hanged."
He means they'd been fucking?
Does he? His closed fist is shaking... it's *you* who's in control. Let them have their moment.
(Whisper) "Kim, we did it."
The lieutenant gives a smile only you can see.
You're in. He's all yours. Questions!
"Whose idea was it to hang him anyway -- hers?"
"Who's *Tibbs*?"
"My brother. He's in the window replacement business."
Tibbs -- that's short for...
"Short for Tiberius?"
Back to cop questions.
"Yeah." He nods. "Good man."
Bet their father's named Atticus Hardie -- Lucretia Hardie would be their sister. Anyway.
Yes. No more small talk.
"You may have noticed our girl's in some shit of her own."
"Thank you for this, Titus. I'll go talk to her -- for the last time." (Conclude.)
"I do -- one of those mercenary buddies of his could've done it. They got guns. Training. Years of bad blood, probably. Or it could've been someone else from Krenel..." He pauses to think.
"She told me some people were after her -- from Oranje. She wouldn't say more."
"Yeah, I told you she's not what she seems. She's had special training -- for something shady."
"I didn't notice anything -- what kind of *shit* are we talking about?"
"The *can't show up on police radar* kind. There are people after her. From the Old Old World -- where she came from."
"These people -- who are they?"
"They're powerful." He looks out the window. "Connected to the Moralintern. She's clearly afraid for her life -- says if she showed up in your systems, she'd be ghosted away."
"And why would you help someone like that? By taking on a murder?"
"Why would help someone like that out?"
"Why *would* I?" He shrugs. "I guess we abide all sorts of runaways and losers here. It's a Martinaise thing."
"Yeah -- she wouldn't. She's fucked if she shows up on police radar."
That's all he knows -- that's all she's told him.
"Oh, you meant *that* kind of training -- like a spy?" He scratches his chin. "Maybe. The kind of people who are after her... I guess she'd have to be."
"Why *would* I?" He looks you in the eye: "I guess we abide all sorts of runaways and losers here. It's a Martinaise thing."
"Not yet. Just some ideas. She says the shot came from outside, behind the window somewhere. So that's a clue."
"What are you thinking?"
"I'm thinking -- someone's past caught up with them. Either hers or his."
"I mean the people after Klaasje. Maybe the shot missed. Maybe it was meant for *her*?"
"Got it. Tell me something else."
"Yeah, sure. You don't need my clues. You're doing a great job on your own." He shakes his head.
"Hers -- you mean..."
"She's got one of those *chequered* pasts. The shot could have missed. Could've been meant for her?"
"I like that." The young guy nods. "Been thinkin' the same thing myself."
"And you had ideas about *his* past too?"
"Tell you what I'd do -- check out the coast for vantage points. Maybe consult with a ballistics buddy of mine -- that's what *I'd* do. If I wasn't too busy doing this clown dance with you."
"Hers?"
"In a manner of speaking."
Remember the two girls? He may be talking about the other one.
"What do you mean?"
"Earlier you said the *girls* asked for your help. Was this the other girl?"
"That's right." He blinks. "It was her idea to hang him -- I liked it, for political reasons. It sent a good message."
"We had... help. From another girl. It was her idea to hang him -- and I liked it, for political reasons. It sent a good message."
"Who is she -- this *other* girl? Do I know her?"
"No," he shakes his head, "you're not gonna be on a first name basis with this person."
"Okay -- *where* is she?"
"Okay -- I get it. Stonewalled."
"Glad you understand that."
"You're not getting to her," he says calmly. "This person is affiliated with the Hardie boys. It's Klaasje you want to talk to."
Hah! Here we go. Jigsaw pieces falling into place...
"You do that." He grabs his beer and swirls it in his hand, then thinks of something. "Hey, cop -- before you go."

"She..." He looks up. "Klaasje came to Martinaise to hide -- many of us did. This is where you wash up when there's nowhere left to go. The Union takes you in -- now, she *refused* that protection, but..."
"But you would *still* prefer if we didn't take her away?"
Suddenly the wind picks up outside. You hear it rattling the large windows in their frames. It carries newspapers, circles the Whirling-in-Rags in a warm column...
"Good bye, Titus." [Leave.]
Still, after all this headache...
"That's right. If we didn't take care of the people who end up here, this place would just be a couple of ruins and some cargo containers."
"We'll take that into account." The lieutenant slides his notebook into his coat pocket. He turns to leave.
A story that fits the occasion, of course! I invented a wonderful *allegory* for all this...
I do not understand. They're just stupid, probably. Too stupid to understand the arguments. Maybe the lieutenant could do it for you.
(Whisper to the lieutenant.) "Kim, I can't keep doing this. You take the wheel."
The lieutenant inclines his head, only slightly. "Thanks for your time, Titus. Case closed." He takes out his notebook and writes a few words. "Let's go, officer."
"Huh?" He looks surprised.
"Really. We're ready to begin our report. I've already started, actually." He turns back to his notebook, and writes as he speaks:
"Yeah, let them know!" The little guy slams his fist on the table. "We'll kill you dead."
"In Martinaise they just kill you because they don't *like* you..."
"I'm gonna tell you a little story about *Kim* here."
"It's her, isn't it -- the missing eighth Hardie? That's the other girl."
The big guy turns to Glen who's about to say something.
"Understood. Can you tell me anything about her? Name, current location?"
"You're going to stonewall me if I ask more about her, aren't you?"
"Glad you understand that."
"Nope," he says. "You're not getting to her. It's Klaasje you want to talk to."
"You know, it's okay for there to be a Hardie girl, Titus."
His face sets like concrete. He shakes his head solemnly. "We're Hardie *boys* and that's *it*."
"It's her, isn't it? The drug trafficker -- the missing eighth Hardie..."
"She's affiliated with the Hardies? So she's, like... a Hardie girl?"
"So the missing eighth Hardie boy... is a Hardie girl?"
A little too far there -- but you're definitely right.
The big guy steps toward you. "Fella, you think too much. Ease off, alright? You're gonna hurt your head."
"I wouldn't go that far. She's just a woman who's sometimes in our company -- who sympathizes with Klaasje. Let's leave it at that."
"You know, actually, some of the guys have been talking, and..."
"No. My answer is no, Glen." He turns to you. "We're Hardie *boys* and that's how it's gonna stay."
"No. Absolutely not. She's just a woman who's sometimes in our company -- who  sympathizes with Klaasje. Let's leave it at that."
"That woman is just *affiliated* with the Hardie boys. You don't know her, anyway. "
He's calm now. Threw all that turmoil away and became himself again.
What just happened between these two?
Right now he's grateful he hasn't gotten his brother into this mess.
These theories -- not bad. Don't buy either one, but still. This guy's not as dumb as he looks.
The blond shuts his mouth before a word escapes.
"I'll say it again..." Titus turns to you. "All the Hardie boys are *right here*, cop. That woman is just *affiliated* with the Hardie boys. You don't know her, anyway. "
The big man laughs, nearly spitting out his beer. "What's that, copper? You want us to help little old ladies now?"
"There's an old catatonic lady in the old fish market, on the other side of the bay. She needs help."
"She had my gun."
"Nope! She didn't have anything of mine."
"No? Well, whatever then, copper." Titus chugs his beer down and wipes his mouth.
"You're *local law enforcement* aren't you?" The lieutenant looks Titus in the eye. "Helping troubled civilians should fall under your jurisdiction."
"You're fucking with me." The big man slams his beer onto the table. "Your gun! She had your fucking gun!"
"Sure did, boss!" The rat-man's face is twisted with a smile. "Heard him loud and clear -- the pig's lost his gun to The Pigs!"
"How did she get like this?"
"Who was she?"
"Boy howdy." He sips his beer, recovering. "Well. We'll get her help. You just stay out of the way. Way far out of the way."
"What's her name? Her real name."
"Where'd she get all her cop gear?"
"Thanks for helping out with this one, Titus." [Leave.]
"Hey," Eugene interjects. "Wasn't Evrart's B Team looking for her the other day? They said something about her... I dunno, finding something?"
"Yeah, I think you're right, Gene." Titus gives him a beer salute and turns to you. "She have something of yours, pig?"
"No, they totally said what it was... What was it..." He's still thinking it over in the corner. "Anyone remember?"
The tattooed man scratches his head with his knuckles. "I don't remember, I was fuckin' drunk."
"Let me know if you figure it out back there," the big man says, turning to you. "Now, anything else we can help you with?"
"No problemo, cop-man. We take care of our mentally ill here in Martinaise. Ain't that right, boys?"
"Sure enough!" Eugene raises his glass in toast. "We're the *real* heroes on these streets!"
The tattooed Mesque sinks into his seat, unsure how to respond. "Yeah... you should be."
"Get wanting to be a cop, you mean? Well, she..." He furrows his brow in thought. "Shit, I don't actually know. Anyone know why she started acting like a pig?"
"No fuckin' clue," the tattooed man shouts. "It's gotta be the crazy. Who'd *want* to be a pig?"
"Someone who wanted to set the world right before it ends. Ever think of that?"
"Fuck you, pig!" He stands. "What the fuck you playing at, huh?"
"More like who *wouldn't*! Cool uniforms, fast machines, packing heat? Sign me up!"
"I didn't want it. Kim has it."
"Law enforcement is a respectable occupation, sir."
"It's been taken care of," the lieutenant replies laconically. "But she hasn't been."
"I can't but feel partially responsible for the unhealthy culture that poor woman latched onto. I'm sorry."
He takes off his cap and scratches his head. "Auntie LePlante, we always called her. Something LePlante?"
"Marianne, *amigo*," he says pouring himself another drink.
"Probably for the best. At least it's not going to do harm there..." He sips his beer, recovering. "Well. We'll get her help. You just stay out of the way. Way far out of the way."
"Marianne Amigo LePlante."
"At least it's in good hands." He sips his beer, recovering. "Well. We'll get her help. You just stay out of the way. Way far out of the way."
The big man stares at you, still stunned. Too stunned to even drink his beer. "Where is it now," he asks slowly. "I don't see it..."
"Yeah, cop, that's some pretty fucking weird shit to say. *The Pigs* level weird." The big man shrugs. "But whatever gets you through the day."
He blinks. "No, I didn't. Because I'm not fucking stupid, *polizonte*."
"It fell into the water."
"You're already signed up, *cerdo*." The man shakes his head. "This guy's seriously damaged, T."
"Respectable professions don't shoot kids, *cerdo*!" He stands, hands wrapped tight around the back of his chair. "They don't beat confessions out of prisoners!"
You absolute fool.
"Marianne LePlante."
"Yeah, yeah. We'll send someone out. Who is -- wait... It's *The Pigs*, isn't it?"
"If you wanna be the local law enforcement, these kind of things fall on your shoulders."
"Easy, Al." The man says soothingly. "Don't let him get to you. Have one for Auntie LePlante, huh?"
The big guy nods, drinking his toast. "Anything else you wanted to know?"

The big man stares at you, still stunned. Too stunned to even drink his beer. "Well," he says after a moment. "At least I can see you got it back. If you have any questions..." He waves in circles, still searching for words.
"Don't disrespect Miss LePlante, copper." The big man finishes off a can. "She's good people. We all get a little crazy sometimes."
"Ah, don't worry about it, Al." The big man smiles, pushing up his cap. "The cops wanna dress up and play policeman. Let 'em. We'll keep doing the real work."
Whatever you do, do not admit to these punks you lost your gun. You will suffer if you do.
The big man shrugs. "Whatever, cop. Don't worry about it. We'll take care of our own."
"Easy there, Al." He turns to the tattooed man, who is taking heaving breaths. "Sit down. We've got one of our own to take care of. So let's not get worked up."
"Dunno," Titus says, shrugging. "She lives by the water. Shit washes up all the time on the beach."

Station 41. A man carries a crate of rusted, unused badges. "You think these would net us something at the annual auction?" A balding detective drags a comb futilely across his head. "Shit, who'd want those? Just dump them into the river."

"Was? Like before? Just an old lady. Her kids moved away years ago. Never come to visit, never took her calls. She gets... out every now and then." He swirls his beer. "She did right by lots of us when we were kids. Always was a little off, but still."
Us kids? That must have been ages ago. She was better then.
"Someone whose only connection to the outside world is Channel 8 and it's cop programs?"
"Oh, don't even get me started on that Gareth Morrand crap!" The Mesque gets visibly agitated. "That racist fucking fuck... motherfucker."
"Easy, Al..." He glances over his shoulder. "We all hate him. The man's all cock and no balls. Can't trust a fella like that."
Must be a local saying.
"Yup. Her."

He pushes up his cap. "God, poor lady. Don't worry. We'll handle this. I think she's got some family in Couron or something... Bastards left her alone when she got sick, we've been getting complaints."
The children kept her together.
"Police paraphernalia doesn't just wash up on the coast, people. It's not like we dump it at night. She bought it, collected it."
Notice how it came together without casting too much suspicion on *Klaasje* -- it was nice and *Ruby-centric* in the end.
What do you mean?
I don't need this criticism right now, this chapter is closed. [Discard thought.]
Anything strike you a bit off about this mish-mash?
Well... the bullet didn't have to come from the roof, it could have come from anywhere on the coast.
The bullet was jacketed -- these don't just lie around everywhere, do they...
So far no one has mentioned hearing the shot.
Perhaps thinking that Ruby's fondness for girls might drive her to murder was a bit sensationalist.
Notice how this hasn't come up at all -- even Hardie and his boys didn't mention it. Neither did you.
No-no, that wasn't sensationalist at all, that is a *perfectly* valid reason for someone to kill someone.
See, even he acknowledges that it's a good reason!
Man, really? You're, like... just the most compromised of them all. Man, maybe you should just fire this one, it's completely useless.
I don't know, my roof route theory was solid.
Yeah, the route was pretty solid. Good work there. Still...
It turned out the bullet was an antique...
True. Strange how you conducted the whole *advanced ballistics analysis* and then hand-waved it?
The footprints in the pinball workshop didn't fit with the Odd Sole's prints on the crime scene...
I'm done thinking about this. [Finish thought.]

That's right. *Finish thought*. Just finish it and conveniently go on. She's watching you leave right now, you know that? Free as a bird on that roof. Lighting up a cigarette and thinking: am I glad Ruby's in this shit and not me!
Absolutely. It could have come from *anywhere*. But you're suddenly so certain it came from the roof behind the window.
Good point. It is rather rare these days... But do continue.
No, they didn't.
Don't listen to this guy. The theory was solid. He's just jealous. Move on, it's no use harassing her further.
You think you have a pretty hot suspect right now, don't you? That Ruby of yours.
Yeah? And?
"The theatrical suicide attempt -- we need to talk about it."
"I wished to embrace The Gloaming ahead of time. The undoing of the atoms called to me."
"Yes. I want to talk about it as well."
"Do we have to?"
"It was a cry for help."
"No, we don't." [Leave.]
"Yes. Well. I was able to re-contextualize it as a dark joke." He pauses thoughtfully. "I will not be able to re-contextualize it the next time."
"I understand you sometimes employ *extreme* interrogation tactics, but I want you to understand: that was *too* extreme."
"We can't have RCM officers going around, putting guns in their mouths. We can't afford to have that image. Few institutions can."
"Understood. 100%. It won't happen again."
"I went with my gut feeling and this time it was wrong."
"It's going to happen again. I'm going to do it again. I'm going try it again *soon*."
"But why did she leave me then?"
"I'm sorry I put you into this position."
"The Gloaming?" He takes off his glasses and cleans them. "Now, that's exactly what we *can't* have. Couldn't have put it better myself. I would need to *re-contextualize* the hell out of that."
He puts his glasses back on. "Now, let's go. And let's keep guns out of our mouths. And not say anything about any gloaming, or anything like that."
"Good. I'm glad we had this talk." He nods. "After you."
"Yes. Very, very, *very* wrong." He nods in agreement. "I'm glad you see it my way. Let's go."
"No need to apologize -- just keep your gun out of your mouth and we'll be all right." He nods. "Let's move."
"No." He takes off his glasses and cleans them. "You're not. You're not going to put your gun into your mouth when we interrogate people. That is never going to happen again."
He puts his glasses back on and repeats: "Never. Now, let's go."
This was your chance to make amends, but you chose not to. Instead you chose to be the bad-ass suicide boiadeiro and now he doesn't like you.
"Whooh..." He takes off his glasses, reaches for a cloth -- pauses -- and puts his glasses back on.
He has an idea who *she* is. Many cops have a *she* or *he* who left. But he just doesn't know what to say.
"No, no. We are talking about it. I was able to re-contextualize it as a dark joke." He pauses thoughtfully. "I will not be able to re-contextualize it the next time."
"We do. I was able to re-contextualize it as a dark joke." He pauses thoughtfully. "I will not be able to re-contextualize it the next time."
"Yes. Well. I was able to re-contextualize it as a *dark joke*." He pauses thoughtfully. "I will not be able to re-contextualize it the next time."
"I don't know why she left you. Let's go."
The right words just don't come to him. He tries, but they don't.
"Don't worry, I will figure this out sooner or later." (Conclude.)
"Why don't you go home and log it into evidence. These men have told you what happened."
Sire, it would be an event most dramatic if you were to produce the bullet and dangle it before their very eyes!
He gives you an indulgent look. "Well there are so many bullets in the world and so many heads..."
"I really don't care." He shrugs and looks over his shoulder.
"I just found a *bullet* -- in the hanged man's head."

"It's bound to happen again, you know." He taps on his right temple. "Just statistically speaking, of course."
"Yeah yeah, I heard him. The fuck do you think I'm doing here? You'd have your ass handed to you if it wasn't for the bossman's word."
"You gonna let him talk to me like that, Titus?" He turns his eyes, full of hurt, to the big man.
"Truly curious. If you *hanged* him, how did it get there?"
It would take an army to bend Titus to its will, but having Evrart back you up like that... did seem to have *some* effect.

"Oh, so you went and talked to my mommy -- and now she's making me play with you?" He spits. "Is that it, lawman?"

Explosive laughter follows. To his men, Titus Hardie is a golden god. They want to laugh at his jokes even before they leave his lips. This guy is a born leader.
"Curious yes, I guess we'll never know... About something else though?"
"I would though," he says, as casually as if he were commenting on the weather.
