dialoguetext: Oh yeah, he's definitely one of us. Smart one too, tactical. He might very well know how to turn back time. Ask him!
But still... he's definitely one of us. Longs for the Old Days - the *Old Ways*. He's likely to know how to turn back time. Ask him!
Deep satisfying rumble runs through your small intestine. It feels affirming.
"How about rekindling that camp fire so we can dry off?"
"Gary, what are you doing there?"
"Don't you remember that method I showed you back in... never mind."
"Seeing if there are any signs of phasmid activity. And taking a leak."
"But everything's so... moist."
"I'd take a bullet for you, but I won't spend another hour out here."
The lieutenant's gaze follows yours and lingers on the reeds, the sand, the water beyond. Then he turns back to you expectantly.
Reach for the trap.
The lieutenant studies the trap with you. "Well, the bait worked on *something*. This doesn't mean it was a reed-monster, though. Unless you see one in there? I just see an empty trap..."
Look around.
You set the apparatus back on the ground, among the reeds.
Say nothing, just put the trap down.
Your voice echoes on the coast, carried by a gust of cold wind.
[Leave.]
This is the last of the traps, the one Morell just set. Checking it over -- he said -- is just a technicality.
This is the trap Morell just set. Checking it over, he said, is just a *technicality*, but...
"No need to grin. I'm not *expecting* to find anything. I'm helping some citizens and getting some fresh air."

A cold gust of air dries your sweaty face and you look to the dark shadow the Feld building in the distance, drawing you to it. What a strange sensation... Once this is done, should you try to ask again?
"No-no. I'm fine. I didn't mean to complain, it's just..." He's short-winded. The sentence ends there.
Nothing has changed about this trap. You need to check the others.
There's nothing else to do with the traps at this time. They're all just lying around, gathering dust and rainwater.
"Maybe they will still attract something?"
You've checked all the traps now. There's nothing else to do with them. The cryptozoologists await your report.
The trap feels light -- and silent -- as you pick it up. Something is different here...
He doesn't want to, but if there is one more cryptozoological run-around, he *must* force the investigation back on track. This better be it...
This trap is also full of panicked locusts. No sign of any cryptozoological beast inside.
Nothing but locusts in this trap as well. Definitely no cryptozoological monstrosity.
"We did *sort of* promise to tell them, didn't we..." He seems to regret the fact.
"Right." It does not look like he thinks you're right. "Anyway, that's for the cryptozoologists to figure out now." He adds, for clarity: "*We're* not cryptozoologists -- we're cops."
No locusts!
Look closer.
"Okay. But after that we get back to our own assignments. We've done a thorough survey of the coast now -- just running around is no longer useful."
"Good, good. We should be courteous and tell the cryptozoologists that one of their traps was empty, but then we can get back to *our* assignment here."

He purses his lips. "Perhaps our cryptozoologists have competition in the form of an actual entomologist? Or someone else is sabotaging them? I could present more theories, but then I would be taking this on as a case -- which I'm *not*."
"Another empty trap," the lieutenant takes a note -- more out of habit than duty.
He stops you. "Don't answer that. It was a rhetorical question."
"Let's keep going. The next one is the *lucky* one."
"How are you enjoying the cardio, lieutenant? I'm quite enjoying it myself."
"I want to make it clear that I don't *actually* believe the phasmid exists, okay?"
Say nothing, just put the trap down.
"Yup. The next one has a *crab* trapped in it." He raises his collar -- it's windy. "These are just crab traps, you do realize?"
"Always up for a good jog -- otherwise, would I still be *on* this case with *you*?" He smiles and raises his collar. It's windy.
"Of course. Noted." He looks at you, incredulously, as you place the trap back in the reeds.
Neither does the lieutenant. He just raises his collar -- it's cold out, as always.
Man, it's lonely doing this alone. The wind seems to howl in a strange manner...
All the traps are stocked now -- and still no sight of the phasmid. Return to Morell and let him know.
"Actually -- I do get the feeling that someone or something may have messed with the trap..."
"Yeah, it probably *wasn't* the phasmid, but still. Morell needs to know."
"But what if it *was* the phasmid? What if it ate them and got out?"
"You're right. But they still need to know."
"You're right. This crypto-research has been stupid."
The reeds continue to hiss around you as you put the empty trap back on the ground. Time to consult the professionals -- Morell and Lena.
"Damn, I was hoping it would be in the *first* one."
"Empty as all of them..." he pants. "*One* more of these and we're done..." His face is red from the cold sea air. He crouches to catch his breath.
"Surely," he repeats and looks at the sea, then at you putting the trap back on the ground. "Anyway, the air is nice and fresh here..."
"It'll be in the next one. *Surely*."
"Bummer it wasn't in here..."
"You getting tired?"
"I *must* stress that I did not expect a cryptozoological monstrosity to be in this trap."
Say nothing, just put the trap down.
The lieutenant stretches his back.
"I'm just..." he breathes out. "Glad we haven't found some poor cat trapped in one of these."
"Of course. Noted." He looks at you, incredulously, as you place the trap back in the reeds.
[Leave.]
"No you weren't." He looks at the sea, then you -- laying the trap back down on the ground.
They're not really going to get the chance to get comfortable here.
"Good. Now that's done. When do you think we will return to our impending apocalypse of a murder investigation?"
Release the locusts into the empty trap.
(Immediately yell.) "It's empty! Morell didn't leave it empty..."
Nothing. No traces of the locusts *or* the Insulindian phasmid. What happened?
Look closer still.
No phasmid either -- but still...
[Leave.]
Locusts are crawling around in the trap, confused but uneaten. You see no carnivorous *reed-phasmid* gorging on them.
"I meant no offence, just..." The lieutenant doesn't know how to finish the sentence. He looks at you, putting the trap back on the ground.
The locusts, dazed from being transported, slowly begin to acclimate to their new surroundings.
"Big surprise." The lieutenant grins mirthlessly. "Anyway -- one down, three to go."
The locusts aren't doing all too well, but they're still in there. This isn't the empty trap. That must have been another one.
[Leave.]
The netting is a little untidy, messier than the others. Like someone or something picked up the trap and shook it before dropping it back down on the ground.
The reeds whisper around the sepulchral trap, as though suddenly filled with fear.
A few locusts trudge along the wall of the trap. The rest are piled in a heap in the corner, dead. No phasmid anywhere.
"Yes. Like a cat, or another teenage psychopath."
"I'm beginning to feel... somewhat sorry for them."
Poor things...
Pause and just stand there.
[Leave.]
The trap stands empty near the reeds. No insect sounds or movement around -- only the reeds' apprehensive hissing.
The later it gets, the colder. Remnants of the camp can still be seen in the sand, the fire that's gone out... you feel strange, somehow.
It's good the cryptozoologists left -- this isn't a very cosy place to stay night after night.
The reeds by the abandoned camp site hiss and shake.
The super fancy topping pie is waiting for you to dig in.
You should eat it slowly, really savour the chef's concept.
Eating this pie will almost certainly make you less of a man. What were you thinking, agreeing to take a wheat-free, meat-free pie from that sleazy bastard?
Consume the pie contemplatively.
"Hey, Kim, share this topping pie with me?"
Leave it for later. [Put the topping pie away.]
Throw the topping pie on the ground. You're not taking any bribes from questionable persons.
You can barely taste what you're eating as you shove the slices in your mouth, but you can tell: it's doing your body good. Soon it's all gone -- just some wheat-free flour left on your hands.
I'm hungover and *famished*! Who cares what's on it? Devour that topping pie!

It's an unexpectedly pleasing combination of flavours and textures -- salty crunch of meatless bacon, butteriness of avocado, sweet bursts of pineapple and fig tempered by the pungency of basil, with a kick from the pepper, paprika, and lime... You have to admit: even the wheat-free crust is pretty good.
Even such a profound experience of topping pie has to come to an end, though. Soon, you have nothing but flour on your hands.
The pie lies sadly face-down on the ground, a waste of culinary creativity, some of its colourful toppings scattered around it.
The lieutenant looks at you wearily. "Please let's not go through this again."
"No, thank you."
"Don't you ever eat?"
"Please, Kim. At least take one slice. It's really too big for me, and it's going to just grow colder and soggier if I keep any part of it..."
"Okay."
The pie is still in your hands, its round face untouched, unbroken.
He sighs. "Don't take it personally."
The lieutenant crosses his arms. "Food of my choice, on my own schedule."
He thinks about it for a moment, then gingerly picks up a slice and starts chewing on it thoughtfully.
"You ate that one man's salami. Why won't you eat my topping pie?"
"I've seen you share the food of other people! Can't help but wonder if you consider me an enemy."
"I just don't want any. Please, enjoy, and then let's move on."

"That's a ridiculous notion. We are not living in a highly ritualistic society where not sharing food with someone indicates animosity. We are in Revachol, where people ought to be free not to eat topping pie when they are not hungry."
"No, but really! You must..!" (Shove the topping pie into Kim's hands.)
"Okay."
The lieutenant takes the pie from you and calmly lets it fall to the ground, face down. "All done. Shall we?"
"Thank you, partner." (Eat the rest of the pie.)
He finishes his slice and brushes the wheat-free flour off his hands. "That wasn't terrible. Well, shall we?"
His tone is almost stern beneath the politeness.
He sighs. "Haven't I already proven that we are comrades or whatever by splitting that sandwich with you?"
"But that was just a sandwich! This is a topping pie!"
"I was just asking out of politeness."
"Every meal we share strengthens our bond!"
"Why won't you share my food with me, Kim?"
He inclines his head. "Why...?" he starts, then thinks better of it.
"I thought it was the symbolism that was important, not the type of..." He takes off his glasses and rubs his forehead. "Please, just... enjoy the pie."
"Well, then: no, thank you."
"That depends on one's perspective." He takes off his glasses and rubs his forehead. "Please, just... enjoy the pie."
You can barely taste what you're eating as you shove the slices in your mouth, but you can tell: it's doing your body good. Soon it's all gone -- just some wheat-free flour left on your hands.
Even such a profound experience of topping pie has to come to an end, though. Soon, you have nothing but flour on your hands.
"Thank you, partner." (Eat the rest of the pie.)
The pie is still in your hands, its round face untouched, unbroken.
He eyes you sceptically. "All right -- what cryptids, precisely? I usually discuss these things with *specialists*, so I don't know what..."
"I know about the most dangerous cryptid -- the Gnome of Geroma."
A moose that looks like any other moose... What's going on here? He's kidding right?
"I know the biggest cryptid -- the Giant of Koko Nur."
"I know about *Cryobacter katlensis*."
"Which cryptid did you *almost* catch? You said before, that you almost caught one."
"I know all about the kind green ape!"
"*Formerly* the most dangerous, yes... But do you know the most dangerous *living* cryptid?"
"Hold on... Does it also attack people?"
"Living? No."
"A lavender shadow..." He smirks.
"I can try to guess."
"That must be the evil apes dukin' it out on the giant ball."
"The what?"
"The evil apes. I suspect I may be one myself."
"We are descended from evil apes and to apes we shall return."
"Oh, you're just talking about *humans*. Well, yes, we are quite dangerous, but we're hardly cryptids." He corrects his hat and says -- as if it's the most sensible thing in the world...
"Just like an ordinary Ardan moose."
"That's what I thought. You haven't *actually* seen it. And I can't imagine how you could either -- the Samarskilt desert region has been embroiled in a civil war for the last eight years."
"The most dangerous cryptid is a carnivorous ruminant, known colloquially as the *dread moose*."
"But that's not all! Some of the slaughterhouse apprentices went hiking by a nearby creek and saw a moose nibbling on an unidentified carcass!"
"That's impressive, I guess." He does not seem that impressed. "But have you *seen* it with your own eyes?"
"Oh, everyone knows about that one, thanks to professor Mijanou being the talk of the town for a time..." He coughs in his fist.
"I'm guessing you heard about it from Lena," he smiles. "The kind green ape is one of her favourites."
"I haven't had a chance to travel to *Koko Nur*, no. And I likely never will. The Samarskilt desert region has been embroiled in a small civil war for the last eight years."
"We travelled to South Safre to look for it once. Gary and I got stuck in a rainstorm, though, and had to spend most of our time there in a little village."
"The search was fabulously unsuccessful -- but the people were very nice. I'm glad they didn't understand what Gary was saying about them..."
"I was lying. I haven't actually seen it. I just wanted to impress you."

"They're very, very thin, almost flat, in fact, and can camouflage themselves easily, wrapping themselves around trees and blending in with the tree bark. In that way, they're not too dissimilar from the phasmid we are looking for here."
"Wait, so I may have seen these willow people without knowing it?"
"How did you almost catch a willow person?"
"You probably have!"
"I'm having trouble remembering..."
"Remarkable! When?"
(Truth.) "No."
"A willow person. It's a long story, one non-specialists would find rather dull."
(Lie.) "Yes."
"What are willow people?"
"Have *you* seen it?"
"They're not people, really -- some argue that they're not even animals, as they seem to have evolved directly from trees." He says it in a self-explanatory, every day manner.
This isn't something unique. Various species of deer have been known to scavenge when plant food is scarce.
"Mijanou liked *extreme* animals, you see. One of the few figures of the academic establishment I respect. Really a shame she disappeared."
"Enough tales then. Let's change the subject."
"A flightless *cursor owl* found in the Semenine isles. Its long legs permit the Nnong Okk to run faster than any other avian, perhaps any other *animal*, who knows?"
"Believe me, you won't *guess* it. You either know, or you don't." He corrects his hat and says -- as if it's the most sensible thing in the world...
"The Nnong Okk?"

"Gary and I painted an entire grove's worth of trees in slow-drying paint. It was a bright lavender colour. I was hoping one of the willow people would get paint on it and not be able to camouflage itself."
"After waiting in hiding for hours, I saw a figure slip from one of the trees, a lavender shadow dashing through the grove..."
"Although -- probably because her life ended as a result of her work in Katla -- no one remembers her contributions to the search for the Nnong Okk."
"Those people were on a different rung of the ladder of civilization, that's all."
"You kept complaining about how dirty they were."
"And I realize that their hygiene habits were completely appropriate for a nascent culture... I just didn't feel comfortable. Let's change the topic."
"I know you think we were snacking on funny mushrooms. It's easier to mock someone than to admit that the world might be more interesting than you've imagined."
"And that's not all! Some of the slaughterhouse apprentices went hiking by a nearby creek and saw a moose nibbling on an unidentified carcass!"
"Okay. What does the dread moose look like?"
"Yes. The dread moose subsists entirely on flesh. It has even been known to dig up fresh graves in search of sustenance."
"Human remains *have* been found deep in the forest, torn apart, then trampled into the mulch by large hooves. Infer from *that* what you will."
"I chased it with a net -- not very elegant, but you can't be elegant in the field -- and, well, it was faster than me!"
"And then?"
"Then how can you tell if it's the ordinary or the dread kind?"
"You can't! That's what makes it so dreadful... and hard to identify."

"No offence, officer, but I'm not much of a *pedagogue* -- I don't know what I would've done if Lena hadn't persuaded me to go back to field research. You should ask her, if you want interesting stories."
"Just tell me about a cool cryptid. Any cryptid."
"I'm not completely sure about this *dread moose*..."
"The bodies found in the forest are just one piece of physical evidence. There's more..."
"What's the other evidence?"
"I think I've heard enough about the dread moose. Let's pick another one."
"Are there any reliable eyewitness accounts of a moose killing other animals for food?" (Conclude.)
"The recent surge in the moose population. As hidden carnivores, the dread moose are effectively removing competition for both themselves and their evolutionary cousins."
"One slaughterhouse at the outskirts of the woods in Vaasa reported that its staff kept seeing moose in the distance."
"The moose would just stare at the building, as though they were waiting for something. Its eyes bloodshot and full of *cruelty*."
"It makes sense that such a majestic animal with natural weapons -- antlers -- would come to rule the forest. The only strange thing is that it took so long."
"But why would it need to hide its carnivorous nature?"
"That does sound suspicious."
"I'm not sure I'm buying it."
"The carnivorous moose are a very young species, the result of a genetic mutation that fared well in the process of natural selection."
"Moose are already being hunted for sport. Can you imagine what would happen if they came to be viewed as predators?"
"What exactly is the relationship between carnivorous moose and regular moose?"
He sees in the dread moose something perversely beautiful and just.
"A lavender shadow?"

"Yes. I know it sounds like we were snacking on funny mushrooms -- but I did see motion and colour. Mine is not a *confirmed* sighting of a cryptid, however. Much goes into *verifying* these things, and my account comes short of a few standards."
He makes it a real point here -- to sound falsifiable.

"Furthermore," he raises his finger. "I am not saying it was a *confirmed* sighting. I am painfully aware of what goes into verifying such things. There is a serious possibility that I saw a squirrel, or a trick of the light. I am my own harshest critic."
"And Lena's sighting of the Phasmid. Is that..."
"Let's talk about a different cryptid."
"Confirmed," he replies quickly. "It's 100% verified and meets all the standards of an authentic cryptid sighting."
The woman nods, thoughtfully, while her hands smooth over the plaid covering her knees.
There is *some* uncertainty in that motion, no? Smoothing the fabric like that, as if looking for some kind of confirmation...
*...we would have to discuss?* he wants to say, but decides against it.
You need to ask him about specific cryptids -- cryptids you've heard about from Lena, or his friend Gary. He won't *just* talk.
*...we would have to discuss?* he wants to say, but decides against it since you've offered to help.
You need to ask him about specific cryptids -- cryptids you've heard about from Lena, or his friend Gary. He won't *just* talk.
A warm wave passes him. Of course the *kind* green ape is her favourite, he thinks.
"WHAT? SOUTH SAFRE?! THEY'RE JUST ON A DIFFERENT RUNG OF THE LADDER, MORELL! I HAD NO *PROBLEM* WITH THEM!"
"REALLY? You kept complaining how dirty everything is, but we digress..."
"THEY'RE A *NASCENT CULTURE*. I just didn't feel comfortable, and... Let's change the topic, okay? Talk about your critters or whatever..." He mumbles something.
Yes. Back to cryptozoology. You don't want to sow disagreement between friends.
He does not want to make it feel like you knowing it is some big deal.
"The... dread moose?"
"Get outta here!"

"No. I will not *get* out of anywhere." He lashes immediately. "The dread moose is a widely reported cryptid from Arda. It subsists entirely on flesh, and has even been known to dig up fresh graves in search of sustenance."
"I am 100% behind the dread moose. I *utterly* believe it exists."
"Of course you do."
"The bodies found in the forest are just one piece of physical evidence. There's more -- sightings in Vaasa, reaching back *four centuries*. But, of course, nothing satiates the scepticism of..."
"A *detective*." He finishes the sentence for him, then his tone turns surprising mild. "Pardon me, I did not wish to seek conflict. It's simply my training to question things."
"Understood, lieutenant." The man tips his hat slightly and then looks to you.
"You're right to." He gives you an approving tip of his hat. "The bodies found in the forest are just one piece of physical evidence. We also have sightings in Vaasa, reaching back *four centuries*."

"In fact, we may be close to capturing a live specimen. Modern genetic methods may prove *crucial* in differentiating the dread variant from the herbivorous one. Anyway..." He gestures for you to continue.
"Another one?" he seems angry for a second, but then settles down.
"Anyway..." He settles down. "There is *more* than enough evidence to justify a thorough *search* for the dread moose. Let's close the subject, before it turns into an argument."
Here is a man who has had more than his fair share of heated arguments -- and would, surprising as it may seem, prefer not to have any more.
"Me -- I'm not a people person, unless you haven't noticed. And I don't make a good lecturer. My strength lies in field work and *persistence*." He brushes an errant strand of hair from his eye.
This is a gruff man who's been ridiculed too many times to feel comfortable talking about what's dearest to his heart. It's in his shoulders, his face, his... everything.
"I fear this mindless barbarism may have wiped out the elusive creature entirely. Sightings of *towering luminosities* have grown rare recently. While they once used to be constant..."
Yes. Sightings of *mirages* are constant. A mirage is a constant phenomenon that people have no time to *report* when a war is going on.
It remains unclear what this has got to do with *you seeing it*, as he was inquiring before. He was just being defensive.
"That's what I thought. You haven't *actually* seen it. In fact, I can't imagine how you could either -- the Samarskilt desert region has been embroiled in a civil war for the last eight years."
"Of course you haven't." He seems satisfied.
A bit of jealousy there. He'd want that glory, truth be told. Even if he'd have to inject *himself* with bacteria to get it.
"Better not to go into the Nnong Okk."
"Yes. Probably." Another cough. His face grows reddish from it.
"When it's not hunting its prey in this manner, the Okk hangs from tree branches, like a bat, waiting to dive on hapless prey below, on the jungle floor."
"When did she disappear?"
"Oh, decades ago. In the Thirties. I didn't know her personally, of course. A chasm of academic pretension still stood before us, even though she had unusual courage for someone from the other side."
"By all means..." He coughs and wipes his mouth.
"Oh," the woman chimes in. "Any time -- just ask. I know those critters in and out. Not quite at the level Morell does, but still..."
"Okay..." He eyes you sceptically. "I already did my best to inform you. I don't really know what else I could discuss with a layman..."
Layman? You always have to prove yourself with this man. Which means -- *you* have to provide the cryptids. *Maybe* he'll answer.
Willow people? Not at *all*.
"All right." He remains guarded.
"Be friendly, dear," the woman says. "The detective really likes these critters, we've talked about them in great *detail*."
Now the man feels embarrassed. Time to move on perhaps?
"Your friend Gary told me about the burning rhino."
"Did he?" He lowers his voice. "That one's a hoax. Some Seraise rice farmers set fire to rhinoceros cadavers and used them scare tourists."
Gary obliviously stares at the stage -- safe in the knowledge the burning rhinoceros exists.
Gary obliviously stares at the stage -- safe in the knowledge the burning rhinoceros exists.
"Have you told Gary this?"
"What if the other cryptids are hoaxes too?"
"I knew it can't be real." (Conclude.)
"Many times. It always turns into an argument. I don't want to repeat it. The rhino holds a special place in his heart -- let it. Myths are part of my field."
It's a *gut feeling*. He knows it exists, fuck the so-called *specialists*.

"Many of them probably are. Statistically speaking, about 20% of all cryptids are verified hoaxes. Uncovering falsehoods deliberately fabricated to fool the public is just as much my calling as finding new species."
If perhaps *slightly* less enjoyable.
"What if you're wrong? What if it's real?" (Conclude.)
"I doubt that. Once confirmed a hoax, so-called sightings of the rhino stopped." A cough. "Was there anything else, or..."
"Did you?" He seems incredulous. "It is almost as difficult to confirm a hoax as it is to confirm a sighting..." A cough.
"See Kim, one of them is a hoax."
"Which one?" He hasn't been paying attention.
"The burning rhinoceros."
"Mhm. The *burning rhino* is where they draw the line." He's unimpressed.
He's a good and loyal man despite his ramblings, the elderly cryptozoologist thinks to himself.
Their relationship transcends Gary's politics. It must -- to work. Plus, a guy like Morell knows a thing or two about being on the fringes himself, though his fringes are... different.
"Let's talk about a different cryptid."
"Honestly, I doubt you'd find any of it comprehensible."
Do you feel that?
Feel what?
That tingle on the back of your neck... like you're being *watched*.
I said I'm *really* not interested in stupid conspiracy theories. [Discard thought.]
What, where? (Look around.)
I don't feel anything.
"Kim, is it true that your people are secretly spying on everyone?"
"My... people? What are you talking about?"
"You don't need to pretend anymore, Agent Kim. I know all about your Seolite spy tech."
"I just want to know what's in my personal file. Who am I? What happened to me? You owe me that much, at least."
The lieutenant sighs, takes off his glasses, and breathes on the lenses, fogging up the glass. As he wipes them clean on his jacket, he begins speaking.
"Now, let's move on. I find this subject tiresome."
"I don't care what that delinquent said."
"Wait, so you can't tell me anything about myself, using spy technology?"
"And no such recordings exist, to my knowledge. Seol has bigger squid to fry."
"In case you've forgotten, men and women in our profession rarely make it to retirement -- and certainly not if they do not trust their partners."
"I'm sorry I doubted you, Kim."
"Why not?"
"I knew it! I knew you couldn't really be a traitor!"
"I respect you as a colleague, and so I will have this conversation with you, but only once."
"There is no Seolite Conspiracy, and even if there were, I would not be a part of it."
"Thanks for clearing that up, lieutenant."
"But Gary said..."

"I was born and raised Revacholian. So was my mother. As for my father, I didn't know him, I don't know who he was. And I don't care. From what I've heard, he wasn't a very pleasant person to be around."
He gestures for you to stop.
"I'm sorry I doubted you even for a moment, Kim." (Lie.)
"At least you were forthcoming with your doubt. Now, let's move on. I find this subject tiresome."
He smirks. "Nothing from surreptitious recordings collected by Seolite agents in an effort to compromise the Militia."
He leans back and studies you with a look of grave concern.
"Yes. Now, let's move on. I find this subject tiresome."
The lieutenant is waiting patiently, tapping his foot lightly to a tune only he can hear.
*Don't* you, though?
Okay, maybe there's *something*. (Look around.)
Nope, everything's normal here. [Discard thought.]
There, *the lieutenant*. Isn't it suspicious how he's always there, *watching* you, *listening* to you?
Isn't that what you've always wanted, to be listened to?
Assume for the sake of argument that there's something to this inane conspiracy... If Seol is keeping tabs on everyone, maybe they can fill in some of your memory holes...
There's nothing suspicious here. [Discard thought.]
"I'm really just interested in the spy tech. How did you get the micro-cassettes so micro?"
"Lots of people out there miss the good old days."
"You think it's gonna be much longer?"
"People are starting to think, waking up."
"Don't you ever wish Hjelmdall was a real place?"
"So many things happening *behind* the scenes."
"People are just scared of the truth."
"I'm just saying, as a *Revacholian*, I am slightly worried."
"What about Revacholian traditions and customs?"
"Gotta be careful what you say these days."
"Quite colourful in here... I mean the lights!"
"I don't mean to sound paranoid or anything, *but*..."
"It's not like I go to meetings or anything."
"Mass-radio can't be trusted. They're all just mouth-pieces."
"If I come to *your* home I respect your way of life, right?"
"It's a bit crowded in here."
"Are you enjoying yourself, darling?"
"There was a confirmed sighting in Mirova in December."
"The evidence is right there -- we can't just ignore it."
"An *unconfirmed* sighting is just a story."
"C'mon, Gary, it's never that black and white."
"God, I hope the traps will hold..."
"Hate to break it to you, Gary, but rhinos don't just combust in flames."
"Gary, do you know how to turn back time?"
"Do I know how to turn back time...?" He gives you a sideways glance. "Is that a trick question?"
"Are you *still* pursuing this?" The lieutenant gives you a tired look.
The lieutenant crosses his arms and turns to look at you.
You'd better be going somewhere case-related with this.
"What's wrong? Material not good enough to send back to your Seolite masters?"
"Yes. This is important."
"I'm not going to dignify that with an answer." The lieutenant's voice is cold and official as he opens his notebook. "Make it quick, we're in the middle of a murder investigation."
"More important than our murder investigation?"
"Now *that's* a trick question, right Gary?" (Wink at him.)
"Potentially more important than *anything* ever before."
"I guess not."
"Ugh... yeah, yeah. I guess." He shrugs, looking confused.
"Make it quick," remarks the lieutenant dryly and opens his notebook. "And the question was rhetorical, not a trick."
"No," the lieutenant replies with a sigh and opens his notebook. "It really isn't. Just please make it quick, so we can get back to our low-priority murder case."
"In that case please make it extra quick, so we can get back to it," says the lieutenant and opens his notebook. "I mean it."
"No?" he asks, surprised. "Because I could've sworn that's what you're doing right now."
"It *will* make sense, I promise."
"Just... please, Kim, trust me on this."
"Fine." He opens his notebook and starts leafing through the pages. "Just make it quick. We need to get back to our case."
"Make what quick?" He shrugs. "You're asking me about time travel. Is this some kind of a trick?"
"I'm all out of tricks, Gary. Tell me what you know."
A question for an answer, huh? The answer must be really obvious.
He gave you a question for an answer. Must mean the answer's obvious.
"Yes, Gary. A trick. Now humour me."
"I don't joke around about time, Gary." (Stare at him intently.)
"Phew..." He scratches his head. "I don't know what to tell you. I mean of course there are *theories* out there..."
The further out, the better.

"Well, there's a very interesting cryptid known as the Semper Maa. And a certain tribe of ancient kipts who practiced 'digital castigation,' though frankly I don't know how *compelling* you'll find that theory..."

"And then you hear rumours..." He flashes a quick side-glance at the lieutenant. "... that the Seolites possess technology that actually lets them move through time like it's a corridor. Back and forth, you see."
"But then, there are rumours going around that the Seolites have developed a technology that allows them to move through time like it's a corridor. Back and forth, you see."
The lieutenant stops writing in his notebook for a moment. It's only a fraction of a second, but you catch it.
No. They haven't.
"What about something pale-related, any theories?"
"Tell me about this cryptid, the Semper Maa."
"You really think the Seolites can really move *through* time?"
"What's this 'digital castigation'?"
"I'm not sure these are realistic options." (Conclude.)
"I don't know what to tell you, officer. I got all my information straight from 'Truth Hunt'. If you can't believe a radio programme called 'Truth Hunt', who *can* you believe?"
Anyone whose livelihood isn't predicated on creating and maintaining preposterous mysteries?

'Truth Hunt' is a popular radio programme. Each week, its two eccentric hosts explore a variety of topics, from cryptids and conspiracy theories to ethnic warfare and the 'historical' Man from Hjelmdall. A radio counterpart to the Graadian fringe science magazine 'Paradox B'.
"Pale-related..." he repeats and pauses to think. "An interesting idea, but I can't say anything really comes to mind, no."
"*Cryptids*, actually. It's a so-called 'colonial animal', presenting as a large singular body, when in actuality, it's a congregation of tiny organisms working in unison."
"It's found in the subtropical jungles of Samara. Extremely difficult to spot as it appears to the untrained eye like common mud. It's thought to be impossible to catch and *very* dangerous."
"Wait, it looks like mud?"

"Yes, it blends in with the jungle floor. Unsurprisingly, it's become the subject of many local myths -- some have even described it as an angry forest spirit or a manifestation of the forest itself."
What if *you* only appear as a large singular body, are actually a congregation of tiny organisms working in unison?
Get out of here, dreamer! Don't you think we'd know about it?
If it were true those organisms would *not* be working *in unison*.
Shut up, we can't hear what he's saying!
That's because some them just don't have the best interests of the colony in mind.
Hey, maybe if the rest of you took a chill-pill every now and then, they'd be more motivated?
"How dangerous is it?"
"I once heard a story about a whole village disappearing overnight, without a trace. Can you imagine that?" He shakes his head. "Just a large patch of mud where the settlement was."
"Whole area is completely abandoned now. Locals won't even go near it. They swear the mud writhes and occasionally grows strange shapes."
"Yes, vividly."
"No, I'm sorry, but I can't."
"I don't *want* to imagine that."
(Scoff.) "I've seen the sky cry blood while everything turns to vapour. I think I can manage, Gary."
"Ahm..." He's so surprised he even forgets to close his mouth. "That's... yes, that's also horrible. I mean in a much grander scale. Exactly what happened to that village."
This event will be beyond all scales.
"I asked you about temporal manipulation, not mud."
Jungles, villages, mud... he better not be wasting your time.
"Gary, are you wasting my time right now?"

"No, no, not at all... You see, the Semper Maa has also evolved a curious defensive mechanism. When threatened, it has the ability to revert back to an earlier stage in its own lifecycle. It may even be able to do this *continually*, ad infinitium..."
So the scary sentient mud is also immortal? That's good news.
"Now, here's where it gets *really interesting*. It's believed that the mechanism by which the Semper Maa reverts actually reverses the flow of time itself..."
"Hang on, I *still* don't see how this immortal mud monster is gonna help me turn back time."
"Okay, I'm convinced. What's our next step?"
"This sounds like a dead end to me, Gary."
He seems to have an unrealistic idea of the RCM's budget and manpower...
"I don't think the RCM is gonna go for it, Gary."
"That would take forever! Isn't there just like a pill I could take or something...?"
"I haven't really heard of any time-travel pills, officer..." He rubs his chin, thinking.
Oh, yes it can. Easily.
"It's true that every expedition up to now has failed, and that several have *vanished* without a trace, but the potential is there, officer. It just can't be denied..."
To be able to revert back to a previous version of yourself, to the one before all the mistakes... that's why we're here!

"Well, first we'd need to secure funding for an expedition, then assemble a team, gather supplies... There's probably a million other little things, but with the resources of the RCM behind you..." He shrugs. "It could be feasible."
"Well, you see, the fascinating thing about it is that this temporal reversion is said to extend to anything *touching* the Semper Maa at the moment of reversal."
"So if I cover myself with this sentient mud..."
"So if I *attack* this sentient mud..."
"Well, if you *cover yourself* in it first, *then* attack it, you could theoretically basically punch your way back to the Franconigerian era!"
Like a diving suit powered by pain.
Like a submarine fuelled by suffering.
Like an exo-skeleton powered by fear.
"... and attack it over and over again, you could theoretically punch your way back to the Franconigerian era!"
"Seems like a dick move."
"Very well. This Semper Maa will pull my ox-cart through the ages."
"There's balance in nature, Gary. Man was not meant to play god."
"Assuming you survive the encounter... But that's way down the line of course..."

"I'm getting there, officer." He smiles. "You see, the Semper Maa has also evolved a curious defensive mechanism. When threatened, it has the ability to revert back to an earlier stage in its own lifecycle. It may even be able to do this *continually*, ad infinitum..."
"Well..." His eyes instinctively dart to the lieutenant before he continues *sotto voce*: "How else did they get so far ahead of everyone in the tech-race?"
"Oh, definitely!" He nod and repeats. "Definitely. How else did they get so far ahead of everyone in the tech-race?"
"By working longer and harder than *everyone* else?"
"By funnelling a larger percentage of their country's budget to research?"
"By seeking answers from behind the veil, from the void?"
"By letting the free market dictate the course of technological progress?"
"I'm sure they have a strong central government keeping things running smoothly."
"Isolation obviously, keeping Seol for Seolites. Very motivating."
"By all joining in solidarity, everyone doing their part to keep the big machine moving?"
"By developing an aesthetics of pure functionality, separated from traditional notions of beauty?"
"Yeah, how *did* you guys get so far ahead?" (Turn to the lieutenant.)
"Strange, I don't have a clue."
"No part of *me* is part of *this* conversation. Oh, no." The lieutenant keeps his eyes fixed on his notebook. "That's a special thing you two are enjoying. With each other."
"Everything's cool. Nothing wrong with a little speculative inquiry." The man shrugs awkwardly. "But really, officer, how *do* you explain how the Seolites developed such a lead over the rest of us?"
He's *really* trying to convey how cool and natural this all is for him.
"Sure, they got the place locked down tighter than a Himean asshole, but that alone?" He's shaking his head. "No way, I don't buy it..."
"Wait, what kind of technological advantages are we talking about?"
"What's their secret, then?"
"Isn't it obvious? *Someone's* been feeding them a little trickle of tech down from someplace *no-one* else can reach..."
"From the blue door in the Whirling!?"
"From the pale?"
"From the future?"

"The blue...? No, *the future*. The Seolites are helping themselves from the future. And every little incremental improvement they receive in the present has *major* ripples all along the timeline..."

"That creates a loop, right? The more advanced tech they send here, the more advanced they become in the future, which means that by smuggling ever more advanced tech down to the past... I'm sure you can see where this is heading."
"Then we have already lost." (Look down at your clenched fist.)
"Gary, that's insane. You are an insane man, sick in the head."
"You lost me there with the loop.
"Yes, that's the only explanation that makes sense."
"Wait, so how did they start the loop in the first place?"
"Sure, the Seolites are hard workers, everyone knows that..." He quickly glances at the lieutenant again. "But hard work alone? I don't buy it..."
"Permission to laugh, officer?" He rolls his eyes. "No way, I don't buy it..."
"Absolutely!" He nods enthusiastically, shooting a quick glance at the lieutenant. "That definitely *helps*, but that alone? I don't buy it..."
The man forces out an unpleasant and artificial laugh. "C'mon, officer, you *know* that's not it. No way!"
"I've personally never witnessed a Seolite commit corporate espionage," he says, determined not to glance at the lieutenant. "*However* there are rumours, articles, respected opinions..."
And he glanced!
He clears his throat and continues. "That's actually peas, nothing, no amount of corporate espionage would ever would ever put them *so far* ahead of everyone else..."
You're underestimating corporate espionage, Gary.
"From the void?" He gives you an intent look and crosses his arms. "I don't think that's it. I think there's a *much* more sinister explanation..."
Cannibalism?
"Could be, could easily be." He nods enthusiastically, shooting a quick glance at the lieutenant. "I mean it definitely *helps*, but the market alone? I don't buy it..."

"Officer," he says with confidence, "the average consumer is a moron. Leave it to them and we'd all be living in fake-bamboo huts, burning carcinogenic incense and playing the bongos. No way that's the reason!"
"Officer, wake up." The man snaps his fingers in front of your face. "No *way* that's the reason why they're winning the race!"
"Like clockwork, I'm sure, no doubt about it. But is that *really* enough to take such an astronomical lead? I don't think so..."

"I don't know... Sounds a bit *incestuous* to me, but sure -- none of my business, I'm not a Seolite." He quickly glances at the lieutenant. "But no way *that's* the reason they're winning the race..."
Oh, trying to keep only one type of people around you is suddenly 'incestuous', Gary?
"Save it for the phyrro-heads," he says with a dismissive hand-wave. "No *way* that's the reason!"
"You know, I don't think that's it." He shakes his head. "I bet there's plenty of beauty over there, art and inspiration too, but that's not why they're winning..."
"I can tell you it isn't something easy and immediately obvious, that's for sure. No way, that would be too easy..."
"Come on, officer, everybody knows about it." He rubs the back of his head, looking down. "The stuff they've got, most people here can't even *dream* of it..."
He's just discovered that he can't think of any examples, though.
"That's crazy, man."
"You think that's crazy, just wait till you learn *how* they've managed to get so far ahead of us..."

"No, why would they be... No, I'm talking about *the future*! The Seolites are helping themselves from the future. And every little incremental improvement they receive in the present has *major* ripples all along the timeline..."

"*Exactly*, officer." He leans in closer. "The Seolites are helping themselves from the future. And every little incremental improvement they receive in the present has *major* ripples all along the timeline..."
"Give me some examples, Gary."
"You're right, I can't even begin to imagine what you're talking about."
"Believe me, it's there. Technology so advanced it defies description..." He's avoiding your gaze.
"Oh, you know like... uhm..." He exhales loudly and continues to massage his neck. "Stealth aerostatics, blaasma-powered weaponry, all kinds of deep-secret projects..."
"But that's nothing. Just wait till you learn *how* they've managed to get so far ahead of us..."
There's no such thing as blaasma-powered weaponry, because there's no such thing as 'blaasma.'
Within this self-contained logic-bubble, -- a loop -- he is not wrong.
"I don't know officer... I think Future-Revachol might also have a few aces up its own sleeve. The people are starting to wake up, you see."
"Hey man..." he spreads his arms wide. "No one likes to hear it, but I'm not here to give you a false sense of security. It is what it is. People are starting to wake up and take notice."
"Now *that* is a paradox," he smiles an all-knowing smile, like he just explained everything.
A statement, seemingly contradictory or opposed to common sense, and yet perhaps true. Or perhaps not.
"You lost me there with the paradox."
"I'm telling you," he nods confidently. "The truth can't be contained, people are starting to wake up and take notice."
A frustrated sigh. "I've been through this with you. I am *not*..." He changes his mind. "Just please make it quick, we're in the middle of a murder investigation, remember?"
You notice the lieutenant flinch and rub his forehead as if hit by a sudden migraine.
God I hope he meant it sarcastically. If not, I don't really see how he can continue being a police detective.
"Oh, people *are* noticing, Gary. They've probably *dispatched* a team already." The pen in the lieutenant's hand glides on the rough paper of his notebook.
"Not to the present, of course, to past-Gary. They prefer to deal with problems before they become *unmanageable*. Just something to think about."
"Hahaha..." His laughter is quick and nervous. "I mean I'm basically just repeating what I heard on 'Truth Hunt' or read in 'Paradox B.' I'm just a messenger, and not even that, really!"
"And I suppose none of this would help *you* manipulate time personally, in any case. So why don't we just forget this whole business?"
Mmmm... the most beautiful smell in the world, fear.

"Well," he glances at the lieutenant. "Essentially it's a grief ritual practiced by certain ancient Semenese tribes. Traditionally, after the death of a village leader, the bereaved are supposed to cut off a segment of their own fingers..."
"Essentially it's a grief ritual practiced by some old kipt tribes. Traditionally, after the death of a village leader, the bereaved are supposed to cut off a segment of their own fingers..."
"The really sick bit is that they bite off bits of their *children's* fingers too. Even babies." He frowns. "Imagine that."
"What makes it really disturbing is the fact that they bite off bits of their *children's* fingers too. Even babies." He frowns. "Imagine that."

Small hut, pregnant with screams of anguish and terror. The lowered head of the mother as she gnaws at the child's joint. Chewing, screams, agony. Finally there's a tiny crunch, followed by the sound of weeping.
Agonizing pain...
"What does any of this have to do with turning back time, Gary?"
"You know what? That's enough for me."
Yes, *imagine* it!
"Gary, you're putting images in my head and I don't like it."

"I'm getting there. See, the practice is derived from Semenese finger counting. Each segment of the finger represents one hour, so they count up to 12 with one hand, disregarding the thumb, of course."
Absolute nonsense across the board.
"By removing one segment from their fingers, they remove the corresponding hour from their life -- that's what they believe, anyway."
"None of this is helpful, Gary."
"So you're saying if I cut off both my hands I can go back to yesterday?"
"No-no..." He laughs nervously. "There's a discrepancy between how these Semenese tribes count and how they tell time."
"No-no..." He laughs nervously. "There's a discrepancy between how the kipts count and how they tell time."
"As I explained, they count up to 12 on their fingers, but they divide the day into 15 parts. But that's a whole other discussion..."
One you absolutely don't have time for. Let's be done with this idiocy.
"This wouldn't help me even if it was *remotely* believable."
"Gary, you owe me at least a finger or two for all my time you've wasted."
"I guess I have to keep looking..."
"Hey, don't blame me, officer." He puts his hands up. "These are barbaric people and barbaric times we're talking about. Dark magic."
In truth, these sound more like scenes from some old fantastique novel, the product of the author's fevered imagination rather than reality.
This guy has proved to be a dead end. (A dissatisfied growl in you abdomen.) But the hard endure and the true kingsman keeps searching. 'Vaillance,' brööder, the night is darkest before the dawn.
Please note: Tales of digital mutilation are a common trope of racist pseudo-histories, completely unsubstantiated by the archaeological record...
"What kind of theories are we talking about here?"
"... by about 4.5 seconds."
"That secret inaccessible bunker near Land's End!?"

"That old thing...? No, *the future*. The Seolites are helping themselves from the future. And every little incremental improvement they receive in the present has *major* ripples all along the timeline..."
"I don't know, this sounds made up to me."
"Hey, you asked me, officer." He puts his hands up. "These are barbaric people and barbaric times we're talking about. Dark magic."
Tropes of fantastique literature combined with mundane racial prejudice -- this is what the term 'pseudo-history' was invented to describe.
"Oh..." He looks surprised. "Well, this is embarrassing, but I'm really not sure what else to tell you..."
"Oh..." He looks surprised. "Well, I suppose there's still the deep-secret Seolite technology to consider."
"Oh..." He looks surprised. "Well, there's still the Semper Maa to consider."
"Listen, there's no problem, officer. There's still the Semper Maa to consider, as well as this advanced Seolite technology."
"Unfortunately, I suppose this *still* doesn't help *you* manipulate time personally." He shrugs. "Sorry about that."
"That said, if you're interested in manipulating time *personally*, I suggest you consider the Semper Maa or digial castigation."
"Though I suppose this still doesn't help *you* manipulate time personally. Perhaps you should consider digital castigation?"
"Though I suppose this still doesn't help *you* manipulate time personally. Perhaps you should consider the Semper Maa?"
"And speaking personally, arranging an expedition seems like the most promising option overall, so I'm not really sure what else to tell you..."
"And personally, it seems easier than accessing deep-secret Seolite technology and more civilised than digital castigation, but to each his own."
"And personally, it seems easier than, say, accessing deep-secret Seolite technology, but to each his own."
"And personally, it seems more civilised than, say, digital castigation, but to each his own."
"I concur, detective," the lieutenant interjects without looking up from his notes. "It's completely *unfeasible*."
His voice betrays relief, he really didn't want to have to argue with you over this.
"Hmmm, what else have you got?"
"Listen, officer. I know it sounds like quite the task, but the potential, it just can't be denied..."
Because he's only now discovering he has no idea what he's talking about.
"How, then?"
"Terrifying..."

"It gets even scarier. You see, the Semper Maa has also evolved a curious defensive mechanism. When threatened, it has the ability to revert back to an earlier stage in its own lifecycle. It may even be able to do this *continually*, ad infinitium..."
"Put your hands where I can see them," the ageing woman under a mountain of police paraphernalia mumbles to herself, then notices you and reaches for the megaphone...

dialoguetext: Nope, not right now. [Leave.]
"We can solve this peacefully, please lower the weapon."
"Ma'am, I'm here to help. Tell me what's wrong."
"COMPLY, OR I WILL LIGHT YOU THE FUCK UP!" she continues to yell as she lumbers about.
"Madam! Please drop the firearm immediately!"
"We can't leave. A delirious civilian is pointing a firearm at us. *Your* firearm. You *need* to solve this."
The woman looks at you, but through you. Like you don't exist. Her eyes gleam feverishly and the rotating police-beacon lights reveal deep scratch marks on her cheeks.
Raise your hands.
"Easy, ma'am, take it easy..."
"Failure to comply. Suspect is displaying aggression! OFFICER UNDER DURESS! OFFICER UNDER DURESS!"
Time to get my gun!
"Back-up?" She lowers the megaphone half-way, but immediately raises it again and screams: "BACK-UP, BACK-UP! STATUS UNCONFIRMED!"
"You're not the police. *I* am the police."
"IT'S THE GODDAMN POLICE, SHIT-BAG," she yells into the megaphone. "HUG THE PAVEMENT, YOU'RE UNDER ARREST!"
"Please identify yourself, ma'am?"
You shouldn't be here. Something's very wrong with her. She's completely out of control.
Scavenged battery-powered police lights protrude from her back. The flickering light-show reveals a gun in her shaking hand.
"Patrol officer Pigs, I need your gun for inspection."
"Ma'am, please..." The lieutenant is trying to maintain eye-contact. "We want to help you, but you need to lower that weapon."
She thinks she's a police officer... Try treating her like a police officer. A *lower-ranking* police officer.
"Patrol officer, I have to sign you up for a disciplinary hearing..." (Slowly shake your head.)
"Show me your hands. This is the Pigs. Show me your hands *RIGHT NOW*," she screams in the megaphone. "SHOW ME YOUR HANDS RIGHT NOW!"
"Superseding event! Split-second decision! Get on the ground! GET ON THE GODDAMN GROUND!"
"Disturbance reported, authorize deadly force. SECTOR, TAKE THE SHOT!" Her head snaps at you. "BIG RED KEY, BIG RED KEY!"
"OFFICER IN NEED OF ASSISTANCE!" Her eyes dart between you and Kim. "SUSPECT AT LARGE, GET ON THE GROUND!"
"Wait, what should we do, Kim?"
"This is bad," the lieutenant whispers. "Getting your weapon back is the priority. We can't have an unhinged civilian running around with a gun."
"I *am* the police! Don't move! DON'T MOVE! Hands on your head! SUSPECT IS ARMED AND DANGEROUS!"
"What's the situation?"
"Let's just talk, alright?"
"Blow her away, lieutenant!"
"You're making it worse, officer," the lieutenant says quietly. His eyes never leave the woman's face.
"THIS IS THE POLICE!" She howls through her megaphone. "UNLAWFUL ENGAGEMENT. HANDS ON THE GROUND, SCUM-BAG!"
"Sir..." She hesitates, looking around in confusion. The three barrelled pepperbox wavers in her hand.
"Wh... what?" She lowers the megaphone and stares at the gun in her hand.
"Patrol officer, you're in gross violation of the RCM Code of Conduct."
"Please, Pigs, just give me the gun."
The woman stands, slumped. She looks catatonic under her mountain of RCM paraphernalia.
Her hand is trembling from some sort of neurodegenerative disease.
"The man appears to be pulling out an object from his pocket!" Her eyes fill with terror. "FEAR UNDER THREAT! FEAR UNDER THREAT!"
Her eyes bulge with terror. Veins protrude on her forehead.
"I wasn't taking anything out of my pocket."
"Ma'am, I just wanna talk to you."
"GET ON THE GROUND! I WANT YOU ON THE PAVEMENT RIGHT NOW! THIS IS THE PIGS!"
"Subject yourself to a FULL BODY CAVITY SEARCH! PROHIBITED MATERIALS CONCEALED IN NOSTRILS, EARS, MOUTH, NAVEL, URETHRA, FORESKIN, VAGINA, AND RECTUM!"
"I'm not moving."
"Ma'am, I need you to calm down. I just want to talk."
"SUSPECT IS ON THE LOOSE! SUSPECT AT LARGE! Officer administers street justice at her own peril!"
"LATERAL VASCULAR NECK RESTRAINT! CAROTID SLEEPER! CAROTID SLEEPER! Critically reducing blood from passing through the neck of the suspect!"
"THAT ONE EXTRA LICK WITH A BATON OR EXTRA KNEE STRIKE ABOVE WHAT WAS ACTUALLY REQUIRED! SUSPECT IS UNDER CONTROL! SUSPECT IS UNDER CONTROL!"
In her mind you're under control now, the next moment you're not. It appears the things she says are very real to her, as long as she's saying them.
"Be careful, detective. Don't do anything that might set her off."
In her mind the cavity search is happening, as long as she's saying it. It appears the things she says are very real to her.
"Careful, I'm packing fire too..." (Flash your piece.)
The woman stands, slumped. She looks catatonic under her mountain of RCM paraphernalia. Nothing more to do here.
Shake her shoulder.
Pick up the RCM cap.

dialoguetext: "You're not getting the porta-reel..."
"It's just a standard flashlight, ma'am. Calm down."
"The sabre is only decorative. It's not a threat to you."
"I don't feel comfortable being separated from my multitool."
"If you want the prybar you're gonna have to... pry it from me."
"No! The tare is mine. I collected it."
"Ma'am... I got a gun."
"Easy, now. They're just chaincutters."
"No! I need this ledger to take notes."
"CONFISCATED CONTRABAND!" The megaphone makes her voice almost painfully metallic. "RESTRICTED ACCESS, TWO KILOS MISSING, EYE-WITNESS REPORT COMPROMISED!"
"Are you on drugs?"
"SUSPECT IS ARMED AND DANGEROUS! REQUESTING IMMEDIATE BACK-UP!" She's now panting heavily. "RESISTING ARREST, BREAKER BREAKER, CUT HIM OFF!"
"DON'T MOVE!" She seems to grit her teeth. "HANDS ON YOUR HEAD, HUMAN SHIELD! HANDS ON YOUR FUCKING HEAD!"
There has to be a way to resolve this situation peacefully.
Confiscate the narcotics. (Wink!)
Leave her be. [Leave.]
You take the phial of pyrholidon and the bottle of speed. As evidence, obviously.
She doesn't even flinch as you reach out and disentangle the familiar-looking lieutenant's cap from her mountain of RCM paraphernalia.

"Of course. Understandably things got a bit hectic before. Don't worry about it." He smiles as he hands you the weapon. "Reunited at last. Let's go now."
"But I think we're done here for now. Let's head out, this is done."
"Titus wants to be the sheriff, I'll tell him where to find you. Maybe he knows your family."
"At ease, patrol officer Pigs, your heart is in the right place." (Bow.)
Quietly leave the old woman alone.
As you turn to leave, the faintest of voices comes from the woman. "Please, leave the radio on..." she mutters. It seems like a reflex, a half-remembered sentence.
She must have built a new -- sadly better -- reality from the only material available: radio waves and cop shows.
Reflex to what? Being left alone?
Exactly. With only the voice of Gareth Morrand to accompany her on Channel 8.
Lieutenant Kitsuragi would probably know what to do, but right now you're just gonna have to leave her like this.
The locals will take care of her. Someone's bound to know her family. Nothing you can do for her anymore.
"Cross me again and I will bury you, Pigs."
The catatonic woman doesn't understand -- probably even hear -- your kind words. She just *is*.
It's a shame. Recognition from an actual police officer would probably mean a lot to her. Too bad she'll never know...
She will *know*. (Hang the Setting Sun medal on her chest.)
Nah, that's not worth it.

"Mr. Morrand... Gareth, thank you. Thank you!" As the sharp end of the pin grazes the flesh, a blessed smile emerges. Then it expires, and like a shadow moving on the ground, all sentience fades again.
Mr. Morrand? Mr. Gareth Morrand, the former cop, turned Channel 8 crime show host? That Gareth Morrand from the radio?
That... was the most honourable thing anyone has ever done.
That... was the most honourable thing *anyone* has ever done. You are virtue embodied.
You weirdo. Get outta here before anyone sees you.
Doesn't look like she would know the difference anyway.
Soon someone might have to. Doesn't look like there's much life left in her.
Take her to the farm. Put her down.
Morrand's from Traffic.
It's all nancies up there in Traffic. I count zero balls.
That... was the most honourable thing anyone has ever done, Harry.
As you turn to leave, the faintest of voices comes from the old lady. It's but a reflex -- nothing else. "Please leave the radio on... Mr. Morrand is on Channel 8..."
As in 'Traffic' police?
A click. Nothing happens. She looks at the useless weapon. "This isn't police issue. Police weapons have bullets. This isn't real! What is this?"
"Wait..."
In there she is alone, trapped in a world of blue and red lights.
Her children and their children, if there were any, stopped coming when it got really bad.
"Understood."
"I've had... disturbances similar to this before. Many calls, but... never this bad."
She stands motionless. Just a heap of clothes and flashers now -- maybe if you search her once more?
The woman stands motionless. Just a heap of clothes and flashers now -- maybe if you search her?
"Necessity-driven architectural design at its finest."
"Don't worry, Mikael, you'll learn all about it."
"Fifty years ago this place was the heart of innovation."
"Feld versus Tricentennial -- I wish we could've witnessed that, Mikael."
"On the outside – ruins. But what are ruins, Mikael? Detritus of lost epochs."
"We are living in *very* interesting times, Mikael."
"Remind me to give you that collection of essays on modern architecture, Mikael."
"The significance of all *this* is hard to overestimate."
You see a once-bright mural towering above you. The signage has peeled off over the years, but you can still make out: 'FELD ELECTRICAL R&D'.
Above the mural -- a collapsed roof, broken windows set in walls that are cracking and will soon also fall, and the coastal breeze rustling and sighing in the remains of the edifice.
Feld *Electrical*. How ironic -- all these dark rooms...
Feld Electrical -- you only know them as a small company that makes ink cartridges. Looks like they used to be... big.
[Turn away.]
A slogan used to intertwine with the loops a long time ago. Now only a shadow of peeled letters remains. It says: 'Tomorrow is just a whisper away'.
Step closer.
"Tomorrow is just a whisper away..."
"Looks like tomorrow never came." The lieutenant raises the collar of his bomber jacket.
"Ah, yes, their famous motto!" You hear the man exclaim behind you. "A fine example of technological optimism, from..." He says something, but the wind blows and you can't hear him.
The wind whispers and whispers.
"Anyway -- we do it the old fashioned way: sector by sector. Go over the whole peninsula, ask the locals, enter the places where we *can* enter first. Like we did in the village."
"I am trying to ask the wind."
(Turn to the lieutenant.) "She could be *anywhere*, how do we find her?"
"And if that fails? If we don't find her?" (Conclude.)
What was I even attempting to do here?
"How *do* we? I was really hoping she'd be in the village..." The lieutenant sighs, then gets a hold of himself: "Okay."
"She's *probably* north of the village and this place is a peninsula. I think there's people west of here, we could ask them..." He looks to his right and cups his ear.
"Because I *hope* you didn't mean to climb that ladder..." He points to the ladder next to the sign and says: "It's *not* safe."
Or spiritual? She could be looking for refuge...

"Then -- if we're desperate -- we can look where we *can't* enter. Bunkers, storm drainage, this place. I'm sure it won't come to that." He looks behind him, at the dark red box crumbling across the chasm.
Listen to the wind -- but for *what*? Ruby whistling? The crackle of her bonfire? Some errant whisper, or a dog barking...
What am I *doing* here?
Shake off the feeling.
*WHAT ARE YOU DOING HERE?* A terrible cold comes over you as you think the words. They echo in your skull, alien suddenly.
For what? A song carried on the breeze? Or children laughing, far away? You walk and walk these city streets and deserted coast, and all it ever tells you -- is cold.
*THERE IS NOTHING ELSE.* The thought makes your bones rattle, like the skeleton of some deserted building ready to collapse.
[Leave.]

He stops to consider your words. "*Ask the wind* sounds like an expression. For when you have no idea. We should continue our search. Perhaps even get a little desperate..."
There has to be a way to use brute force. Climbing sounds unsafe. Brute force is safe. Look around and find something to break if the ladder fails.
"Perhaps *you* can climb them. *We're* not climbing anything. I'm 43 years old -- and I plan to live to see 70."
"We've looked everywhere else."
Where does it go?
He shrugs. "So how do we get in there? The doors were on the collapsed side of this building... they're gone, basically."
"The wind told me."
"Right," he shrugs. "How do we get in there? The doors were on the collapsed side of this building... they're gone, basically."

Suddenly, all is quiet. There is no cold hand brushing against your forehead, no rustle in the reeds. The wind has died down, or gone behind a corner? You only hear distant waves washing the coast.
Trying to talk to the wind, or the city? Whatever you thought would happen did not, and now you're just standing there with your hands fallen to your side.
Indeed. You hear what sounds like two men arguing where the lieutenant is pointing.
Listen to the wind.
No. There is something else. In the wind.
As if said by someone else. Someone outside you. Around you. Not you.
The lieutenant looks at you shiver, worried suddenly. "We should go. It gets cold if you stand in one place too long."
Just blow on your hands for warmth.
"Who said that?"

"I am performing *black magic*."

[Leave.]
"Yeah, I don't know..."

He looks around. "Like -- maybe we can get shovels and dig?" A quiver of a smile. "Don't mind that -- a bad attempt at humour."
For what? God? God is very, very silent. Too silent. Even the wind seems tired...
"Ever since I woke up -- maybe even before -- I've been getting these strange *cold spells*."
"Good, good, yes. Cold spells..." He seems incredulous. "So basically your *hangover* is telling you she's down there?"

Say: "I think she's down *there*. Below this building."

In through the collapsed roof, flowing down a concrete staircase -- to the basement, sweeping away footprints in the dust on the stairs. And then the beach below the boardwalk, its winding tunnels... a whisper away.
"Okay -- why?"
Finally, my time to shine!

What is happening...

You try to peer in but there are no windows on this side. Only the disinterested whistle of the wind.

A prayer of sorts? To Revachol.
She could be *anywhere*, how do I find her?
An adventure awaits! An adventure on the windswept urban coast.
Buckle up and raise your collar -- this search is going to be wet and cold.

Or spiritual? She could be looking for refuge...
And then there's the church. You look at the bell tower rising into the clouds -- a prominent place to hide, but maybe she's reckless?
Indeed. About 70 metres west from here.

First you need to tune in to the coast, get to know its residents. Then you can search where you can't enter: bunkers, storm drainage, this building here. You can always come back and talk to the wind again -- look where it already got you.

"Well..." The man behind you hesitates for a moment. "I was *trying* to explain to Mikael what it is the officer keeps returning here for -- then I realized I don't know."
No one. You're just talking to yourself again -- the letters slowly peeling off the mural seem to form a malevolent smile.
"In case she's underground? Don't mind that -- a bad attempt at humour."
He stops to consider your words. "*Ask Revachol* sounds like an expression. For when you have no idea. We should continue our search. Perhaps even get a little desperate..."
"Of course. We should continue our search."
"I am trying to ask Revachol."
"I'm just thinking. This is me thinking. Nothing strange here."
"Ask the wind or 'Aska i Vinden' is the name of a Vaasan lullaby," he remarks. "Maybe that helps?"
"Blood spatter reading, rooster sacrifice -- still quite common in Revachol," he remarks. "Hope it helps."
"I am performing *black magic*."
"I am trying to ask the wind."
"'Ask Revachol' is the name of a war time radio show the communists used to address civil issues," he remarks. "Maybe that helps?"
"Of course. Didn't mean to imply otherwise."
It doesn't.

Even though you're *sure* you succeeded, all is quiet. There is no cold hand brushing against your forehead, no rustle in the reeds -- the wind has died down. The ruin in front of you is silent as a tomb.
Listen to the wind again.
The once-bright mural towers above you, saying "FELD ELECTRICAL R&D."
There's something in the wind. Sometimes the only way to go forward is to fail first.
Walk the coast, the old boardwalk, the reeds... You can always come back here and talk to the wind again. Look where it already got you.
You felt it, before, when it rained in Martinaise and you *felt* the cold of the rain. The feeling persists. It has been in you ever since.
Why single out this one building?
The ruin in front of you is silent as a tomb.
Somewhere in Martinaise, Lieutenant Kitsuragi is consulting his notebook... A sudden draught turns a page between his hands. You're going to need him if you want to listen to the wind.
Lieutenant Kitsuragi stands in front of a mirror, fixing his orange bomber jacket. You should be asking him that question.
The long abandoned industrial building towers above you in silence.
A breeze, like a quiet sigh, moves over you. The cool air breaks across your body. It brings the salt of the sea into your lungs.
GO TO THE CHILDREN OF THE BIG SEA.
What the hell was that?
Yes. I understand.
Yes, Comrade Zephyr. I shall find them. Girl Child Revolution and Girl Child Communism!
The big sea... The Big C? That can only mean one thing: Communism.
The wind rushes away, leaving you where you were -- on the rotting boards of the Feld Building.
BOY CHILD FREEDOM. BOY CHILD JUSTICE.
"Officer?" The lieutenant watches you attentively. "Are you okay? It looked like we lost you for a second."
"Did I have a seizure, Kim?"
"I think I need to talk to some kids in the village."
"The wind told me to talk to children. Let's roll."
"I need to go to the children, Kim. Girl Child Communism. Boy Child Freedom."
"Doesn't look like it to me." He pauses to study you for a moment. "Probably not, anyway."
"When you're ready." The lieutenant nods.
"Right. Well, I'm sure that after..." The lieutenant's words come to a slow halt. He pinches the bridge of his nose.
"This is part of the investigation now."
"Okay..." The lieutenant looks down the coast, toward the shacks. "When you're ready, officer."
"Communism is a murder investigation, Kim. It's about understanding whose bootheel killed the human spirit."
Pull on your knowledge to understand what caused the twins to hear radio in their heads.

Land's End? You took in the sights there with Lilienne. Ruby wasn't up the disused radio tower, among the reeds, or beneath the boardwalk.
The alcoholics never mentioned seeing Ruby either. Idiot Doom Spiral gave an exhaustive account of recent events, but never mentioned seeing Ruby.
You've searched the whole coast for Morell's traps. Just as you didn't find the Insulindian phasmid, you did not find her.
Nor is Ruby in the Church. Some criminals still seek sanctuary from sacred buildings, even though sanctuary laws were abolished decades ago. But Ruby wasn't such a one.
Does that mean she's *here*?
If she's here on the coast, she'll be *here.* And besides, something weird happened to the twins around here. It'd be nice to know what caused that. Another fact for your collection!

Suddenly there's a sigh, carried on the molecules around you, moving, flowing from high pressure to low pressure. Like that of a woman emptying her lungs. She wraps the collapsing stone box in front of you in her breath, flowing through it...
"I see. Political theory as detective work. Right." The lieutenant looks down the coast, toward the shacks. "After you, officer."
Judging eyes, like he's a fucking brain doctor. What the hell does he know?
"You mean we should do that *right now*, don't you?" the lieutenant asks, his usually even tone wavering slightly. "Can that be done *after* the murder investigation?"
"The wind didn't tell me to wait."
"True...  But how do we even get in there? The doors were on the collapsed side of this building... they're gone, basically."
"The twins did hear the radio from here, so *something* is happening..."

... Well, in fairness, you haven't seen much more of the coast. But you do know one last thing: ULAN. Ruby dabbles in advanced radio theories. ULAN, the Speedfreaks mystery -- it might just be related.

And, while you might not have seen much of the coast, you were probably right: The ULAN frequency is likely connected to all this. Ruby dabbles in advanced radio theories. The Speedfreaks FM case is a radio mystery. That may not be coincidence.
That isn't a fact *yet*. But it's a compelling suspicion.
So I was right! ULAN -- she *is* here!
"We should look into that before we move on."
The lieutenant glances down the coast, toward the fishing village. "There's also still the question of how the twins tuned into Speedfreaks FM..."
"Can we look into that later?"
A shuffle of nylon as the lieutenant shrugs. "I don't know... It's your call, detective. If you drop the radio lead now, just be prepared to live without having done it."
A shuffle of nylon as the lieutenant shrugs. "It's your call, detective. If you drop the radio lead now, just be prepared to live without having done it."
"You just want to dial your favourite radio station, don't you?"

A shuffle of nylon as the lieutenant shrugs. "I'm only observing that there's another lead you wanted to follow. And that if you drop the radio lead now, just be prepared to live without having done it."
A rusty ladder leads to the rooftop. Some of the rungs are missing.
"Yeah, that doesn't look good at all."
You shouldn't attempt to get to the roof without the lieutenant here. What if you fall and need to be rushed to the hospital?
"It won't hurt to try."
You're not ready to do this yet. [Leave.]
"Oh yes. It could hurt. A lot."
He is restraining himself from using a parental tone with you right now.
Yes. Teleportation is completely not a thing. Perhaps if you were to, instead, climb the ladder with your eyes closed? This way it's less scary.
Grab the first rung.
It doesn't crumble in your hand, as one might expect. In fact, it doesn't even bend.
"Officer, be careful! Officer!"
The ladder gleams arrogantly with what remains of its metallic lustre as you hit the barrel and tumble onto the ground.
Assess the situation.
The distances between the remaining rungs are rather *wide*. You'd have to use the mounting brackets. However, they seem corroded and the peeling rust is razor-sharp.
Your fingers slip from the rung...
Grab the second rung.
Brace yourself!

"C'mon, Kim. Where's your adventurous spirit?"
"Teleportation *is* a thing. Just needs a bit of concentration..."
"This really has nothing to do with... adventure. We're dealing with basic physics here."
"Okay, let's say teleportation is a thing. Wouldn't you need some kind of... scientific apparatus to create a teleportation field? You can't just do it without apparatus."
Teleport to the roof.

Do it.
*ZOOT*! *ZAP*! *POW*! *CRINKLE*! It's like magic, you feel yourself disappear, your atoms fading out of existence...
"Oh my god! I can't believe it!"
*BAM*! You find yourself on the roof... having mastered the art of physical displacement.
"I did it, Kim! I teleported!"
"I just *saw* you climb the ladder," the lieutenant shouts from below. "You just climbed it, like a regular person."
The wind at the top of the building starts howling loudly, blowing away the lieutenant's voice... faintly you hear...
"Never mind... find a way to let me in when you get inside! Don't go adventuring without backup, especially if we think the suspect may be hiding here."
In addition, the first rung is going to be *tough* to reach. It's, what, three metres above ground, and you're -- 180...?

One-ninety. I'm a giant.

ASTRAL PROJECTION! Be *open-minded* about this.

Where the dead body used to hang, clearly visible from the roof. But no longer.

There is the tiniest bit of flattery in there -- the way her eyes move from your shoulder to shoulder.
"Like riding a 'copocycle.'" She takes a sip of her coffee.
"Ah, I can see that you have, officer." She nods.
"You're doing just fine -- after all, your path has led you back to me."
Her hair is still slick from the shower.
"Ah, I see." She takes a pensive drag of her menthol cigarette.
Be careful. Ask something else first. When you go *there*, use words like 'I hear you have been through something difficult.'
No need to dilly-dally. She's tough.
I'll go straight to it. I don't wanna sound like a namby-pamby.
Thanks Coach, but I think I'll *dilly dally* this time.
YOU'LL SOUND LIKE A NAMBY-PAMBY!
Good on you, boy. She can take it.
Coach Physical Instrument is overdoing it -- even by my standards. Say something else first.
"You ain't seen nothing yet. There's a *karaoke* stage downstairs."
