dialoguetext: "Wow..." She shakes her head in silent disbelief, breathing in the coffee smell.
"Johnny Law is about to tear it up. Sad-style."
"That's the one! The Small Sad Church Song! I've missed it, I really have."
"You have? Why?"
"The Small Sad Church Song tells it like it is, detective -- *sad*."
"I assure you, he is not about to tear it up in *any* style. In fact..."
We'll show him. You'll tear it up ALL the styles!
It's no mere turn of phrase. This young woman has a deeply rooted understanding of what *sad* means.
"Things are only getting easier for me. I'm a police man: Too-doo-roo-doo!" (Imitate a siren.)
"No comment."
"Actually, Johnny Law isn't going to tear it up, that would be unprofessional."
"It would, wouldn't it? It would be *strange*. You see..."
No, it wouldn't. It would be thematic.
"That is not actually what a police siren sounds like." The lieutenant turns to the young woman.
"Oh, I've got a couple of good years left on my warranty..." She looks down at her body shimmering in the silver jumpsuit.
"I can see that." She nods. "I'm glad all this *onward going* has brought you to me."
No. She reached the end of her elasticity about two months ago -- from here on out, every chip and knick and blow stays in there somewhere.
"You must have me confused with someone else. I'm just a regular, down-to-earth law official."
"I would never do anything interesting like that. I'm trying to become the world's most regular cop."
"I would like to withdraw the comment I made earlier. Given the situation we find ourselves in now, it seems out of place."
"I stand by my words."
She tilts her head to the side and smiles. Vapour rises from her coffee cup.
"Say nothing."
"See?" She turns to the lieutenant. "'Say nothing'. So strange. Who says that? What is going on here?"
"And what is that situation?" She looks at the lieutenant.
It's almost imperceptible in the cold wind, but the blood vessels on her cheeks and neck dilate.
"I doubt it." She shakes her head. "You can't bury that kind of fire. What brought you back to me, Fire Man?"
"It's okay, it's absolutely okay to be that." She nods compassionately. "What is this about, officers?"
"I'm sorry. I'm the Sorry Cop."
"No. That's not me anymore. I am a Superstar Cop now."
"No. That's not me anymore. I am the Cop of the Apocalypse now."
"That's not me anymore. I am just a regular cop now. Regular law official."
"Those days are behind me. I am here to ask questions."
Do *not* go along with this.
"An unnecessary development, if you ask me." She shakes her head. "What brings this supposedly *regular* law official back to me?"
"I stand corrected. What brings you back to me -- superstardom?"
"I stand corrected. What brings you back to me -- the coming apocalypse?"
"Questions? What about?"
"Hear that, Kim? I am a *huge* deal around here."
"I am sad to say I have shifted *copotype* since we last saw each other. I am a different cop now."
"Martinaise is very lucky. Only one in a *thousand* cops wakes up as the Superstar Cop."
"Of course there are. Look at him..." She looks at you, then turns back to the lieutenant. "He is The Phoenix. What brings The Phoenix back to me?"
"Wow..." Vapour rises from the coffee cup in her hand.
"Wow." She turns to the lieutenant. "What brings *The Phoenix* back to me?"
"Miss, I don't know what he's told you, but there are no superstars among police officers."
"Yes. *Wow*." (Lean in.) "I am now a herald of the Planetary Slaughterhouse. The Abattoir To Come."
"No. Not wow." (Lean in.) "I am the most boring cop in the world now. Nothing like *that* will ever happen again."
"Things are very far from *wow*, little miss." (Lean in.) "I am a changed man, a cop reborn to *repent* my shortcomings -- I am the Sorry Cop."
"This is part of the... khm... *thing* I told you about."
"Yes, I understood that, officer." He turns to the young woman.
"Kim, I swear I have no idea what she's talking about."
The Phoenix is one of the many nicknames of Guillaume le Million, Revachol's second greatest (male) disco artist. This is an honour.
"A penitent cop-monk..." she says to herself. "What brings this *changed man* to me?"
"I very much doubt that. What brings this *so-called* boring cop back to me?"
"Wow indeed... And what brings this herald back to me?"
"I'm disappointed it's dragging out like this. What a farce..." (Look around.)
(With contempt written all over your face.) "Fucking *end* already."
"New information has come to light -- it is a matter of *weeks* now. A great reckoning of the classes. Revachol explodes in vigilante violence. It's foretold."
"Know that I am no longer the Cop of the Apocalypse. The prophecy was wrong. The signs meant nothing. The hangover has passed."
"Oh." She pauses. "Well, you know... I'm sad to hear that."
"Wow, there are *copotypes*..." Vapour rises from the coffee cup in her hand.
"I can assure you -- there really, really are *not*."
"Yeah, man." Her face wrinkles into a rock 'n' roll smile.
"I know," she says with great melancholy. "What now?"
What is there to do now -- stranded here? The question is personal to her. More than humour.
"Wow..." Vapour rises from her coffee cup. "Can it be stopped? And if not, what are we to do with the time left?"
"I am sure it has. In the time we've spent together, I must have covered 30 kilometres. He has a *track and field* approach to police work."
Isn't that odd? How *can* you run so much?
Why not? You're a powerhouse.
"And what brings this track-and-field god all the way up here?"
Actually, yeah... How? You have mediocre lungs.
Indeed. You don't strike yourself like a powerhouse at all.
It's about DEDICATION, son. That and you're *probably* a gym teacher. Only a former gym teacher can think these thoughts and drink so much.
"What is your name, miss? For the record."
"What is this wild flower?" (Show her the flower.)
Wait what? I'm a what?
Gym teacher?
Doesn't matter! The flow of events is already passing you by! The woman said something, now the man's saying something... KEEP YOUR HEAD IN THE GAME, SON!
Then how am I able to do it...
Doesn't matter.
Doesn't matter! The flow of events is passing you by! The woman said something, now the man's saying something... KEEP YOUR HEAD IN THE GAME, SON!
"Officer." She nods to you in greeting. "It's a fine day for questions."
The woman doesn't flinch, but there is something in her light brown eyes... a sadness.
The woman doesn't flinch, but there is something in her eyes -- the same sadness? Yes, from when she first told you about the hanging, in the hallway.
She nods approvingly. "They also say that's why the cleaning lady quit. Because of the *Infernum*."
"I doubt you will succeed." She shakes her head. "So, what is this about, officers?"
"They tell us you were raped."
"Right." She turns to face the wind, letting it dry her hair.
"Let's return to this later, miss." [Leave.]
"Why not? I'll be here until 23.00, drinking coffee most likely..."
"Klaasje Amandou."
"And where are you from?"
"Vredefort, Republic of Oranje."
Wasn't the tattoo on the hanged man an *Oranjese* Map of the Waterways? The thought begins to form in your head, then dissipates -- something for later.
"What is Oranje?"
"What do you do, miss? What is your *specialization*?"
"Could I see your passport, please?"
Same name that Titus gave you. Like her accent, it sounds Oranjese.
Same name that Titus gave you. It sounds Oranjese -- as does her accent.
Her birthmarks also signal Oranje. You don't know why, but Oranjese girls tend to come speckled with them.
The victim's ethnicity *could* have been Oranjese... -- something for later?
"A bad memory, officer."
"A bad memory of what?"
"Understood, miss."

"Of lilacs and lightning." She squints her eyes as if to see them in the distance. "Parks, glass, duraluminium -- Vredefort is a conference city. It's always autumn there. And night. At least it was for me."

The Republic of Oranje is a democratic nation on the Mundi isola, north of here, over the sea and across the pale. It is one of the six major Occidental nations to hold stake in the continued occupation of Revachol (the Coalition). People consider it a *reasonable* superpower.
Reasonable?
They will make you into a fiscal colony, divert your natural resources, hold patents and shares, but they won't threaten to *wipe you out any time* like Revachol did in its prime.
"And what's so bad about that?"
"Nothing -- if you're no longer there."
The conference centres are filled with people who get angry at you if you do something *wrong*.
"It's the past." She takes a sip of her coffee. "People can't go back to the past."
"How old are you?"
"I'm 28." She takes a drag.
"Did you do something wrong?"
Let it be.
"Sooner or later, everyone does."
Thankfully -- it's implied.
"Something stupid."
"What's that?"
"What's so bad about that?"
Wanna hear what's stupid? Somewhere in a one room apartment on Boogie Street a young man shows Patrol Officer Tillbrook his genital warts, asking if they're *cancer*.
"You're a cop?"
"Oranjese lit."
"Oranjese lit?"
"Oranjese literature. It's what I studied *at the university*." She raises both eyebrows.
"What is Oranjese literature about?"
"Fear of failure, fear of death. How it *sucks* to be Oranjese. All national literatures are -- only the name of the nation changes."
"Revacholian literature too?"
"No!" She seems glad that you asked. "Revacholian lit is about how *magnificent and serious* Revachol is. It's about how you have to save the world."
"No-no. *More* stupid -- Oranjese lit."

His partner Émile Mollins can't be there -- he's in another apartment with another man who's showing him a dead dog under the radiator. 'It's dead,' Mollins says. "No," the man replies. "I touched him. He's warm."
"He's warm," Mollins replies, "because he's under the radiator."
"I have no intention of doing that."
"I do feel the urge to save the world, yes. I guess that's why I'm on this case."
"The world is unimportant -- I want to hear about you."
"That's just a phase the Revacholian hero goes through..." She breathes in the menthol-flavoured fumes, savouring it...
"That's the natural state of the Revacholian hero..." She breathes in the menthol flavoured fumes, savouring it -- then breathes out.
"Strange, usually the Revacholian hero does not save women..." She breathes in the menthol flavoured fumes, savouring it...
"Back to you."
"Back to me." She breathes in the menthol-flavoured fumes, savouring it in her lungs.
"How do you make money then? Money is very important." (Show her some money.)
"Nothing. I do nothing with it."
...then breathes out. "Before they plunge into full-core humanity- and world-saving."
...then breathes out: "It's a frivolous pursuit. He saves all of mankind instead."
"Oranjese lit -- what do you *do* with it?"
"Cool." She looks at the black note in your hand. "I've made more money by just *being* than I have with Oranjese lit."
"Cool."
"Sure." She takes a drag.
What about Revacholian literature? People sometimes reveal things about themselves when they discuss such matters...
"It's not very cool, but what can you do?"
"How do you make money then? Money is very important -- everyone tells me that."
"Cool." She looks at the white cents in your hand. "I've made more money by just *being* than I have with Oranjese lit."
"Oranjese lit certainly hasn't helped. I've made more money by just *being* than I have with Oranjese lit."
"Being what?"
"Many things. A roller skating instructor, a secretary, Miss Oranje '37." She smiles.
It's the world's most tired smile.
"What is Miss Oranje '37?"
"What is a beauty pageant?"
"Understood." (Conclude.)
"You were 14?"
"It's a beauty pageant. Held in the year of our century '37 -- in Oranje."
"It's a competition." She takes a drag. "For stupid girls. Men look at them and choose the most beautiful."
She was 14 at the time.
"What is beauty?"
"When you have the fewest deviations from the norm. I've been told it's a type of mediocrity that I possess."
"So you were the most beautiful?"
"So you were stupid and mediocre?"
"No." She cranes her neck. "I was the *most* stupid and mediocre. And I got a crown and a sash -- and a sceptre -- for it. And a scholarship to study Oranjese lit."
"Yes. And for that I got a crown and a sash -- and a sceptre. And a scholarship to study Oranjese lit."
"Indeed."
Her voice is indifferent to the number.
"I don't think I've ever been 14."
"Cool." (Raise your thumb.)
(Lower your thumb.) "I disapprove of this custom."
"I don't think I've ever heard anything less relevant to any investigation."
"Supercool." She raises her coffee cup as though making a toast. "Full disclosure -- I was Miss *Teen* Oranje '37. The pageant was discontinued recently."
"It was okay." She shrugs. "And it was called Miss *Teen* Oranje '37, actually. You'll be glad to hear the pageant was discontinued."
"Mhm." She gestures toward the table. "I would offer you coffee, but it's garbage -- literally tastes like poison." She takes a sip.
"I'm afraid you can't, officer."
"C'mon, detective, cut him some slack. These may be the final hours of human existence."
"C'mon, detective, cut him some slack. This guy's been through some heavy-duty emotional stuff."
"C'mon, detective, he's the most repentant law official in the land. I don't mind."
"It's okay, he's just getting his bearings. The world of beauty pageants *is* bewildering."
"It's okay, I don't mind. The world of beauty pageants is absurd and bewildering."
"It's okay. This is what superstar law officials do. I'm getting used to it."
"It's okay. This is just him being a scintillating wordsmith. I'm used to it."
"Neither do I," she says calmly. "I think it's *alcohol* that makes you feel like that. It must have something to do with partying."
Another innocent tradition bulldozed by the march of ethical *progress*!
The march of ethical progress continues.
"Thank you. That's it -- for the record."
"Why is that?"
"Okay."
"Why?"
"Thank you for your understanding." She looks a little surprised.
"'The record' -- so official!"
"Because it's buried in a sealed plastic bag at an undisclosed location on the coast. Along with cash and airline tickets."
"Thank you for your candour -- why?"
"Why?"
"They say so in your tourist brochure -- keep travel documents away from your person when west of the river."
"I'm pretty sure I have the legal right to demand your passport, miss."
"How do I know you've told us your real name?"
"Okay then." (Conclude.)
"Officer, I like this place, but I don't want to be stuck *wandering* the city like a ghost after being robbed of my travel documents."
"I don't want to become an indentured servant in a brothel on Boogie Street -- and I don't want my relatives to pay the ransom."
There are plenty of other reasons for hiding your documents from the law.
"That's not why you hid it, though."
"It's *also* why I hid it."
"Why else?" He's suddenly very attentive.
"Why else?"
"I'm an unpopular girl." She takes a drag. "There are people back home who don't like me -- if they show up, I'm in a *hurry*."
"The kind of hurry where you can't afford to *not* find your documents -- but don't worry. This has *nothing* to do with your investigation."
"What kind of *people* are these -- the ones that don't like you?"
"I would *love* to change the subject. It's not important. Unless I'm some kind of... suspect?" She arches an eyebrow.
"Earlier you said I would have to *interrogate* you. Suspects are interrogated."
"Not yet."
"No. I've just come to talk."
Didn't she say you would have to *interrogate* her? Before? And that she *didn't do it*? What was up with that?
"Well-well." She leans back. "It seems I either underestimated you -- or overestimated your hangover, officer."
"You might be."
"If I were to lie to you, I would come up with a more *mainstream* name than *Klaasje Amandou*. It's... a weird name."
She seems to be telling the truth, sire.
"If I didn't know better, I'd say you feigned that 'fuck-having' line to get me to say something stupid. Was that so?"
"Okie-dokie." She pours herself more coffee.
If any of this made her nervous, it certainly doesn't show in her expression or her movements.
"Totally."
"Turns out it did suck -- for *you*."
"No, that was *sincere*."
"I'm flattered. You told us about the investigation Friday night. Downstairs. At a table full of local kids and dockworkers. You told pretty much everyone. After you showed them your gun..."
"Cool. You told us about the investigation Friday night. Downstairs. At a table full of local kids and dockworkers. You told pretty much everyone. After you showed them your gun, that is..."
"Not too hard. You told us about the investigation Friday night. Downstairs. At a table full of local kids and dockworkers. You told pretty much everyone. After you showed them your gun..."
"Whooh..." She wipes her brow.
"No, I'm not." She waves you off.
She doesn't seem to be overly distressed. Or distressed at all, really.
"Whooh..." She wipes her brow.
"My colleague has an *exploratory* sense of humour. Don't hold it against him."
He's thinking: "I like this kind of prodding, whatever the situation. It may lead somewhere yet..."
Playfully. She doesn't seem to be overly distressed. Or distressed at all, really.
"What are you doing here -- in the Whirling-in-Rags?"
(Look around.) "Hate to say it, but you've got *Sad* all over the place."
"Where does that door lead to?" (Point to the door on the roof.)
"That window is new."
"I have other questions for you."
"Yeaaah..." She draws out the vowel. "I've contaminated it pretty bad."
"Is that why you're out here?"
She nods. "The Contamination spreads from room to room. First I escaped upstairs. The Sad got that too. Then I found the handle for the summer door..."
"What if you contaminate the *this* too?" (Spread your hands.)
"The World?" She looks around.
"What exactly is the nature of this 'Contamination'?"
A squall of seagulls under the low-hanging sky. Distant machinery from the harbour. It's wide open and cold.
"It's hard to contaminate such a wide open space -- even for me. At least I hope so. If I do..." She smiles a quivering smile. "Where will any of us go?"
"For me it's a mix of *me* with a lack of cleaning services. How about you?"
"Talk around the establishment is you have an industrial Sad-spill in there." She taps the roof with her heel.
Somewhere below, military-grade Sad is dripping off the walls... you should say the first thing. It's honest. It will lead to introspection.
"Something is bad," point to your head, "in my head. In the past."

dialoguetext: "I hate objects. I am part of the Anti-Object Task Force."
"It's a demon who smells of betrayal. And apricots."
"For me it's alcoholism, miss."
"That's where it always comes from, isn't it? From the head -- and from the past."
"I love apricot chewing gum!"
"So do I."
"I *hate* apricot chewing gum. It betrayed me."
"That's pretty hard core," she nods. "I'm part of the Anti-Human Task Force myself."
"It's a feeling. Acidic and crawling with doom. Gaseous. Invisible. Deadly. It's everywhere."
(Nod.) "Anyway."
"It's a feeling. White and filled with doom. Gaseous. Invisible. Deadly. It's everywhere."
"Yeah."
That *yeah* is the kind that consoles and sweeps under the rug at the same time.
"Sounds like an advanced form of what I've got. With a bit of old love sprinkled on top."
"Doesn't feel like love at all."
"Probably, yeah."
"Are you sure? Love is *terror*..." She breathes in a large billow of menthol-infused smoke, savours it, then lets it out slowly.
Brother, blast a ziggy now! Press that pleasure button, let the pain recede!
"Love is terror." She breathes in a large billow of menthol-infused smoke, savours it, then lets it out slowly...
"Betrayed by the things we love -- what a rotten deal..." She breathes in a large billow of menthol-infused smoke, then lets it out slowly...
Oh my...
"Don't be alarmed, but Mr. Garte implied there's an industrial Sad-spill in there." She taps the roof with her heel.
"I don't know what it is."
"Cool. I think I'm developing a pinch of that too. It hasn't done wonders to my taste in interior decoration."
"Mhm, it's a *mystery*." She takes a drag. "An alcohol-related mystery."
"I have no idea, officer." She looks at it calmly.
"You kicked it down -- you tell me."
"Nice room you've got here."
"Yeah, it's pretty *De Luxe*."
"I'm wintering."
"How long have you been staying here?"
She calculates. "About four months. I came in November."
The bills downstairs concur.
"How long have you been wintering?"
"Why here?"
"Here in the Whirling, here in Martinaise, or here in Revachol?"
"Understood."
"Funkytown," she says and takes a sip of her coffee.
"Here in the Whirling."
"Here in Martinaise."
"Here in Revachol."
"Here on the Insulindian isola."
"Because it's the funkiest building in Martinaise. And because all the other buildings are bombed to hell."
"I heard this is where the washed up disco has-beens go."
"I always wanted to see 'The Only City in the World' in the worst time of the year. It's a tourist thing."
"Came to see the New New World," she shrugs. "It's a tourist thing."
"What happened to the old New World?"
"What happened to the Old World?"
This is by far not the only reason she's here -- and she isn't really hiding it, either.
This is by far not the only reason she's here -- she isn't overtly hiding it, either.
"You came to the right place."
"You're too young to call yourself a disco has-been."
"No. This is Sassytown. It's where the future of dance lies."
"If you say so, officer -- if you say so."
She smirks. "I'm really not."
She looks at you and nods.
"It turned out to be a tzaraath-infested third-world slum."
"Conference centres. A lot of them."
"All right." She takes a long, pensive drag of her Astra Menthol.
Watching herself reflected in the bedroom window -- tall and sparkling and draped in smoke.
"Okay." She takes a pensive drag of her cigarette.
Called Iilmaraa. And it didn't. Even after the Mesque colonized it seven ways from Sunday it's an industrial power house.
"Yeah?"
"It is." She moves slightly to your left to check her reflection in it.
An evasive manoeuvre. Ask a follow up!
The lieutenant makes a note in his notebook.
He finds the answer unsatisfying.
"When was it changed? During your stay?"
Let her be.
Harry, you're becoming soft.
"Yeah... I'm trying not to lie to you here. Stop making it hard."
What was that? Funkytown?
"What's funky?"
"Believe me, you don't wanna get into that shit." She flicks the ash from her cigarette.
"I do."
"You're right."
She nods, inspecting your sideburns. "You've got it bad as it is."
"No-no." She leans in to inspect your sideburns. "You've got it bad as it is."

Funk is an aggressive resurgence of *The New* aesthetic of the Revacholian Thirties, but this time originating in Graad. It's brought there by the Iilmaraan diaspora. Funk is more masculine and guitar-oriented than disco. Even more *dangerous*.
"Then tell the truth."
"Then lie to me."
"Okay then -- I'll cut you some slack."
"Thanks." She smiles. It's a sad little smile, like she's some miniature bird or tiny field mouse.
Behind it is deep, boundless gratitude.
"I don't want to lie to the law. It's not my style." She smiles. It's a sad little smile, like she's some miniature bird or tiny field mouse.
Then she whispers: "I'm just a girl whom windows break around."
"The truth is I'm a horrible girl. Windows break around me. It's not their fault."
You hear the scribbling of the lieutenant's pen.
Feels like success.
She looks at the dried petals in your palm, then lightly touches one with her fingernail.
Chipped white polish covers the nail. It's long and sharp, like a mini dagger. The petal crumbles on contact.
"Pretty. Looks like a dried *may bell* -- is that the one you caught? Sam Bo-style?"
"Why was it there?"
"Sudden change of topic!"
"Why was there a flower on the roof? I don't know, officer. Because of the wind?"
"Any admirers, miss?"
"Admirers? I'm too old to be a débutante." She looks over the railing at the plaza below. "And this place is no fashionable society."
Or an admirer?
"What's Sam Bo?"
"A martial art, sir." She raises an eyebrow. "Is that it?"
Question avoided. Let's conclude that she has admirers. Plenty of them.
"All right." She nods and takes a drag. "I like it sudden."
"Yes. Why was it there?"
Say nothing.
She watches you pocket the petals, then closes her eyes as she breathes in the cigarette fumes...
Samaran boxing, or Sam Bo. Graceful martial arts stuff. 'Sam Bo- style' implies stealth and cool.
"I was just thinking -- what a nice day for questions." She lights a cigarette. "Pertaining to a murder investigation."
"Officer. What brings you up here in the rain?" She leans back against the railing.
Something in her demeanour has changed. She's tired, consigned to her fate -- to being here with you and what's to come.
"It's always good to see you." She cracks a weary smile, leaning back against the railing.
The chorus of the '35 single "Megafoning The Entire Human Race," instills you with the fuck-it-all swagger that prompts one to plough into grannies on your morning stroll.
"Hello again, officer." She sounds tired now. All the pep is gone.
"That door there..." (Point to it.) "Did you know it leads to a downstairs *elevator*?"
"There's a peep hole on the other side, looking into your bedroom."
She looks at the door. Suddenly, her eyes widen. "Oh... Do you think *Ruby* could have gotten in that way? To the *roof*? She could have come up through there!"
"I did not." She takes a drag of her cigarette and smiles. "Mystery solved then. I kept wondering where it led."
"Okay..." There's a pause as she processes this information.
"A peep hole? You mean like a hole in the wall?"
"That's all for now." (Conclude.)
"Mhm..." She flicks the ash from her cigarette absent-mindedly.
"I did not." She takes a drag of her cigarette. "Do you think this has something to do with what happened?"
"Huh. This isn't good."
She's lost in thought -- eyes narrowed, forehead furrowed...
"It's possible."
"It's possible."
"Not really."
She keeps looking at the door with a worried expression. The wind ruffles her hair.
"I don't know..." She frowns, uncertain. "Was there anything else? Back there?"
"There were tracks on the floor. They're recent."
"It's an old pinball workshop. The room back there. This place used to be a pinball arcade."
"Yes. Looking into your bedroom, miss." The lieutenant points to her window. The unmade bed is visible through the glass.
"Looking into your bedroom, miss."

"Had I the physical robustness and social support, *I* would be tearing it up *Soldier of the Apocalypse*-style..."
"Did he tell you he had actually *done* any of those things? Here in Martinaise, I mean."
"Can you say any more about what's on the tape?"
"I'll ask one last time: Do you still deny that he assaulted you in any way?"
"That'll be all about the tape. Thank you for your time."
"Any time, officer." She removes her cigarette from between her lips. Smoke trails from her mouth.
"I'm quite sure he didn't, officer." The young woman looks at you, bored, but smiles politely.
"The tape? Hm..." She searches her memory. Slowly, she starts smiling a strange smile.
"I think he said *whore* a lot... He said this wasn't Revachol. He said it was a fucking village with village elephants and that he was gonna do us all *Co Hoi-style*."
"Coping mechanism?"
"Running joke. I was gonna say running joke -- and that tape didn't even get the good bits. Lely's punchlines got way, way funkier."
"Catch phrase?"
"Did you learn this from studying Oranjese lit? Sounds psychological."
"People who go to the University know how to use words like *internalize* and *integrate*, officer... now what was that expression?" She's still looking for it.
There's more to this. She has an index in her head of pathologies and how to exploit them. You can almost see her turning the pages.
"Co Hoi, huh?"
"Why'd he say things like that? Was he bragging?"
"Was he bragging?"
"He liked the way it *sounded* when he said it. As for Co Hoi..." The young woman lights a new cigarette with the butt of her old one.
"Why did he say *whore* so much?"
"He wasn't actually there -- not from what he told me, at least. But he might as well have been. I could see he'd lived his own little Co Hoi. It was in his... *everything*."
"Oh no, I'm pretty sure he *did* terrible things -- then integrated them into his idea of normalcy. To keep on living. Until they just... sort of turned into his... What's the word I'm looking for?"
"He was like the Semenese conflict, the Co Hoi massacre, and the '36 famine in Yeesut all rolled into one person, then encased in Oranjese ceramic armour. Which he wore in bed *and* in the shower..."
"No, I'm pretty sure he *did* terrible things -- and then had to internalize them to keep on living. Until they just... sort of turned into his... What's the word I'm looking for?"
"Does it matter that he said *whore*? I said it too."
She's quite observant about the human character -- trained almost...
"It suits you, officer. You should say it more. As for Co Hoi..."
"It's not a problem." She touches his shoulder. "As for Co Hoi..."
She clearly enjoys siding with you.
She clearly enjoyed saying that to you.
"Do you think he was trying to scare people?"
"I don't see how your problems are relevant right now, officer," the lieutenant says in a quick, clipped, *annoyed* tone.
You can trust Pillar-Bookhead, by the way. As far as I can tell, he's not singing to her tune... the *only* one besides me.
"Persona?"
"That's enough. I get the picture."
"Mhm." She looks down at her feet, still smiling slightly. "Anything else, officer?"

Co Hoi, a village that was the site of infamous war crimes in the South Safre conflict, the ongoing proxy war between Graad and Safre. It has been hot for 12 years, with atrocities piling up daily. Mostly committed by Graad.
Oh, come on -- you know better than that!
A memory surfaces in her damaged neocortex -- it's not entirely unpleasant.
Wait! Where's Kim? The man with all the notes -- he *needs* to be here for this.
You should record her responses, but you do not have a notebook. Kim, on the other hand, does.
Hold up. Don't go it alone -- it's a marathon, and you'll need support. Get Kim before you go any further.
"Hm? Oh -- I'm guessing your partner should be here too?" She taps the ash from the end of her cigarette while you stand there in silence.
It isn't much closure, but it is enough. She is ready to talk about him now.
"He went to Killer Academy in Vredefort. Then he killed some people on the Semenine islands. And on other islands too -- all of the islands. After this he came to Revachol and got killed himself."
"Yes?" She looks at the note in your hand.
"Thank you. A few more questions..."
"I ran the serial number on his boots. I know his name."
She blows a long column of smoke and watches it disperse overhead. After a moment, she says: "Good for you."
"His name was Ellis. Ellis Kortenaer."
"I bet you're playing aloof because you wanna know really, really bad."
"Hmh..." She doesn't smile. She taps the ash from her cigarette and shrugs. "Sounds oddly feminine..."
"You don't want to know?"
"Not really," she says with complete uninterest. "I just think Lely's good enough. But go ahead. You look like you *want* to tell me."
"Not really." Curls of smoke leave her mouth with each word. "Lely's good enough for me."
"I'll respect that."
"Thank you." She smiles, takes a puff on her cigarette.
"Ellis. Ellis Kortenaer was his name."
"You mentioned he liked showing off his tattoos -- how?"
"How?" She leans back. "Imagine him lying in bed, *freakish* musculature laid out on the sheets. Scarred, of course. Tattooed. The sheets are dirty for some reason."
Is this Oranjese lit?
Don't interrupt.
"You were the woman in this?"
"He's smoking and drinking, of course. And his chest and shoulders and arms are studded with stars. Tens, hundreds of them. Maybe even thousands."

"And he says..." She lowers her voice, comically. "'That was *too* hard core. Don't ask me about that.' So she goes: 'Okay. But what's this, baby?' And he's like: 'Saw some bad shit there, killed some loincloths.'"
"Oh yeah." She nods.
"And the woman goes like..." She points at the air with her sharp-nailed finger, picking out an imaginary tattoo-star. "'What was this, baby?'"
"And so it goes -- star after star, port after port, third world country after third world country. And he's done horrible things in every single one of them."
"Is this Oranjese lit?"
"Yes. This is the very *essence* of Oranjese lit -- a moment's respite. Dark and hopeless as the struggle itself." She leans even further back to demonstrate.
She wouldn't, she doesn't have the Full Hoi in her.
"This means his race was Occidental, which fits the statements of another witness," the lieutenant says, pleased.
This does not surprise her.
Everything left to be clarified is in the column on the left.
The last missing pieces of a puzzle of flesh.
No love for Möther Oranje? Wasn't he a *söldier*?
"Revachol chooses carefully."
"True -- it did *not* love him."
She understands what autopsies entail. It doesn't get her off-balance.
The lieutenant blinks -- his expression does not change.
All right. Let's see where this is going.
This is one of her manoeuvres. The others are fast asleep, as always... it's hard to say what the truth is.
What? Huh? The truth? All the world's a stage! Aren't we *all* just actors?
"What was what?"
"It was nothing."
"You mean the sweating and the fidgeting when he mentioned her name?"
"Yes."
"Yes."
"It's an art thing. You wouldn't understand."
"Try me."
'Tis art.
"The victim? Is there something I should know before we talk to her?"
"I think I know that woman."
"It's not nothing, you were coming apart at the seams." He looks you in the eye: "Do you know the assault victim?"
"You looked strange when he mentioned the assault victim's name." He looks you in the eye: "Do you know that woman?"
He's not leaving you a lot of room to back off from this.
"Yes."
"No."
He repeats: "Officer, before we interview this woman -- is there something I should know?"
"Is there something I should know before we talk to her?"
"I met her. In the hallway, after I woke up."
"She knows I didn't remember being a cop."
"I tried to hit on her..."
"She knows I did some pretty crazy stuff before I passed out. That I partied hard. And not very mental-healthily."
"I asked her where we are, what city is this, maybe even *what year*. Something like that."
"That's it." [Leave.]
"I didn't rape her."
"What you're saying is..." he says in a low, calm voice. "*You* raped her?"
Ice is forming on the inside of your chest cavity, cold sweat trickles down your neck...
"No."
"Then don't *ever* say that again." There's a pause.
"Understood -- you were not in good shape on Monday."
"What else?"
Whatever you do, don't say the first thing.
"Okay," he nods. "That's manageable."
"It *is*," he nods. "This would have been good to know *before*."
"It didn't come up."
"Okay."
"Anything else?"
"It should have. Anything else?"
"So she overheard you? Or did you *party* together?"
So this is what it feels like to be *interviewed*...
Not very fun.
I got nothing to hide.
Fun.
I wouldn't say it is.
What if you do -- but you just don't *remember* that you do?
You'll get through it.
You'll get through it, you slippery fuck! Blast some insane-o at him, throw him off.
Of course it is, you slippery fuck! Blast some insane-o at him, throw him off.
"She overheard me listening to music and doing weird things. From her room. It's the one next to yours."
"Yeah, we partied all right. Partied all night like the Inzany Boys."
"I'm not going to answer that, lieutenant."
"I'm going to assume she overheard you -- anything else?"
"Wonderful. I'm going to assume she overheard you -- anything else?"
"Anything else?"
He shrugs. "That's clearly your interrogation technique. Anything else?"
"This is unprofessional." He repeats: "Not sharing information with me is *unprofessional*."
He nods. "We'll be all right, officer. This is nothing."
His opinion of you has lowered considerably.
You feel fortified by his assurance. It's going to be all right.
"Understood." He's stone-faced.
"It went pretty okay, I guess."
"She said I'm going to have to interrogate her later and it's going to *suck* for me."
"Better not to add anything to that."
"It doesn't matter how it *went* officer -- what else?"
"Mhm," he nods. "What else did you do?"
"And the... sort of... quivering jello thing with the eye?" (Point to your twitching eye.)
Is it, though? 'Nothing'? You're still in for a bumpy ride here, try not to mess it up.
"Hello again, officer."
You made the right call there. It feels good. Pure.
About what?
[Discard thought.]

I'm talking about your zero tolerance policy toward *the mania of Narco*! You're in the *right* there. Powerful stance. Would you like to take it up a notch? Would you like to become an anti-narcomania zealot?
I seem to have an absolutely *massive* speed habit myself... Is this really a good idea?
Okay, but don't I have to stop, like, taking pyrholidon first?
I am pure and steadfast. Totally uncorrupted by Narco.
That's *not* a problem. At all. The more drugs you do, the more zealous you can be in combating them. Drugs give you the *vigour* to fight drugs.
Yeah -- and the intimate knowledge of their damaging effects.
Yeah. Sure.
Yes. You're pure. Unravaged by Narco. Of course it's pretty obvious you've done a lot of drugs in the past -- and will probably do more in the future -- but that doesn't matter.
Doesn't it hurt that I smoke like beast?
Me drinking -- moribundly -- that isn't gonna be a problem, is it?
You're right. I can't think of any objections.
No. Alcohol is a powerful anti-narco agent. Seventy-eight percent of people who use alcohol daily feel no need to use it's opposite -- narcohol. If anything, you should drink more. It cleanses.
No. By supporting the *traditional* tobacco industry, you keep the narco mills in check. If anything, you should smoke *more*. Tobacco smoke also wards off narco spirits.
Of course not. You've always been anti-narco militant material. You kept *her* off a *dark* course with that interjection! Are you ready to *save lives*?
And not only that!
Isn't that a bit... stupid?
No.
"I'm ready to start saving lives." (Opt in.)
"I'm gonna pussy out at the last moment, like a degenerate." [Discard thought.]
"What?" The lieutenant waves you off. "Never mind."
"That's good to hear." The lieutenant acknowledges your strange mumbling. He does not have any narcotics visibly on him as he says it. Good.
"That's wonderful to hear." The young woman takes a sip of coffee. Good un-narcotic coffee. Wholesome to look at.
"That's an odd thing to say to yourself, officer." The young woman takes a sip of coffee. It does not seem to have narcotics in it.
I seem to have a slight speed habit myself, though. Is this really a good idea?

dialoguetext: And my proclivity for smoking doesn't hurt?
My drinking problem... isn't going to be a problem, is it?
Your words sound hollow and unconvincing. You're a weakling, a servant to the dark arts of narcomania.
You say the words loudly to yourself. That makes them very convincing. The world applauds you -- you are finally on the holy warpath against narcomania!
I seem to have a drug habit or two myself. Is this really a good idea?

"This is the Insulindian Lily." The lieutenant corrects his glasses. "Called 'May bells' or 'Lucille's tears' during the Revolution. Girls used to pin these on soldiers before sending them off to battle."
"What is the Revolution?"
"Very well." (Put the flower back in your pocket.)
"Who pinned them? Which side?"
Blow on your fingers.
"Does this flower blossom in early spring?"
Water flows under the channel bridge -- dark water. You rub your sides for warmth but there is none.
...the wrinkled fingers of an old man crush flower petals. Then sprinkle them in the stream, like white salt.
"A big political and military conflict. Ask around, or buy a book." He seems annoyed by the question.
"The revolutionaries: so the communards and the anarchists. White's their colour. But the custom started in the Suzerain's army so it held meaning for the kingsmen too."

"It's about girls and boys more than *sides*. Girls sending off boys who are going to their deaths -- then also dying themselves in the ruins, from dysentery and consumption. It's a symbol of the Civil War."
"Yes, but not *this* early -- not to my knowledge..." He observes the petals: "It looks dried. Preserved."
Inland, above the Martinaise distributary, the channel that brought waste water from the silk mills of Jamrock; and then dead bodies during the War...
Stand still.
The feeling recedes.
The petals feel dry and fragile in your hand.
Six crumbling petals rest on your palm. They're white, a bell-shaped crown.
Somewhere in Central Jamrock, Lieutenant Kitsuragi steps into the public library, rows of shelves pass on either side... you feel he should be here for in-depth flower analysis.
"What is this, Kim?"
This flower is a spring flower, but it's a bit early for that, isn't it?
"Is it a coincidence -- it being on the roof?"
"Maybe -- maybe not." He makes a note in his little note book. "We'll see."
Never mind [Leave.]
"As I said -- an Insulindian Lily, or a May bell. Girls pinned them on their boys during the Revolution."
René! That old man in the uniform. Maybe you should show it to him when you get the chance.
Wait, have you noticed there's a *war veteran* playing a ball game -- on the plaza? You should ask him about the flowers.
"You think this will make them cooperate?"

"Nothing will make them respect the RCM. But it will disrupt the game they prepared for us. We just stripped off one layer of whatever it is. Her decision to not corroborate their story was *definitely* not part of the plan."
"Got it. Let's go." [Leave.]
(Say in a hushed voice.) "Why *did* she tell us all of that?"
"What else could she have done? Lie? She saw there was no way to lie and get away with it."
You would have caught it.
(Nod.) "I would have caught it."
"I'm not sure she *had* to lie. I wouldn't have known."
"I have reason to doubt my ability to see through her lies."
"If not you, then me. It was a smart move from her."
Like hell you would have -- remember?
"She seems candid."
(Whisper) "I know she's manipulative."
"Something is off here."
"You think so?" A shadow runs across his face. "Being candid is the best way to lie. The appearance of candour, with some facts thrown in, draws attention away from whatever one chooses to omit."
"She may be trying to control the pace of the investigation. Anyway, we should move. I suspect our inquiries will bring us back here soon enough."
"You think so?" A shadow runs across his face. "She seemed forthcoming... Unusually so. Being forthcoming about some things is a good way to obscure other things."
"The best liars are always forthcoming... Anyway, we should move. I suspect our investigation will bring us back here soon enough."
"So you said to her.... What did you *mean* by it?"
"What do you mean by that?"
(Whisper.) "She has half my skillset compromised, singing her tune. My assessments of her are untrustworthy."
"She seemed forthcoming to me... Unusually so. Being forthcoming with some things is a good way to obscure other things. But I wouldn't call myself compromised..."
"Perhaps that's because you *are*?"
"Well. I am, anyway."
"I am not easily swayed by young women. But on the other hand... the best liars are candid. And she was candid."
"Anyway, we should move. I suspect our investigation will bring us back soon enough."
The lieutenant seems oddly sure he is not compromised, not psychologically at least. Is it hubris?
"I understand." She puts her coffee mug on the table.
This is good. Clear the air first -- between you two -- then move on to questions.
No, it's not good. It's the opposite of that. This will let her dictate the terms of your...
"Hold on there. The Hardie boys are *not* the law -- I am."
"Cool. I'm satisfied with this explanation."
"Who among us, having been in love, can say they haven't *thought* about it?"
She definitely called the cops. That was *task complete*. It could not hath been a *lie*. That is impossible.
Oh god. That was a lie too. Who made the call then?
She did, of course.
Who... what... Dear god, you've been lied to! She could have killed her lover and lied to everyone! She's not *candid* at all, she's smoke and mirrors and will-o-wisps!
Look at her! Her hands, her nails, the cigarette... Every second you stall, you become more entangled in this spider's *web of lies*. Arrest her immediately!
"She has this *thing* for me -- ever since I met her and the boys downstairs. She's been pretty frank about what she wants..."
"Okay, I'll keep you here, miss. For now." (Back off completely.)
Who?
"That's all good, but I think we should still take you in -- just in case." (Step a little bit closer.)
"Okay. That's it for Ruby." (Wrap it up.)
Okay? And WHAT?!?
Arrest the liar! Now.
"Let's talk about you and Ruby again."
Just like that. No resistance -- her shoulders are slouched, her feet long and straight.
"You sent us on a run-around."
"You *lied* to us, miss."
"You don't look surprised. You were expecting this."
"I knew there was a chance you'd get them to tell you. It's what you do. You're the police."
Shush. I can't hear what she's saying.
Let the miss speak. She's tall and thin and tired -- a twig trying so hard not to break...
"Why *did* you waste our time then?"
"Why *did* you waste my time then? If you knew I would find out."
"Because of the Hardies -- I couldn't just dispense with them, they were only trying to help me." She looks at her feet. "Out of the shit I'd gotten into."
"That's not a good enough reason."
"I know that. But the people around here -- they don't see it that way. And if I am to stay here I need to get along with them."
Is it? Something is off here...
Is she implying the Hardie boys are THE LAW?!
A grand expanse of water reaches over the bay and to the horizon. Grey and pale violet in the morning light...
A grand expanse of water reaches over the bay and to the horizon. Wine dark in the evening light...
A grand expanse of water reaches over the bay and to the horizon. Golden grey in the noon light...
What lies beyond it?
The pale. The Mundi isola. The Occident. And then -- *Oranje*. The Old Old World.
Never mind...
"Is that why you're looking over your shoulder? You're afraid of the Moralintern?"
"Is this about the people you mentioned, the ones who are *angry* at you?"
"Has this got something to do with you being... Miss Oranje '37?"
The conference centres... the people who are angry at her. Her past.
She smiles, cautiously. "I wish it did. But sadly no."
She winces. "For what it's worth, I'm sorry for wasting your time."
"It was a mistake." She winces. "I'm sorry for wasting your time."
"I didn't lie. Not a lot. I've done my absolute best *not* to. I just..."
'Tis true, the laedy hath tried to avoid falsehoods.
C'mon. She lied through her teeth. And you know it.
"I know." She looks down for a moment, hiding her eyes behind her bangs. "For what it's worth, I'm sorry. For all of this, for wasting your time."
"I am not. There is more here, miss."
Briefly glancing over her shoulder to the sea -- as she's done time and time again.
"I sense you're being sarcastic. Okay. The thing is -- you're on the payroll of the Moralist International..." She stops to fish a new cigarette out of the pack.
"It is." She nods. "They're after me. And they have friends in the Moralintern -- some *are* Moralintern. If I show up in your records, officer, they will find me. They will..."
"You share a database with them. You send people to their courts." She lights the cigarette.
"What's the RCM's involvement with the Moralintern got to do with this?"
"I don't answer to *anyone*. Mother fucking anyone, butch."
"I think you meant to say *bitch* there."
"I thought I did."
"I know what I meant -- I meant to say *butch*, you have a problem with it?"
She nods. "You share a database with them. You send people to their courts." She lights the cigarette.
What the fuck WAS that!?! You don't fucking answer to FUCKING ANYONE.
"Officer. Regain control of yourself." He turns to the woman: "What does our *limited cooperation* with the Moralintern have to do with this?"
"Wow. Someone has their testosterone cranked up to neolithic. Let me just forcefully re-rail this talk for you, okay? Are you okay with that? Here we go..."
"You didn't." There's a short pause.
Until the lieutenant loses patience: "What does our *limited cooperation* with the MI have to do with this?"
"Is this part of why Oranje is a *bad memory* for you?"
"What happened here -- the night he died?"
"Did you kill him?"
"Why did you call the cops if you're hiding?"
"I think we're done here -- for now." (Conclude.)
"What did you do to have these *people* after you?"
"What happened after you ran downstairs?"
Run, woman! Run past them and out into the street where it's dark and people move -- to the lorries at the intersection. As far as you can...
"I already *ran*. I ran from an entire isola. There is... I can't run any further. Not with these people. This is as far as it gets."
"What happens if they do?"
"They will kill me, sir. If you file my name -- take me in for questioning -- enter me into the Moralintern mill..."
"Why didn't you run away from here? As a matter of fact -- why are you here now?"
Say nothing.
She pulls on the cigarette, looking up at the sky. Her hair ripples in the breeze as she stands there, silent.
"What's going on? What did you do?"
"Just business -- but *bad* business for some people in the Moralintern. If I show up in your records, officer, they will find me. They will..."
"It's not nice -- but it's not illegal, not here in Revachol. Or even in Oranje."
"Industrial espionage. I joined a business collective with the intention of betraying them. I did my job well enough to be asked to do it again."
"With a bigger company -- the kind you really, really don't fuck with. I took their ledgers -- two decades' worth of accounting."
"What *exactly* did you do?"
"What *exactly* did you do?"
"Understood."
She takes a drag, then glances over her shoulder.
"I'm sure there are people who have done much worse than that."
"That's a lot of shit you've gotten yourself into."
"You're right. This is bad. You've destroyed what people have built."
Looskap -- these people engineer financial disasters in second world countries. The conglomerate also includes The Bank of Consecration, Eeirberg and the popular Pappa Lollo line of dairy products.
"Who did you do this to? And on whose behalf?"
"I need the names of the companies involved. And who hired you." He taps on his notebook.
"The job was Loosduin County Savings Bank -- they sound small but they're part of the Looskap conglomerate. That was the second job. The first was some printer company. You wouldn't know them."

"As to who hired me for the job -- I don't know. But *they're* after me too. Along with Looskap, and their friends in the MI." She breathes out, heavily. "Once you're done in the competitive intelligence circuit, you don't have allies. You're radioactive."
"Pappa Lollo!"
"Yeah. Pappa fucking Lollo wants to kill me." She smiles.
"Serves them right. When I am king, this Savings Bank will be first against the wall."
"Sure. I'm not a war criminal -- but it was bad. People lost their jobs. Good people too, not just C-Suite..." She shakes her head at the thought.
"It is. Many people lost their jobs. Not just C-Suite. Ordinary people. What I did to get to accounting..." She shakes her head at the thought.
"This was not a joke. Real people lost their jobs. Not just in the C-Suite either -- good people. What I did to get to accounting..." She shakes her head at the thought.
"I am. I am a destroyer. People lost their jobs -- good people. Not just C-Suite assholes. And the way I got into accounting..." She shakes her head at the thought.
She says it quickly. Like she's said it a hundred times -- to herself? To get used to the idea?
Out of guilt.
"That's bad. How do you live with yourself?"
"I don't." She shrugs. "How do *you* live with yourself?"
"I do drugs."
"I drink."
"I'm a cop. What I do is *right*."
"By not remembering a single god damn thing."
"That would do the trick, yes." She has almost devoured the cigarette she lit. She looks at it sadly.
"By bargaining then..." She takes a drag. "I do that too. It's not all that effective."
"Drugs are good," she looks to the sea. "I also do those. I try to *bargain* with myself too."
"I just try to smoke as much as possible."
"That doesn't really work, does it?" She has almost devoured the cigarette she lit. She looks at it sadly. "Not without a drink to wash it down..."
"I do that too, yes. It's unbelievably effective. Especially when combined with cigarettes. And drugs."
Around her -- a drop in atmospheric pressure. Not long from now it will get dark. And the air will start moving faster, circling the box she stands on...
"We were there." She points to the window -- the silhouette of the bed is visible. "Together. In bed, I mean."
"I turned back to him." She breathes out. A moment's silence. "His eyes were looking through me and his mouth was open, dumb... I could see... I could..."
"Tell me *exactly* what happened."

"Okay..." She takes a deep breath. "He was in a kneeling position, he had just entered me. I was on my back, looking at him. I heard the window behind me shatter and I turned to look -- there was a hole in the glass..."
"I waited for the second shot to come -- for me. I thought there would be one. It never came."
"I knew he was dead. Before he fell down on top of me."
"Your cigarette, miss."
"I'm sorry this happened to you."
"Are you sure you're not making this up?"
(Shake your head.) "That's a motherfucker."
A great pain moves through her, a dark and indefinite wave. She continues in spite of it.
"Sylvie was tending the bar." She looks down. "A lot of people were there. The Hardies were at the table in front of the stage, I think the Union box was full..."
"Yeah, it was a real *motherfucker*... ouch..." She looks down. Her cigarette has singed her fingers.
"Then what happened?"

"He was heavy. I pushed him off and he fell to the floor -- there." She points through the window. "He only had his boots on. I bit the pillow... not to scream, then ran downstairs..." There's a long pause. She just stands there, her arms at her sides.
She's forgotten about her cigarette. The butt has burned right down to her fingernails...
(Just nod.) "There are a few questions I have to ask for my report."
"So am I." She looks down. Her cigarette has singed her fingers.
"I'm not lying to you..." She looks down, wincing. Her cigarette has singed her fingers.
"Oh..." She looks at it and quickly tosses the butt aside.
She throws it away and immediately proceeds to light another one.

"She would have seen us. My bed is right next to..." She's forgotten her cigarette in the ash tray.
"No." She shrugs it off. "No -- why would she do that to herself? No, I just remembered you told me about it, and..."
"You mean to suggest -- she made it?"
She's not really sure. It *was* right above the bed -- she could have seen all sorts of things from there.
Don't let your imagination run wild here, sire. Keep it on track.
Then slipped back downstairs without anyone noticing? That *is* possible...
Her! Stop letting her distract you.
"Okay." She looks relieved.
"Thank you." She cradles herself for warmth. "Thank you. You won't regret it."
Something tells you: you will.

"*Still...*" she says, her voice breaking. "After all this. Sir, please... it's a shitty world and I know I'm shitty too, I know..." Her hand turns into a fist, slowly, crushing the cigarette she's still holding.
"But I don't deserve to be sent to the Moralintern and ground into paste just because I disturbed the *sanctity* of accounting. At some multinational..."
"What do you deserve then?"
"What *other* option do I have?"
"I don't know..." She throws away the cigarette. "To spend my days with smoke and drink and dance -- wallowing in shit. Just like everyone else."

"You have those *station calls*, right? Where I have to show up at the station or I'll become a fugitive. You can write me one. You don't have to take me in right now... I promise I won't go out anymore, at night. I'll be right here."
"Kim, arrest her before this drags out any longer." (Arrest her.)
"I will escort you to the motor carriage outside, miss."
"I do have a form..." He looks at his notes.
"You do have the form..." He looks at your ledger.
That's it. I'm calling it. Kim is beyond compromised.
Definitely, sire.
"Let's write you a Station Call. If you miss it -- I can't help you anymore." (Write a Station Call.)
"What will have changed in two months? Or one month?"
"*Everything* could change." She looks around. "This city, the extradition rules... The people after me could be in jail. Or maybe Revachol..." She falls silent.
"I won't, sir..." She exhales, shaking visibly. Then she collects herself.
"I'll let you off the hook -- for now. Don't make me regret it." (Don't arrest her.)
With a muffled whimper, she extends her wrists. They're white, bony -- exposed below the rolled-up sleeves of her jumpsuit.
Waiting for your teeth and talons to cut into...
He puts the handcuffs away. "These won't be necessary. I will take you to Station 57 myself -- and slow the extradition process as much as I can."
"It may be possible to stall it indefinitely. But you *will* be safer there for the purposes of this investigation." He turns to you.
"I won't..." She takes the slip, shaking visibly. Then she collects herself.
This may have been a *grave* mistake, sire.
Maybe. Maybe not. Mercy is rarely a *complete* mistake.
By god, she's playing him too! Like a fiddle, sire... Who would have known?
"I can do this on my own. She's not an immediate flight risk. See you tomorrow morning, officer. Downstairs, at the Whirling-in-Rags."
"Maybe Revachol could be free? I could be tried in a free Revachol? An independent state that doesn't hand its detainees over to the Moralintern."
A free Revachol... There is a low, distant rumble on the motor tract. A great machine, shaking the pillars down south. Electricity runs up your spine.
"The world can change. It's changed before." Her round light brown eyes shining with tears.
"Okay. Well..." Her round light brown eyes shine with the tears.
"Don't. The world can change. It has changed before..." She looks at you, frozen to her spot.
That's not the answer she was hoping for. Thought that you were some kind of patriot, or communard, did she?
"When it happened -- did you hear a gunshot?"
"When he was shot?" She thinks. "I may have. I don't know. I couldn't hear anything over the glass exploding."
The gunshot wasn't that loud? This is something to keep in mind when assessing the distance of the shot.
"I know you can do that -- just let me come in on my own. In two months. Or maybe even one month. That's all I need..."
There is desperation there -- in that silence. A cornered animal looking for a way out.
"I also find it hard to believe."
"I do like the sound of that... another Revachol. Free. Independent."
"Not on my watch."
"This has got nothing to do with anything."
"I find that hard to believe, miss." The handcuffs jingle in his hands...
What was that feeling?
IT'S COMING.
The political gambit has failed.
Her political overture has succeeded, we see?
"I know, but..." She doesn't know what to say.
This was her last card. There is nothing more she can say. The final decision is yours -- you alone stand on the throne of your Mind.
"You said you studied *Oranjese lit*. What is with this fugitive stuff?"
"I *did* -- I also had a side job selling insurance that I was really good at. Got picked up by a bank. *Competitive intelligence*, they called it."
"After that I sort of..." She smiles. "Transitioned out of the whole culture scene."
"West of the boardwalk, in the reeds? I need to check this buoy out." (Accept task.)
"Fine. Tell me one more thing." (Move on.)
"Of course." She nods.
The lieutenant makes a note of it.
"You're welcome to it. It's in the reeds northwest of here, past a broken sewage pipe. Right near the waterline."
"You're welcome to it. It's in the reeds northwest of here, past a broken sewage pipe. Right near the waterline."
The grand expanse of water is barely visible in the darkness of the night. The horizon is there, somewhere...
The light refracts. She takes out her lighter.
"Chill. I'm the cool cop, remember?"
She cracks a weary smile. "I'm sorry for wasting your time. I should have known you'd... that you'd find out."
"If you knew we would find out eventually -- why *did* you waste our time?"
"Why *did* you waste my time then?"
"You're right... there's more."
"More?"
"You answer to the Coalition Government -- and, by extension, the *Moralintern*..." She reaches for a new cigarette.
"The RCM isn't the lapdog of the Moralintern. You don't have to worry."
She nods. "I have people after me. And they have friends in the Moralintern -- some *are* Moralintern. If I show up in your records, officer, they will find me. They will..."
"What happens if they find you?"
"They will kill me, officer. If you file my name, take me in for questioning, enter me into the Moralintern mill..."
There's a wince and a pained little smile. "Well, then I'm fucked. For nothing. This murder didn't have anything to do with me."
Fucked? People after her? *Moralintern* people? This isn't Oranjese lit!
Here we go. For once you seem to have her off-guard.
Nothing to do with her? You'll be the judge of that.
"A lot of people got hurt," she concludes. "But that's just more of my shit you shouldn't have to deal with. You're solving a murder."
"I..." She looks down, then into your eyes. "One of them killed themselves. Because of me."
That can wait. Look into her eyes -- there's more.
"What did you *do*?"
Let's not pry. It's not part of this case.
Of course. This case takes precedence.
"That's..." (Shake your head.) "Not easy to deal with."
The young woman looks at her cigarette -- with melancholy. It's almost gone.
(Nod.) "Let's get back to what happened here, okay?"
"How do you deal with anything? It's all just..." She looks at you with pleading eyes. "How do *you* do it?"
"I *don't* either."
"There you have it." She's already almost devoured the cigarette she just lit and looks at it sadly. "The way of the warrior."
She's already in prison here. For what happened. And she is prepared to never leave. Even after his death.
Around her -- a drop in atmospheric pressure. Not long from now it will get dark. The rain will come. And the air will start moving faster, circling the box she stands on...
Her chest rises and falls with each word. She keeps herself together, and says it...
"You don't have to continue if you don't want to."
"No. I want to. Let's get this done."
"It's okay. Tell us as much as you're comfortable with." He waits for her to continue.
"Alright. Tell me as much as you're comfortable with."
"Did you hear or see the shooter -- at any point?"
Wait -- Titus said she was gurning her jaw off. Much more than usual.
This doesn't fit with the testimony of Titus Hardie. He said she was higher than usual.
"Titus said you looked pretty high."
It doesn't matter. Better not to mention it.
Of course. Keep your eyes open for the killer instead.
Of course. Keep your eyes open for the killer instead.
"Oh yeah..." She tilts her head. "I did one of his lines. Just to clear my head."
Good thinking. Clear your head. You should clear *your* head... get into his mindset.
"No -- not just yet." He turns to the woman. "Who is *Ruby*?"
*Let's go on*, what are you talking about? Did you forget how to cop? There's a new actor in the investigation -- change the question immediately!
I don't understand what you're doing detective -- *go on*? A new name just emerged -- Ruby! This is important. Change the question immediately.
I can't restrain this one. The need to *cop* is too strong. You just need to ask it.
Ruby?!
"Would you say she is the..." He looks at you. "Eighth Hardie boy?"
"Why not."
"Would you say she is... the eighth Hardie boy?"
They tampered with the body to disguise the cause of death.
To mislead you! They were tampering with the body.
"How could we have *missed* that..." He shakes his head. "And when was the tampering -- twenty minutes after death?"
"What did you do while they were hanging him?"
"Ruby said to wait here. She also said I wouldn't see her for a while; that we should lay low or something... so I did."
There is something suspicious about that theory, but you can't put your finger on it.
It could have been a *desire* murder. Maybe an act of jealousy?
"It's okay if you did it in self defence."
"I did not kill him to defend myself from rape," she says. "I told you before. That wasn't what happened."
"We'll try to make it less stressful, miss. But these are questions we *need* to ask."
"Relax. One more thing."
"Sure." She nods and relaxes her hands.
"No." She shakes her head. "People don't take drugs to kill each other -- they take them to feel okay with each other."
"I don't."
...or maybe you should take her to the station? For safekeeping. She *lied* to you. And she's a flight risk.
No. That won't be necessary. Just leave her alone, she's been through enough. She doesn't need this... police brutality.
Multi-Face! I'm beginning to doubt your judgement -- are you sure you're not sleeping on the post? You have to wake this one up -- with force -- if you want to continue pushing her.
You're not done. She's a flight risk and she lied to you -- wake up, man.
You're not done. She *lied* to you. And she's a flight risk -- wake up, man.
If you have doubts, just give us *one* example of deceit! Just one, and we will gladly change our minds.
This guy won't budge. You have to wake  Multi-Face up -- forcefully -- if you want to continue pushing her.
It looks like this one's not waking up. You'll have to do it without pushing her further. At least for now.
This one's *still* not budging. You'll have to do it without pushing her further.
"You log your work *every week*. It's *all* transmitted to COMINSUR. I couldn't just beg you not to enter my name... So I lied."
Yes they can! For *lying*!
"I agree." The lieutenant turns to her. "You wouldn't give us your real name -- not when people are after you."
Wait, wait, everyone -- just *wait*. What is this? Derail this whole thing immediately and *investigate*.
"Go on."
"Before we do..." He turns to her, the cuffs still in his hand. "What exactly in your relationship made you think she's romantically interested in you?"
Well, I'll be damned! That's one more thing we know about the world!
Could it be that Ruby was cleaning up after herself? That the lynching was a cover-up for *her* -- and she organized the boys to do it?
It's ominous -- you buying into her theory and running with it. Be careful with this Logic guy.
No, wait! Look at her! Teeth like pearls, face like a pebble -- she looks like a Twenties movie star. You can almost see her in Automatik Polychrome. Those posters in Ruby's lorry...
Look at her: teeth like pearls, face like a pebble -- she looks like a Twenties movie star. You can almost see her in Automatik Polychrome. Those posters in Ruby's lorry...
She was her type.
"You've been trying to kick that door down, right?" She points to the barred door, next to the window. "Maybe it leads downstairs?"
"You've been through there, right? I saw you come out." She points to the door that leads to the pinball workshop. "It leads downstairs."
"She could have had access to the roof." She points to the barred door next to the window. "You've noticed that door there, right? Maybe it leads downstairs?"
"She could have come up through there, then taken the shot -- right here, where I stand. It was too dark outside, I wouldn't have seen her."
"Yes. She's been up here many times. She used to come to drink on the roof when..." The young woman falls silent -- her mouth moves without a sound.
"Yes, of course. She's been up here many times, jacking private stations off the ring antenna. She used to come here, to drink on the roof with me. Before it got... weird."
"She could have come to the roof through that, then taken the shot -- right here, where I stand. It was dark outside, I wouldn't have seen her."
"She could have come to the roof through that, then made the shot right here, where I stand. It was dark outside, I wouldn't have seen her."
Why? She told us some pretty interesting things there.
Don't arrest her. Push her a bit more but then let her off. That Ruby theory was solid. (And she's beautiful.)
She's stuck here. She's already in prison -- look around! She's only trying to help you...
She knows something!
"I've made my choice." (Decide what to do with her.)
She looks at you in silence, her face filled with fear, lips parted...
She's gearing up for a last stand. This is it.
She probably didn't give you her real name either -- why would she? Arrest her immediately, before she further entangles you in her *web of lies*!
She probably didn't make the god damn call either. And her name is not Klaasje Amandou -- why would she give her real name? Arrest her immediately!
Samaran boxing, or Sam Bo. Graceful martial arts stuff -- stealth, cleverness, and cool.
"It's a shame we never got around to doing a thorough autopsy..." He shakes his head. "And when was the tampering -- twenty minutes after death?"
Wait! If you arrest her, Kim will have to transport her. You'd be without your partner for the rest of the day...
SHUT UP! He's making a decision and it's *his* to make.
In her bedroom, inside?
Not now...
Yes -- you see the glass sparkling out of the corner of your eye...
Still you see the glass sparkling out of the corner of your eye...
Where the cold oceanic expanse lies -- and behind it, another world.
Actually -- this murder did have *a little* to do with her.
But she *really* destroyed them. She still feels it.
Oops...
She's getting scared now. Of you -- the downstairs people. All of it.
True, sire. 'Tis true.
Which *is* an indicator of truth...
Very good, sire. She will never admit to it, but we can *see* that she didn't.
She fears an arrest right here and now. This has been an awful turn of events for her.
(Now that Kim's here) "What if I told you you're under arrest, miss."
You *are*. This is not the end of this.
That is *a little* strange... people don't usually keep things together under stress like that.
"I promise I will be right here all the time -- nights too. I'll help you *any* way I can in this investigation and I *will* be at Station 41 in six weeks." She repeats. "I promise."
Wait, stop -- that man, bloated beyond all recognition, was 42?
It's what she said, yes.
[Discard thought.]
Below the damage, the weeks of decomposition, all the swollen indignity of mortality -- he was 42 years old?
Where is this going?
How old are *you*? That's where this is going. Forty-five thousand litres of raw alcohol has left its disfigurements. What lies beneath, you wonder.
"Kim, how old do you think I am?"
(Turn around.) "Miss, how old do you think I am?"

dialoguetext: "Huh?" The lieutenant isn't quite sure he heard you.
"How old do I look?"
"Nothing." [Finish thought.]
"How old? Fifty-eight."
"Maybe you're wrong. You were wrong about the deceased too, he was *way* younger."
"What if you're wrong? We were both wrong about the deceased -- he turned out to be 40!"
"You're probably right. That's about what I look."
"Oh my god, that's really old -- really?"
"You asked." He shrugs.
"He was *deceased*. He had been decomposing for a week."
"I feel like I've been decomposing for longer than that."
"Forty-two. And he was *deceased*. He had been decomposing for a week."
"Actually, make that 54." He squints. "Alcoholism has severely impacted your appearance."
"And I *was* wrong about the age of the deceased. "
"Alcoholism has a similar effect on living tissue, I hear."
"You're right. I'm probably 62. Let's leave it at that."
"I didn't say 62, I said 58." He squints, looking at you for a second.
There's silence.
Then a little more.
Here it comes -- mercy.
"Sure -- you're 42." He squints. "Let's go?"
"On the bright side, you've been getting *a lot* of exercise lately."
"Huh?" She leans in closer. "How old do I think you are?"
She's buying time to formulate the best answer.
Look who's finally awake!
"I don't know... Twenty-one? Seventeen? Sixteen? When does the male libido peak?"
"I don't know... one million years old? Twenty-one? Seventeen? How old are superstar police officers usually?"
"I don't know... 80? One hundred? One year old? I don't know what I'm supposed to say? How old is the *sorriest* age?"
"I don't know... one? Two? I don't know what I'm supposed to say? How old is a newborn cop who doesn't remember he's a cop?"
"I don't know... Forty-one? Forty-five? What am I supposed to say? What's the most *boring* age a human being can be?"
"I don't know... As old as time itself? *Ageless*? Fifty-thousand years old? I don't know what I'm supposed to say? How old *is* an Apocalypse Cop?"
"I don't know... 40? I was like 9 when OO peaked. That was, what? Nineteen years ago? I liked them when I was 9. You couldn't have liked it when you were 40..."
"Let's say you were twenty-something. Twenty five. A good disco age. Twenty five plus nineteen is forty four. I'm gonna say you're 44."
Wow!
"Wow."
"Forty four? I'm young!"
"Forty four? You think so?"
"Yeah. I have a university degree, you know." She flicks ash from her cigarette.
"Absolutely. Age is just a number, man."
"Look -- at the end of the day, age is just a number, you know."
"I think I'm circa 55."
"I think I'm circa 45."
"I think I'm circa 35."
Wait! This requires *scientific* measurements.
Bring it on. I am not afraid of the truth.
I don't want to think about this anymore.
To the Laboratorium!
Okay. Seek not the truth. Cower in barbarism, you 58-year-old man-child.
"You're not." He's squinting at you.
"Sure he is. You know. Age is just a number."
"Yes. But for him that number is *much* larger than 35."
"Sure. Age is just a number, you know." She extinguishes her cigarette. "It's all in your *head*."
"You're not." He's squinting at you.
"Sure he is. You know, age is just a number."
"Yes. But for him that number is higher than 45."
"Sure, yeah. And if you're not -- age is just a number anyway."
"You're not." He's squinting at you.
"Sure he is. You know, age is just a number."
"Yes. But for him that number is 56."
"That's pretty much it, but... Age is just a number anyway, you know." She extinguishes her cigarette.
You could ask either one of them.
"Yes miss, but..." The lieutenant disagrees. "For him that number is *56*."
